With $\delta=\frac1{14}-c$, $\tau=\delta$, $\phi=\delta/(12(n+1))$ and $\sigma=\frac14\delta$ one has $c_1-3n\phi>c$, and the product $\omega_0\prod_q\omega_q$ gives the bound of the difference with the rate $c$ and with numbers independent of the larger side $\ell$; on $T_{\ell'}$ itself the bound is Lem.~\ref{C-360-10}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The flow with an insertion]\label{C-360-20}
Let $\ell=2L^m$ be any side, $0<\mathsf b_-\le\mathsf b\le\mathsf b_+$, $\beta=L^K\mathsf b$, $n\ge1$, $\mathsf d>0$ and $f_i$ real Lipschitz; let $S_\varkappa=\sum_l\varkappa(l)\,{\rm dn}_l$ be an insertion of brick densities ${\rm dn}_l$ (gauge invariant polynomials on boxes of at most five sites along each axis, each holding a plaquette, vanishing at $\mathbf 1$) of the order $r$, and let two of the $n+1$ sets formed by the carrier of $S_\varkappa$ and the ${\rm supp}\,f_i$ be at sup distance $\ge\mathsf d$, the others in any position. For $\gamma$ small enough in terms of the other constants there are $C,p,K_0$, depending on $\ell,\mathsf b_\pm,n,\mathsf d$ and the type, such that for $K\ge K_0$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] if $r\ge3$ and $|\varkappa|_\infty\le\beta h$: $|\langle S_\varkappa;\mathcal O(f_\cdot)\rangle|\le CK^pL^{-\lambda_LK/4}h\prod_i\|f_i\|_\sharp$; no norm of $\varkappa$ but its supremum enters;
\item[(b)] if $r=2$, $0\le\sigma\le1$, $|\varkappa|_\infty\le L^{\sigma K}h$ and $0<\epsilon\le1$: $|\langle S_\varkappa;\mathcal O(f_\cdot)\rangle|\le C_\epsilon K^pL^{-(1-\sigma-\epsilon)K}h\prod_i\|f_i\|_\sharp$; in particular $|\langle\mathcal O(w);\mathcal O(f_\cdot)\rangle|\le C_\epsilon a^{-\epsilon}\max|w|\prod_i\|f_i\|_\sharp$ for every real weight $w$, in contact with the $f_i$ or not;
\item[(c)] if $r=2$, the insertion is real with $|\varkappa|_\infty\le\beta h$, and its densities are of derivative kind, that is, $|G_\nu(b)|^2$ or $\Psi_{\lambda(p)}(p)$: $|\langle S_\varkappa;\mathcal O(f_\cdot)\rangle|\le CK^pL^{-c_nK}h\prod_i\|f_i\|_\sharp$, $c_n=\lambda_L/(4(6+3n))$; for every $0<\theta_1<1$ and every real insertion of the order $2$ with $|\varkappa|_\infty\le\beta h$, $\langle S_\varkappa-J_{t_1};\mathcal O(f_\cdot)\rangle$ obeys the same bound with $L^{-\lambda_L\theta_1K/4}$, the numbers $C,p,K_0$ depending besides on $\theta_1$, where $t_1=K-\lceil\theta_1K\rceil$ and $J_{t_1}$ is the classical value of the insertion at the background of the level $t_1$, a function of the block field.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Run the chain with the insertion, as in Lem.~\ref{C-360-9}(a), down to a level $t$ at which the large fields are rare. A transfer inequality bounds the cumulant by
\[
2\delta_t(\varkappa)\prod_i\bigl(8nM_t\|f_i\|_\sharp\bigr)+{\rm Con}_t+4\,{\rm op}_{n+1}\mathsf R_t\sup|S_\varkappa|\prod_i\bigl(6\ell^3L^{4K}\sup|f_i|\bigr),
\]
with $\delta_t$ the oscillation of the conditional mean of the insertion given the block field of the level $t$, $M_t$ the inverse radius of the sources at that level, and ${\rm Con}_t$ the mixed derivative of the constants of the chain, which is small by locality when a pair of sets is separated (when the separated pair is the insertion and one source, the constants of the sources that meet the insertion are handled by a slow cut-off at the scale $\mathsf d$, at the price $(2+480M/\mathsf d)^{n-1}$). By power counting an insertion of the order $r$ has the size $|\varkappa|_\infty L^{(3-2r)i}$ at the level $i$, and what the steps make of it is forgotten at the rate $L^{-\lambda_L/2}$ per level, $(L/2)^{-x}=L^{-\lambda_Lx}$; this gives (a) and (b).

For (c) two levels are used. Let $0<\theta_1<1$, $\tau_1=\lceil\theta_1K\rceil$, $t_1=K-\tau_1$, and $t=K-\tau$, $\tau=\lceil\theta K\rceil$, $\theta=\lambda_L\theta_1/(4(7+3n))<\theta_1$. The insertion is put into the chain only up to the level $t_1$, as early members; there it equals its classical value $J_{t_1}$ on the background of the level $t_1$ plus what the steps up to $t_1$ made of it, which in level-$t_1$ terms has the size $C|\varkappa|_\infty L^{-(t_1-1)}L^{-\lambda_L\tau_1/2}$ (what a step makes of an insertion of the order $2$ is forgotten at the rate $L^{-\lambda_L/2}$ per level). From the level $t_1$ to the level $t$ this part is forgotten by the factor $L^{-(t-t_1)}$ of the run, on the field cut of the level $t$; at the level $t$ the histories with a large field are discarded, at a cost below every power of $L^{-K}$, and the volume $N_t=\ell^3L^{3\tau}$ and Cauchy's estimates in the $n$ sources cost $L^{3(n+1)\tau}$ up to powers of $K$; the mixed derivatives of the constants of the chain in the sources are small by locality, two of the sets being separated.

The derivative in the insertion is taken as a difference quotient at a small step $s$, its second derivative being bounded crudely. Together the exponent is $(7+3n)\tau+1-\frac12\lambda_L\tau_1\le-\frac14\lambda_L\theta_1K+8+3n$: this is the second clause of (c), for every $\theta_1$. For the first clause the classical part is bounded besides: $J_{t_1}$ is a function of the block field of the level $t_1$, its cumulant with the sources is bounded by Cauchy's estimates in the sources at that level, at the price $L^{3n\tau_1}$, times its supremum, and for densities of derivative kind the supremum is at most $\beta\ell^3L^{3K}\,C\varepsilon_{t_1}^2(1+K\log L)^2L^{-6t_1}$ by the estimate below; the exponent is $K+3K-6(K-\tau_1)+3n\tau_1=-2K+(6+3n)\tau_1$, which at $\theta_1=1/(6+3n)$ is at most $-K+6+3n$.

With the second clause at this $\theta_1$ the rate is $\min\{1,\frac14\lambda_L\theta_1\}=c_n$. For a lattice field $B$ on a box of radius $R$ with $|B|\le A_0$ and $|{\rm div}^+B|,|{\rm curl}^-B|\le\epsilon_1$, the div--curl estimate $|\partial^\pm_jB_i|\le C_*[A_0/R+\epsilon_1(1+\log R)]$ on the quarter box, applied with the Bianchi identity on a cube, gives $|G_\nu(b)|^2,|\Psi_{\lambda(p)}(p)|\le C\varepsilon_i^2\eta_i^6(1+i\log L)^2$ at the regular backgrounds of the level $i$, $\eta_i=L^{-i}$, which is the order that (c) needs.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The mean plaquette]\label{C-360-21}
Let $0<g\le\gamma$, $\ell\in\mathfrak L(g)$, $n\ge1$, and $E(\beta)=\langle a_p\rangle$ on a periodic lattice of $N_s$ sites along each axis (it does not depend on $p$).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For every $R\ge3$, $N_s\ge R$ and $\beta$ with $116R^3(\beta/2)^{-1/2}\le\frac15$ and $\bar\eta(R,\beta)\le\frac14$, $|\beta E(\beta)-1|\le2\bar\eta(R,\beta)^{1/2}$, with $\bar\eta(R,\beta)\le\frac{9\log(2\beta)+55}{R^3}+\frac{18\log(1+256R^3)+15}R+1.21\cdot10^9R^9\beta^{-1/2}$: at $R=\lceil\log\beta\rceil$ this tends to $0$ uniformly in all volumes $N_s\ge\log\beta$.
\item[(b)] On the side $\ell$, with $N_s=\ell L^K$: there are $C,K_0$, depending on $g,\ell,n$, such that $\sup_{\mathsf b'\in I(g)}|\beta^nE^{(n-1)}(\beta)-(-1)^{n-1}(n-1)!|\le CK^{2n+3}L^{-K/20}$ for $\beta=L^K\mathsf b'$ and $K\ge K_0$.
\item[(c)] For all real Lipschitz $f_1,\dots,f_n$ on $T_\ell$, with nothing asked of the supports, $|a_K^3S^T_{n;K,\ell,L^K\mathsf b'}(f)-3(n-1)!\,\mathsf b'^{-n}\int_{T_\ell}\prod_if_i|\le CK^{2n+3}L^{-K/20}\prod_i\max\{\sup|f_i|,\frac{40}{\sqrt3}M{\rm Lip}_\infty f_i\}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(a) Cut the lattice into blocks of $R$ to $2R$ sites along each axis, and in each block take a comb tree. Bounding the partition function with plaquette weights $\beta_p\in[\beta_-,\beta_+]$ from above (dropping a few plaquettes) and from below (freezing a few bonds), both bounds become the same Gaussian integral, $\sum_B(2|B|-2)\log\mathsf g(\beta_B)-\mathsf D$ with $\mathsf g(\beta)=(2/\pi)^{1/2}\beta^{-3/2}$ and a number $\mathsf D$ of the geometry, up to an error $N\eta$ that is small per site; this uses weak coupling on blocks of $R\le\beta^{1/20}$ spacings alone. The convexity of $\log Z$ in $\beta$ then pins down its first derivative. (b) For the higher derivatives analyticity in $\beta$ is needed.

On a torus of a fixed physical side, Thms.~\YMMref{AJ}{673} and~\YMMref{AD}{607} write $Z[\zeta f]=\exp(E+\sum_{j,X}e_j(X;\zeta f))\widetilde Z(\zeta f)$ for real $f$ with $\max\{\sup|f|,\frac{40}{\sqrt3}M{\rm Lip}_\infty f\}\le1$, with $|e_j(X;w)|\le C_{\rm S}e^{-\kappa d_j(X)}$, $|\widetilde Z|\le e^{C_{\rm S}\ell^3}$ and $\widetilde Z(0)\ge e^{-C_g\ell^3}$; the factor $\widetilde Z$ may vanish. Put $N=(\ell L^K)^3$, $h_f(\zeta)=\widetilde Z(\zeta f)/\widetilde Z(0)$ and $D_f(\zeta)=(3N)^{-1}[\sum_{j,X}e_j(X;\zeta f)+\sum_p\log(1-\zeta f(x(p))/\mathsf b')]$, the per-site exponent; by the count of polymers $|D_f|\le M_0$ on a disc $|\zeta|<\rho_1$, with $M_0$ and $\rho_1$ free of $K$. Then $h_f(0)=1$, $h_f>0$ on the real axis and $|h_f|\le e^\Gamma$ with $\Gamma=(C_{\rm S}+C_g)\ell^3$, a number free of $K$.

First, Cauchy's estimate on circles of radius $\frac12\rho_1$ gives $|h_f-1|\le\frac12$ on $|\zeta|\le\frac14\rho_1e^{-\Gamma}$, so that $\log h_f$ is defined there and $|(\log h_f)^{(n)}(0)|\le n!\,(4e^\Gamma/\rho_1)^n$: this member does not grow with the cutoff, and it is of the order $1/N$ per site. Second, the Poisson--Jensen formula and Harnack's inequality, applied to the non-negative function $\Gamma-\log|h_f|$, give $\int_{-\rho_1/2}^{\rho_1/2}|\log|h_f(x)||\,\mathrm{d}x\le9\rho_1\Gamma$; with this, the two-sided real-axis bound of (a), at the plaquette weights $\beta(1-xf(x(p))/\mathsf b')$, controls the per-site exponent in $L^1$ on the segment: $\int_{-\rho_1/2}^{\rho_1/2}|D_f(x)|\,\mathrm{d}x\le\rho_1\delta$ with $\delta=\frac13(2\bar\eta(R,\beta)+Ra_K+R^{-3})+3(C_{\rm S}+C_g)L^{-3K}$.

Third, A.~Markov's inequality for the derivatives of the Taylor polynomial of $D_f$ of the order $\mathsf m=\max\{n,\lceil\log_2(M_0/\delta)\rceil\}$, with Cauchy's estimate for the rest of the series, gives $|D_f^{(n)}(0)|\le4\,(2/\rho_1)^n\mathsf m^{2n}(\mathsf m+1)^2\delta$, and at $R=\lfloor\beta^{1/20}\rfloor$ this is the rate. By Jensen's formula $h_f$ has at most $\Gamma/\log2$ zeros in $|\zeta|<\frac12\rho_1$, a number that does not grow with the cutoff; the bound on $(\log h_f)^{(n)}(0)$ above does not need it. At $f\equiv1$, where $S^T_n(1,\dots,1)=a_K^{-n}(-1)^{n-1}3N\,E^{(n-1)}(\beta)$, the identity of (c) below gives (b). (c) is the same argument at a general $f$: $S^T_n(f,\dots,f)=(n-1)!\mathsf b'^{-n}\sum_pf(x(p))^n+3ND^{(n)}_f(0)+(\log h_f)^{(n)}(0)$, with the per-site exponent $D_f$ and the factor $h_f$ of Thms.~\YMMref{AJ}{673} and~\YMMref{AD}{607}; polarisation gives distinct entries.
\end{proof}

Use the separated regions and the actual averaging constraints of
Prop.~\ref{prop:weighted-system-L2}, with its block-number and
small-triple hypotheses in addition to the width condition below.
Require also the geometric and regularity hypotheses of
Thm.~\YMMref{I}{225} and Prop.~\YMMref{29.1}{231},
with their block-number, torus-size and gap floors. The matrix-valued
plaquette-divergence bound in that theorem follows from the regular
curvature and current bounds by equation~\YMMref{(579)}{288},
with a factor $2$ absorbed in the regularity ceiling. These are
numerical floors and small-radius conditions on the data, not
assumptions about the inverse estimate to be proved.
Also retain the four local-system radii at most $a_H$, the block
floor $\mathfrak M\ge M_H$, and the permitted decay rate of
Lem.~\ref{lem:ordinary-holder-kernels}.
Write $\xi=\eta_k$ and $\ell_n=\xi L^n$ for the physical layer scale.
For clarity distinguish $D_0$, the covariant differential from sites
to bonds, from $D_1$, the covariant differential from bonds to
plaquettes. Let $U$ be a real background, critical for the unweighted
action on the kernel of the averaging constraint, regular at radius
$\alpha\le\alpha_{\rm lin}(L)\le(16L^2)^{-1}$, with curvature bounded
by the envelope $e(x)=\varepsilon_{j(x)}$ in the scaled norm below,
and $\sup e\le e_0(L)$. The layer radii satisfy
$0<\varepsilon_j\le\varepsilon_{j+1}\le L\varepsilon_j$.
Require
$R_1\mathfrak M\ge w_{\rm lin}(L)$.

At each bare site $x_*$ of layer $n\ge2$, fix a real adjoint gauge
$g_{x_*}$ on the cube of physical sup radius $\ell_n/4$ such that
\[
 |g_{x_*}(b_-)\operatorname{Ad}U(b)g_{x_*}(b_+)^{-1}-I|
       \le L^2\alpha/L^n.
\]
The gauge hypotheses are part of the setting. All H\"older quotients
below compare components of the same orientation in these gauges.
The cube for a potential is the concentric cube of radius
$\ell_n/8-2\xi$; those for a curvature and a source two-form have radius $\ell_n/4$. Quotients are taken over distinct admissible base points
in the indicated cube, with the usual physical Euclidean distance.

We use the following scaled spaces. For a field of inverse
length degree $r$, put
\[
 |f|_{r,h}=\sup_i\frac{\ell(i)^r|f(i)|}{h(x_i)},\qquad
 [f]_{r,1/2,h}
 =\sup_{n\ge2,x_*}\frac{\ell_n^{r+1/2}}
                              {h(x_*)}[g_{x_*}f]_{1/2;C(x_*)}.
\]
For an index $i$, let $\ell(i)$ be the largest layer scale of the
sites in the stencil defining that field value or first difference.
For a row use its prescribed scale $\xi_c$. The envelope is read at
the indicated base point $x_i$. This fixes the norm convention also
for indices meeting a layer boundary. The adjacent-layer comparison
of Lem.~\YMMref{21.2}{141} makes it equivalent, with constants
depending only on $L$, to the base-point scale convention. Set
$\|f\|_{r,1/2,h}=|f|_{r,h}+[f]_{r,1/2,h}$.
For the first two layers only the supremum term is required; their
ratios $\ell_n/\xi\le L$ are uniformly bounded. The curvature
hypothesis above means $\|F_U\|_{2,1/2,e}\le1$.

The row units are dimensionless. If $Q_{\rm ph}$ is the physical
averaging derivative with row pairing of weight $\xi_c^3$, put
\[
 QA(c)=\xi_c Q_{\rm ph}A(c),\qquad
 \omega(c)=\xi_c^3\omega_{\rm ph}(c).
\]
Use the row pairing of weight $\xi_c^{-1}$ for $Q^{\mathsf T}$.
Then $Q^{\mathsf T}\omega=Q_{\rm ph}^{\mathsf T}\omega_{\rm ph}$,
since both pairings with $A$ are
$\sum_c\frac12\operatorname{tr}(Q_{\rm ph}A(c)\omega(c))$.
This conversion changes units only; it retains the same row set and
averaging germ. Row data $b$ and multipliers have degree zero.

Let $h=e\theta$, where $\theta>0$ and
$|\log\theta(x)-\log\theta(x')|\le c_Ud(x,x')$.
Choose $c_U$ at most one eighth of each decay rate used below and
at most $1/(6L)$. Thus, for fixed constants
$C_h=C_h(L)$ and $0<\nu\le\delta_2/2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:linear-input-envelope}
       h(z)/h(y)\le C_h e^{\nu d(y,z)}.
\end{equation}
Take the same condition on the local comparison cubes. Define
\begin{align*}
 \|(A,\omega)\|_{\mathcal X_h}
  &=\|A\|_{1,1/2,h}+\|D_1A\|_{2,1/2,h}
       +|D_0^{\mathsf T}A|_{2,h}+|\omega|_{0,h},\\
 \|(Y,f,b)\|_{\mathcal F_h}
  &=\|Y\|_{2,1/2,h}+|f|_{3,h}+|b|_{0,h}.
\end{align*}
The ordinary and divergence sources are read only through
$f+D_1^{\mathsf T}Y$. For a complex anisotropy ${\rm an}$, its size
$t({\rm an})$ is its supremum plus the scaled H\"older-$1/2$
seminorm on the same plaquette cubes.

\begin{lemma}[Linear response at a variable anisotropy]\label{C-360-22}
There are positive numbers
$w_{\rm lin},\allowbreak\alpha_{\rm lin},\allowbreak e_0,\allowbreak t_{\rm lin},\allowbreak K_{\rm lin}$,
depending only on $L$, such that the following holds in the setting
above. If $t({\rm an})\le t_{\rm lin}\le1/4$, the system
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-linear-response-system}
 QA=b,\qquad
 T_\tau A=f+D_1^{\mathsf T}Y+Q^{\mathsf T}\omega,
 \qquad \tau=1+{\rm an},
\end{equation}
has a unique solution, linear in the data, with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-linear-response-bound}
 \|(A,\omega)\|_{\mathcal X_h}
      \le K_{\rm lin}\|(Y,f,b)\|_{\mathcal F_h}.
\end{equation}
Here
$T_\tau=D_1^{\mathsf T}\tau cD_1+V_0'+D_0RD_0^{\mathsf T}$
is the second variation of the weighted action at the reference
field, with the slice term. The coefficient $c_p$ is determined by
$\partial U(p)=c_pI+i\xi^2F_U(p)$, and $V_0'$ contains the
curvature commutator terms of that second variation. The nonlinear
block-constraint remainder and its multiplier are kept in the
forcing when the lemma is applied to the nonlinear equation.
The row and slice conventions are those of the setting. All
constants are uniform in the volume, the number of layers and the
permitted envelopes. For the mean-scheme rows of a label, rotated
into the comb frame, the same estimate holds with $2K_{\rm lin}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the linear estimate]
We first treat the unweighted operator. The block constraint must be
retained in this argument: the inverse of the gauge-fixed operator
without the constraint is not the required Green operator. Put
\[
 T=T_\tau\big|_{{\rm an}=0},\qquad
 G=(T+Q^{\mathsf T}Q)^{-1},\qquad
 M=QGQ^{\mathsf T},
\]
and define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:endpoint-constrained-inverses}
 H=GQ^{\mathsf T}M^{-1},\qquad
 \widetilde G=G-HQG.
\end{equation}
Thus $QH=1$, $Q\widetilde G=0$ and
$\widetilde GT=1-HQ$. The rows are the interior and outward
determining bonds; inward bonds are discarded, so there are no edge
rows. On a row of level $j$, the derivative of the iterated comb
average is
\[
 Q A(c)=\xi\,
   \bigl(\mathbf Q(W_{j-1})\cdots\mathbf Q(W_0)A\bigr)(c).
\]
The factors read only the double block beneath that row. Separation
keeps these blocks inside the domains on which the averages are
defined. The row conversion above therefore identifies this $Q$
with the physical averaging derivative in the regular constrained
system, without changing the set of constraints.

The regular current bound supplies the matrix-divergence hypothesis
used for that system. Indeed, at a full bond the quaternion
decomposition gives
\[
 D_U^{\mathsf T}\partial U=aI+i\xi^2J(U),\qquad
 |a|\le\xi^{-1}\max_{p\ni b}|\partial U(p)-I|^2.
\]
Since the adjacent plaquette scale is at least the bond scale and
the latter is at least $\xi$, the regularity bounds give
$|D_U^{\mathsf T}\partial U|\le2\alpha\xi^2\ell(b)^{-3}$.
This is equation~\YMMref{(579)}{288}; our choice
$2\alpha_{\rm lin}\le a_Q$ permits the application below.

Here are the unweighted bounds that will be used. Write
$|f|_{(r)}=\sup_i\ell(i)^r|f(i)|$ and
$\|A\|_X=\max\{|A|_{(1)},|\nabla A|_{(2)}\}$. For sufficiently
small regularity radius, there are $K_1,K_7\ge1$, depending only
on $L$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:endpoint-six-bounds}
\begin{gathered}
 \|\widetilde Gf\|_X\le K_7|f|_{(3)},\qquad
 \|Hb\|_X\le K_1\sup|b|,\qquad
 \sup|H^{\mathsf T}f|\le K_1|f|_{(3)},\\
 \sup|(D_1H)^{\mathsf T}Y|\le3K_1|Y|_{(2)},\qquad
 \sup|(D_0^{\mathsf T}H)^{\mathsf T}\lambda|
       \le3K_1|\lambda|_{(2)},\qquad
 |R\lambda|_{(2)}\le(1+K_1^3)|\lambda|_{(2)}.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
These estimates are unchanged by passing to the units of any layer.
The averaging rows are dimensionless, their pairing has weight
$\ell(c)^{-1}$, and their transposes are taken for that pairing.
They are precisely the bounds of
Prop.~\YMMref{29.1}{231}, applied after the row identification
just made. Its proof also records their exponential versions.
For the transpose estimates, test against a datum supported at one
row $c$. The row pairing contributes a factor $\ell(c)$, while
the number of bonds or plaquettes in a cell of scale $\ell_y$ is
at most $3(\ell_y/\xi)^3$. The resulting kernel sum has factor
$\ell(c)/\ell_y$, which is absorbed by the exponential decay.
The same calculation with the first differences gives the fourth
and fifth estimates, including the zero-extension terms at the
boundary. These are equations~\YMMref{(459)}{235} and the
following divergence estimate. The scalar estimate follows from
$R=1-G'Q'^{\mathsf T}(Q'G'^2Q'^{\mathsf T})^{-1}Q'G'$.
At a bond meeting the complement of the ambient region, the
zero-extension difference has local scale $\xi$ and is bounded by
$|A|_{(1)}$. Thus these estimates also include boundary differences.
For an empty ambient region all spaces are zero. The operators
preserve real fields, so the estimates extend to complex fields by
their real and imaginary parts, with constants enlarged by a fixed
factor.

The same operators have exponential decay in the weighted distance.
Their first-difference H\"older estimates follow from the ordinary
kernel estimates in Lem.~\ref{lem:ordinary-holder-kernels}.
Multiplying the input at $z$ and output at $y$ by the envelope ratio
costs $h(z)/h(y)$. The permitted growth of this ratio consumes only
part of the exponential decay. The remaining kernel is summable by
Lem.~\YMMref{21.2}{141}. This gives the envelope versions of
\eqref{eq:endpoint-six-bounds}, with constants independent of the
torus and the number of layers.

For $q=f+D_1^{\mathsf T}Y$, elimination of the multiplier in
$TA=q+Q^{\mathsf T}\omega$, $QA=b$, gives the exact formulas
\begin{equation}\label{eq:endpoint-elimination}
 A=\widetilde Gq+Hb,\qquad
 \omega=H^{\mathsf T}(THb-q).
\end{equation}
Indeed $(T+Q^{\mathsf T}Q)A=q+Q^{\mathsf T}(\omega+b)$,
and applying $QG$ determines $\omega+b$. The identity
$M^{-1}=H^{\mathsf T}TH+1$ gives the displayed formula for
$\omega$. The six bounds control the ordinary forcing, the lift,
and all multiplier terms. The remaining issue is the first-slot
divergence $D_1^{\mathsf T}Y$.

Cover each layer of index at least two by cubes of size comparable
to its layer scale. In the local gauges, write
$U=e^{i\xi a}$, with $a$ and its first differences bounded in the
units of that layer. A partition of unity reduces the divergence
source to the flat equation on these cubes. Convolution with the
lattice Laplace Green kernel gives a local potential; its first
differences involve second differences of that kernel. These
preserve the H\"older exponent by Lem.~\YMMref{19.4}{115}.
The cancellation in that lemma is essential: a bound on the
absolute kernel alone would give a logarithmic loss.

Cut off these local potentials and carry them back to the original
gauge. Their sum $\Phi$ satisfies
\[
 T\Phi=D_1^{\mathsf T}Y+J,\qquad
 |J|_{3,h}\le C\|Y\|_{2,1/2,h}.
\]
Here $J$ consists of cutoff commutators, the terms containing the
local potential and curvature, the lower-order term $V_0'\Phi$,
the term $-D_0(1-R)D_0^{\mathsf T}\Phi$, and the untreated
sources in layers zero and one. The first differences of the local
gauge potential bound the coefficient terms; the cutoff derivatives
have the inverse powers of the local scale. In the first two layers
the scale-to-spacing ratio is bounded by $L$, so a bare difference
is bounded by the corresponding scaled supremum. These are
ordinary sources of degree three. The parametrix identity is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:endpoint-parametrix}
 \widetilde GD_1^{\mathsf T}Y
       =\Phi-HQ\Phi-\widetilde GJ.
\end{equation}
The row datum $Q\Phi$ is bounded in the dimensionless row norm:
each average reads a double block on which the scale and envelope
are comparable, and the factor $\ell(c)$ in the physical path
average cancels the scale $\ell^{-1}$ of $\Phi$.
The remainder $J$ has the degree-three norm displayed above.
Thus both correction terms lie in the ordinary-input classes of
Lem.~\ref{lem:ordinary-holder-kernels}. Its estimates are read
at $s=1$, with the same rows and their row pairing. This proves
the required potential and curvature bounds. The first-difference
H\"older bounds for the correction terms are the ordinary kernel
bounds; those for $\Phi$ are the same-exponent Green-kernel
bounds just used. Their supremum estimates also bound the
divergence. To pass from the comparison cubes
of radius $\ell/56$ to the cubes in the norm, cover the latter
by comparison cubes and use the local gauge transition bounds.
On an overlap those transitions have differences bounded by
$C(L)\alpha/\ell$; the H\"older product inequality and the
supremum bound therefore control the change of gauge. The
bounded overlap gives a constant depending only on $L$.
No H\"older estimate is
obtained here by applying an estimate with a positive loss of
exponent at zero loss.

For completeness, the potential H\"older norm can also be read
directly from its curvature and divergence. On a cube $C_R$ in
bare units, let the adjoint transports differ from the identity by
at most $v/R$. If $6v\le\sigma_H$, then
\[
 \sup_{C_{R/2-2}}|E|+(R/2-2)^{1/2}[E]_{1/2;C_{R/2-2}}
 \le 2C_H\bigl((R-1)^{-3/2}\|E\|_2
                 +R|DE|+R|D_0^*E|\bigr).
\]
To obtain it, apply Prop.~\YMMref{18.1}{102} to each
component, whose flat Laplacian is the divergence of its flat
curvature and divergence. Replacing the covariant quantities by
the flat ones adds at most $Cv$ times the supremum on the next
larger cube. On radii increasing from $3R/4$ by
$R/8,R/16,\ldots$, choose $v$ so that this factor is at most
$1/12$. Iteration absorbs the supremum; the terminal error is at
most $12^{8-\log_2R}\|E\|_2$. A second application on cubes
of radius $R/4$ gives the H\"older bound. For $R<64$ the
supremum is bounded by the finite-volume $\ell^2$ norm. At
$R=L^n/4$, the condition follows by reducing the regularity
radius so that $\alpha\le\sigma_H/(8L^2)$.

We have proved the estimate at zero anisotropy with a constant
$K^{(0)}$. At a nonzero anisotropy, the same solution solves the
unweighted system with data
\[
 (Y-{\rm an}\,cD_1A,\ f-V_0'[{\rm an}]A,\ b).
\]
The H\"older product inequality bounds the first change by
$Ct({\rm an})\|D_1A\|_{2,1/2,h}$; the second is bounded by
$C|{\rm an}|_\infty\alpha|A|_{1,h}$. Choose
$K^{(0)}Ct_{\rm lin}\le1/2$ and absorb these terms. The bound
holds with $K_{\rm lin}=2K^{(0)}$.

The real part of the form of $T_\tau$ on $N(Q)$ is coercive
at these radii, as proved below. Hence a homogeneous solution has
$A=0$, by pairing its equation with $\bar A$, and then
$Q^{\mathsf T}\omega=0$ gives $\omega=0$. The finite square
system is therefore invertible. This proves existence and
uniqueness as well as the estimate.

Finally, the mean-scheme rows of a label, rotated into the comb
frame, have the form $Q+E$. Their comparison kernel is supported
in the double block of the row and obeys
\[
 |EA|_{0,h}\le c_E\alpha|A|_{1,h},\qquad
 |E^{\mathsf T}\omega|_{3,h}\le c_E\alpha|\omega|_{0,h}.
\]
The system with these rows is the one just solved with data
$(Y,f+E^{\mathsf T}\omega,b-EA)$. Taking
$K_{\rm lin}c_E\alpha\le1/2$ proves its bound, with
$2K_{\rm lin}$, by a contraction. This is the row comparison
needed when the estimate is applied to a label.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The energy of the displacement]
\label{lem:weighted-field-energy}
In the setting of Lem.~\ref{C-360-22}, decrease the regularity
radius and the envelope ceiling by constants depending only on
$L$. Put
\[
 \mathcal E(A)=\xi^3\sum_p|D_1A(p)|^2
                +\xi^3\sum_b\ell(b)^{-2}|A(b)|^2,
 \qquad |b|_{\rm row}^2=\sum_c\ell(c)^{-1}|b(c)|^2.
\]
For the linear solution with data $(Y,f,b)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-field-energy-linear}
 \mathcal E(A)\le K^{(2)}\left(
       \xi^3\sum_p|Y(p)|^2+
       \xi^3\sum_b\ell(b)^2|f(b)|^2+|b|_{\rm row}^2\right).
\end{equation}
For the small fixed point with zero block datum,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-field-energy-nonlinear}
 \mathcal E(A[{\rm an};0])
      \le C|{\rm an}|_\infty^2\xi^3\sum_p|F_U(p)|^2.
\end{equation}
At a permitted complex block datum $b_0$, the difference
$A'=A[{\rm an};b_0]-A[0;b_0]$ instead satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-field-energy-difference}
 \mathcal E(A')\le C|{\rm an}|_\infty^2
       \left(\xi^3\sum_p|F_U(p)|^2+|b_0|_{\rm row}^2\right).
\end{equation}
The constants are independent of the number of layers and the
volume. The last two statements concern fixed points in the small
ball of the linear estimate.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We need an estimate on the field energy, including the forcing from
the nonlinear block constraint. A contraction in a stronger energy
norm of the field and multiplier is unnecessary.

At zero anisotropy the operator $T+Q^{\mathsf T}Q$ is real,
symmetric and positive by Thm.~\YMMref{I}{225}. Its
restriction to $N(Q)$ is $T$, so the constrained Green operator
is positive on that subspace. Apply the first estimate of
\eqref{eq:endpoint-six-bounds} to an eigenvector of the largest
eigenvalue of $\ell^{-1}\widetilde G\ell^{-1}$. If that
eigenvalue is $\lambda$, it gives
\[
 \lambda\sup_b\ell(b)^2|g(b)|
       \le K_7\sup_b\ell(b)^2|g(b)|.
\]
Thus the quadratic form of $T$ on $N(Q)$ controls the weighted
potential square sum with constant $K_7^{-1}$. Its expression as
a curvature form, a slice term and $V_0'$ gives the second lower
bound. The plaquette coefficient satisfies $c_p\ge1/2$, while
the form of $V_0'$ is bounded by $C_V\alpha$ times the weighted
potential square sum. Since $|{\rm an}|_\infty\le1/4$, reducing
$\alpha$ so that $3C_VK_7\alpha\le1$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-field-energy-floor}
 \operatorname{Re}(\bar A,T_\tau A)_\xi
    \ge c^{(2)}\mathcal E(A)+\tfrac12\|RD_0^*A\|_\xi^2,
 \qquad A\in N(Q),
\end{equation}
where $c^{(2)}=\min\{1/8,(4K_7)^{-1}\}$. Pairing the equation
with $\bar A$ removes the multiplier. Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the
remaining pairing by $\mathcal E(A)^{1/2}$ times the square root
of the first two data sums in
\eqref{eq:weighted-field-energy-linear}.

For nonzero row data use the lift $A^\circ=Hb$. Then
$A-A^\circ\in N(Q)$ and its equation has the additional forcing
$-T_\tau A^\circ$. The bounds on $H$, its first differences and
their transposes in \eqref{eq:endpoint-six-bounds}, applied by the
weighted Schur test, give
\[
 \mathcal E(A^\circ)+\|D_0^*A^\circ\|_\xi^2
                   \le C_H|b|_{\rm row}^2.
\]
The row weight is $\ell(c)^{-1}$; using an unweighted row sum
would not give a constant uniform in the layers. Apply
\eqref{eq:weighted-field-energy-floor} to $A-A^\circ$ and use
this lift estimate. This proves
\eqref{eq:weighted-field-energy-linear}.

At the nonlinear fixed point the data are
\[
 \bigl(-{\rm an}F_U-Y_3(A),\
       -f_3(A)+(dC_2(U,A))^{\mathsf T}(\omega_0+\omega),\
       -C_2(U,A)\bigr).
\]
Here $Y_3,f_3$ are the terms of order at least two in the
displacement in the first variation, and $C_2$ is the nonlinear
remainder of the block constraint. The last entry is not zero.
The small-ball bound on $A$ and the multiplier implies that the
square-sum norm of the nonlinear data is at most
$c_{\rm ms}\sup e\,\mathcal E(A)^{1/2}$.
To see the row estimate in the same units, write $l(c)=\ell(c)/\xi$.
The Taylor kernel of the block average and Cauchy--Schwarz give
\[
 |C_2(U,A)(c)|\le C l(c)^{-1}
                  \sum_{b\ {\rm beneath}\ c}|\xi A(b)|^2.
\]
There are at most $Cl(c)^3$ bonds beneath the row, their scales
are comparable to $l(c)$, and each bond lies beneath at most a
constant number of rows. Hence the row square sum is bounded by
$C(\sup_b\ell(b)|A(b)|)^2\mathcal E(A)$. The same bilinear
kernel bounds the transposed derivative paired with
$\omega_0+\omega$, whose scaled supremum is at most $C\sup e$.
The plaquette and bond remainders are treated by their local
product bounds, using one small factor and one energy factor.

Choose the envelope ceiling so that
$K^{(2)}c_{\rm ms}^2(\sup e)^2\le1/16$.
The nonlinear data can then be absorbed in
\eqref{eq:weighted-field-energy-linear}. The remaining forcing
is $-{\rm an}F_U$, which proves
\eqref{eq:weighted-field-energy-nonlinear}.

At ${\rm an}=0$ and datum $b_0$ the same argument gives
$\mathcal E(A[0;b_0])\le4K^{(2)}|b_0|_{\rm row}^2$.
Subtract the two fixed-point equations at the same $b_0$.
The terms linear in ${\rm an}$ are bounded by its supremum times
the square root of
$\xi^3\sum|F_U|^2+\mathcal E(A[0;b_0])$.
The remaining differences have the factor $C\sup e$; the
multiplier difference is bounded by testing against the same row
lift. One further reduction of the envelope ceiling absorbs
these differences. This proves
\eqref{eq:weighted-field-energy-difference}.
\end{proof}


\begin{lemma}[Complex scalar gauge transfer]\label{hyp:complex-scalar-transfer}
Use the regular-reference setting of Lem.~\ref{C-360-22}.
After decreasing its envelope ceiling and the admitted radii
by constants depending only on $L$, the following estimates
hold. Consider a complex potential $a$ in a sufficiently small
ball for $\mathcal X_e$ and the small gauge
$e^{i\lambda}$ relative to its real reference configuration. Define
$N$ and $q$ by the exact identities
\[
 \begin{split}
 D^*a^{e^{i\lambda}}&=D^*a-D^*D\lambda+N(a,\lambda),\\
 T^{-1}i^{-1}\log\mathcal R(a;e^{i\lambda})
        &=Q'\lambda+q(a,\lambda).
 \end{split}
\]
Here $\mathcal R$ is the induced gauge at the retained block tops,
and $T$ is the orthogonal transport in its linearization; these are
the maps in the proof of Lem.~\YMMref{30.4}{242}. Their linear
scalar system is precisely the compression $\mathbb K^{[2]}$ of
Section~\YMMref{23.2}{179}, in the covariant form of
Section~\YMMref{25}{189}:
\[
 \mathbb K^{[2]}(\lambda,w,\sigma)
  =(\Delta'_a\lambda+w,\ \Delta'_aw-Q'^*\sigma,\ Q'\lambda),
 \qquad \Delta'_a=\Delta_D+Q'^*\mathsf a'Q'.
\]
Here $\Delta_D$ is the scalar Dirichlet Laplacian; the boundary
identity is $RD^*D=R\Delta_D$. Let $\mathcal S(f,b)$ be the first
component of the solution with data
$(f+Q'^*\mathsf a'b,0,b)$. Its first and third rows give
$w=f-\Delta_D\lambda$, while its second row says $Rw=0$.
Consequently the two desired gauge conditions are exactly the fixed
point $\lambda=\mathcal S(D^*a+N(a,\lambda),-q(a,\lambda))$.
The mass term $Q'^*\mathsf a'b$ is necessary when $b\ne0$.
Put
$\|\lambda\|_{\mathcal Z_h}
 :=|\lambda|_{0,h}+\|(D\lambda,0)\|_{\mathcal X_h}$.
For $\lambda,\tilde\lambda$ in one common small ball
for $\mathcal Z_e$, and every admitted envelope $h$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:complex-scalar-transfer}
 \begin{split}
 \|\mathcal S(N(a,\lambda)-N(a,\tilde\lambda),
                  -q(a,\lambda)+q(a,\tilde\lambda))\|_{\mathcal Z_h}
       &\le\tfrac12\|\lambda-\tilde\lambda\|_{\mathcal Z_h},\\
 \|(a^{e^{i\lambda}}-a,0)\|_{\mathcal X_h}
       &\le C\|\lambda\|_{\mathcal Z_h}.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
The scalar fixed-point map preserves a sufficiently small common
complex ball for $\mathcal Z_e$. The estimates also hold for
differences about a given solution and for a cutoff repair with
its commutator forcing, in the exponentially weighted envelopes.
All constants are independent of the volume and number of layers.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{The divergence remainder.}
The divergence remainder has a uniform complex estimate.
Let $a$, $\lambda$ and $\widetilde\lambda$ lie in one sufficiently
small ball for the unlocalized norms $\mathcal X_e$, $\mathcal Z_e$,
and let the sum of their norms be at most $r$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:complex-scalar-divergence-part}
 |N(a,\lambda)-N(a,\widetilde\lambda)|_{2,h}
 \le C(L)r\sup e\,
              \|\lambda-\widetilde\lambda\|_{\mathcal Z_h}.
\end{equation}
Here a localized norm measures the difference; the other factor
in each product is bounded on the common unlocalized ball.

For completeness, put $k(l)=(e^{i\operatorname{ad}l}-1)/
(i\operatorname{ad}l)$, with its value at zero defined by the
power series. At a site $x$, use the outgoing and incoming
bond logarithms
\[
 \Psi_{\rm out}(l;u,d)=i^{-1}\log(e^{il}e^{iu}e^{-i(l+d)}),
 \qquad
 \Psi_{\rm in}(l;u,d)=i^{-1}\log(e^{i(l-d)}e^{iu}e^{-il}).
\]
On a fixed complex ball these are holomorphic and have the form
\[
 \Psi(l;u,d)=\operatorname{Ad}(e^{il})u-k(l)d
                         +\Psi^{(2)}(l;u,d),
 \qquad
 |\Psi^{(2)}|\le14|d|\max\{|u|,|d|\}.
\]
The signed bond sum therefore gives the exact identity
\[
\begin{split}
 N(a,\lambda)(x)
 ={}&[\operatorname{Ad}(e^{i\lambda(x)})-1]D^*a(x)
       -[k(\lambda(x))-1]D^*D\lambda(x)\\
 &+\xi^{-2}\sum_{b\ni x}\epsilon_{x,b}
      \Psi^{(2)}_{x,b}
       (\lambda(x);\xi a_{x,b},\xi D\lambda_{x,b}).
\end{split}
\]
Incoming values are transported to $x$ by the real reference
configuration, and $\epsilon_{x,b}$ is the divergence sign.
The holomorphic remainder vanishes for $d=0$ and has no terms
of degree less than two in $(u,d)$. On a smaller fixed ball,
Cauchy's estimate bounds its differential by products containing
one variation and at least one additional small factor, with a
constant independent of the lattice.
Subtract the formula at $\lambda$ and $\widetilde\lambda$.
Every term contains one difference, among
$\lambda-\widetilde\lambda$, $D(\lambda-\widetilde\lambda)$
and $D^*D(\lambda-\widetilde\lambda)$, and a small factor
bounded by $Cr e$ in its scaled degree. Adjacent scales and
envelopes are comparable with constants depending only on $L$.
Dividing by $h$ and multiplying by the degree-two scale gives
\eqref{eq:complex-scalar-divergence-part}.

\emph{The induced top factors.}
The complex tower estimates of Prop.~\YMMref{30.2}{238}
give the top remainder a common complex domain. To verify
this without iterating estimates for complex group angles, fix
a retained top $y$ of level $j$ and work on its tower. Here
$\xi_j=\ell_j=\xi L^j$ is the layer scale, $B^j(y)$ is the
block beneath $y$, and $\mathsf P^j(y)$ is its tower bond set,
as in the cited proposition. Write $\alpha^{(j)}$ for the local
bound on the reference plaquette angles at that scale. Put
\[
 a_y=\xi_j\sup_{\mathsf P^j(y)}|a|,\qquad
 d_y(\lambda)=\max\left\{
       \sup_{B^j(y)}|\lambda|,
       \xi_j\sup_{\mathsf P^j(y)}|D\lambda|\right\}.
\]
For $a_y+d_y(\lambda)$ below a fixed number of $L$, the
complex bond logarithm for $a^{e^{i\lambda}}$ is defined and
obeys
\[
 \xi_j\sup_{\mathsf P^j(y)}|a^{e^{i\lambda}}|
             \le C\{a_y+d_y(\lambda)\}.
\]
Use the straightened averages and their accumulated factors
$v_i[a]$, for both $a$ and $a^{e^{i\lambda}}$. Their complex
tower estimates give, with constants independent of $j$,
\[
 |v_j[a]^{\pm1}-1|\le C(L)a_y,\qquad
 |v_j[a^{e^{i\lambda}}]^{\pm1}-1|
               \le C(L)\{a_y+d_y(\lambda)\}.
\]
In particular the expression
\[
 r_j(a,\lambda)(y)
      =v_j[a^{e^{i\lambda}}](y)^{-1}
                      e^{i\lambda(y)}v_j[a](y)
\]
and its small logarithm are holomorphic on a common complex
ball independent of the depth. The factorization identity
for the mean scheme identifies $r_j$ with the induced gauge
at real arguments. The identity continues to the complex
ball. Apply the same bounded-factor formula at every
intermediate level $i\le j$. Factorization identifies the
straightened averages of $a^{e^{i\lambda}}$ with those of $a$
transformed by $r_i$, so every intermediate factor and small
logarithm used by the recursion is admitted on this ball.

At $\lambda=0$ one has $r_j=1$. The derivative at $(a,\lambda)
=(0,0)$ of $T^{-1}i^{-1}\log r_j$ in $\lambda$ is
$Q'+E'$, where $E'$ is the comparison of the scalar mean
and comb averages. Its local bound is
\[
 |E'\lambda(y)|\le\kappa_F\alpha^{(j)}
                                    \sup_{B^j(y)}|\lambda|.
\]
The Taylor expansion of $q(a,\lambda)-E'\lambda$ contains only
terms involving $\lambda$ and of total degree at least two in
$(a,\lambda)$. Cauchy's estimate on a smaller common complex
ball therefore gives
\[
\begin{split}
 |q(a,\lambda)(y)-q(a,\widetilde\lambda)(y)|
 \le C(L)\{\alpha^{(j)}+a_y+d_y(\lambda)
             +d_y(\widetilde\lambda)\}
                           d_y(\lambda-\widetilde\lambda).
\end{split}
\]
For the weighted setting, the layer index is constant on
$B^j(y)$ and is $j$ at a retained top. Consequently $e=e(y)$
there and the internal bond scales are $\xi_j$. Its diameter
in the weighted distance is bounded by a number depending only
on $L$. The envelope condition therefore gives
$h(x)\le C(L)h(y)$ for $x\in B^j(y)$. The local reference
curvature parameter obeys $\alpha^{(j)}\le C(L)e(y)$:
use the bound on $F_U$ in the same pillar and the comparison
between the small real plaquette angle and its vector part.
For $a$, $\lambda$ and $\widetilde\lambda$ in the same
unlocalized radius-$r$ ball as above, division by $h(y)$
now yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:complex-scalar-top-part}
 |q(a,\lambda)-q(a,\widetilde\lambda)|_{0,h}
 \le C(L)(1+r)\sup e\,
                  \|\lambda-\widetilde\lambda\|_{\mathcal Z_h}.
\end{equation}
At level zero $q=0$.

\emph{The scalar inverse and repaired field.}
The scalar inverse has the stronger norm required here. Its
three equations are
\[
 \Delta'_a\lambda+w=f+Q'^*\mathsf a'b,
 \qquad \Delta'_aw-Q'^*\sigma=0,
 \qquad Q'\lambda=b.
\]
The scalar solution seminorms and forcing degrees are
those of equations~\YMMref{(327)--(328)}{177}; the regional
inverse is Thm.~\YMMref{G}{204}, with its scalar
compression. The solution seminorm retains
$|\lambda|_{0;y}$, $|D\lambda|_{-1;y}$ and
$|w|_{-2;y}$; its forcing seminorm retains
$|f_2|_{-2;y}$, $|f_3|_{-4;y}$ and $|f_4|_{0;y}$.
The regional inverse estimate is
$|\mathbb E^{[2]}g|_y\le B\sup_z e^{-\delta d(y,z)}|g|_z$.
Apply it with $g=(f+Q'^*\mathsf a'b,0,b)$.
At a bare site of the cell of a level-$j$ top $y$,
$Q'^*\mathsf a'b$ is the value
$\varkappa_j\xi_j^{-2}b(y)$, transported by the real
reference configuration, with $\varkappa_j\le1$.
The input therefore has the claimed degrees, uniformly
in the cell size. The envelope inequality
\eqref{eq:linear-input-envelope}, with its exponent
strictly below $\delta$, bounds the weighted supremum
in the regional inverse estimate. It gives
\[
 |\lambda|_{0,h}+|D\lambda|_{1,h}+|w|_{2,h}
       \le C_{\rm sc}(L)(|f|_{2,h}+|b|_{0,h}).
\]
The first and
third rows therefore imply
\[
 \Delta_D\lambda=f-w,
 \qquad
 |\Delta_D\lambda|_{2,h}
       \le C(L)(|f|_{2,h}+|b|_{0,h}).
\]
At a site meeting the boundary of the first region,
$\Delta_D\lambda-D^*D\lambda$ is the missing-neighbour
mass $\xi^{-2}n\lambda$. Such sites have layer zero and
layer scale $\xi$, so this term has the same bound.

To add the H\"older terms, put $B=D\lambda$. The exact
covariant curl of this gradient is reference curvature acting on
a transported value of $\lambda$, and its divergence has just
been bounded. Apply the local curl--divergence estimate proved
in the proof of Lem.~\ref{C-360-22} to $B$ in the same
comparison gauges. It gives the degree-one H\"older estimate
for $D\lambda$, uniformly in the bare spacing. The pointwise
gradient bound also makes $\lambda$ locally Lipschitz after
transport. The reference curvature is H\"older, so the exact
formula for $D_1D\lambda$ gives its degree-two H\"older norm
by the product rule. The first two layers require only supremum
bounds. No additional regularity of the scalar forcing is used.
We have proved
\begin{equation}\label{eq:complex-scalar-inverse-norm}
 \|\mathcal S(f,b)\|_{\mathcal Z_h}
       \le K_{\rm sc}(L)(|f|_{2,h}+|b|_{0,h}).
\end{equation}
The regional solution seminorm also retains $|Dw|_{3,h}$
and $|\sigma|_{4,h}$. For general three-row forcing
$g=(g_1,g_2,g_3)$, the same inverse and the same local
regularity calculation give
\[
 \|[\mathbb E^{[2]}g]_\lambda\|_{\mathcal Z_h}
       +|[\mathbb E^{[2]}g]_w|_{2,h}
       +|D[\mathbb E^{[2]}g]_w|_{3,h}
       +|[\mathbb E^{[2]}g]_\sigma|_{4,h}
 \le K_{\rm sc}(L)
       (|g_1|_{2,h}+|g_2|_{4,h}+|g_3|_{0,h}),
\]
after enlarging $K_{\rm sc}$. Indeed its first and third
rows bound $\Delta_D\lambda=g_1-w-Q'^*\mathsf a'g_3$;
the rest of the H\"older argument is unchanged.

The field repaired by this scalar has the full stated
norm. The bond logarithm is a holomorphic function of
$\lambda$, $\xi a$ and $\xi D\lambda$, with its linear
term $\xi(a-D\lambda)$. Its product and difference
estimates on a fixed smaller complex ball give
\[
 \|a^{e^{i\lambda}}-a\|_{1,1/2,h}
                       \le C(L)\|\lambda\|_{\mathcal Z_h}.
\]
For its divergence use the exact formula for $N$ above.
For its curl use the exact plaquette identity
\[
 \partial(e^{i\xi a}U)^{e^{i\lambda}}(p)
   =e^{i\lambda(x_p)}
       \partial(e^{i\xi a}U)(p)e^{-i\lambda(x_p)},
\]
before taking differences. The one-plaquette expansion
in the complex potential has the form
\[
 F_{e^{i\xi a}U}(p)
       =F_U(p)+M_U(a)(p)D_1a(p)+R_U(a)(p),
\]
where $M_U(a)$ and its inverse are bounded on the common
ball. More explicitly, with the notation of the
one-plaquette calculation, one can take
$M_U(a)=c_p\mathsf f(-i\xi\operatorname{ad}a_1)^{-1}$,
where $c_p=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}\partial U(p)$,
$\mathsf f(z)=(e^z-1)/z$, $\mathsf f(0)=1$, and
$a_1$ is the potential at the first positively oriented
bond of the plaquette based at $x_p$;
the terms left in $R_U$ are linear in $a$ with coefficient
$O(\xi F_U)$, or of order at least two in the four
potential values. The reference plaquette is small, so
$c_p$ stays away from zero.

Write $a'=a^{e^{i\lambda}}$ and $B=a'-a$.
Subtracting the last identity and using plaquette
conjugation gives
\[
\begin{split}
 M_U(a')D_1B={}&
       (\operatorname{Ad}(e^{i\lambda(x_p)})-1)
                       F_{e^{i\xi a}U}\\
   &+(M_U(a)-M_U(a'))D_1a
                       -R_U(a')+R_U(a).
\end{split}
\]
Every term on the right contains $\lambda$ or $B$.
The quadratic holomorphic remainder has difference
bound $C(|a|+|a'|)|B|$, while its curvature term costs
$C\xi|F_U||B|$. The same estimates hold in the scaled
H\"older norm by the product rule on the fixed comparison
cubes. In these gauges a reference bond transport differs
from the identity by $O_L(\alpha\xi/\ell)$; its scaled
H\"older seminorm is bounded by $C(L)\alpha$, using the
supremum bound at distances at least $\xi$.
For the curvature norm on the larger cube, cover it by a
fixed number of smaller comparison cubes. On overlaps
the two real gauges have relative first difference
$O_L(\alpha/\ell)$, because both transformed reference
bond fields have the stated small bound. Product norms
therefore pass between these gauges with a uniform
constant. Pairs of points farther apart than a fixed
fraction of $\ell$ are controlled by the supremum norm.
The preceding bound for $B$ and the reference
curvature and $D_1a$ bounds therefore give the
degree-two supremum and H\"older estimates for $D_1B$.
No second difference of $\lambda$ is estimated by
separately differencing a bond logarithm. Together with
the divergence identity this proves
\begin{equation}\label{eq:complex-scalar-repaired-field}
 \|(a^{e^{i\lambda}}-a,0)\|_{\mathcal X_h}
                         \le C(L)\|\lambda\|_{\mathcal Z_h}.
\end{equation}
Subtracting the formulas at two scalars proves the
corresponding localized difference bound on the same
ball.

Combining \eqref{eq:complex-scalar-divergence-part},
\eqref{eq:complex-scalar-top-part} and
\eqref{eq:complex-scalar-inverse-norm}, the nonlinear
scalar map has Lipschitz constant at most
$C(L)K_{\rm sc}(1+r)\sup e$. Reduce the envelope ceiling
so that this is at most $1/2$. On the unlocalized ball
of radius $2K_{\rm sc}|D^*a|_{2,e}$ the same map is
invariant, since $N(a,0)=q(a,0)=0$; reduce the admitted
radius of $a$ so that this ball lies in the common
complex ball above. Its fixed point exists and is
holomorphic. For localization, retain the auxiliary variables of the scalar
system. If $a$ already lies in the slice, put $f=D^*a$.
Then $Rf=0$ and there is a top field $\sigma_0$ with
$\Delta'_af=Q'^*\sigma_0$. Thus
$\Psi_0=(0,f,\sigma_0)$ satisfies
$\mathbb K^{[2]}\Psi_0=(f,0,0)$.
The retained inverse seminorm gives
$|Df|_{3,h}+|\sigma_0|_{4,h}\le C(L)|f|_{2,h}$.
Multiply the scalar and top slots by the same slow cutoff,
read at their own base points. Subtract the resulting
$\chi\Psi_0$ from the scalar system with first datum
$D^*(\chi a)$. Its forcing is
\[
 ([D^*,\chi]a,0,0)-[\mathbb K^{[2]},\chi]\Psi_0.
\]
It is supported in the enlarged collar where the cutoff varies:
the Laplacian reads adjacent sites, and every scalar averaging
row reads one tower block of bounded weighted diameter.
If the cutoff has scaled first and second differences
bounded by $C/w$ and $C/w^2$, its commutator is bounded
in degrees $(2,4,0)$ by $C(L)(w^{-1}+w^{-2})$ times
the retained solution seminorm on that collar. In
particular its second row uses both $Df$ and $\sigma_0$.
This is the local scalar system used in the cutoff comparison,
with coefficients agreeing where the compared backgrounds agree.
Use the general three-row inverse estimate above for this
forcing, whose second row need not vanish.
The localized inverse and the nonlinear estimates therefore
localize the scalar correction. Subtracting a given small
solution uses the difference estimates on the same complex
ball. Together with \eqref{eq:complex-scalar-repaired-field},
this proves the cutoff and difference assertions.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The re-filing of the counterterms]\label{C-360-23}
Let $1\le j\le K$, $m'<m+K-j$, $b_0,b_1,\kappa'>0$ and let $c'$ be a complex function of the plaquettes. For a site $z$ of the level $j$ let $\square_z$ be the cube of $\pi_j$ (of side $M$ in level-$j$ units) that holds $z$, and $X_z=\square_z^\sim$ the block of the $3\times3\times3$ cubes of $\pi_j$ about it, the box of the site $z$: $X_z\in\mathcal D_j$, $z\in X_z$, $d_j(X_z)\le7$ for the linear size $d_j$ of \YMMref{72}{607} (the definitions of $\mathcal D_j$ and $d_j$ at its beginning) (Section~\YMMref{72}{607} (the definitions of $\mathcal D_j$ and $d_j$ at its beginning)), every plaquette $p$ with $h^{(j)}_z(p)\ne0$ has its four corners in $X_z$ and its four bonds in ${\rm Bd}(X_z)$, and at most $M^3$ sites $z'$ have $X_{z'}=X_z$, namely those of $\square_z$ (the tent domains and support assertions are those preceding equation~\YMMref{(762)}{376} and in Lem.~\YMMref{49.7}{376}).

Here $h^{(j)}_z$ is the tent of the level $j$ at $z$, the product of the hat functions $\max\{1-|u_\mu|,0\}$ of the coordinates in level-$j$ units, read at the barycentres (equation~\YMMref{(760)}{375}): $0\le h^{(j)}_z\le1$, $h^{(j)}_z(y)\ne0$ exactly when $|y-z|_\infty<1$ in level-$j$ units, $\sum_zh^{(j)}_z=1$, and $\sum_ph^{(j)}_z(p)=3\eta_j^{-3}$ (Prop.~\YMMref{49.6}{375} and the plaquette-count calculation in the proof of Lem.~\YMMref{49.7}{376}). For a complex weight $c$ and a complex bare configuration $\mathbf U$ put $A^\eta(c,\mathbf U)=\eta^{-1}\sum_pc(p)a_p(\mathbf U)$ (equations~\YMMref{(6)--(7)}{13}), and for a triple $P=(U,A',J)$ of a level $q$ let $\mathbf U_P=e^{i\eta_qA'}U$ be its configuration. The tent family at the weight $c'$,
\[
\begin{multlined}
A^t[c'](X,P,z)=A^{\eta_j}\bigl(c'h^{(j)}_z,\mathbf U_P\bigr)=\eta_j^{-1}\sum_pc'(p)h^{(j)}_z(p)a_p(\mathbf U_P)\ \relax \ \relax \text{if }X=X_z,\qquad A^t[c'](X,P, \\
z)=0\ \relax \ \relax \text{for the other }X\in\mathcal D_j,
\end{multlined}
\]
$z\in X$ a site of the level $j$, is, on the cores $\mathcal U^\circ_j(X;b_0,b_1)$, a pointed family of the level $j$ at $(b_0,b_1)$ (Defs.~\YMMref{49.4}{375} and~\YMMref{49.5}{375}), complex linear in $c'$ and $0$ at the trivial triple; its size \YMMref{(759)}{375}, the supremum of $e^{\kappa'd_j(X)}|A^t[c'](X,P,z)|$ over the $X\in\mathcal D_j$, the sites $z\in X$ and the triples $P$ of the core, obeys $\|A^t[c']\|_{j,\kappa'}\le\frac32|c'|_\infty b_0^2e^{7\kappa'}$; at $c'=1$ it is the tent family of equation~\YMMref{(762)}{376}; and $A^{\eta_j}(c',\mathbf U)=\sum_zA^{\eta_j}(c'h^{(j)}_z,\mathbf U)$ for every complex $\mathbf U$. Consequently, let $1\le n\le K$ with $m'<m+K-n$, and let $E^{(i)}$, $1\le i\le n$, be pointed families of the levels $i$ at $(\alpha_0,\alpha_1)$ with complex counterterms $e_i$, let ${\rm an}$ be a complex weight with $|{\rm an}|_\infty=s$, and $\hat E^{(i)}=E^{(i)}-e_iA^t_i[{\rm an}]$, $A^t_i$ the tent family of the level $i$; let $P$ be a triple of one level $k\ge n$ on the whole torus whose restrictions $\rho_XP=\rho^{k\to i}_XP$ to the domains $X$ of the levels $i\le n$ lie in the cores; since $\eta_iL^{-(k-i)}=\eta_k$, the configuration of $\rho_XP$ is $\mathbf U_P$ on $X$. Then, identically in $P$,
\[
\begin{multlined}
\sum_i\Bigl[\sum_z\sum_{X\ni z}\bigl(E^{(i)}(X,\rho_XP,z)-E^{(i)}(X,\mathbf 1,z)\bigr)-e_iA^{\eta_i}(1+{\rm an},\mathbf U_P)\Bigr]=\sum_i\Bigl[\sum_z\sum_{X\ni z}\bigl(\hat E^{(i)}(X, \\
\rho_XP,z)-\hat E^{(i)}(X,\mathbf 1,z)\bigr)-e_iA^{\eta_i}(1,\mathbf U_P)\Bigr],
\end{multlined}
\]
$\hat E^{(i)}(X,\mathbf 1,z)=E^{(i)}(X,\mathbf 1,z)$, and $\|\hat E^{(i)}-E^{(i)}\|_{i,\kappa'}\le\frac32s|e_i|\alpha_0^2e^{7\kappa'}$.

On the label $\mathcal S$ of a history $h\in\mathcal H_k$ with regular regions $\Lambda_j$, assume $m'<m+K-j$ at every level used. The same identity then holds in the following form. Let $\varphi_j$ be the profile of $\Lambda_j$ (equation~\YMMref{(666)}{349} and the definition of $\varphi_j$ following it): $0\le\varphi_j\le1$, $\varphi_jh^{(j)}_z=h^{(j)}_z$ at the sites $z$ of $\Lambda_j^{\sim-1}$, which is $\Lambda_j$ less one layer of its cells, and $\varphi_j(x(p))\ne0$ only if all the corners of $p$ lie in $\Lambda_j$ (the tent identity in Section~\YMMref{44.4}{349}; the corner assertion also follows since a nonzero profile is more than one quarter of a cell width from $Z_j$, while every plaquette corner is less than one bare spacing from its center). The exponent on the label (equation~\YMMref{(1476)}{600}) holds, besides its Wilson term and its vacuum constant, the regular sums in equation~\YMMref{(1474)}{600}, over the set $\mathsf{Ix}^{\rm rs}_j(\mathcal S)$ of the places $(z,X)$ with $X\subset\Lambda_j$ and $z\in\Lambda_j^{\sim-1}$, with the counterterms $-e_jA^{\eta_j}(\varphi_j,\cdot)$, and the boundary sums in equation~\YMMref{(1475)}{600}, which hold the made boundary entries $\mathscr B(j,X,{\rm mk})$ at the filing places $X\in\mathsf{Ix}^{\rm mk}_j(\mathcal S)$ and the edge parts of equation~\YMMref{(1388)}{571} of the families, the members with base points outside $\Lambda_j^{\sim-1}$, at the places $X\in\mathsf{Ix}^{\rm ed}_j(\mathcal S)$ (the index sets and domains preceding Prop.~\YMMref{62.2}{571}); each member is filed at exactly one place (by the separate level, domain and origin indexing in Prop.~\YMMref{62.2}{571}); the entries are boundary terms of their filing places, additive in the exponent, of the sizes $\le\mathsf B\,e^{-\kappa d_j(X)}$ of a well filed system (Prop.~\YMMref{62.2}{571}, on its stated layered output spaces); with the anisotropy the counterterms are $-e_jA^{\eta_j}((1+{\rm an})\varphi_j,\mathbf U_P)$.

For a site $y$ of the level $j$ outside $\Lambda_j^{\sim-1}$ put $\epsilon_y=1$ if $X_y\subset\Lambda_j$ and $\epsilon_y=0$ otherwise, and
\[
r_{(j,y)}=-e_j\eta_j^{-1}\sum_p{\rm an}(p)\bigl[\varphi_j(x(p))-\epsilon_y\bigr]h^{(j)}_y(p)\,a_p(\mathbf U_P).
\]
Then the exponent formed with the families $E^{(j)}$, the entries $\mathscr B$ and the counterterms $-e_jA^{\eta_j}((1+{\rm an})\varphi_j,\mathbf U_P)$ equals, identically, the exponent formed with the families $\hat E^{(j)}$ at the regular places and in the edge parts, the entries $\mathscr B(j,X,{\rm mk})+\sum\{r_{(j,y)}:y\notin\Lambda_j^{\sim-1},\ X_y=X\}$ and the counterterms $-e_jA^{\eta_j}(\varphi_j,\mathbf U_P)$. Here $r_{(j,y)}=0$ unless the tent of $y$ meets the set where $\varphi_j\ne\epsilon_y$, a collar of the boundary of $\Lambda_j$, and then $X_y\in\mathsf{Ix}^{\rm mk}_j(\mathcal S)$; $r_{(j,y)}$ is linear in ${\rm an}$, reads $\mathbf U_P$ in $X_y$ alone and is $0$ at the trivial triple; and on the space of the filing place $(j,X_y,{\rm mk})$, namely the layered output space at level $j$ specified before Prop.~\YMMref{62.2}{571}, where the plaquettes concerned have their plaquette variables within $r_0\eta_j^2$ of $\mathbf 1$, $r_0=\mathsf r_0((j,{\rm out});j)$ being the prescribed output-layer curvature radius at level $j$ (the same radius used for the edge-tent estimate in the proof of Prop.~\YMMref{58.22}{541}), $|r_{(j,y)}|\le\frac32s|e_j|r_0^2$; in a frame of Thms.~\YMMref{AJ}{673} and~\YMMref{AD}{607} the radius of the level is at most $\alpha_0/(1+\beta_{\rm s})<\alpha_0$. The values at the trivial triple are unchanged.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The room condition gives $2L^{m+K-j-m'}\ge2L$ cubes of
$\pi_j$ in each coordinate direction. The three consecutive cubes
in each projection of $X_z$ therefore determine its middle cube.
Thus $X_{z'}=X_z$ exactly for the $M^3$ level-$j$ sites
$z'\in\square_z$.

On the cores $|\partial\mathbf U_P(p)-\mathbf 1|<b_0\eta_j^2$ at the plaquettes with their bonds in ${\rm Bd}(X_z)$, and $a_p=\frac12\det(\partial\mathbf U_P(p)-\mathbf 1)$ for a matrix of determinant $1$, so $|a_p|\le\frac12b_0^2\eta_j^4$; with $h^{(j)}_z\ge0$ and $\sum_ph^{(j)}_z(p)=3\eta_j^{-3}$ this gives $|A^t[c'](X_z,P,z)|\le\eta_j^{-1}|c'|_\infty\cdot3\eta_j^{-3}\cdot\frac12b_0^2\eta_j^4=\frac32|c'|_\infty b_0^2$, and $d_j(X_z)\le7$ gives the factor $e^{7\kappa'}$. Each member is a polynomial in the entries of the $U(b)^{\pm1}$ and $e^{\pm i\eta_jA'(b)}$ at the bonds of ${\rm Bd}(X_z)$, entire in $(A',J)$, a function of the pair, gauge invariant, and $0$ at the trivial triple (Lem.~\YMMref{49.7}{376}).

The tents form a partition of unity, so $A^{\eta_j}(c',\mathbf U)=\sum_zA^{\eta_j}(c'h^{(j)}_z,\mathbf U)$; at $\mathbf U=\mathbf U_P$ the counterterm $e_iA^{\eta_i}({\rm an},\mathbf U_P)$ is the sum over the sites $z$ of the members $e_iA^t_i[{\rm an}](X_z,\rho_{X_z}P,z)$, which vanish at the trivial triple, and moving each from the counterterm into the family of its box is the display, term by term: the two members differ by $\sum_ie_i\eta_i^{-1}\sum_p{\rm an}(p)[a_p(\mathbf U_P)-a_p(\mathbf U_P)]=0$, the counterterm and the families being read at the one configuration $\mathbf U_P$. On a label, by the partition of unity and $\varphi_jh^{(j)}_z=h^{(j)}_z$ on $\Lambda_j^{\sim-1}$, for every rule $\epsilon_y\in\{0,1\}$,
\[
A^{\eta_j}({\rm an}\,\varphi_j,\mathbf U)=\sum_{z\in\Lambda_j^{\sim-1}}A^{\eta_j}({\rm an}\,h^{(j)}_z,\mathbf U)+\sum_{y\notin\Lambda_j^{\sim-1}}\epsilon_yA^{\eta_j}({\rm an}\,h^{(j)}_y,\mathbf U)+\sum_{y\notin\Lambda_j^{\sim-1}}A^{\eta_j}\bigl({\rm an}\,(\varphi_j-\epsilon_y)h^{(j)}_y,\mathbf U\bigr).
\]
For $z\in\Lambda_j^{\sim-1}$ the place $(z,X_z)$ is a regular place, and for $y\notin\Lambda_j^{\sim-1}$ the domain $X_y$ is an edge place exactly when $X_y\subset\Lambda_j$; the exponent with $\hat E^{(j)}$ holds $-e_jA^t_j[{\rm an}]$ at the regular places and in the edge parts, which are the first sum and the members of the second with $\epsilon_y=1$: this is why $\epsilon_y=1$ at the edge places and $\epsilon_y=0$ elsewhere, and $-e_j$ times the third sum is $\sum_yr_{(j,y)}$, the contribution to the made boundary entries. This identity also holds at $e_j=0$. If ${\rm an}(p)[\varphi_j(x(p))-\epsilon_y]h^{(j)}_y(p)\ne0$, the corners of $p$ lie in $X_y$, and in $\Lambda_j$ (by the profile corner property just stated if $\varphi_j(x(p))\ne0$; and if $\varphi_j(x(p))=0$, then $\epsilon_y=1$ and $X_y\subset\Lambda_j$); as $\Lambda_j\subset\Omega_j$, its bonds lie in the bonds of the label in $X_y$, and its base point, a corner, is a site of $X_y$ and of $\Omega_j$, so that $X_y$ and $\Omega_j$ have a bare cube in common; and as $y\in X_y$ lies outside $\Lambda_j^{\sim-1}$, $X_y\in\mathsf{Ix}^{\rm mk}_j(\mathcal S)$: this index set consists precisely of domains sharing a bare cube with $\Omega_j$ and not contained in $\Lambda_j^{\sim-1}$, as defined before Prop.~\YMMref{62.2}{571}.

The size: $|\varphi_j-\epsilon_y|\le1$, the mass $3\eta_j^{-3}$ of the tent and $|a_p|\le\frac12r_0^2\eta_j^4$ on the space of the filing place give $\frac32s|e_j|r_0^2$; in a frame of Thms.~\YMMref{AJ}{673} and~\YMMref{AD}{607}, $r_0\le\alpha_0/(1+\beta_{\rm s})$. The tent families and $\varphi_j$, $\epsilon_y$ read no history beyond the label, and the values at the trivial triple are unchanged, the tent families vanishing there.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Proofs of the theorems}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Thms.~\ref{C-360-2}--\ref{C-360-5}, \ref{C-360-13} and \ref{C-360-14}, and of the remarks]
\emph{Step 1: Thm.~\ref{C-360-2}(a)--(c).} (a) is Lem.~\ref{C-360-6} for the rough entries $F_a=\mathcal O(w_a)$, and its second bound is the second decomposition in the sketch of that lemma, applied to the weights $u_a\mathbf 1\{\lambda(\cdot)=\lambda_a\}$; for a weight that vanishes the cumulant is $0$. (b) Let $\ell'=2\mathsf l$, $\mathsf d=\min\{\mathsf d_0,\frac{\mathsf l}{4n},\frac12\}$, and let $K_1$ be the least $K\ge K_0(r,\mathsf d)$, $2\le r\le8n$, with $a_K\le\frac{\mathsf l}{4n}$. For $K\ge K_1$ cut each $f_i$ into at most $(\frac R\rho+2)^3$ pieces in balls of radius $\rho=\frac{\mathsf l}{8n}$; each choice of pieces lies, for a suitable offset (a pigeonhole on the $n$ centres), in cells of a board of side $\mathsf l$ at sup distance $\ge\frac{\mathsf d}2$ from the walls, so that the mirror copies stay $\ge\mathsf d$ apart, and Lem.~\ref{C-360-7} with (a) gives
\[
\Bigl\|\prod_{a\le r}(\mathcal O(w_a)-c_a)\Bigr\|_{\rm ch}\le e^{G_g\mathsf l^3}\Bigl[\sum_\pi\prod_{I\in\pi}k(\#I,\mathsf d)\Bigr]^{1/8}\prod_a\sup|w_a|,
\]
$\pi$ over the partitions of $8r$ points into blocks of at least two; the moment--cumulant formula, $\langle F_1;\dots;F_n\rangle=\sum_\pi(-1)^{|\pi|-1}(|\pi|-1)!\prod_{B\in\pi}\langle\prod_{a\in B}(F_a-c_a)\rangle$, gives a bound $T_n(\mathsf d)$. For $K<K_1$ we use $|\mathcal O(f)|\le m_K(R)\sup|f|$, $m_K(R)=6a_K^{-1}(\frac{2R}{a_K}+1)^3$, increasing in $K$; so $C_n=\max\{(\frac R\rho+2)^{3n}T_n(\mathsf d),\,m_{K_1}(R)^n\sum_\pi(\#\pi-1)!\}$. On $T_\ell$ the same board is placed with $\ell\ge L\ell'$, and a periodic Gibbs state is dominated through its conditional laws (Lem.~\ref{C-360-7}). The bound on $\nu'-\nu$ is the case $n=1$ with the centring at the mean of the torus. (c) The bounds of (b) give equicontinuity in the sup norm, and a diagonal argument over a countable dense family of tuples gives a convergent subsequence; the lattice symmetries and the reflection positivity of the states pass to the limit, at the three coordinate mirrors in both cases and, for periodic Gibbs states, also at the six diagonal mirrors; the translations by all $v\in\mathbb R^3$ follow through $v_j\in a_{K_j}\mathbb Z^3$, $v_j\to v$, and the Lipschitz continuity of the limits; the growth in $n$ follows by cutting into $\lceil\frac{2\mathsf l}{\mathsf d_0}\rceil^3$ cells and counting, with $B=2e^{3+p}(\frac{8R}{\mathsf l}+2)^3\mathsf d_*^{-p}\max_{r\le P}[e^{G_g\mathsf l^3}{\rm Bl}_{8r}^{1/8}]^{1/r}$, $\mathsf d_*=\min\{\mathsf d_0,\frac{\mathsf l}4,\frac12\}$, $P=\lceil\frac{2\mathsf l}{\mathsf d_0}\rceil^3$; the sum over the planes is the scalar cumulant by linearity.

\emph{Step 2: Thm.~\ref{C-360-2}(d).} Put $\sigma=\lfloor K/(1260n)\rfloor$. (i) Let $s=\lfloor\sigma/(8n+3)\rfloor$ be the coarse depth, $T=K-s$, and $\nu=\sigma-s\ge(8n+2)s$ the number of the levels between the fine depth $\sigma$ and the coarse one. By forgetting, with the never-large term and the sources switched on at the level $K-\sigma$, each $\mathcal O(w_a)$ is exchanged for the weighted energy, plane by plane, of the background over the block field $\mathcal M^{K-\sigma}U$: what a source creates at the levels between $K-\sigma$ and $T$ is forgotten by $L^{-\nu/2}$ over these $\nu$ levels. For the $n$ sources, at mutual corner distances $\ge\mathsf d'=\frac12\mathsf d$, the cumulants of the $\mathcal O(w_a)$ and of the energies differ by at most
\[
\mathsf K_n\bigl[2L^{4n}\mathsf V_\ell(b)L^{-(b+1)s}+n\,C_{\rm fg}(\nu+1)^{2\mathfrak p_0+2}L^{-\nu/2}+2e^{3-L^s\mathsf d'/M}\bigr]\prod_ay_a,\qquad y_a\le4\ell^3L^{4s}\sup|w_a|,
\]
for every real $b\ge4n$, with numbers $\mathsf K_n$, $C_{\rm fg}$ and $\mathsf V_\ell(b)$ that read no $K$: the sup norms of the sources are paid at the coarse depth, which brings the factor $L^{4ns}$, and the histories with a first creation of a large field up to the level $T$ bring $\mathsf V_\ell(b)L^{-(b+1)s}$; the member $2e^{3-L^s\mathsf d'/M}$ is the factor of the distance of the mixed parts at the level $T$ (Lem.~\ref{C-360-24}(a), (e)), read under the conditions $L^s\mathsf d'\ge3M$ and $\mathsf h_2(s)\le1$ of Lem.~\ref{C-360-24}(e) at $t=T$, which hold for $K\ge K_1$, since $s$ grows with $K$ and $\mathsf h_2(s)\to0$ as $s\to\infty$. At $b=4n+1$, $L^{4ns}L^{-(4n+1)s}=L^{-s}$; and $L^{4ns}L^{-\nu/2}\le L^{-s}$ since $\nu\ge(8n+2)s$; so this error is at most $C\ell^{3n}K^{2\mathfrak p_0+2}L^{-s}\prod_a\sup|w_a|$, the factor $\ell^{3n}$ of $\ell^{3(n+1)}$ in the statement coming from $\prod_ay_a$ (the further $\ell^3$ comes from (iii)), and $s\ge\theta_nK-2$. (ii) For one block field at the level $t$ and the cutoffs $K$, $K+1$ at equal label the plane-wise energies of the two backgrounds, formed with the coefficient function $\mathsf c$ of the weights, differ per block site by $Ct^{1/2}L^{-t/2}(\sup|\mathsf c|+L^{t-K}{\rm Lip}_\infty\mathsf c)$.

For the sum of the three planes this is equation~\YMMref{(2156)}{795}. For one plane, retain the parallel-plaquette support in the proof of Prop.~\YMMref{15.1}{79}. More precisely, for a set $S$ of coarse plaquettes and a finer real field $W$ with $\varpi=\varpi_{\mathcal N(S)}(W)\le\varpi'_L$,
\[
\Bigl(\sum_{p'\in S}a_{p'}(\mathcal M(W))\Bigr)^{1/2}\le L^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{p\in\mathcal N^{\mathsf W}(S)}a_p(W)\Bigr)^{1/2}+\sqrt{12}\,C^{\rm SO}_0\,\varpi\Bigl(\sum_{p\in\mathcal N(S)}a_p(W)\Bigr)^{1/2},
\]
where $\mathcal N(S)$ consists of the fine plaquettes in the cones of $S$, and $\mathcal N^{\mathsf W}(S)$ consists of those parallel to a corresponding plaquette of $S$. To verify the estimate, put $f_W(p)=|\partial W(p)-1|$. Lem.~\YMMref{14.9}{68} bounds $f_{\mathcal M(W)}(p')$ by $(\mathsf Wf_W)(p')+C^{\rm SO}_0\varpi_{p'}^2$. The kernel in Lem.~\YMMref{14.8}{68} uses only parallel plaquettes, so its squared-norm bound is $L\|f_W\|^2_{\mathcal N^{\mathsf W}(S)}$. Equation~\YMMref{(146)}{80} gives
\[
 \sum_{p'\in S}\varpi_{p'}^4
 \le12\varpi^2\|f_W\|^2_{\mathcal N(S)}.
\]
The triangle inequality and $f_W(p)^2=2a_p(W)$ give the displayed energy bound. Applied to the plaquettes of one plane at which the coefficient exceeds a level $\lambda$, and integrated over $\lambda$, this bounds the plane-wise energy of the block average by that of the finer background up to the factor $1+C_{\rm en}\varpi$ and up to the variation of the coefficient over a block; this is the one place where the Lipschitz constants enter, with the factor $L^{-\sigma}$. (iii) The laws of the block fields of depth at most $\lceil K/1260\rceil$ at the two cutoffs at equal label differ, on every bounded Borel gauge invariant function $F$, by at most $C_{\rm bf}\ell^3K^{p'}L^{-K/10}\sup|F|$: this is Cor.~\textup{\ref{IV-62-66}}(a), \textup{(\ref{IV-62-68})}, with the number $C_{\rm bf}$ of Def.~\textup{\ref{IV-62-62}}(5) and the exponent $p'=2\mathfrak p_0+\frac12$, the exponent defined before Thm.~\YMMref{AR}{810} at $n=0$.

With $\sigma=\lfloor K/(1260n)\rfloor$ and $s=\lfloor\sigma/(8n+3)\rfloor$ the three errors are at most $L^{-s}\le L^2L^{-\theta_nK}$, $L^{4n\sigma}L^{-(K-\sigma)/2}\le L^{-K/3}$ and $L^{4n\sigma}L^{-K/10}\le L^{-K/11}$, which gives $\theta_n$ and the exponent $\max\{2\mathfrak p_0+2,p',1\}$ of $K$; it equals $2\mathfrak p_0+2$, since $p'=2\mathfrak p_0+\frac12$ and $\mathfrak p_0\ge1$. The comparison of two lattices at equal label, Thm.~\YMMref{AR}{810} in the setting (E) of \S\ref{sec:cutoff-calibration}, applies: it asks $\mathsf b\ge\gamma^{-2}$, which holds because $\mathsf b>g^{-2}+\bar B>\gamma^{-2}$, and $MR(\mathsf b)\le L^{m-1}$, which holds because $L^{m_{\mathfrak L}(g)}\ge LM\,R(L(g^{-2}+\bar B))$ by the definition of the sides (equation~\YMMref{(1528)}{615}), $\mathsf b\le L(g^{-2}+\bar B)$ and $R$ increases.

For $\mathsf b\ge2\max\{\gamma^{-2},x_{\rm J}\}$ and $g=(\mathsf b/2)^{-1/2}$ we have $g^{-2}=\frac{\mathsf b}2\ge x_{\rm J}$ and $\mathsf b\in I(g)$. On a compact interval of labels the numbers are monotone in $\mathsf b$; the dilation is the change of units $x\mapsto L^zx$, which carries $\mu_{K,\ell,\beta}$ to $\mu_{K-z,L^z\ell,\beta}$ and multiplies the label by $L^z$. For continuous $\phi_a$ with supports at sup distances $\ge2\mathsf d$, uniform approximation by Lipschitz functions with supports at distances $\ge\mathsf d$ and the bound of (b), uniform in $K$, make $(G_K)$ a Cauchy sequence. With one plane field among action densities, (ii) is needed for the plane field alone, the action densities being compared at the two cutoffs by the comparison of two lattices at equal label (Thm.~\YMMref{AR}{810}).

The plane field is a connected function at both cutoffs: with the tent $\theta_K(y)=\max\{0,1-(2/a_{K+1}){\rm dist}_\infty(y,{\rm Bc}_\lambda)\}$ about the barycentres ${\rm Bc}_\lambda$ of the plaquettes normal to $\lambda$ at the cutoff $K+1$, $k_0=k\,\theta_K$ is Lipschitz, ${\rm supp}\,k_0\subset{\rm supp}\,k$, $\sup|k_0|\le\sup|k|$, and $k_0(x(p))=k(x(p))\mathbf 1\{\lambda(p)=\lambda\}$ at the plaquettes of both cutoffs, $L$ being odd; so $\langle\mathcal O_\lambda(k);\mathcal O(f_\cdot)\rangle=S^T_{n+1}(f_1,\dots,f_n,k_0)$ at both cutoffs. The comparison statements on two cutoffs at equal label (Thm.~\YMMref{AR}{810} with the lemmas on which it rests, Def.~\textup{\ref{IV-62-62}} and Cor.~\textup{\ref{IV-62-66}}) hold, with the same proofs, at any two depths $u<s$ in the places of the depths there: their proofs read of the depths only conditions on the cutoff, which hold for $K\ge K_0$ when $u$ and $s$ are fixed fractions of $K$.

Take $u=\lceil K/(80(3n+8))\rceil$, at whose level $t_1=K-u$ the sources are carried by the run, and $s=\lceil K/20\rceil$, at whose level $K-s$ the plane field is compared. Three members are left, each with the factor $L^{3nu}$ of Cauchy's estimates in the $n$ sources at the level $t_1$. What the plane field makes below the level $K-s$ is forgotten over the $s-u$ levels up to $t_1$, by $L^{-(s-u)}$, against the volume $L^{3u}$ of the level $t_1$ and the size $L^{s/2}$ of its first variation at the level $K-s$: the exponent $(3n+4)u-\frac12s\le-\frac1{80}K+3n+4$. The forgetting of the run between the two depths, against the size of the first variation at the level $t_1$, gives the exponent $(3n+\frac{15}2)u-s\le-\frac3{80}K+3n+8$.

The classical comparison of the plane-wise energies of the two backgrounds at the level $K-s$, as in (ii), with the factor $K^{1/2}L^{-(K-s)/2}(\sup|k|+L^{-s}{\rm Lip}_\infty k)$ against the volume $L^{3s}$, bounds the difference of the two first variations at the real points of the polydisc of the sources; at its complex points the first variations are bounded crudely, and the estimate with two constants for holomorphic functions, with the exponents $\frac34$ and $\frac14$, gives the exponent $3nu+\frac{23}4s-\frac38K\le-\frac6{80}K+3n+6$. The histories with a first creation of a large field up to the level $t_1$, and the mixed derivatives of the constants of the run in the sources, which are small by locality, cost less than every power of $L^{-K}$.

The largest of the three exponents gives the rate $L^{-K/80}$, and the powers of $K$ of Cauchy's estimates in the $n$ sources give $K^{2\mathfrak p_0(n+2)+2}$. For the sharpness: $L$ being odd, the barycentres of $a_K\mathbb Z^3$ are barycentres of $a_{K+1}\mathbb Z^3$ in the same plane, of density $L^{-3}$ among them; so the indicator of the points of a ball that are barycentres at an even cutoff and at no smaller cutoff samples to a weight of density close to $1$ in the ball at the even cutoffs and close to $L^{-3}$ at the odd ones, and for suitable smooth spectators the cumulants along the even and along the odd cutoffs have different limits.

\emph{Step 3: Thm.~\ref{C-360-2}(e)--(g).} (e) $\mathcal O_\lambda(f)=\mathcal O(f\chi_\lambda)$, $\chi_\lambda$ the indicator of the plaquettes normal to $\lambda$. Prop.~\YMMref{126.4}{846}, the two-point law on a torus of small side against the lattice kernel, is stated for every test pair of $\mathfrak T_{T_\ell}(\mathsf d;\vartheta)$ and every shape parameter $\vartheta\in(0,1)$, with a tolerance $\epsilon_g(s(\mathsf d))$ that depends neither on $\vartheta$ nor on $a_K/\mathsf d$. A pair of non-negative Lipschitz functions, neither identically $0$, carried by balls of radius $\mathsf d$ whose supports are between $\mathsf d$ and $6\mathsf d$ apart, is a test pair for every $\vartheta\in(0,1)$ below four positive numbers formed from their masses, their sup norms and their Lipschitz constants ({\cite[Lem.~I.1]{YMM2}}).

For non-negative weights $w_1,w_2$ carried by balls of radius $\mathsf d-a_K$ about $x_0,y_0$ with $3\mathsf d\le|x_0-y_0|\le4\mathsf d$, the functions $\sum_pw_a(p)\,{\rm pk}_p$, ${\rm pk}_p$ the tent of height $1$ and sup radius $\frac12a_K$ at $x(p)$, are Lipschitz, take the values $w_a$ at the barycentres, so that $\mathcal O(\sum_pw_a(p){\rm pk}_p)=\mathcal O(w_a)$, and form such a pair; so Prop.~\YMMref{126.4}{846} applies to them with its tolerance; real weights are differences of two non-negative ones (four terms), complex weights have real and imaginary parts (sixteen terms). This applies to the weights $f\chi_\lambda$, $h\chi_{\lambda'}$, which depend on the plane, and the kernel bounds of equations~\YMMref{(2245)--(2246)}{824}, with the bounds that enter the template sums of Prop.~\YMMref{121.2}{824} and Lem.~\ref{lem:ward-fluctuation-template}, compare the lattice kernel with $\mathbb K_3$ plane by plane at the Lipschitz pair $(f,h)$.

The lower bound on $\mathcal K_{\lambda\lambda'}$ follows from the masses and the Lipschitz constants of test pairs. For $\mathcal O_1-\mathcal O_2$: with $\hat u=u/|u|$ and $\mathbb K_3(u)_{\lambda\mu}=(3\hat u_\lambda\hat u_\mu-\delta_{\lambda\mu})/(4\pi|u|^3)$,
\[
\begin{multlined}
[\mathbb K_3(u)_{11}]^2-2[\mathbb K_3(u)_{12}]^2+[\mathbb K_3(u)_{22}]^2=\frac{(3\hat u_1^2-1)^2-18\hat u_1^2\hat u_2^2+(3\hat u_2^2-1)^2}{16\pi^2|u|^6} \\
=\frac{9(\hat u_1^2-\hat u_2^2)^2-6(\hat u_1^2+\hat u_2^2)+2}{16\pi^2|u|^6},
\end{multlined}
\]
which is at least $(32\pi^2|u|^6)^{-1}$ where $\hat u_1^2+\hat u_2^2\le\frac14$, the bracket being then at least $2-\frac32$; this holds at all $u\in{\rm supp}\,f-{\rm supp}\,h$ for the test pairs of the statement, for instance for those carried by balls of radius $\mathsf d$ whose centres are $4\mathsf de_3$ apart. With $|u|\le10\mathsf d$ there ({\cite[Lem.~I.1]{YMM2}}(a)) and the masses $\ge\vartheta\mathsf d^3\|f\|_\infty$, $\vartheta\mathsf d^3\|h\|_\infty$ of the non-negative pair ({\cite[Lem.~I.1]{YMM2}}), the main term of the two-point function of $\mathcal O_1-\mathcal O_2$ is at least $\frac32\mathsf b^{-2}(32\pi^2)^{-1}10^{-6}\vartheta^2\|f\|_\infty\|h\|_\infty$, and its error is at most $4$ times the error of the display, one for each of the four two-point functions of the planes $1,2$; so it is positive for small $\mathsf d$, whereas a plane field that is a multiple of $\mathcal O$ would make $\mathcal O_1-\mathcal O_2$ vanish.

The combination $\mathcal O-2\mathcal O_m$ has coefficients of modulus $1$ in three planes, whence the factor $9$ for two entries. Multilinearity gives one further factor $\mathsf b$ in both the main term and the error for each entry multiplied by $\mathsf b$. (f) For free photons, expansion of
$\log\det(1-\mathsf b^{-1}M_\lambda)^{-3/2}$, where
$M_\lambda=\sum_a\lambda_aQ^{\rm T}{\rm diag}(w_a)Q$,
gives $3\mathsf b^{-n}\mathcal K_K^{(n)}$ exactly.
For the interacting weights the lattice comparison is
$\mathrm{(Q_n)}$. The kernel comparison and bound
\YMMref{(2245)--(2246)}{824}, applied to the factors of each
ring and telescoped plane by plane, give the displayed
$C'_n$ error; multilinearity gives the factors for plane
combinations and rescaled entries. (g)(i) Lem.~\ref{C-360-7} on $T_{\ell_g}$, applied to the Wick monomials of the tuple, whose eight mirror copies have as mean a mixture over histories, with jets that are nearly constant at the working level and with large fields that are rare on the small side.

A real multilinear form that is invariant under the lattice translations and bounded by $\mathsf a$ at every choice of signs of a packing of $N_c\sim\mathsf d^{-3(1-\sigma)}$ translates of the tuple in one cube of side $\sim\mathsf d^\sigma$ is bounded by $\mathsf a/N_c$; this gives the factor $\mathsf d^{3(1-\sigma)}$. Each derivative in a source is paid by Cauchy's estimate on the polydisc of the height, which costs $(\frac43\bar{\mathsf b}/\mathsf d)^{[\frac n2-1]_+}$, $\bar{\mathsf b}=L(g^{-2}+\bar B)$; the sizes at the working depth give a factor $\Lambda(\mathsf d)\le C(\log\frac1{\mathsf d})^c$; so $\mathsf e'_n=2^{n-1}(\frac{42L}M)^3(\frac43\bar{\mathsf b})^{[\frac n2-1]_+}[c^\circ_nQ_0\Lambda(\mathsf d)]^n\mathsf d^{3(1-\sigma)-[\frac n2-1]_+}$ with $c^\circ_n=n2^{3n}(1+n4^{n-1})$ and $Q_0$ a constant of the stability bounds on $T_{\ell_g}$.

Every periodic Gibbs state is a state at $g$. (ii) For real weights, the mean of the product of the eight mirror copies of the Wick polynomials $\Xi_B$, centred at the cumulants of $T_{\ell'}$, is exactly the sum over the partitions of the copies all of whose blocks link different copies of the products of the cumulants of the blocks (an identity of formal power series). Hypotheses $\mathrm{(Q_m)}$, $2\le m\le8n$, apply to the real plaquette weights without an upper bound on their mutual distances. Together with the following Gaussian ring bound, they show that a linking cumulant is at most $\mathsf e_m+\mathsf v_m$, where $\mathsf v_m=\frac32(m-1)!(81(1+3C_{\rm lat}))^m(\frac{4\mathsf d}{\ell'})^6$ bounds the linking lattice rings, two copies in different cells being $\ge\frac14\ell'$ apart; with ${\rm Bl}_N(k)=\sum_\pi\prod_{I\in\pi}k_{\#I}$ over the partitions of $N$ points into blocks of at least two, Lem.~\ref{C-360-7} gives the second display with $\eta^\sharp=2^ne^{G_g\mathsf l^3}\max_{m\le n}{\rm Bl}_{8m}(\mathsf e+\mathsf v)^{1/8}$ and $\mathsf e^\sharp_n=\mathsf e_n+\eta^\sharp(1+\eta^\sharp)^{n-1}$.

\emph{Step 4: Thm.~\ref{C-360-2}(h).} (i) On the least torus a pair of narrow bumps, of width $\rho$ at the distance $\mathsf d$, is treated at the level $k_1=\max\{K-s(\mathsf d),2\}$ of the distance $\mathsf d$, the working level of Lem.~\ref{C-360-24} at the depth $s(\mathsf d)$: there the jet of each bump at the background is a constant plus an explicit quadratic form of the curvature, up to errors that the bounds of Thm.~\YMMref{D}{8} make summable over the levels. The induction over the levels with the two sources runs upward from the level $k_1$ to the last level $K$, at which the block field is trivial and the quadratic form vanishes, and carries this to the Gaussian value, the explicit part $\frac32\mathsf b^{-2}\sum f_1f_2(C^{\rm free}_K)^2$, with the error $\epsilon^{\rm nar}_2(g,\mathsf d)(\rho/\mathsf d)^6$ in natural sizes, $\epsilon^{\rm nar}_2\le C(g)(\log\frac1{\mathsf d})^{19\mathfrak p_0}\mathsf d^{1/2}$.
