\mathsf F[\![X_1,\dots,X_m]\!]:=\partial_{s_1}\cdots\partial_{s_m}\,\mathsf F\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^ms_iX_i\Bigr);
\]
this expression is symmetric and multilinear in $X_1,\dots,X_m$, and $\mathsf F[\![A,\dots,A]\!]=m!\,\mathsf F(A)$. For an index $\mathsf i=(b,a)$, where $b$ is a positively oriented bond of $\Omega$ (a free bond if $\Omega=\Lambda_n$) and $a\in\{1,2,3\}$, let $\delta_{\mathsf i}$ be the form which equals $\mathsf e_a$ at $b$ and $0$ at all other positively oriented bonds. We put $\mathsf C(\mathsf i,\mathsf i'):=\delta_{aa'}\,\mathsf C(b,b')$ for $\mathsf i'=(b',a')$, and $\mathsf E_p^a:=\mathsf E_p(\cdot)\,\mathsf e_a$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] (Symmetry factors.) Let $\mathsf F_1,\dots,\mathsf F_r$ be homogeneous polynomials of degrees $m_1,\dots,m_r$. Then $\langle\mathsf F_1;\dots;\mathsf F_r\rangle_0=\sum_{\mathsf n}\mathsf{val}(\mathsf n)$. The sum extends over the symmetric matrices $\mathsf n=(n_{vv'})_{v,v'=1}^r$ of non-negative integers such that $2n_{vv}+\sum_{v'\ne v}n_{vv'}=m_v$ for every $v$ and such that the graph on $\{1,\dots,r\}$ with $n_{vv'}$ edges between $v$ and $v'\ne v$ is connected; and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf{val}(\mathsf n)=\Bigl[\prod_{v<v'}n_{vv'}!\prod_v2^{n_{vv}}\,n_{vv}!\Bigr]^{-1}&\sum\ \prod_{v=1}^r\mathsf F_v[\![\delta_{\mathsf i(v,1)},\dots,\delta_{\mathsf i(v,m_v)}]\!]\\
&\times\prod_{\text{lines }\{e,e'\}}\mathsf C\bigl(\mathsf i(e),\mathsf i(e')\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here, for every such $\mathsf n$, we fix one pairing of the slots $(v,1),\dots,(v,m_v)$, $v=1,\dots,r$, with exactly $n_{vv'}$ pairs between the slots of $v$ and those of $v'$, and $n_{vv}$ pairs among the slots of $v$; its pairs $\{e,e'\}$ are called lines, and the sum extends over all indices $\mathsf i(e)$ attached to the slots $e$. In (a), in (b) and in the proof of the lemma the symbol $\mathsf n$ stands for such a matrix; in the formula for $\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}$ and in \eqref{IV-73-54} below it is the number $\mathsf n=3$ of the setting.
\item[(b)] (Colour.) For every plaquette $P$, every real kernel $\mathsf c$ on pairs of bonds, symmetric or not, and every form $X$,
\[
\sum_{\mathsf i,\mathsf i'}\mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![\delta_{\mathsf i},\delta_{\mathsf i'},X]\!]\,\mathsf c(b,b')\,\delta_{aa'}=0\qquad(\mathsf i=(b,a),\ \mathsf i'=(b',a')).
\]
Consequently $\mathsf{val}(\mathsf n)=0$ if $n_{vv}\ge1$ for some $v$ with $\mathsf F_v=\mathsf a_P^{(3)}$, and also if $n_{vv'}=2$ for some $v,v'$ with $\mathsf F_v=\mathsf a_p^{(2)}$ and $\mathsf F_{v'}=\mathsf a_P^{(3)}$.
\item[(c)] (Classes.) Let $\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}$ and $\Gamma_q$ be defined by the formulas of Def.~\ref{IV-73-29}(5), with the Gaussian family and the vertices of $\Omega$. Then
\[
\mathsf B_1^\Omega(p,q;\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})=\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}+\mathsf T_1+\mathsf T_4+\mathsf T_{4'}+\mathsf T_5+\mathsf T_6 ,
\]
where, with $P,P'$ denoting plaquettes and $\mathsf i,\mathsf i',\mathsf j,\mathsf j',\dots$ indices of $\Omega$,
\begin{align*}
\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}&:=-\mathsf n\,\Pi(p,q)\sum_{b,b'}\mathsf E_p(b)\,\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}(b,b')\,\mathsf E_q(b'),\\
\mathsf T_1&:=\tfrac12\sum_{P,P'}\sum_{a,a'}\sum_{\mathsf i,\mathsf j}\mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![\mathsf E_p^a,\mathsf E_q^{a'},\delta_{\mathsf i}]\!]\,\mathsf C(\mathsf i,\mathsf j)\,\mathsf a_{P'}^{(3)}[\![\mathsf E_p^a,\mathsf E_q^{a'},\delta_{\mathsf j}]\!],\\
\mathsf T_4&:=-\tfrac14\sum_P\sum_{a,a'}\mathsf a_P^{(4)}[\![\mathsf E_p^a,\mathsf E_p^a,\mathsf E_q^{a'},\mathsf E_q^{a'}]\!],\\
\mathsf T_{4'}&:=\tfrac14\sum_a\sum_{\mathsf i,\mathsf j}\mathsf C(\mathsf i,\mathsf j)\bigl\{\mathsf a_q^{(4)}[\![\mathsf E_p^a,\mathsf E_p^a,\delta_{\mathsf i},\delta_{\mathsf j}]\!]+\mathsf a_p^{(4)}[\![\mathsf E_q^a,\mathsf E_q^a,\delta_{\mathsf i},\delta_{\mathsf j}]\!]\bigr\},\\
\mathsf T_5&:=-\tfrac12\sum_P\sum_a\sum_{\mathsf i,\mathsf i',\mathsf j,\mathsf j'}\mathsf C(\mathsf i,\mathsf j)\,\mathsf C(\mathsf i',\mathsf j')\bigl\{\mathsf a_q^{(3)}[\![\mathsf E_p^a,\delta_{\mathsf i},\delta_{\mathsf i'}]\!]\,\mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![\mathsf E_p^a,\delta_{\mathsf j},\delta_{\mathsf j'}]\!]\\
&\qquad\qquad+\mathsf a_p^{(3)}[\![\mathsf E_q^a,\delta_{\mathsf i},\delta_{\mathsf i'}]\!]\,\mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![\mathsf E_q^a,\delta_{\mathsf j},\delta_{\mathsf j'}]\!]\bigr\},\\
\mathsf T_6&:=\tfrac16\sum\mathsf a_p^{(3)}[\![\delta_{\mathsf i_1},\delta_{\mathsf i_2},\delta_{\mathsf i_3}]\!]\,\mathsf a_q^{(3)}[\![\delta_{\mathsf j_1},\delta_{\mathsf j_2},\delta_{\mathsf j_3}]\!]\prod_{\varsigma=1}^3\mathsf C(\mathsf i_\varsigma,\mathsf j_\varsigma),
\end{align*}
the last sum extending over all indices $\mathsf i_1,\mathsf i_2,\mathsf i_3,\mathsf j_1,\mathsf j_2,\mathsf j_3$. By the first half of $\mathsf T_{4'}$, resp.\ of $\mathsf T_5$, we mean the term with the first summand in braces, by the second half the term with the second summand. On $\Omega=\mathbb Z^3$ the formulas hold provided the sums converge absolutely, which is shown in Lem.~\ref{IV-73-55}. Moreover, if the summands of $\Gamma_q$ are taken in the order of Def.~\ref{IV-73-29}(5), the second and the third being grouped together, then
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-54}
\begin{aligned}
\tfrac{\mathsf n}2\sum_{b,b'}\Gamma_q(b,b')\,\mathsf E_p(b)\,\mathsf E_p(b')&=\bigl[\text{first half of }\mathsf T_{4'}\bigr]\\
&\quad+\bigl[\text{first half of }\mathsf T_5\bigr]+\mathsf T_4+\mathsf T_1
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
term by term, the four groups of summands of $\Gamma_q$ producing the four terms on the right in this order; the same holds with $p$ and $q$ exchanged and with the second halves of $\mathsf T_{4'}$ and $\mathsf T_5$.
\item[(d)] (Vertices.) For forms $X,Y,Z$ we have $\mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![X,Y,Z]\!]=\sum\mathsf t_P(X',Y',Z')$, the sum extending over the six orderings $(X',Y',Z')$ of $(X,Y,Z)$, where
\[
\mathsf t_P(X,Y,Z):=-\Bigl\langle\mathrm{d}X(P),\sum_{i<j}s_is_j\,Y(b_i)\times Z(b_j)\Bigr\rangle ,
\]
with $b_i=b_i(P)$ and with the complex bilinear extensions of $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and of $\times$. The standard writing of $\mathsf a_P^{(4)}$ consists of monomials of three kinds: with four plain legs (these come from $\frac12|\mathfrak z_1|^2$), with one curl leg and three plain legs, and with four curl legs.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1: proof of (a).} Writing $A_{\mathsf i}:=A^a(b)$ for $\mathsf i=(b,a)$, we have $A=\sum_{\mathsf i}A_{\mathsf i}\,\delta_{\mathsf i}$, and multilinearity together with $\mathsf F_v(A)=\frac1{m_v!}\mathsf F_v[\![A,\dots,A]\!]$ gives the finite sum
\[
\mathsf F_v=\frac1{m_v!}\sum_{\mathsf i_1,\dots,\mathsf i_{m_v}}\mathsf F_v[\![\delta_{\mathsf i_1},\dots,\delta_{\mathsf i_{m_v}}]\!]\,A_{\mathsf i_1}\cdots A_{\mathsf i_{m_v}} .
\]
We use the multilinearity of cumulants and Lem.~\ref{IV-73-21}, applied to the monomials $A_{\mathsf i(v,1)}\cdots A_{\mathsf i(v,m_v)}$, with the slots $(v,1),\dots,(v,m_v)$ as legs and with the covariance $\langle A_{\mathsf i}A_{\mathsf i'}\rangle_0=\mathsf C(\mathsf i,\mathsf i')$ of Def.~\ref{IV-73-19}(1). We find that $\langle\mathsf F_1;\dots;\mathsf F_r\rangle_0$ is $\prod_v\frac1{m_v!}$ times the sum, over all indices and over all pairings of the slots with connected graph on $\{1,\dots,r\}$, of $\prod_v\mathsf F_v[\![\cdots]\!]\prod_{\text{pairs}}\mathsf C$. As the forms $\mathsf F_v[\![\cdot]\!]$ are symmetric, the contribution of a pairing, summed over the indices, depends only on its matrix $(n_{vv'})$; and the graph of a pairing is connected if and only if that of its matrix is.

It remains to count the pairings with a given matrix $\mathsf n$. At each vertex $v$ we decide which slots are joined to which $v'\ne v$ and which are paired among themselves: there are $m_v!/[\prod_{v'\ne v}n_{vv'}!\,(2n_{vv})!]$ possibilities. For each pair $v<v'$ we match the chosen slots of $v$ with those of $v'$: $n_{vv'}!$ possibilities. At each $v$ we pair the $2n_{vv}$ slots reserved for this purpose: $(2n_{vv})!/(2^{n_{vv}}n_{vv}!)$ possibilities. Since $\prod_v\prod_{v'\ne v}n_{vv'}!=\prod_{v<v'}(n_{vv'}!)^2$, the number of pairings is
\[
\prod_vm_v!\Big/\Bigl[\prod_{v<v'}n_{vv'}!\prod_v2^{n_{vv}}\,n_{vv}!\Bigr],
\]
and multiplication by $\prod_v\frac1{m_v!}$ gives the factor in $\mathsf{val}(\mathsf n)$.

\emph{Step 2: proof of (d) and (b).} By \eqref{IV-73-10}, $\mathsf a^{(3)}_P(A)=\langle\mathrm{d}A(P),\mathfrak z_1(P)\rangle$ with $\mathfrak z_1=-\sum_{i<j}s_is_j\,A(b_i)\times A(b_j)$; thus $\mathsf a_P^{(3)}(A)=\mathsf t_P(A,A,A)$ with the trilinear form $\mathsf t_P$, and \[
 \partial_{s_1}\partial_{s_2}\partial_{s_3}\,\mathsf t_P\bigl(\sum s_iX_i,\sum s_iX_i,\sum s_iX_i\bigr)
\] is the sum of $\mathsf t_P$ over the six orderings of $X_1,X_2,X_3$. The three kinds of monomials of $\mathsf a_P^{(4)}$ are those of the three terms $\frac12|\mathfrak z_1|^2$, $\langle\mathrm{d}A(P),\mathfrak z_2\rangle$, $-\frac1{24}|\mathrm{d}A(P)|^4$ of \eqref{IV-73-10}, written as in Def.~\ref{IV-73-19}(3).

For (b) we insert (d): $\mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![\delta_{(b,a)},\delta_{(b',a)},X]\!]$ is a sum of terms, each the product of a real number which depends on $b$, $b'$ and on the ordering, but not on $a$, with one of $\langle\mathsf e_a,\mathsf e_a\times X'\rangle$, $\langle\mathsf e_a,X'\times\mathsf e_a\rangle$, $\langle X',\mathsf e_a\times\mathsf e_a\rangle$, where $X'$ is a value of $X$ or of $\mathrm{d}X$. Summed over $a$, each of these three expressions vanishes, since $Y\times X'$ is orthogonal to $Y$ and $Y\times Y=0$; multiplying by $\mathsf c(b,b')$ and summing over $b,b'$ we obtain (b). A line between two slots of a vertex $\mathsf a_P^{(3)}$ produces exactly the sum in (b) with $\mathsf c=\mathsf C$.

By the rule for $\mathsf a_p^{(2)}$ in Step~3 below, two lines from $\mathsf a_p^{(2)}=\frac12\sum_a((\mathrm{d}A)^a(p))^2$ to the same vertex $\mathsf a_P^{(3)}$ produce the sum in (b) with $\mathsf c(b,b')=\mathsf E_p(b)\,\mathsf E_p(b')$. In both cases $\mathsf{val}(\mathsf n)=0$.

\emph{Step 3: rules for (c).} From $\mathsf a_p^{(2)}=\frac12\sum_a((\mathrm{d}A)^a(p))^2$ we obtain $\mathsf a_p^{(2)}[\![\delta_{\mathsf i},\delta_{\mathsf i'}]\!]=\delta_{aa'}\,\mathsf s_p(b)\,\mathsf s_p(b')$, where $\mathsf s_p(b_i(p))=s_i$ and $\mathsf s_p(b)=0$ for the bonds $b$ which do not belong to $p$. Since $\sum_b\mathsf s_p(b)\,\mathsf C(b,b'')=\mathsf E_p(b'')$, a line from a slot of $\mathsf a_p^{(2)}$ to a slot of another vertex inserts $\mathsf E_p^a$ into that slot, the colour $a$ being summed together with the other slot of $\mathsf a_p^{(2)}$. A line from $\mathsf a_p^{(2)}$ to $\mathsf a_q^{(2)}$ produces $\Pi(p,q)$ and identifies the colours of the two remaining slots. A vertex $\mathsf a^{(2)}$ carrying a line between its own two slots is not connected to the other vertices.

\emph{Step 4: enumeration for (c).} We go through the seven cumulants of \eqref{IV-73-24} and list the matrices $\mathsf n$ with connected graph whose value does not vanish by (b) or by Step~3; in particular there are no lines between two slots of a vertex $\mathsf a^{(2)}$ or $\mathsf a^{(3)}$. We index these matrices by names of the vertices: the vertices $\mathsf a_p^{(m)}$ and $\mathsf a_q^{(m)}$ are called $p$ and $q$, the vertices $\mathsf a_P^{(m)}$ and $\mathsf a_{P'}^{(3)}$ coming from $\mathsf S_3$ or from $\mathsf V_2$ are called $P$ and $P'$, and a quadratic local term $\mathsf F$ of $\mathsf V_2$, taken as a vertex, is called $\mathsf F$. Thus $n_{pq}$ is the number of lines between the slots of $p$ and those of $q$, $n_{qq}$ the number of lines joining two slots of $q$, and similarly for the other entries.
\begin{itemize}
\item $\langle\mathsf a_p^{(3)};\mathsf a_q^{(3)}\rangle_0$: here $n_{pq}=3$, with the factor $\frac1{3!}=\frac16$; this is $\mathsf T_6$.
\item $\langle\mathsf a_p^{(2)};\mathsf a_q^{(4)}\rangle_0$: here $n_{pq}=2$ and $n_{qq}=1$, with the factor $\frac1{2\cdot2}$; this is the first half of $\mathsf T_{4'}$. In the same way $\langle\mathsf a_p^{(4)};\mathsf a_q^{(2)}\rangle_0$ gives the second half.
\item $\langle\mathsf a_p^{(2)};\mathsf a_q^{(3)};\mathsf a_P^{(3)}\rangle_0$, from the term $-\langle\mathsf a_p^{(2)};\mathsf a_q^{(3)};\mathsf S_3\rangle_0$: the conditions $n_{pq}+n_{pP}=2$, $n_{pq}+n_{qP}=3$, $n_{pP}+n_{qP}=3$ force $n_{pq}=n_{pP}=1$ and $n_{qP}=2$, with the factor $\frac12$; with the sign of \eqref{IV-73-24} and the sum over $P$ this is the first half of $\mathsf T_5$. In the same way $-\langle\mathsf a_p^{(3)};\mathsf a_q^{(2)};\mathsf S_3\rangle_0$ gives the second half.
\item $\langle\mathsf a_p^{(2)};\mathsf a_q^{(2)};\mathsf F\rangle_0$ with a quadratic local term $\mathsf F$ of $\mathsf V_2$: here $n_{pq}=n_{p\mathsf F}=n_{q\mathsf F}=1$, with the factor $1$, and the value is $\Pi(p,q)\sum_a\mathsf F[\![\mathsf E_p^a,\mathsf E_q^a]\!]=\Pi(p,q)\sum_a\sum_{b,b'}\mathsf E_p(b)\,\mathsf E_q(b')\,\partial_{b,a}\partial_{b',a}\mathsf F$.
\item $\langle\mathsf a_p^{(2)};\mathsf a_q^{(2)};\mathsf a_P^{(4)}\rangle_0$: either $n_{pq}=n_{pP}=n_{qP}=n_{PP}=1$, with the factor $\frac12$ and the value
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\Pi(p,q)\sum_a\tfrac12\sum_{\mathsf i,\mathsf j}\mathsf C(\mathsf i,\mathsf j)\,\mathsf a_P^{(4)}[\![\mathsf E_p^a,\mathsf E_q^a,\delta_{\mathsf i},\delta_{\mathsf j}]\!]\\
&\qquad=\Pi(p,q)\sum_a\sum_{b,b'}\mathsf E_p(b)\,\mathsf E_q(b')\,\langle\partial_{b,a}\partial_{b',a}\mathsf a_P^{(4)}\rangle_0
\end{aligned}
\]
(by (a) for the quadratic polynomial $\partial_{b,a}\partial_{b',a}\mathsf a_P^{(4)}$, whose polarisation is $\mathsf a_P^{(4)}[\![\delta_{(b,a)},\delta_{(b',a)},\cdot,\cdot]\!]$); or $n_{pP}=n_{qP}=2$, with the factor $\frac14$, which with the sign of \eqref{IV-73-24} and the sum over $P$ gives $\mathsf T_4$. The matrix with $n_{pq}=2$ has a disconnected graph.
\item $\langle\mathsf a_p^{(2)};\mathsf a_q^{(2)};\mathsf a_P^{(3)};\mathsf a_{P'}^{(3)}\rangle_0$: subtracting the conditions at $p$ and $q$ from those at $P$ and $P'$ we get $n_{PP'}=1+n_{pq}$. For $n_{pq}=2$ the graph is disconnected. For $n_{pq}=1$ we get $n_{PP'}=2$ and either $n_{pP}=n_{qP'}=1$ or $n_{pP'}=n_{qP}=1$, each with the factor $\frac12$; summed over $P,P'$ and multiplied by the $\frac12$ of \eqref{IV-73-24}, they give
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\Pi(p,q)\sum_a\tfrac12\sum\mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![\mathsf E_p^a,\delta_{\mathsf i},\delta_{\mathsf i'}]\!]\,\mathsf a_{P'}^{(3)}[\![\mathsf E_q^a,\delta_{\mathsf j},\delta_{\mathsf j'}]\!]\,\mathsf C(\mathsf i,\mathsf j)\,\mathsf C(\mathsf i',\mathsf j')\\
&\qquad=\Pi(p,q)\sum_a\sum_{b,b'}\mathsf E_p(b)\,\mathsf E_q(b')\,\langle\partial_{b,a}\mathsf S_3;\partial_{b',a}\mathsf S_3\rangle_0 ,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the sum on the left extends over $P,P'$ and all indices, and the equality is (a) for two quadratic polynomials. For $n_{pq}=0$ we get $n_{PP'}=1$ and $n_{pP}+n_{qP}=2=n_{pP'}+n_{qP'}$; the possibilities $(n_{pP},n_{qP})=(2,0)$ and $(0,2)$ vanish by (b), and there remains $n_{pP}=n_{qP}=n_{pP'}=n_{qP'}=1$, with the factor $1$; with the $\frac12$ of \eqref{IV-73-24} this is $\mathsf T_1$.
\item We collect the terms with $n_{pq}=1$ found above, with the signs of \eqref{IV-73-24}. By the definition of $\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}$ in Def.~\ref{IV-73-29}(5) they add up to $-\Pi(p,q)\sum_a\sum_{b,b'}\mathsf E_p(b)\,\mathsf E_q(b')\,\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}(b,a;b',a)$. The argument on the colour structure given there applies in the box as well and shows $\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}(b,a;b',a)=\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}(b,b')$ for every colour $a$; summing over the three colours we obtain $\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}$.
\end{itemize}

\emph{Step 5: proof of \eqref{IV-73-54}.} Let $\partial=\partial_{b,a}$, $\partial'=\partial_{b',a'}$, $\delta=\delta_{(b,a)}$, $\delta'=\delta_{(b',a')}$. By (a),
\begin{align*}
\langle\partial\partial'\mathsf a_q^{(4)}\rangle_0&=\tfrac12\sum_{\mathsf i,\mathsf j}\mathsf C(\mathsf i,\mathsf j)\,\mathsf a_q^{(4)}[\![\delta,\delta',\delta_{\mathsf i},\delta_{\mathsf j}]\!],\\
\langle\partial\mathsf a_q^{(3)};\partial'\mathsf S_3\rangle_0&=\tfrac12\sum_P\sum\mathsf C(\mathsf i,\mathsf j)\,\mathsf C(\mathsf i',\mathsf j')\,\mathsf a_q^{(3)}[\![\delta,\delta_{\mathsf i},\delta_{\mathsf i'}]\!]\,\mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![\delta',\delta_{\mathsf j},\delta_{\mathsf j'}]\!],\\
\langle\mathsf a_q^{(2)};\partial\partial'\mathsf S_4\rangle_0&=\tfrac12\sum_P\sum_{a''}\mathsf a_P^{(4)}[\![\delta,\delta',\mathsf E_q^{a''},\mathsf E_q^{a''}]\!],\\
\langle\mathsf a_q^{(2)};\partial\mathsf S_3;\partial'\mathsf S_3\rangle_0&=\sum_{P,P'}\sum_{a''}\sum_{\mathsf i,\mathsf j}\mathsf C(\mathsf i,\mathsf j)\,\mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![\delta,\mathsf E_q^{a''},\delta_{\mathsf i}]\!]\\
&\qquad\times\mathsf a_{P'}^{(3)}[\![\delta',\mathsf E_q^{a''},\delta_{\mathsf j}]\!];
\end{align*}
in the last line the three polynomials are quadratic, the only connected matrix has one line between any two of them, and its factor is $1$. We contract these expressions, and the one obtained from the second by exchanging $(b,a)$ and $(b',a')$, with $\frac12\sum_a\mathsf E_p^a\otimes\mathsf E_p^a$; that is, we set $a'=a$, multiply by $\frac12\,\mathsf E_p(b)\,\mathsf E_p(b')$ and sum over $b,b',a$. Since $\Gamma_q(b,a;b',a)=\Gamma_q(b,b')$, this turns $\Gamma_q$ into the left side of \eqref{IV-73-54}. By multilinearity, and with the signs of Def.~\ref{IV-73-29}(5), the first summand of $\Gamma_q$ produces the first half of $\mathsf T_{4'}$; the second and the third, whose contributions coincide after the symmetric contraction, together produce the first half of $\mathsf T_5$; the fourth produces $\mathsf T_4$; and the fifth produces $\mathsf T_1$. Exchanging $p$ and $q$ gives the statement for the second halves.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Convergence of the graph sums on $\mathbb Z^3$]\label{IV-73-55}
Let $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}>0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] On $\mathbb Z^3$, for all plaquettes $p,q$, the sums over the positions of the local terms of $\mathsf S_3$ and $\mathsf V_2$ in \eqref{IV-73-24}, taken monomial by monomial in the standard writing and pairing by pairing, converge absolutely. Consequently $\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(p,q;\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})$ is defined, the formulas of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-53}(c) hold on $\mathbb Z^3$, and $\sup_{p,q}|\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}(p,q;\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})|<\infty$.
\item[(ii)] (Uniform form.) Let $\mathsf c_0\ge1$, let $\Omega=\mathbb Z^3$ or $\Omega=\Lambda_n$, and substitute for $\mathsf C,\mathsf E,\Pi,\mathsf D,\mathsf g$ arbitrary real kernels which satisfy, with the base points $b_-$ of the bonds and $x_p$ of the plaquettes,
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-56}
\begin{gathered}
|\mathsf C(b,b')|\le\frac{\mathsf c_0}{\langle b_--b'_-\rangle},\qquad|\mathsf E_p(b)|\le\frac{\mathsf c_0}{\langle x_p-b_-\rangle^{2}},\\
|\mathsf D(b;b')|\le\frac{\mathsf c_0}{\langle b_--b'_-\rangle^{2}},\qquad|\Pi(p,q)|\le\frac{\mathsf c_0}{\langle x_p-x_q\rangle^{3}},\qquad|\mathsf g(b)|\le\mathsf c_0 .
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
Then the sum of the absolute values of all terms of the seven cumulants of \eqref{IV-73-24}, over monomials, pairings and positions, is at most $C\,\mathsf c_0^5$, with a pure constant $C$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1.} By Lem.~\ref{IV-73-51}, the kernels $\mathsf C$, $\mathsf E$, $\Pi$, $\mathsf D$ of $\mathbb Z^3$ are, as functions of the difference of the base points, elementary lines of the degrees $1,2,3,2$, with finitely many different symbols. Lem.~\ref{IV-73-39}(a), applied with $s=-2,-1,0,-1$ and $\gamma=0$, bounds them by constants times $\langle\cdot\rangle^{-1}$, $\langle\cdot\rangle^{-2}$, $\langle\cdot\rangle^{-3}$, $\langle\cdot\rangle^{-2}$, and $\mathsf g=\frac13$ on $\mathbb Z^3$ by Def.~\ref{IV-73-15}(2). Hence these kernels satisfy \eqref{IV-73-56} with some $\mathsf c_0=\mathsf c_0(\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})$, and (i) follows from (ii): the bound $C\mathsf c_0^5$, which does not depend on $p,q$, is the absolute convergence required in Def.~\ref{IV-73-19}(3), so that $\mathsf B_1^{\mathrm{lat}}$ is defined and those rearrangements made in the proof of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-53}(c) are allowed whose terms are bounded by the majorants of Step~2 below, such as regroupings of whole terms of positions and regroupings which split one curl leg or, as in Step~5 of that proof and for $n_{pq}=n_{pP}=n_{qP}=n_{PP}=1$ in its Step~4, curl legs at $P$ or $P'$ joined to $p$ or $q$, whose lines then have the degree $2$ which these majorants have there.

For the kernels of $\mathbb Z^3$ we obtain the equality of the display for $n_{pq}=1$ in Step~4 of that proof, whose right side splits the curl legs at $P$ and at $P'$ joined to $p$ and to $q$, as in $\Pi(p,P)=\sum_b\mathsf s_P(b)\,\mathsf E_p(b)$, by regrouping one vertex at a time, with $u,z,w$ as in Step~2. At $P$ we write $\mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![\mathsf E_p^a,\cdot,\cdot]\!]=\sum_b\mathsf E_p(b)\,\mathsf a_P^{(3)}[\![\delta_{(b,a)},\cdot,\cdot]\!]$, split the quadratic polynomial $\partial_{b,a}\mathsf a_P^{(3)}$, whose polarisation is the last factor, into its two terms as in \eqref{IV-73-58}, which follows from \eqref{IV-73-10} by the Leibniz rule, and keep the vertex at $P'$ in the standard writing; the resulting terms, indexed by $(P,b,P')$, the monomials and the pairings, are bounded by $C\langle z\rangle^{-2}\langle w-z\rangle^{-n_3}\langle u-w\rangle^{-n_5}$, with a constant $C$ which depends only on $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}$, as the kernels of $\mathbb Z^3$ satisfy \eqref{IV-73-56} with $\mathsf c_0=\mathsf c_0(\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})$, and with the four pairs $(n_3,n_5)$ of Step~2, for which the computation there holds for every $n_1\ge2$; so they may be grouped by $(b,P')$, and the sum over $P\ni b$ turns the first entry into $\partial_{b,a}\mathsf S_3$.

Next, with $z,w$ the positions of $b,P'$ relative to the base point of $p$ and with $C=C(\tau_{\mathrm{gf}})$, we have $|\langle\partial_{b,a}\mathsf S_3;\partial_{b',a}\mathsf a_{P'}^{(3)}\rangle_0|\le C\langle w-z\rangle^{-3}$: by \eqref{IV-73-58}, a monomial of $\mathsf u_{b,a}$ has a curl leg and a plain leg, so that the two lines joining it to a monomial of $\partial_{b',a}\mathsf a_{P'}^{(3)}$ have degrees of sum at least $3$, and \eqref{IV-73-56} applies; and $\mathsf d_{b,a}$ contributes $\sum_{P\ni b}\mathsf s_P(b)\,\mathsf F(P)$ with $\mathsf F(P):=\langle\langle\mathsf e_a,\mathfrak z_1(P)\rangle;\partial_{b',a}\mathsf a_{P'}^{(3)}\rangle_0$, by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-53}(a) and Lem.~\ref{IV-73-51} a finite sum of products $K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}$ of elementary lines in the base point of $P$ with $n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}\ge2$; since the four plaquettes containing $b$ form two pairs, each of one dual direction, with base points differing by one of the vectors $e_1,e_2,e_3$ and with opposite signs, this is a sum of two first differences in the base point of $P$, which Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(c) with $|\gamma|=1$ bounds by $C\langle w-z\rangle^{-3}$.

At $P'$, by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-53}(a) for two quadratic polynomials, the term of $(b,P')$ so obtained is the sum over $b'$ of $\mathsf E_p(b)\,\mathsf E_q(b')\,\langle\partial_{b,a}\mathsf S_3;\partial_{b',a}\mathsf a_{P'}^{(3)}\rangle_0$; these terms, indexed by $(b,P',b')$, are bounded by $C\langle z\rangle^{-2}\langle w-z\rangle^{-3}\langle u-w\rangle^{-2}$, the pair $(3,2)$ of Step~2; so they may be grouped by $(b,b')$, and the sum over $P'\ni b'$ gives the right side of that display. Thus this equality holds on $\mathbb Z^3$, and the sum over $b,b'$ in the formula for $\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}$ converges absolutely: for the summand $-\langle\partial_{b,a}\mathsf S_3;\partial_{b',a}\mathsf S_3\rangle_0$ of $\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}$ by these majorants, and for the summands of $\langle\partial_{b,a}\partial_{b',a}\mathsf V_2\rangle_0$, which by \eqref{IV-73-17} and \eqref{IV-73-56} are bounded and of finite range, or bounded by $8\mathsf c_0^2\langle b_--b'_-\rangle^{-4}$, by the sums of Step~2.

\emph{Step 2.} We prove (ii). We write every vertex in the standard writing and count a curl leg as one leg (Lem.~\ref{IV-73-53}(d)); at every position there are finitely many monomials, with coefficients independent of the position. We follow the enumeration in the proof of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-53}(c); at fixed positions all sums there are finite. By \eqref{IV-73-56} a term is bounded, up to a bounded factor, by $\prod_\ell\mathsf c_0\langle y_\ell\rangle^{-n_\ell}$, where $\ell$ ranges over its lines, $y_\ell$ is the difference of the positions of the two vertices joined by $\ell$, and $n_\ell=1+\#$(curl legs at $\ell$); the bounded factor accounts for shifts of length at most $3$ between the base points of the legs and the positions of the vertices, since $\langle y\rangle\le4\langle y+v\rangle$ for $|v|\le3$.

Every term has at most five lines, $\mathsf c_0\ge1$, and the numbers of monomials and pairings are pure constants; it therefore suffices to bound the sums over the positions of the products $\prod_\ell\langle y_\ell\rangle^{-n_\ell}$ by pure constants. Let $u$ be the base point of $q$ minus that of $p$, and let $z,w$ be the positions of $P,P'$ (or of the bonds of the local terms of $\mathsf V_2$) relative to the base point of $p$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathsf T_1$: the lines starting at $p$ or ending at $q$ carry a curl leg of $p$ or of $q$, so their degrees are at least $2$, and the line between $P$ and $P'$ has degree at least $1$. As $\langle\cdot\rangle^{-n}$ decreases in $n$, the sum is at most the sum in Prop.~\ref{IV-73-47}(i) with $(n_1,\dots,n_5)=(2,2,1,2,2)$, which satisfies the hypotheses of that proposition.
\item The terms of $\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}$ with two cubic vertices, or with the ghost loop, have sums of the form
\[
\begin{gathered}
\langle u\rangle^{-3}\sum_{z,w}\langle z\rangle^{-n_1}\langle w-z\rangle^{-n_3}\langle u-w\rangle^{-n_5},\\
n_1,n_5\in\{2,3\},\qquad n_3\ge2,\qquad n_1+n_3+n_5=8 ;
\end{gathered}
\]
the factor $\langle u\rangle^{-3}$ comes from $\Pi(p,q)$, and $\langle w-z\rangle^{-n_3}$ from the two lines between the cubic vertices, resp.\ from $\mathsf D(b;b')\mathsf D(b';b)$. The possible pairs are $(n_3,n_5)=(2,3),(3,2),(3,3),(4,2)$, and for each of them Lem.~\ref{IV-73-40}(c) gives $\sum_w\langle w-z\rangle^{-n_3}\langle u-w\rangle^{-n_5}\le C\langle u-z\rangle^{-2}\lg\langle u-z\rangle$. Next, $\sum_z\langle z\rangle^{-2}\langle u-z\rangle^{-2}\lg\langle u-z\rangle\le C$: by $\lg t\le2t^{1/2}$ for $t\ge1$ and by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-40}(c) with $(a,a')=(2,\frac32)$ this sum is at most $C\langle u\rangle^{-1/2}\lg\langle u\rangle\le C$. Finally $\langle u\rangle^{-3}\le1$.
\item The other terms of $\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}$ (with a line between two slots of the quartic vertex at $P$, with the Haar term, with the ghost tadpole) have sums bounded by $\sum_z\langle z\rangle^{-2}\langle u-z\rangle^{-2}\le C$, by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-40}(c).
\item $\mathsf T_4$ leads to $\sum_z\langle z\rangle^{-4}\langle u-z\rangle^{-4}$, and $\mathsf T_5$ to $\sum_z\langle z\rangle^{-n_X}\langle u-z\rangle^{-n_Y}$ with $n_X,n_Y\ge2$, the line between $p$ and $q$ being bounded by $\mathsf c_0$; both sums are bounded by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-40}(c). The sums of $\mathsf T_{4'}$ and $\mathsf T_6$ are finite, as these classes have no vertex besides $p$ and $q$.
\item The graphs which vanish by colour in Lem.~\ref{IV-73-53}(b) vanish pairing by pairing, so they contribute no terms. Indeed $\langle\mathrm{d}A,A_i\times A_j\rangle=\sum\epsilon_{abc}(\mathrm{d}A)^aA_i^bA_j^c$, so every monomial of $\mathsf a_P^{(3)}$ has three legs of three different colours, while $((\mathrm{d}A)^a(p))^2$ has two legs of one colour; since the covariance is diagonal in the colours, a line between two legs of one monomial of $\mathsf a_P^{(3)}$, or two lines from $((\mathrm{d}A)^a(p))^2$ to one monomial of $\mathsf a_P^{(3)}$, give the factor $0$.
\end{itemize}
In the box the positions range over subsets of $\mathbb Z^3$, and the same bounds apply.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Elementary terms, their expansions, the local parts}

\begin{lemma}[Elementary terms and their degrees]\label{IV-73-57}
Let $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}>0$, let us work on $\mathbb Z^3$, let $p=p_{[\iota]}(x_p)$ and $q=p_{[\iota']}(x_q)$ be plaquettes, and put $u':=x_q-x_p$. We write every vertex occurring in the formulas of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-53}(c) in the standard writing (Def.~\ref{IV-73-19}(3), Lem.~\ref{IV-73-53}(d)), we carry out the sums over the colours, and we write every contraction as an elementary line by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-51}. Then there are finite index sets $\mathfrak G_\bullet=\mathfrak G_\bullet(\iota,\iota')$, real numbers $c_G$ and elementary lines $K^G_\bullet$, all independent of $x_p$ and $x_q$, such that the following representations hold; every $G$ is called an elementary term. We omit the index $G$ on the lines, and $*$ denotes the convolution of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $\mathsf T_1=\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_1}c_G\,\mathsf T^G(u')$, where every $\mathsf T^G$ is a kite as in Prop.~\ref{IV-73-47}, with degrees satisfying the hypotheses of that proposition and with $\varDelta=5$. Here $K_1$ and $K_2$ are contractions of $(\mathrm{d}A)(p)$ with legs at $P$ and at $P'$, $K_4$ and $K_5$ are contractions of legs at $P$ and at $P'$ with $(\mathrm{d}A)(q)$, and $K_3$ is the contraction of a leg at $P$ with a leg at $P'$.
\item[(4)] $\mathsf T_4=\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_4}c_G\,(X*Y)(u')$, where $X=K_1K_2$ and $Y=K_3K_4$ with $n_i\in\{2,3\}$, and $(n_X,n_Y):=(n_1+n_2,n_3+n_4)\in\{(4,4),(5,4),(4,5),(6,6)\}$, with $(n_X,n_Y)=(4,4)$ for the monomials of $\frac12|\mathfrak z_1|^2$.
\item[(4$'$)] The first half of $\mathsf T_{4'}$ equals $\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_{4'}}c_G\,K_1(u')\,K_2(u')$, where $n_i\in\{2,3\}$ and $K_1,K_2$ are contractions of $(\mathrm{d}A)(p)$ with legs at $q$.
\item[(5)] The first half of $\mathsf T_5$ equals $\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_5}c_G\,K_0(u')\,(X*Y)(u')$ with $Y=K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}$. Here $K_0$ and $X$ are contractions of $(\mathrm{d}A)(p)$ with a leg at $q$, resp.\ at $P$, and $n_0,n_X\in\{2,3\}$; $K_{\mathrm a},K_{\mathrm b}$ are contractions of legs at $P$ with legs at $q$, and $n_{\mathrm a},n_{\mathrm b}\in\{1,2,3\}$; finally $n_0+n_X+n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}=8$, so that $n_Y:=n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}\in\{2,3,4\}$.
\item[(6)] $\mathsf T_6=\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_6}c_G\,K_1(u')\,K_2(u')\,K_3(u')$, with $n_1+n_2+n_3=5$.
\item[(I)] $\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}=-\mathsf n\,\Pi(p,q)\sum_{\mu,\nu}\bigl(K^\to_{\iota\mu}*\Sigma_{\mu\nu}*K^\leftarrow_{\nu\iota'}\bigr)(u')$, where $K^\to_{\iota\mu}(y):=\mathsf E_{p_{[\iota]}(0)}((y,\mu))$ and $K^\leftarrow_{\nu\iota'}(y):=\mathsf E_{p_{[\iota']}(y)}((0,\nu))$ are elementary lines of degree $2$, and $\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(y):=\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}((x,\mu),(x+y,\nu))$, which does not depend on $x$. With $\mathsf s_P(b):=s_i$ if $b=b_i(P)$ and $\mathsf s_P(b):=0$ otherwise,
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-58}
\begin{gathered}
\partial_{b,a}\mathsf S_3=\mathsf d_{b,a}+\mathsf u_{b,a},\\
\mathsf d_{b,a}:=\sum_{P\ni b}\mathsf s_P(b)\,\langle\mathsf e_a,\mathfrak z_1(P)\rangle,\qquad\mathsf u_{b,a}:=\sum_{P\ni b}\langle\mathrm{d}A(P),\partial_{b,a}\mathfrak z_1(P)\rangle ;
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
the monomials of $\mathsf d_{b,a}$ have two plain legs, those of $\mathsf u_{b,a}$ a curl leg and a plain leg. Moreover
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-59}
\Sigma_{\mu\nu}=\mathsf q^0_{\mu\nu}+\sum_{G\in\mathfrak G_{\mathrm I}(\mu,\nu)}c_G\,\mathsf f_G(\nabla)\bigl[K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}\bigr],
\end{equation}
where $\mathsf q^0_{\mu\nu}$ has finite support (it comes from the line between two slots of the quartic Wilson vertex, from the Haar term and from the ghost tadpole); $\mathsf f_G(k)$ is the product of two trigonometric polynomials, each a line symbol of degree $0$ or $1$, of total degree $d_G\in\{0,1,2\}$; $\mathsf f_G(\nabla)$ is the finite difference operator which multiplies symbols by $\mathsf f_G$; $n_{\mathrm a},n_{\mathrm b}\in\{1,2,3\}$; and $n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}+d_G=4$. The terms $G$ are the ghost loop $-8\,\mathsf D(b;b')\,\mathsf D(b';b)$, with $d_G=0$, and the terms of $-\langle\partial\mathsf S_3;\partial'\mathsf S_3\rangle_0$ multiplied out by \eqref{IV-73-58}, with $d_G$ the number of entries $\mathsf d$.
\end{enumerate}
The second halves of $\mathsf T_{4'}$ and $\mathsf T_5$ have the same forms, with $p$ and $q$ exchanged and $u'$ replaced by $-u'$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We use two counting rules: every monomial of $\mathsf a^{(3)}$ has exactly one curl leg and $\mathsf a^{(2)}$ has two (Def.~\ref{IV-73-19}(3)); and the degree of a line is $1+\#$(its curl legs) (Lem.~\ref{IV-73-51}). By the consequence stated in Lem.~\ref{IV-73-51}, every contraction is an elementary line in the difference of the base points of the two vertices which it joins, its symbol depending only on the two legs; the shifts between the base points of the legs and those of the vertices are absorbed into the lines.

(1) A kite has five lines. There are four curl legs at $p$ and $q$ and one at each of $P$ and $P'$, hence $\sum_in_i=5+6=11$ and $\varDelta=5$. For $i\in\{1,2,4,5\}$ one end of the line $i$ is a curl leg of $p$ or of $q$, so that $n_i\ge2$, and $n_i\le3$. Besides the two curl legs of $p$, the lines $1,2,3$ carry at most two further curl legs, one of $P$ and one of $P'$; hence $n_1+n_2+n_3\le2+2+1+2=7$, and the same count applies to the lines $3,4,5$. With the base points $x_p+z$ and $x_p+w$ of $P$ and $P'$, the sum over $P,P'$ becomes the sum over $z,w$ and over the dual directions of $P,P'$, and the five lines become functions of $z$, $w$, $w-z$, $u'-z$, $u'-w$.

(4) Each of the four lines carries a curl leg at $p$ or at $q$; it has degree $2$, or degree $3$ if its leg at $P$ is a curl leg. The three kinds of monomials of $\mathsf a_P^{(4)}$ (Lem.~\ref{IV-73-53}(d)) give $(n_X,n_Y)=(4,4)$; $(5,4)$ or $(4,5)$; and $(6,6)$. With the base point $x_p+z$ of $P$, the two lines from $p$ make up $X(z)$, the two lines to $q$ make up $Y(u'-z)$, and the sum over $z$ is $(X*Y)(u')$.

(4$'$) There are two lines from $p$ to $q$, each with its curl leg at $p$; the line between two slots of the vertex at $q$ is a number, independent of the positions, and it is absorbed into $c_G$.

(5) There are four lines, and there are $2+1+1$ curl legs, at $p$, $q$ and $P$; hence $\sum n=4+4=8$. With the base point $x_p+z$ of $P$, the line from $p$ to $P$ is $X(z)$, the two lines from $P$ to $q$ make up $Y(u'-z)$, and the line from $p$ to $q$ is $K_0(u')$.

(6) There are three lines, and there are $1+1$ curl legs, at $p$ and $q$; hence $\sum n=3+2=5$.

(I) In the formula for $\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}$ we write $b=(x,\mu)$ and $b'=(x',\nu)$ with $x=x_p+z$, $x'=x_p+w$. By translation invariance $\mathsf E_p(b)=K^\to_{\iota\mu}(z)$ and $\mathsf E_q(b')=K^\leftarrow_{\nu\iota'}(u'-w)$, and by the translation covariance in Def.~\ref{IV-73-29}(5) $\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}(b,b')=\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(w-z)$; this gives the formula for $\mathsf T_{\mathrm I}$. The functions $K^\to_{\iota\mu}$ and $K^\leftarrow_{\nu\iota'}$ are elementary lines of degree $2$ by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-51}, the second because $K^\leftarrow_{\nu\iota'}(y)=\mathsf E_{p_{[\iota']}(0)}((-y,\nu))$. By Def.~\ref{IV-73-29}(5) and \eqref{IV-73-17}, with $\partial=\partial_{b,a}$ and $\partial'=\partial_{b',a}$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}(b,b')={}&\Bigl[\langle\partial\partial'\mathsf S_4\rangle_0+\bigl(\tfrac23+\tfrac43\mathsf g(b)\bigr)\delta_{bb'}\Bigr]\\
&-4\bigl[\mathsf D(b;b')\mathsf D(b';b)+\mathsf D(b';b)\mathsf D(b;b')\bigr]-\langle\partial\mathsf S_3;\partial'\mathsf S_3\rangle_0 .
\end{aligned}
\]
The bracket has finite range and is translation invariant; it gives $\mathsf q^0_{\mu\nu}$. The middle term is the ghost loop $-8\,\mathsf D(b;b')\,\mathsf D(b';b)$, a product of two elementary lines of degree $2$ in $y$ (Lem.~\ref{IV-73-51}), with $\mathsf f_G=1$. From \eqref{IV-73-10} and the Leibniz rule we have
\[
\partial_{b,a}\langle\mathrm{d}A(P),\mathfrak z_1(P)\rangle=\mathsf s_P(b)\,\langle\mathsf e_a,\mathfrak z_1(P)\rangle+\langle\mathrm{d}A(P),\partial_{b,a}\mathfrak z_1(P)\rangle ,
\]
which gives \eqref{IV-73-58}. For a function $\mathsf F$ on the plaquettes of one dual direction, the map $b\mapsto\sum_{P\ni b}\mathsf s_P(b)\,\mathsf F(P)$ is a difference operator whose symbol is $\pm\overline{\mathsf k_\alpha}$ up to a factor $e^{ik\cdot y_0}$, a line symbol of degree $1$; this operator yields the factor of $\mathsf f_G$ which belongs to an entry $\mathsf d$. An entry $\mathsf u$ we split into its monomials and treat each of them separately. By the consequence stated in Lem.~\ref{IV-73-51}, the contraction of a leg with base point $x+\xi$ with a leg with base point $x+y+\xi'$ is an elementary line in $y$ in which the shifts $\xi$ and $\xi'$ are already contained; hence the factor of $\mathsf f_G$ which belongs to an entry $\mathsf u$ is $1$, a line symbol of degree $0$ with leading part $1$, just as for the ghost loop.

By Lem.~\ref{IV-73-53}(a), the cumulant of two quadratic monomials is a sum of two products of two lines. Hence every term of $-\langle\partial\mathsf S_3;\partial'\mathsf S_3\rangle_0$, multiplied out by \eqref{IV-73-58}, has the form $c_G\,\mathsf f_G(\nabla)[K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}]$, with $d_G$ the number of entries $\mathsf d$ and with $n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}=2+\#$(curl legs on the two lines). As $\mathsf d$ has no curl leg and $\mathsf u$ has one, $n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}=2+(2-d_G)$. The second halves of $\mathsf T_{4'}$ and $\mathsf T_5$ are treated in the same way, the roles of $p$ and $q$ being exchanged.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Expansions of the elementary terms, with errors]\label{IV-73-60}
Let the setting be that of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-57}, let $r':=|u'|$ be large, and let $K^h:=\mathcal F^{-1}_{\ne0}\sigma^h$ for every line $K$ with symbol $\sigma$. For the bubbles $X$ and $Y$ let $\mathsf q_X$ and $\mathsf q_Y$ be the kernels $\mathsf q$ of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(c), and put $X':=X-\mathsf q_X$, $Y':=Y-\mathsf q_Y$. Then the elementary terms of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-57} have the following expansions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(6)] $K_1K_2K_3(u')=K_1^hK_2^hK_3^h(u')+O(r'^{-6})$.
\item[(5)] $K_0(u')\,(X*Y)(u')=K_0(u')\,(\mathsf q_Y*X)(u')+K_0^h(u')\,(X*Y')^h(u')+O(r'^{-6}\lg r')$, where $(X*Y')^h$ is the second component of the leading data of $X*Y'\in\mathfrak K(n_X+n_Y-3)$.
\item[(4)] $(X*Y)(u')=(\mathsf q_X*Y)(u')+(\mathsf q_Y*X)(u')+\mathsf U_G(u')+O(r'^{-6}\lg r')$, where $\mathsf U_G:=(X'*Y')^h$ if $(n_X,n_Y)=(4,4)$ and $\mathsf U_G:=0$ otherwise.
\item[(1)] The expansion of Prop.~\ref{IV-73-47}(iii) holds, with the error $O(r'^{-6}\lg r')$.
\item[($*$)] In all four cases the function of degree $-5$ in the expansion (that is, $K_1^hK_2^hK_3^h$, $K_0^h(X*Y')^h$, $\mathsf U_G$, resp.\ the function $\mathsf U$ of Prop.~\ref{IV-73-47}) is determined by the leading parts $\sigma^h$ of the lines alone; it is multilinear in them, it belongs to $C^1(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$, and it is rotation covariant as in Prop.~\ref{IV-73-47}(iv).
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(6) By Lem.~\ref{IV-73-39}(a),(c), $K_i(u')=O(r'^{-n_i})$, $K_i^h(u')=O(r'^{-n_i})$ and $K_i(u')=K_i^h(u')+O(r'^{-n_i-1})$. As $n_1+n_2+n_3=5$, the product $K_1K_2K_3(u')$ differs from $K_1^hK_2^hK_3^h(u')$ by $O(r'^{-6})$, and $K_1^hK_2^hK_3^h$ is homogeneous of degree $-5$.

(5) The line $X$ is an elementary line of degree $n_X\in\{2,3\}$, so $X\in\mathfrak K(n_X)$ by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-39}(c). The bubble $Y=K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}$ has $n_{\mathrm a},n_{\mathrm b}\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $n_Y\le4$, so $Y'\in\mathfrak K(n_Y)$ by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(c). We write $X*Y=\mathsf q_Y*X+X*Y'$. Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(b) applies to $X$ and $Y'$, as $n_X,n_Y\le4$ and $n_X+n_Y=8-n_0\ge5$; it gives $X*Y'\in\mathfrak K(n_X+n_Y-3)$, and (K3) with $\gamma=0$ gives $X*Y'=(X*Y')^h+O(r'^{-(n_X+n_Y-3)-1}\lg r')$. Moreover $K_0=K_0^h+O(r'^{-n_0-1})$ by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-39}(c), and $K_0$, $K_0^h$, $X*Y'$, $(X*Y')^h$ are bounded by the corresponding powers of $r'$. As $n_0+(n_X+n_Y-3)=8-3=5$, the claim follows.

(4) Multiplying out $X*Y=(\mathsf q_X+X')*(\mathsf q_Y+Y')$ we obtain
\[
X*Y=\mathsf q_X*Y+\mathsf q_Y*X-\mathsf q_X*\mathsf q_Y+X'*Y',
\]
and $\mathsf q_X*\mathsf q_Y$ vanishes off $\{|u'|\le2\}$, because $\mathsf q_X$ and $\mathsf q_Y$ vanish off $\{0,\pm e_j\}$. If $(n_X,n_Y)=(4,4)$, then $X',Y'\in\mathfrak K(4)$ by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(c), and Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(b) gives $X'*Y'\in\mathfrak K(5)$ and $X'*Y'=(X'*Y')^h+O(r'^{-6}\lg r')$. Otherwise we apply Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(a) to $X'$ and $Y'$, with $a_X=\min\{n_X-3,2\}$ and $a_Y=\min\{n_Y-3,2\}$. Its hypotheses hold by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(c), which bounds the differences of a bubble of degree $n$ by $C_\gamma\langle x\rangle^{-n-|\gamma|}$ (the kernels $X',Y'$ differ from $X,Y$ at finitely many points only) and the symbol of $X'$, resp.\ $Y'$, by $|\mathsf I-\tilde{\mathsf Q}|\le C|k|^{\min\{n-3,2\}}$. The three exponents in the bound of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(a) are $-2-4$, $-1-5$, $3-9$ for $(n_X,n_Y)=(5,4)$, the same by symmetry for $(4,5)$, and at most $-8$ for $(6,6)$; so $X'*Y'=O(r'^{-6}\lg r')$ in these cases.

(1) This is Prop.~\ref{IV-73-47}(iii) with $\varDelta=5$ (Lem.~\ref{IV-73-57}(1)), so that $r^{-\varDelta-1}\lg r=r'^{-6}\lg r'$.

($*$) In the case (6) this follows from Lem.~\ref{IV-73-39}(b). In the cases (5) and (4), Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(b) shows that the second component of the leading data of a convolution depends only on the leading data of the two factors, bilinearly and rotation covariantly. By Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(c) the leading data of $Y'$, and of $X'$ in the case (4), are $(\mathsf I^h,K_{\mathrm a}^hK_{\mathrm b}^h)$, where $\mathsf I^h$ depends only on $\sigma_{\mathrm a}^h,\sigma_{\mathrm b}^h$, bilinearly and rotation covariantly, by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-42}(a); the leading data of the lines $X$ and $K_0$ are $(\sigma^h,K^h)$ with $K^h=\mathcal F^{-1}_{\ne0}\sigma^h$, by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-39}(b),(c). The functions $K^h$ and the second components of leading data are smooth off the origin. In the case (1) the assertions are Prop.~\ref{IV-73-47}(iii),(iv).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A local insertion with vanishing moments]\label{IV-73-61}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[beginpenalty=10000]
\item[(a)] Let $\gamma_{\mu\nu}$, $1\le\mu,\nu\le3$, be functions of finite support on $\mathbb Z^3\times\mathbb Z^3$ whose symbols
\[
\hat\gamma_{\mu\nu}(\kappa_1,\kappa_2):=\sum_{y,y'}\gamma_{\mu\nu}(y,y')\,e^{-i(\kappa_1\cdot y+\kappa_2\cdot y')}
\]
vanish at $\kappa=0$ together with their gradients, and let $K_1,K_2,K_3$ be elementary lines of degree $2$. Then
\[
\Bigl|\sum_{\mu,\nu}\sum_{y,y'}\gamma_{\mu\nu}(y,y')\,K_\mu(u+y)\,K_\nu(u+y')\Bigr|\le C\,|u|^{-6}\qquad(u\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}),
\]
where $C$ depends on the $\gamma_{\mu\nu}$ and on the symbols of the $K_\mu$.
\item[(b)] Let $\mathsf q$ be a function of finite support on $\mathbb Z^3$ with $\hat{\mathsf q}(k):=\sum_y\mathsf q(y)\,e^{-ik\cdot y}=O(|k|^2)$ at $k=0$, and let $K_1,K_2$ be elementary lines of degree $2$. Then $|(K_1*\mathsf q*K_2)(u)|\le C\langle u\rangle^{-3}$ for all $u\in\mathbb Z^3$, where $C$ depends on $\mathsf q$ and on the symbols of $K_1,K_2$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(a) As the $\gamma_{\mu\nu}$ have finite support, only points $y,y'$ in a fixed ball occur; let $|u|$ be large. By Lem.~\ref{IV-73-39}(a) with $s=-1$, $K_\mu(u)=O(|u|^{-2})$, $\nabla K_\mu(u)=O(|u|^{-3})$, and the second differences of $K_\mu$ near $u$ are $O(|u|^{-4})$. We write $K_\mu(u+y)-K_\mu(u)$ as a sum of first differences along a nearest-neighbour path from $u$ to $u+y$ and compare each of them with $\nabla_jK_\mu(u)$; this gives
\[
K_\mu(u+y)=K_\mu(u)+\sum_jy_j\,\nabla_jK_\mu(u)+O(|u|^{-4}).
\]
We insert this expansion for $K_\mu(u+y)$ and for $K_\nu(u+y')$. The terms of the orders $|u|^{-4}$ and $|u|^{-5}$ then carry the coefficients
\[
\sum_{y,y'}\gamma_{\mu\nu}(y,y')=\hat\gamma_{\mu\nu}(0),\qquad\sum_{y,y'}\gamma_{\mu\nu}(y,y')\,y_j,\qquad\sum_{y,y'}\gamma_{\mu\nu}(y,y')\,y'_j ,
\]
and the last two are $i$ times the derivatives of $\hat\gamma_{\mu\nu}$ with respect to $\kappa_{1,j}$, resp.\ $\kappa_{2,j}$, at $0$. All three vanish by hypothesis, and the remaining terms are $O(|u|^{-6})$. For $u\ne0$ in a bounded set the left side is bounded and $|u|^{-6}$ is bounded below, so the bound holds for all $u\ne0$ after enlarging $C$.

(b) The trigonometric polynomial $\hat{\mathsf q}$ is smooth and vanishes at $0$ together with its gradient, hence $\hat{\mathsf q}\in\mathcal S^2$. The kernel $\mathsf q*K_2$, a finite combination of translates of $K_2$, has the symbol $\hat{\mathsf q}\sigma_2\in\mathcal S^1$, where $\sigma_2\in\mathcal S^{-1}$ is the symbol of $K_2$; by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-39}(a) it is $O(\langle x\rangle^{-4})$ and lies in $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3)$, as does $K_1=O(\langle x\rangle^{-2})$. By Plancherel's theorem $K_1*(\mathsf q*K_2)$ is the kernel with the symbol $\sigma_1\hat{\mathsf q}\sigma_2\in\mathcal S^0$, and Lem.~\ref{IV-73-39}(a) with $s=0$ gives the bound $C\langle u\rangle^{-3}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The local parts vanish to the second order]\label{IV-73-62}
Let $\tau_{\mathrm{gf}}>0$; we work on $\mathbb Z^3$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] (Self-energy.) In \eqref{IV-73-59} let $\mathsf q_G$ be the kernel $\mathsf q$ of the bubble $K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}$ in the sense of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(c), and put
\[
\mathsf q^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}:=\mathsf q^0_{\mu\nu}+\sum_Gc_G\,\mathsf f_G(\nabla)\mathsf q_G,\qquad\mathsf W_{\mu\nu}:=\sum_Gc_G\,\mathsf f_G(\nabla)\bigl[K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}-\mathsf q_G\bigr],
\]
so that $\Sigma_{\mu\nu}=\mathsf q^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}+\mathsf W_{\mu\nu}$. Then $\mathsf q^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ has finite support. Each $\mathsf f_G(\nabla)[K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}-\mathsf q_G]$ belongs to $\mathfrak K(4)$, and the first component of its leading data is $\mathsf f_G^h\,\mathsf I_G^h$, where $\mathsf f_G^h$ is the leading part of $\mathsf f_G$ and $\mathsf I_G^h$ is the homogeneous part of the symbol $\mathsf I_G$ of the bubble (Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(c), Lem.~\ref{IV-73-42}(d)). Hence $\mathsf W_{\mu\nu}\in\mathfrak K(4)$, and its leading data are functions of the leading parts $\sigma^h$ and of the $\mathsf f_G^h$ occurring in \eqref{IV-73-59} alone. Moreover the symbol of $\mathsf q^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ satisfies $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(k)=O(|k|^2)$ at $k=0$.
\item[(b)] (Vertex.) Let $q=p_{[\iota']}(x_q)$. Let $\gamma_q(b,b')$ be the symmetric kernel of finite range defined below; then, for every plaquette $p$ with $|u'|$ large, $\frac{\mathsf n}2\sum_{b,b'}\gamma_q(b,b')\,\mathsf E_p(b)\,\mathsf E_p(b')$ is the sum of the following terms of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-60}: the first half of $\mathsf T_{4'}$; the terms $c_G\,K_0(u')\,(\mathsf q_Y*X)(u')$ of the first half of $\mathsf T_5$; the terms $c_G\,(\mathsf q_Y*X)(u')$ of $\mathsf T_4$; and the terms $c_G\sum_{z,w}\mathsf q_{\mathsf q}(z,w)\,K_1(u'-z)\,K_2(u'-w)$ of $\mathsf T_1$. The kernel $\gamma_q$ is defined as follows. Each of $K_0$, $X$, $K_1$, $K_2$, at the points where it is evaluated in these terms, is either a value $\mathsf E_p(b)$ with $b$ a bond near $q$, or a value $\Pi(p,P)=\sum_is_i\,\mathsf E_p(b_i(P))$ with $P$ a plaquette near $q$.

Substituting this term by term in the four sums we obtain a quadratic expression in the values $\mathsf E_p(b)$, and $\frac{\mathsf n}2\gamma_q$ is its coefficient kernel, symmetrised. This kernel does not depend on $p$. Indeed, by the rule for $\mathsf a_p^{(2)}$ in the proof of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-53}(c), the plaquette $p$, with its base point and its dual direction, enters the four sums only through the forms $\mathsf E_p^a$ inserted into the two slots joined to $p$, that is, only through the values of $K_0$, $X$, $K_1$, $K_2$ just described. An elementary term $G$ of these sums is given by the monomials at the vertices at $q$, $P$, $P'$ and by the choice of their legs which are contracted with $p$, with $q$ and with one another, so that the numbers $c_G$ do not involve $p$; and the kernels $\mathsf q_Y$, $\mathsf q_{\mathsf q}$ and the line between two slots of the vertex at $q$ are built from lines among $q$, $P$, $P'$ alone.

We define $\gamma_q$ through this way of writing, since the numbers $\sum_{b,b'}\gamma_q(b,b')\mathsf E_p(b)\mathsf E_p(b')$ alone would not fix a kernel. Let $\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(y,y'):=\gamma_q((x_q+y,\mu),(x_q+y',\nu))$. Then the symbols $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$, defined as in Lem.~\ref{IV-73-61}(a), vanish at $\kappa=0$ together with their gradients.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1: a trace formula.} Let $\mathsf m^1,\dots,\mathsf m^{\mathsf r}$, $\mathsf r\le3$, be real symmetric matrices indexed by $\mathsf i=(x,\mu,a)$, that is, by a bond $(x,\mu)$ and a colour $a$, each with finitely many non-zero entries. For $y\in\mathbb Z^3$ let $\mathsf m_y$ be the translate of $\mathsf m$ by $y$, $(\mathsf m_y)_{(x,\mu,a),(x',\mu',a')}:=\mathsf m_{(x-y,\mu,a),(x'-y,\mu',a')}$, and let $\hat{\mathsf m}(l',l)$ be the $9\times9$ matrix, indexed by $(\mu,a)$ and $(\mu',a')$, with the entries
\[
\sum_{x,x'}e^{-il'\cdot x}\,\mathsf m_{(x,\mu,a),(x',\mu',a')}\,e^{il\cdot x'} .
\]
Then $\hat{\mathsf m}_y(l',l)=e^{-i(l'-l)\cdot y}\,\hat{\mathsf m}(l',l)$, and $\hat{\mathsf m}(l,l)$ is the symbol of the translation invariant matrix $\sum_y\mathsf m_y$, in the sense that $\sum_y\mathsf m_y$ maps $e^{il\cdot x}\alpha$ to $e^{il\cdot x}\,\hat{\mathsf m}(l,l)\,\alpha$. We insert $\mathsf C(\mathsf i,\mathsf i')=\delta_{aa'}\int_{\mathbb T}e^{il\cdot(x-x')}\,\hat{\mathsf C}_{\mu\mu'}(l)\,d^\circ l$ and let $\hat{\mathsf C}(l)$ act on the nine-dimensional space as $\hat{\mathsf C}(l)$ in the directions and as the identity in the colours. For $\mathsf r=3$ we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{IV-73-63}
\begin{aligned}
&\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[\mathsf m^1\mathsf C\,\mathsf m^2_{y_2}\mathsf C\,\mathsf m^3_{y_3}\mathsf C\bigr]\\
&\qquad=\iint e^{i(\kappa_2\cdot y_2+\kappa_3\cdot y_3)}\Bigl\{\int\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf m}^1(l_3,l)\,\hat{\mathsf C}(l)\,\hat{\mathsf m}^2(l,l_2)\,\hat{\mathsf C}(l_2)\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\hat{\mathsf m}^3(l_2,l_3)\,\hat{\mathsf C}(l_3)\bigr]\,d^\circ l\Bigr\}\,d^\circ\kappa_2\,d^\circ\kappa_3 ,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
with $l_2:=l+\kappa_2$, $l_3:=l+\kappa_2+\kappa_3$, all integrals being over $\mathbb T$. Indeed, the sums over the indices are finite and the integrals over the variables $l,l_2,l_3$ of the three covariances converge absolutely; Fubini's theorem allows us to carry out the sums first and then to pass to the variables $\kappa_2=l_2-l$, $\kappa_3=l_3-l_2$. For $\mathsf r=2$ one omits $\mathsf m^3$, the last factor $\hat{\mathsf C}$ and $\kappa_3$; for $\mathsf r=1$ one has $\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf m^1\mathsf C]=\int\operatorname{tr}[\hat{\mathsf m}^1(l,l)\,\hat{\mathsf C}(l)]\,d^\circ l$. For the quadratic forms $\mathsf F_j:=\frac12(A,\mathsf m^jA)$, Lem.~\ref{IV-73-53}(a) gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
\langle\mathsf F_1\rangle_0=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf m^1\mathsf C],\qquad\langle\mathsf F_1;\mathsf F_2\rangle_0=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf m^1\mathsf C\,\mathsf m^2\mathsf C],\\
\langle\mathsf F_1;\mathsf F_2;\mathsf F_3\rangle_0=\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf m^1\mathsf C\,\mathsf m^2\mathsf C\,\mathsf m^3\mathsf C].
\end{gathered}
\]

The formula \eqref{IV-73-63} also identifies integrands. For a leg $\ell$ of colour $a$ we define $\mathsf v_\ell(k)\in\mathbb C^3$ by $\ell(e^{ik\cdot x}\alpha\,\mathsf e_a)=\mathsf v_\ell(k)\cdot\alpha$, where $e^{ik\cdot x}\alpha\,\mathsf e_a$ denotes the form $(x,\mu)\mapsto e^{ik\cdot x}\alpha_\mu\mathsf e_a$; thus $\mathsf v_\ell(k)=e^{ik\cdot\xi}e_\nu$ for the plain leg at the bond $(\xi,\nu)$, and $\mathsf v_\ell(k)=e^{ik\cdot\xi}\bigl(\mathsf c_{\iota,\nu}(k)\bigr)_{\nu=1,2,3}$ for the curl leg at $p_{[\iota]}(\xi)$. The contraction of $\ell$ with the translate by $y$ of a leg $\ell'$ of the same colour is $\int e^{-ik\cdot y}\,\mathsf v_\ell(k)^{\mathsf T}\,\hat{\mathsf C}(k)\,\mathsf v_{\ell'}(-k)\,d^\circ k$, and the Hessian $\mathsf m$ of the product $\ell_1\ell_2$ of two legs has
\[
\hat{\mathsf m}(l',l)=\mathsf v_{\ell_1}(-l')\,\mathsf v_{\ell_2}(l)^{\mathsf T}+\mathsf v_{\ell_2}(-l')\,\mathsf v_{\ell_1}(l)^{\mathsf T},
\]
the colour indices being those of the legs. The matrices $\mathsf m^j$ used below are sums of Hessians of monomials in legs. Multiplying out, we find that for all $(l,\kappa)$ the integrand in braces in \eqref{IV-73-63} is a sum of products of the symbols of $\mathsf r$ lines evaluated at $\pm l,\pm l_2,\pm l_3$, and that these products are, term by term, the integrands of the one-loop functions (Lem.~\ref{IV-73-42}, Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(c), Prop.~\ref{IV-73-47}) of the elementary terms of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-57}, up to substitutions $l\to\pm l+\lambda(\kappa)$ with $\lambda$ linear. At $\kappa=0$ the integrand in braces is the sum of the integrands of these one-loop functions at $\kappa=0$, up to the substitution $l\to-l$ in single terms. We express this by saying that the two sides agree integrand by integrand.

\emph{Step 2: the Hessians at a constant abelian field.} By \eqref{IV-73-7} with $t=1$, $a_p(e^{iA})=\sum_m\mathsf a_p^{(m)}(A)$. Let $\mathsf N_j(B)$ and $\mathsf h_q^{(j)}(B)$ be the parts of degree $j$ in $B$ of the Hessians $\mathsf N(B)$ and $\mathsf h_q(B)$ of Def.~\ref{IV-73-29}(1). Since $\mathsf S_3$ is cubic and $\mathsf S_4$ quartic, $\mathsf N_1(B)$ is the Hessian of the quadratic polynomial $\sum_{b,a}B^a(b)\,\partial_{b,a}\mathsf S_3$, and $\mathsf N_2(B)$ is that of $\frac12\sum B^a(b)\,B^{a'}(b')\,\partial_{b,a}\partial_{b',a'}\mathsf S_4$; the matrix $\mathsf h_q^{(j)}(B)$ is obtained in the same way from $\mathsf a_q^{(2+j)}$.

Let $\mathsf H_b$ be the Hessian of $\partial_{b,3}\mathsf S_3$, and let $\mathsf H_b^{\mathsf u}$ and $\mathsf H_b^{\mathsf d}$ be those of $\mathsf u_{b,3}$ and $\mathsf d_{b,3}$ in \eqref{IV-73-58}; these matrices are translation covariant, $\mathsf H_{b+y}=(\mathsf H_b)_y$. For the constant field $Y_\gamma$ of Def.~\ref{IV-73-29}(2), with $\mu(b)$ the direction of $b$, we have
\[
\sum_b\gamma_{\mu(b)}\,\mathsf d_{b,3}=\sum_P\langle\mathrm{d}Y_\gamma(P),\mathfrak z_1(P)\rangle=0
\]
(as a quadratic form, every entry of its Hessian being a finite sum), because $\sum_b\gamma_{\mu(b)}\,\mathsf s_P(b)\,\mathsf e_3=\mathrm{d}Y_\gamma(P)$ and $\mathrm{d}Y_\gamma=0$. Hence $\mathsf N_1(Y_\gamma)=\sum_b\gamma_{\mu(b)}\,\mathsf H_b^{\mathsf u}=\sum_\mu\gamma_\mu\sum_y(\mathsf H^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\mu)})_y$, and by Step~1 and Def.~\ref{IV-73-29}(2) its symbol is
\[
\sum_\mu\gamma_\mu\,\hat{\mathsf H}^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\mu)}(l,l)=\bigoplus_e\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1}(l;\gamma)
\]
in the basis $\mathsf e_e$ of the colours.

\emph{Step 3: the structure in (a).} Let $K\in\mathfrak K(n)$ have the symbol $\sigma$ and the leading data $(\sigma^h,K^h)$, and let $y_0\in\mathbb Z^3$. The kernels with the symbols $e^{ik\cdot y_0}\sigma$, $\mathsf k_\mu\sigma$ and $\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}\sigma$ lie in $\mathfrak K(n)$, $\mathfrak K(n+1)$ and $\mathfrak K(n+1)$, respectively, with the leading data $(\sigma^h,K^h)$, $(ik_\mu\sigma^h,\partial_\mu K^h)$ and $(-ik_\mu\sigma^h,-\partial_\mu K^h)$. Indeed, the symbol $\mathsf k_\mu\sigma$ belongs to the kernel $\nabla_\mu K$. For (K2) we write
\[
\mathsf k_\mu\sigma-\chi\,ik_\mu\sigma^h=\mathsf k_\mu(\sigma-\chi\sigma^h)+(\mathsf k_\mu-ik_\mu)\,\chi\sigma^h=O(|k|^{n-1}\lg|k|),
\]
and for (K3), by Taylor's formula and the homogeneity of the derivatives of $K^h$,
\[
\nabla^\gamma(\nabla_\mu K-\partial_\mu K^h)=\nabla^{\gamma+e_\mu}(K-K^h)+\nabla^\gamma(\nabla_\mu-\partial_\mu)K^h=O(|x|^{-n-2-|\gamma|}\lg|x|);
\]
at the finitely many points with $|\gamma|+1\le|x|<|\gamma|+2$ the left side is a finite number, which is absorbed into the constant. Next, $\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}=-e^{-ik_\mu}\mathsf k_\mu$. For the shift, $(e^{ik\cdot y_0}-1)\,\chi\sigma^h=O(|k|^{n-2})$ and $\nabla^\gamma[K^h(\cdot+y_0)-K^h]=O(|x|^{-n-1-|\gamma|})$. By Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(c), $K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}-\mathsf q_G\in\mathfrak K(n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b})$, with the leading data $(\mathsf I_G^h,K_{\mathrm a}^hK_{\mathrm b}^h)$; that lemma applies, since $n_{\mathrm a},n_{\mathrm b}\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}=4-d_G\le4$. A trigonometric polynomial $\mathsf f$ is a finite sum of terms $c\,e^{ik\cdot y_0}$.

As a line symbol of degree $0$ it has the leading part $\mathsf f(0)$. As a line symbol of degree $1$ it has $\mathsf f(0)=0$, its leading part is its linear part at $0$, and $\mathsf f$ is a finite sum of terms $c\,e^{ik\cdot y_0}\mathsf k_\mu$: indeed $\mathsf f$ is a linear combination of the functions $e^{ik\cdot y}-1$, and each of these is a telescoping sum, along a nearest-neighbour path from $0$ to $y$, of terms $\pm e^{ik\cdot y_0}\mathsf k_\mu$ (with $\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}=-e^{-ik_\mu}\mathsf k_\mu$ for the steps in the negative direction). Since $\mathfrak K(n)$ is a linear space and the leading data depend linearly on the kernel, multiplication of the symbol by $\mathsf f$ maps $\mathfrak K(n)$ into $\mathfrak K(n)$, resp.\ $\mathfrak K(n+1)$, and multiplies the first component of the leading data by $\mathsf f^h$.

Applying this once for each of the two factors of $\mathsf f_G$, we obtain $\mathsf f_G(\nabla)[K_{\mathrm a}K_{\mathrm b}-\mathsf q_G]\in\mathfrak K(n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}+d_G)=\mathfrak K(4)$, with $\mathsf f_G^h\,\mathsf I_G^h$ as the first component of its leading data. Hence $\mathsf W_{\mu\nu}\in\mathfrak K(4)$. The first component of its leading data, $\sum_Gc_G\,\mathsf f_G^h\,\mathsf I_G^h$, depends only on the leading parts $\sigma^h$ (Lem.~\ref{IV-73-42}(a)) and on the $\mathsf f_G^h$; by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(d) the second component is determined by the first, linearly. Finally $\mathsf q^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ has finite support, since $\mathsf q^0_{\mu\nu}$ and the $\mathsf q_G$ have and $\mathsf f_G(\nabla)$ is a finite difference operator.

\emph{Step 4: the value of $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ at $0$.} The symbol of $\mathsf q_G$ is $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G$, whose value at $0$ is $\mathsf Q_G(0)$, and $\mathsf f_G(0)=0$ if $d_G\ge1$. Hence
\[
\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(0)=\hat{\mathsf q}^0_{\mu\nu}(0)+\sum_{G:\,d_G=0}c_G\,\mathsf f_G(0)\,\mathsf Q_G(0).
\]
For $d_G=0$ we have $n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}=4$, so that the bubble symbol has $\omega=1$, and Lem.~\ref{IV-73-42}(c), with the data of the bubble given in the proof of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(c), yields $\mathsf Q_G(0)=\int_{\mathbb T}\sigma_{\mathrm a}(-l)\,\sigma_{\mathrm b}(l)\,d^\circ l$. The terms with $d_G=0$ are the ghost loop and the terms of $-\langle\mathsf u_{b,3};\mathsf u_{b',3}\rangle_0=-\frac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf H_b^{\mathsf u}\mathsf C\,\mathsf H_{b'}^{\mathsf u}\mathsf C]$ (Step~1). We compute $\frac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu$ times each contribution to $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(0)$.
\begin{itemize}
\item Gluon loop. By \eqref{IV-73-63}, $-\frac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf H^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\mu)}\mathsf C\,\mathsf H^{\mathsf u}_{(y,\nu)}\mathsf C]$ is the kernel in $y=b'_--b_-$ with the symbol $\kappa_2\mapsto-\frac12\int\operatorname{tr}[\hat{\mathsf H}^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\mu)}(l_2,l)\,\hat{\mathsf C}(l)\,\hat{\mathsf H}^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\nu)}(l,l_2)\,\hat{\mathsf C}(l_2)]\,d^\circ l$, and this symbol is $\sum c_G\,\mathsf f_G\,\mathsf I_G$, summed over the corresponding $G$, integrand by integrand. At zero momentum the integrand is $-\frac12\operatorname{tr}[\hat{\mathsf H}^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\mu)}(l,l)\,\hat{\mathsf C}(l)\,\hat{\mathsf H}^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\nu)}(l,l)\,\hat{\mathsf C}(l)]$, and by Step~2
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\tfrac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\Bigl(-\tfrac12\int\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf H}^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\mu)}(l,l)\,\hat{\mathsf C}\,\hat{\mathsf H}^{\mathsf u}_{(0,\nu)}(l,l)\,\hat{\mathsf C}\bigr]\,d^\circ l\Bigr)\\
&\qquad=-\tfrac14\sum_e\int\operatorname{tr}\bigl[(\hat{\mathsf C}\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1})^2\bigr]\,d^\circ l=\int_{\mathbb T}\mathfrak s^{(1)}(l;\gamma)\,d^\circ l .
\end{aligned}
\]
\item Gluon tadpole. Let $\mathsf H_{bb'}$ be the Hessian of $\partial_{b,3}\partial_{b',3}\mathsf S_4$, and let $\mathsf m:=\frac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\sum_y\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\,\mathsf H_{(0,\mu),(y,\nu)}$, a finite sum. By Step~2 and translation covariance $\mathsf N_2(Y_\gamma)=\sum_x\mathsf m_x$, hence $\hat{\mathsf m}(l,l)=\bigoplus_e\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,2}(l;\gamma)$, and Step~1 with $\mathsf r=1$ gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tfrac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\sum_y\langle\partial_{(0,\mu),3}\partial_{(y,\nu),3}\mathsf S_4\rangle_0&=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf m\,\mathsf C]\\
&=\tfrac12\int\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf m}(l,l)\,\hat{\mathsf C}(l)\bigr]\,d^\circ l=\int_{\mathbb T}\mathfrak s^{(2)}(l;\gamma)\,d^\circ l .
\end{aligned}
\]
\item Haar term: $\frac12\cdot\frac23|\gamma|^2=\frac13|\gamma|^2=\int\mathfrak s^{(5)}$. Ghost tadpole: $\frac12\cdot\frac43\cdot\frac13|\gamma|^2=\frac29|\gamma|^2=\int\mathfrak s^{(4)}$, since by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-31}(c) $\int\mathfrak s^{(4)}=\sum_{e=\pm1}\frac4{12}\sum_\mu\gamma_\mu^2\int|\mathsf k_\mu|^2|\mathsf k|^{-2}\,d^\circ k$, and $\int|\mathsf k_\mu|^2|\mathsf k|^{-2}\,d^\circ k=\frac13$.
\item Ghost loop. Here $\mathfrak s^{(3)}=4\bigl(\sum_\mu\gamma_\mu\sin k_\mu\bigr)^2|\mathsf k|^{-4}$. By Lem.~\ref{IV-73-51} the symbols of $y\mapsto\mathsf D((x,\mu);(x+y,\nu))$ and of $y\mapsto\mathsf D((x+y,\nu);(x,\mu))$ are $\frac12(1+e^{ik_\nu})\,\overline{\mathsf k_\mu}\,|\mathsf k|^{-2}$ and its image under $\mu\leftrightarrow\nu$, $k\to-k$. Since $(1+e^{ik_\nu})\,\overline{\mathsf k_\nu}=-2i\sin k_\nu$, the ghost loop $G$, for which $c_G=-8$ and $\mathsf f_G=1$, has $\mathsf Q_G(0)=\int\frac14(-2i\sin l_\mu)(-2i\sin l_\nu)\,|\mathsf k(l)|^{-4}\,d^\circ l$, and $\frac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\,(-8)\,\mathsf Q_G(0)=\int\mathfrak s^{(3)}$.
\end{itemize}
Summing up, we find $\frac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\,\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(0)=\sum_{i=1}^5\int\mathfrak s^{(i)}=\frac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\bigl(\sum_ic^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}\bigr)\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu$ for small $\gamma$ (Def.~\ref{IV-73-29}(3)); hence $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(0)+\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\nu\mu}(0)=2\sum_ic^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}$, and this number vanishes, because by Thm.~\ref{IV-73-34} the five matrices $c^{(i)}$ add up to zero, $\sum_{i=1}^5c^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}=0$ for all $\mu,\nu$. It remains to show that $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(0)=\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\nu\mu}(0)$. Let $\hat\Sigma_{\mu\nu}:=\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}+\hat{\mathsf W}_{\mu\nu}$ be the symbol of $\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$.

Since $\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is symmetric and translation covariant, $\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(y)=\Sigma_{\nu\mu}(-y)$, and the uniqueness of Fourier coefficients gives $\hat\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(k)=\hat\Sigma_{\nu\mu}(-k)$ for almost every $k$. As $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma$ is continuous and $\hat{\mathsf W}(k)\to0$ for $k\to0$, by (K2) for $\mathsf W\in\mathfrak K(4)$, letting $k\to0$ gives the symmetry, and therefore $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(0)=0$.

\emph{Step 5: the gradient of $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ at $0$.} The function $\hat\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ is integrable on $\mathbb T$, with the Fourier coefficients $\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(y)$. Lem.~\ref{IV-73-37}(c) with $c=0$, for which $(x,\mu)^R=(-x-e_\mu,\mu)$, gives
\[
\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(y)=\Sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}\bigl((-e_\mu,\mu),(-y-e_\nu,\nu)\bigr)=\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(-y+e_\mu-e_\nu),
\]
hence $\hat\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(k)=e^{-ik\cdot(e_\mu-e_\nu)}\,\hat\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(-k)$ for almost every $k$, by the uniqueness of Fourier coefficients. With $\varphi(k):=\frac12(k_\mu-k_\nu)$ the function $\tilde\Sigma(k):=e^{i\varphi(k)}\hat\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(k)$ is therefore even. By (K2) for $\mathsf W_{\mu\nu}\in\mathfrak K(4)$, $\hat{\mathsf W}_{\mu\nu}=\hat{\mathsf W}^h+O(|k|^2\lg|k|)$ near $0$, where $\hat{\mathsf W}^h=\sum_Gc_G\,\mathsf f_G^h\,\mathsf I_G^h$ is homogeneous of degree $1$ and even: by Lem.~\ref{IV-73-42}(a) the parity of $\mathsf f_G^h\mathsf I_G^h$ is $(-1)^{d_G}(-1)^{\omega_G+1}$, where $\omega_G=n_{\mathrm a}+n_{\mathrm b}-3$, and $\omega_G+d_G=1$.

Consequently the odd part of the smooth function $e^{i\varphi}\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}=\tilde\Sigma-e^{i\varphi}\hat{\mathsf W}_{\mu\nu}$ equals the odd part of $-e^{i\varphi}\hat{\mathsf W}^h+O(|k|^2\lg|k|)$, which is $O(|k|^2\lg|k|)$, because $\hat{\mathsf W}^h$ is even and $(e^{i\varphi}-1)\hat{\mathsf W}^h=O(|k|^2)$. So the gradient of $e^{i\varphi}\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ at $0$ vanishes; as $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(0)=0$ by Step~4, the gradient of $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ at $0$ vanishes as well. Since $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}$ is a trigonometric polynomial, this proves $\hat{\mathsf q}^\Sigma_{\mu\nu}(k)=O(|k|^2)$ and completes the proof of (a).

\emph{Step 6: set-up for (b).} Let $\Gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(y,y'):=\Gamma_q((x_q+y,\mu),(x_q+y',\nu))$. In the rest of the proof $c_G$ denotes $\frac2{\mathsf n}$ times the number $c_G$ of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-57}; the reason is that the sums with the numbers $c_G$ of that lemma equal $\frac{\mathsf n}2\Gamma_q$, by \eqref{IV-73-54}, resp.\ $\frac{\mathsf n}2\gamma_q$, by the definition of $\gamma_q$ in (b). By the first, second, third and fourth summand we mean the four groups of summands of $\Gamma_q$ as in \eqref{IV-73-54}. In each summand the derivatives $\partial_{b,a}$ and $\partial_{b',a'}$ of Def.~\ref{IV-73-29}(5) act on two legs of the vertices at $q$, $P$, $P'$; we call these two legs the outer legs.

In the terms on the right of \eqref{IV-73-54} the outer legs are the legs which are contracted with the two curl legs $(\mathrm{d}A)(p)$, namely the legs at which the lines $K_1$, $K_2$ of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-57}(4$'$), (4) and (1), resp.\ the lines $K_0$, $X$ of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-57}(5), end. An outer leg is either plain or a curl leg; in the second case we speak of an outer curl leg. The symbol of a kernel on $\mathbb Z^6$, such as $\Gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$, is defined as in Lem.~\ref{IV-73-61}(a), so that $\kappa_1$ is the variable dual to $y$ and $\kappa_2$ the variable dual to $y'$; accordingly we say that the outer leg on which $\partial_{b,a}$ acts, $b=(x_q+y,\mu)$, carries the momentum $\kappa_1$, and that the outer leg on which $\partial_{b',a'}$ acts, $b'=(x_q+y',\nu)$, carries the momentum $\kappa_2$.

By \eqref{IV-73-54} and Lem.~\ref{IV-73-57}, $\Gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ is a finite sum of kernels on $\mathbb Z^6$ with the symbols
\[
c_G\,\mathsf f_{G,1}(\kappa_1)\,\mathsf f_{G,2}(\kappa_2)\,\mathsf J_G(\kappa),
\]
symmetrised under $(\mu,\kappa_1)\leftrightarrow(\nu,\kappa_2)$. Here the $\mathsf f_{G,i}$ are trigonometric polynomials, line symbols of degree $0$ if the corresponding outer leg is plain and of degree $1$ if it is a curl leg. Further, $\mathsf J_G=1$ for the first summand; $\mathsf J_G$ is the bubble symbol $\mathsf I_G(\pm\kappa_2)$ of $Y$ for the second summand, the outer leg at $q$ carrying the momentum $\kappa_1$; $\mathsf J_G=\mathsf I_G(\pm(\kappa_1+\kappa_2))$ for the third summand, both outer legs sitting at $P$; and $\mathsf J_G=\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}(\pm\kappa)$ for the fourth summand, the Fourier representation being \eqref{IV-73-48}.

By the definition of $\gamma_q$ in (b), the symbol $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ is the same sum with $\mathsf J_G$ replaced by $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G$, where $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G:=1$ for the first summand, which is entirely local (the line between two slots of the vertex at $q$ is a number, a factor of $c_G$), and otherwise $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G$ is the function $\tilde{\mathsf Q}$ of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(c), resp.\ $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_{\mathsf q}$ of Prop.~\ref{IV-73-47}, taken at the argument of $\mathsf J_G$. Indeed, each of the local terms listed in (b) arises from the corresponding full term of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-57} by replacing a single kernel by its local kernel, while the lines which end at the outer legs are left as they are.

In the first half of $\mathsf T_5$ the full term is $K_0(u')\sum_zY(z)\,X(u'-z)$, and the local term has $\mathsf q_Y$ in place of $Y$, in accordance with $X*Y=\mathsf q_Y*X+X*Y'$; in $\mathsf T_4$ the full term is $\sum_zY(z)\,(K_1K_2)(u'-z)$, and again $Y$ is replaced by $\mathsf q_Y$. In $\mathsf T_1$ the substitution $(z,w)\to(u'-z,u'-w)$ turns the full term into
\[
\sum_{z,w}\bigl[K_4(z)\,K_5(w)\,K_3(z-w)\bigr]\,K_1(u'-z)\,K_2(u'-w),
\]
where the bracket, a kernel in $(z,w)$, has the symbol $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}$ by the second identity of \eqref{IV-73-48}; the local term has $\mathsf q_{\mathsf q}(z,w)$, with the symbol $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_{\mathsf q}$, in place of the bracket. The first half of $\mathsf T_{4'}$ is entirely local and is its own local term. In each case the symbol $\mathsf J_G$ of the replaced kernel turns into $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G$, while the number $c_G$, the factors $\mathsf f_{G,1}$, $\mathsf f_{G,2}$ and the argument of $\mathsf J_G$ remain the same. Let $\hat\Gamma:=\hat\Gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ be the sum of the symbols of $\Gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$; in $\hat\Gamma-\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ the first summand cancels.

\emph{Step 7: counting degrees.} Let $d_{G,i}\in\{0,1\}$ be the degree of $\mathsf f_{G,i}$ and $d_G:=d_{G,1}+d_{G,2}$, the number of outer curl legs; for $G$ in the second, third and fourth summand let $\omega_G$ be the number $\omega$ of $\mathsf J_G$. We use again that the degree of a line is $1+\#$(its curl legs) (Lem.~\ref{IV-73-51}), and that $\mathsf a^{(2)}$ has two curl legs and every monomial of $\mathsf a^{(3)}$ one (Def.~\ref{IV-73-19}(3)). In the second summand the vertices at $q$ and $P$ have two curl legs, of which $2-d_G$ lie on the two bubble lines, so that $\omega_G=2+(2-d_G)-3=1-d_G$. In the fourth summand the vertices at $q$, $P$, $P'$ have four curl legs, of which $4-d_G$ lie on the three lines of $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}$, so that $\omega_G=3+(4-d_G)-6=1-d_G$.

In the third summand the bubble lines carry the two curl legs at $q$: for the monomials of $\frac12|\mathfrak z_1|^2$ we get $(d_G,\omega_G)=(0,1)$; for the monomials of $\mathsf a_P^{(4)}$ with one curl leg we get $(1,1)$ or $(0,2)$, according as this leg is outer or not; for those with four curl legs we get $(2,3)$. Thus $d_G+\omega_G=1$, except for these last three kinds, for which $d_G+\min\{\omega_G,2\}\ge2$ and $\omega_G\ge1$.

\emph{Step 8: expansion of $\hat\Gamma-\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$.} We show that for almost every $\kappa$ with $|\kappa|\le c$, $c$ small,
\[
\begin{gathered}
\hat\Gamma-\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}=\hat\Gamma^h+O\bigl(|\kappa|^2\lg|\kappa|\,\Lambda(\kappa)\bigr),\\
\hat\Gamma^h:=\sum_{G:\,d_G+\omega_G=1}c_G\,\mathsf f_{G,1}^h\,\mathsf f_{G,2}^h\,\mathsf J_G^h,\qquad|\hat\Gamma^h|\le C|\kappa|\,\Lambda(\kappa).
\end{gathered}
\]
Here $\mathsf J_G^h$ is the homogeneous part of $\mathsf J_G$ (Lem.~\ref{IV-73-42}(d)), taken at the argument of $\mathsf J_G$, and $\Lambda\ge1$ is the function $\Lambda$ of Lem.~\ref{IV-73-42} for $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}$. The function $\hat\Gamma^h$ is homogeneous of degree $1$ and even, each of its terms having the parity $(-1)^{d_G}(-1)^{\omega_G+1}=1$. Let $\kappa'$ denote the argument of $\mathsf J_G$; then $|\kappa'|\le\sqrt2|\kappa|$. For $d_G+\omega_G\ge2$, Lem.~\ref{IV-73-46}(c) gives
\[
\bigl|\mathsf f_{G,1}\mathsf f_{G,2}\,(\mathsf J_G-\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G)\bigr|\le C|\kappa|^{d_G}\,|\kappa'|^{\min\{\omega_G,2\}}\le C|\kappa|^2 .
\]
For the other $G$ we have $\omega_G\le1$, hence $\deg\mathsf Q_G\le1$ and $\mathsf Q_G-\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G=O(|\kappa'|^3)$, and Lem.~\ref{IV-73-42}(b) gives
\[
\mathsf J_G-\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G=\mathsf J_G^h+O\bigl(|\kappa'|^{\omega_G+1}\lg|\kappa'|\,\Lambda_G(\kappa')\bigr)+O(|\kappa'|^3),
\]
where $\Lambda_G$ is bounded for the bubbles and equals $\Lambda$ for $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}$. Moreover $\mathsf f_{G,i}(\kappa_i)=\mathsf f_{G,i}^h(\kappa_i)+O(|\kappa_i|^{d_{G,i}+1})$, and the functions $t\lg t$ and $t^2\lg t$ are increasing on $(0,1]$, their derivatives being $-\log t$ and $t(1-2\log t)$. We go through the summands.
\begin{itemize}
\item Third summand, $\omega_G=1$, $d_G=0$: $|\mathsf J_G^h|\le C|\kappa'|\le C|\kappa|$, and the errors are $O(|\kappa|^2\lg|\kappa|)$.
\item Fourth summand: $\kappa'=\pm\kappa$, $|\mathsf J_G^h|\le C|\kappa|^{\omega_G}\Lambda$ and $|\mathsf f_{G,1}\mathsf f_{G,2}|\le C|\kappa|^{d_G}$; the leading term is $O(|\kappa|\Lambda)$, and the errors are $O(|\kappa|^2\lg|\kappa|\,\Lambda)$.
\item Second summand: $\kappa'=\pm\kappa_2$, and $\omega_G=-1$ occurs. We take the factor of the outer leg at $P$, which carries the momentum $\kappa_2$, together with $\mathsf J_G$. As $d_{G,2}+\omega_G=1-d_{G,1}\ge0$, we have $|\mathsf f^h_{G,2}(\kappa_2)\,\mathsf J_G^h|\le C|\kappa_2|^{1-d_{G,1}}$ and $|\mathsf f^h_{G,1}\mathsf f^h_{G,2}\,\mathsf J_G^h|\le C|\kappa_1|^{d_{G,1}}|\kappa_2|^{1-d_{G,1}}\le C|\kappa|$. Replacing $\mathsf f_{G,i}$ by its leading part costs a factor $|\kappa_i|$, and
\[
|\mathsf f_{G,1}\mathsf f_{G,2}|\,|\kappa_2|^{\omega_G+1}\lg|\kappa_2|\le C|\kappa_1|^{d_{G,1}}\,|\kappa_2|^{2-d_{G,1}}\lg|\kappa_2|\le C|\kappa|^2\lg|\kappa| .
\]
\end{itemize}
The symmetrised terms are treated in the same way, with the indices $1$ and $2$ exchanged.

\emph{Step 9: the value of $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ at $0$.} We have $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(0)=\sum c_G\,\mathsf f_{G,1}(0)\,\mathsf f_{G,2}(0)\,\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G(0)$, the sum extending over the $G$ with two plain outer legs, as an outer curl leg gives $\mathsf f_{G,i}(0)=0$. For such $G$ in the first summand, $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G=1$, and the line between two slots of the vertex at $q$, contained in $c_G$, is the integral of its symbol (the case $\mathsf r=1$ of Step~1). For such $G$ in the other summands, $d_G=0$, hence $\omega_G\ge1$ by Step~7, and $\tilde{\mathsf Q}_G(0)=\mathsf Q_G(0)$ is the integral of the integrand at $\kappa=0$ (Lem.~\ref{IV-73-42}(c)). By Step~1 the four summands of $\Gamma_q(b,3;b',3)$ have the trace forms
\[
\begin{gathered}
\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf m_{bb'}\mathsf C],\qquad-\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf m_b\mathsf C\,\mathsf H_{b'}\mathsf C]-(b\leftrightarrow b'),\\
-\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf h_q^{(0)}\mathsf C\,\mathsf H_{bb'}\mathsf C],\qquad\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf h_q^{(0)}\mathsf C\,\mathsf H_b\mathsf C\,\mathsf H_{b'}\mathsf C],
\end{gathered}
\]
where $\mathsf m_{bb'}$, $\mathsf m_b$ and $\mathsf H_{bb'}$ are the Hessians of $\partial\partial'\mathsf a_q^{(4)}$, $\partial\mathsf a_q^{(3)}$ and $\partial\partial'\mathsf S_4$ ($\partial=\partial_{b,3}$, $\partial'=\partial_{b',3}$), $\mathsf H_b$ is the Hessian of $\partial_{b,3}\mathsf S_3$ (Step~2), and $\mathsf h_q^{(0)}$ is the Hessian of $\mathsf a_q^{(2)}$. By Step~2,
\[
\begin{gathered}
\sum_{b,b'}\tfrac12\gamma_{\mu(b)}\gamma_{\mu(b')}\,\mathsf m_{bb'}=\mathsf h_q^{(2)}(Y_\gamma),\qquad\sum_b\gamma_{\mu(b)}\,\mathsf m_b=\mathsf h_q^{(1)}(Y_\gamma),\\
\sum_\mu\gamma_\mu\,\hat{\mathsf H}_{(0,\mu)}(l,l)=\bigoplus_e\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,1}(l;\gamma),\\
\sum_{\mu,\nu}\sum_y\tfrac12\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\,\hat{\mathsf H}_{(0,\mu),(y,\nu)}(l,l)=\bigoplus_e\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,2}(l;\gamma),
\end{gathered}
\]
the sums in the first line being finite; and $\hat{\mathsf h}(l,l)$ is the matrix of the form $(e^{il\cdot x}\alpha'\mathsf e_e,\mathsf h\,e^{il\cdot x}\alpha\,\mathsf e_e)$, which for $\mathsf h=\mathsf h_q^{(j)}(Y_\gamma)$ is $\bigoplus_e\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e,j}(l;\gamma)$ by Def.~\ref{IV-73-29}(2). The parts of the Hessians which come from an outer curl leg drop out here, since $\mathrm{d}Y_\gamma=0$; they belong to the $G$ with $\mathsf f_{G,1}(0)\,\mathsf f_{G,2}(0)=0$. We use \eqref{IV-73-63} at $\kappa=0$, integrand by integrand, and write $\hat{\mathsf h}_j:=\bigoplus_e\hat{\mathsf h}_{q,e,j}$ and $\hat{\mathsf N}_j:=\bigoplus_e\hat{\mathsf N}_{e,j}$. The four summands contribute to $\frac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\,\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(0)$ the amounts
\[
\begin{gathered}
\tfrac12\!\int\!\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf h}_2\hat{\mathsf C}\bigr],\qquad\tfrac12\cdot2\cdot\bigl(-\tfrac12\bigr)\!\int\!\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf h}_1\hat{\mathsf C}\hat{\mathsf N}_1\hat{\mathsf C}\bigr],\\
-\tfrac12\!\int\!\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf h}_0\hat{\mathsf C}\hat{\mathsf N}_2\hat{\mathsf C}\bigr],\qquad\tfrac12\!\int\!\operatorname{tr}\bigl[\hat{\mathsf h}_0\hat{\mathsf C}\hat{\mathsf N}_1\hat{\mathsf C}\hat{\mathsf N}_1\hat{\mathsf C}\bigr]
\end{gathered}
\]
(integrals over $\mathbb T$ with respect to $d^\circ l$), and these are $\int\mathfrak v_q^{(j)}(l;\gamma)\,d^\circ l$, $j=1,\dots,4$, by Def.~\ref{IV-73-29}(4). Hence, by Def.~\ref{IV-73-29}(4) and Thm.~\ref{IV-73-36},
\[
\tfrac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\,\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(0)=\tfrac12\sum_{\mu,\nu}\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu\sum_{j=1}^4\mathsf g^{(j)}_{q;\mu\nu}=0
\]
for all small $\gamma$. Since $\gamma_q$ is a symmetric kernel, $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(0)$ is symmetric in $\mu,\nu$, and therefore $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(0)=0$.

\emph{Step 10: the gradient of $\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ at $0$.} Lem.~\ref{IV-73-37}(c) with $c=x(q)$, for which $R_cq=q$, gives
\[
\Gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(y,y')=\Gamma_{q;\mu\nu}(\mathsf o-e_\mu-y,\ \mathsf o-e_\nu-y'),\qquad\mathsf o:=2\bigl(x(q)-x_q\bigr),
\]
and the uniqueness of Fourier coefficients gives $\hat\Gamma(\kappa)=e^{-2i\varphi(\kappa)}\,\hat\Gamma(-\kappa)$ for almost every $\kappa$, with the real linear form $\varphi(\kappa):=\frac12[\kappa_1\cdot(\mathsf o-e_\mu)+\kappa_2\cdot(\mathsf o-e_\nu)]$; hence $e^{i\varphi}\hat\Gamma$ is even almost everywhere. Since $\hat\Gamma^h$ is even, the odd part of $e^{i\varphi}\hat\Gamma^h$ is $O(|\kappa|^2\Lambda)$. By Step~8 the odd part of the smooth function $e^{i\varphi}\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ is therefore $O(|\kappa|^2\lg|\kappa|\,\Lambda)$ almost everywhere near $0$. The function $\Lambda$ is bounded on an open cone. Indeed, for $\hat{\mathsf T}_{\mathsf q}$ we have $(l_1,l_2,l_3)(\kappa)=(\kappa_1,-\kappa_2,0)$ (Step~2 of the proof of Prop.~\ref{IV-73-47}), so that the differences $l_i(\kappa)-l_j(\kappa)$, $i<j$, are $\kappa_1+\kappa_2$, $\kappa_1$ and $-\kappa_2$. Let
\[
\mathsf K:=\bigl\{\kappa\in\mathbb R^6:\ \min\{|\kappa_1|,|\kappa_2|,|\kappa_1+\kappa_2|\}>\tfrac12|\kappa|\bigr\}.
\]
This set is open, it is invariant under $\kappa\to t\kappa$ for real $t\ne0$, and it is not empty, since it contains $(v,v)$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$: there $|\kappa|=\sqrt2\,|v|$, while $|\kappa_1|=|\kappa_2|=|v|$ and $|\kappa_1+\kappa_2|=2|v|$. On $\mathsf K$ each of the three terms $\log_+\bigl(|\kappa|/|l_i(\kappa)-l_j(\kappa)|\bigr)$ in the definition of $\Lambda$ is at most $\log2$, so that $\Lambda\le1+3\log2$ there. On $\mathsf K$ the odd part is therefore $O(|\kappa|^2\lg|\kappa|)$ almost everywhere near $0$. The odd part of the smooth function $e^{i\varphi}\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu}$ differs from its linear part $\kappa\mapsto\kappa\cdot\nabla(e^{i\varphi}\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu})(0)$ by $O(|\kappa|^3)$.

Hence $|\kappa\cdot\nabla(e^{i\varphi}\hat\gamma_{q;\mu\nu})(0)|\le C|\kappa|^2\lg|\kappa|$ for almost every, and by continuity for every, $\kappa\in\mathsf K$ with $|\kappa|\le c$.
