Then the gauge-invariant operators of $Y_1$ and of $Y_2$ generate those gauge-invariant operators of $Y_1\cup Y_2$ that commute with the gauge transformations of $\mathsf R_2$ by central elements that are constant on each component of $I$ and $1$ off $I$; for connected $I$, all of them. For two plaquettes with exactly one common bond (seven bonds, six sites), the gauge-invariant operators of the two plaquettes generate all those of their union. (b) Let connected subgraphs $\Gamma_i$ (boxes) cover the graph, such that at every site $x$ any two boxes at $x$ are joined by a chain of boxes at $x$ in which consecutive boxes meet in a component at $x$ with two independent cycles.

Let $Z$ be the sign fields $c$ with $c(C')=1$ for every closed path $C'$ in one box, $B$ the coboundaries and $\mathsf H=Z/B$. On an open set $X_0$ of full Haar measure, invariant under gauge transformations and sign fields: for $V\in X_0$, a configuration $V'$ looks as $V$ in every box up to the gauge transformations of the box if and only if $V'=g\cdot(cV)$ with a gauge transformation $g$ and $c\in Z$; the Borel sets invariant under gauge transformations and under $Z$ agree on $X_0$ with the sets of the $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal S_{\rm add}$ that the boxes generate; and for every character $\kappa$ of $\mathsf H$ there is a closed path $C_\kappa$ with $c(C_\kappa)=\kappa([c])$, such that every bounded gauge-invariant Borel $F$ is $\sum_\kappa\Phi_\kappa s_\kappa$ on a set of full Haar measure in $\mathcal S_{\rm add}$, $s_\kappa={\rm sign}\,{\rm tr}\,V(C_\kappa)$, $\Phi_\kappa$ $\mathcal S_{\rm add}$-measurable with $\sup|\Phi_\kappa|\le\sup|F|$. (c) For a cyclic chain of boxes $\Gamma_1,\dots,\Gamma_n$ with components $\Delta_i\subset\Gamma_i\cap\Gamma_{i+1}$ that hold two independent cycles, frames $\mathfrak f_i(V)\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ formed from two holonomies of $\Delta_i$ at a site $y_i$, and paths $C_i$ in $\Gamma_i$ from $y_{i-1}$ to $y_i$: the entries of $T_i=\mathfrak f_{i-1}^{\rm T}{\rm Ad}(V(C_i))\mathfrak f_i$ are invariant under gauge transformations and under $Z$, measurable for $\Gamma_i$ and of modulus $\le1$, and $\chi_1(V(C_1\cdots C_n))={\rm tr}(T_1\cdots T_n)$ on $X_0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(a) Write $\mathfrak F(Y)$ for the bounded operators of the bonds of $Y$, acting on $L^2(G^Y)$ and tensored with $1$, $\Gamma_Y(g)$ for the gauge transformation by $g$ on the bonds of $Y$ alone, $\Gamma$ for $\Gamma_{\mathsf B}$, and $\Sigma_*=\Sigma(Y_1)\cap\Sigma(\mathsf R_2)$ for the common sites, which lie in $\Sigma(I)$ by hypothesis. \emph{Fullness.} A spanning tree of a connected set $J$ of bonds with $n\ge1$ independent cycles fixes the gauge at all but one site, so the gauge action $\Gamma_J$ on $L^2(G^J)$ is induced from the conjugation action of $G$ on $L^2(G^n)$; by Peter--Weyl every irreducible representation of the gauge group of the sites of $J$ with trivial total central character occurs in it, since every irreducible representation of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ occurs in the conjugation action of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ on $L^2(\mathrm{SU}(2))$: $J$ is full.

\emph{Contained in.} $\mathfrak F(Y_1)$ commutes with $\Gamma_{\mathsf R_2}(\zeta)$; on $\mathfrak F(Y_2)$ the adjoint action of $\Gamma_{\mathsf R_2}(\zeta)$ is that of $\Gamma(\zeta)$, because $\Gamma_I(\zeta)=1$, both ends of a bond of $I$ lying in one component, on which $\zeta$ is a constant central element; so the invariant operators of $Y_2$ commute with $\Gamma_{\mathsf R_2}(\zeta)$. \emph{Contains,} in three steps. (1) The bonds of $Y_1\cup Y_2$ are those of $Y_1$ and of $\mathsf R_2$, so its operators are weak limits of sums of products $AC$, $A\in\mathfrak F(Y_1)$, $C\in\mathfrak F(\mathsf R_2)$; averaging over the gauge group and over the $\Gamma_{\mathsf R_2}(\zeta)$, and writing $C$ as a weak limit of sums of members of multiplets, the right member is the weakly closed span of the sums $\sum_kA_kD_k^*$, where $(A_k)$ in $\mathfrak F(Y_1)$ and $(D_k)$ in $\mathfrak F(\mathsf R_2)$ are multiplets of one irreducible representation $\sigma$ of $G^{\Sigma_*}$, invariant under the gauge transformations at the other sites, $\sigma$ of trivial central character on the sites of each component of $I$, the mean over the $\zeta$ removing the other $\sigma$. (2) The common sites lie in $\Sigma(I)$, so the gauge group of $\Sigma_*$ acts on the bonds of $I$ (here the hypothesis on the common sites is read), and each component of $I$ is full; so there are multiplets $\chi^{(\mathsf r)}$ of $\sigma$ in $\mathfrak F(I)$, invariant at the sites of $I$ off $\Sigma_*$, with $\sum_{\mathsf r}\chi_k^{(\mathsf r)*}\chi_{k'}^{(\mathsf r)}=\delta_{kk'}$, the partial sums bounded by $1$: a multiplet of $\sigma$ in $\mathfrak F(I)$ is an intertwiner from $V_\sigma\otimes L^2(G^I)$ to $L^2(G^I)$, every type in $\sigma\otimes\Gamma_I$ has trivial central character on each component of $I$ and so occurs in $\Gamma_I$, and partial isometries between the copies of each type give the $\chi^{(\mathsf r)}$. (3) Then $\sum_kA_kD_k^*=\sum_{\mathsf r}a^{(\mathsf r)}b^{(\mathsf r)}$ with $a^{(\mathsf r)}=\sum_kA_k\chi_k^{(\mathsf r)*}$ and $b^{(\mathsf r)}=\sum_k\chi_k^{(\mathsf r)}D_k^*$; $a^{(\mathsf r)}$ is gauge invariant of $Y_1$, by the unitarity of $\sigma$, and $b^{(\mathsf r)}$ is gauge invariant of $Y_2$, because the sites of $I$ off $\Sigma_*$ are no sites of $\mathsf R_2$ and the sites of $\mathsf R_2$ off $\Sigma_*$ no sites of $I$, $\Sigma(I)$ lying in $\Sigma(Y_1)$.

For connected $I$ every $\sigma$ that occurs is trivial on the constant central elements of $\Sigma_*$, a constant central gauge transformation of all the sites of $\mathsf R_2$ acting trivially on $\mathfrak F(\mathsf R_2)$; so the condition of commutation is void. \emph{The two plaquettes.} On the space of the gauge-invariant vectors of a periodic layer with $N_1,N_2\ge4$ the invariant operators of two plaquettes with one common bond generate those of their seven bonds, by the argument with the full algebras of single plaquettes as cells that the last paragraph of the proof of Thm.~\ref{C-363-7}(b), on two plaquettes with one common bond, gives on $L^2(G^7)$ itself (spin labels, Lem.~\ref{C-363-27}, one plaquette made large, a monotone path, and the identity for the cross term at the ends of the common bond), every closed sign field of the seven bonds being a coboundary.

This is a statement on the abstract graph of the seven bonds: if the complement of a set $Y$ of bonds of a finite graph is connected, holds a cycle and meets every site, then $X\mapsto XP$, $P$ the projection on the gauge-invariant vectors, is injective on the invariant operators of $Y$, because such an operator is a sum of blocks $1\otimes\mathcal B(\mathsf K_\tau)$ over the types $\tau$ of $\Gamma_Y$, all of trivial total central character, and the block of $\tau$ is killed by $P$ only if the conjugate type does not occur in the gauge action on the complement, which, full and meeting every site, holds it. In a periodic layer with $N_1,N_2\ge4$ the complement of two plaquettes with a common bond is connected, holds cycles and meets each of their six sites. (b) Two elements of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ that do not commute have the centraliser $\{\pm1\}$: in a component with two independent cycles the two holonomies at a site fix the gauge transformation there up to the centre, and the chains carry this along; the quotients by the compact gauge groups are standard Borel spaces, and the sign of the trace of a loop that detects a character separates the classes. (c) Under a gauge transformation the frames turn by ${\rm Ad}(g(y_i))$, which keeps scalar and vector products; sign fields do not change ${\rm Ad}$; and $\chi_1(V(C))={\rm tr}\,{\rm Ad}(V(C))$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Sharp loops and flips on one lattice]\label{C-363-25}
On a torus $\Lambda_{K,\ell}$ at the coupling $\beta$, with $N=\ell L^K$ sites on a side and $\langle\cdot\rangle$ the Wilson measure: (a) for a rectangular path $\gamma$ with sides of at least three and at most $N-2$ bonds, $\gamma'$ its bonds but the two at each corner, $n'=\#\gamma'$, and bounded Borel $F$ of the other bonds, $|\langle\frac12{\rm tr}\,U(\gamma)F\rangle|\le(I_2(4\beta)/I_1(4\beta))^{n'}\sup|F|$; (b) on a cubic torus at $\beta\ge1$, $\langle a_p\rangle\le(21+3\log\beta)/\beta$ for every plaquette; (c) for a state $\omega$, a bounded $V$ and a projection $Q_0$ with $Q_0VQ_0=0$, and bounded $X,Y$ commuting with $Q_0$: $|\omega(XVY)|\le2\|X\|\|V\|\|Y\|\omega(1-Q_0)^{1/2}$; for the flip $\mathsf V_\zeta$ of a dual path $\zeta$ of a layer with an end plaquette $p_0$ and $Q_0=M_{\mathbf 1\{a_{p_0}<1\}}$, $Q_0\mathsf V_\zeta Q_0=0$ and $\omega(1-Q_0)\le\omega(M_{a_{p_0}})$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(a) Two bonds of $\gamma'$ lie in no common plaquette: collinear neighbours share none; bonds of two adjacent sides could share one only at a corner, and the corners are removed; and two parallel bonds lie in a common plaquette only at the distance of one bond, while two opposite sides of $\gamma$ are at least three bonds apart in the plane of $\gamma$ and, as each side has at most $N-2$ bonds, at least two bonds apart also across the seam of the torus. Given all other bonds, the weight factorises over the bonds of $\gamma'$, and $\frac12{\rm tr}\,U(\gamma)$ is linear in each of them. For a bond $b$ the sum $A_b$ of the four staples of its plaquettes is $a\,g$ with $0\le a\le4$ and $g\in\mathrm{SU}(2)$, and by the character expansion $\int Ue^{\frac\beta2{\rm tr}(UA_b)}\,\mathrm{d}U/\int e^{\frac\beta2{\rm tr}(UA_b)}\,\mathrm{d}U=\frac{I_2(\beta a)}{I_1(\beta a)}g^{-1}$, a ratio that increases with its argument; the product over $\gamma'$ gives the bound. (b) $\log Z(\beta)$ is convex with $Z(0)=1$, so $\langle\sum_pa_p\rangle_\beta\le-\log Z(\beta)/\beta$; restricting the integral to $|U_b-1|\le\epsilon$ at all bonds, where $a_p=\frac12|\partial U(p)-1|^2\le8\epsilon^2$ and the Haar measure of $\{|U-1|\le\epsilon\}$ is $\ge8\epsilon^3/3\pi^3$, and using that a cubic torus has as many bonds as plaquettes, $\langle a_p\rangle\le[\log(3\pi^3/8)+3\log\epsilon^{-1}]/\beta+8\epsilon^2$; at $\epsilon^2=1/8\beta$ this is $\le(7+\frac32\log\beta)/\beta$. (c) $XVY=X(1-Q_0)VY+XQ_0V(1-Q_0)Y$; the Schwarz inequality for $\omega$, with $X(1-Q_0)X^*\le\|X\|^2(1-Q_0)$ and $Y^*(1-Q_0)Y\le\|Y\|^2(1-Q_0)$, bounds each term by $\|X\|\|V\|\|Y\|\omega(1-Q_0)^{1/2}$. $\mathsf V_\zeta$ reverses $t_{p_0}$, the end plaquette having exactly one crossed bond, so it carries $\{a_{p_0}<1\}$ onto $\{a_{p_0}>1\}$; and $\mathbf 1\{a_{p_0}\ge1\}\le a_{p_0}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Haar-null sets under the block map]\label{C-363-26}
Let $0\le k<K$ and let $\mathcal M$ be the block-averaging map of one step from the configurations of the fine lattice $\mathbb T^{(k)}$ to those of the coarse lattice $\mathbb T^{(k+1)}$ (equations~\YMMref{(37)--(39)}{20}). For every Haar-null Borel set $N$ of coarse configurations, $\mathcal M^{-1}(N)$ is a Haar-null Borel set of fine configurations; so the same holds for every iterate $\mathcal M^n$. Hence, in the setting of Thm.~\ref{C-363-7}(g), the laws $\mu^K_d$ of the block fields, $K\ge\max\{d,1\}$, are absolutely continuous for the Haar measure $\mathsf h_d$, and so are the limit laws $\mu_d$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The positively oriented fine bonds are the disjoint union of the bonds with both ends in one block and of the sets $X_c$, $c$ a positively oriented coarse bond, where $X_c$ is made of the $L^2$ fine bonds that lie over $c$, parallel to $c$, one at each offset across $c$: each coarse bond has $L^2$ fine bonds of its own. $\mathcal M(U)(c)$ depends only on the values of $U$ on the bonds inside the two blocks of $c$ and on $X_c$ (Prop.~\YMMref{4.5}{20}). At fixed values $\iota$ of the bonds inside the blocks, $\mathcal M(\iota,\cdot)$ is thus a product over $c$ of Borel maps $\Psi^\iota_c$ of the bonds of $X_c$, and by Fubini's theorem it suffices that, for $\iota$ off a null set, every $\Psi^\iota_c$ pulls null sets back to null sets, a property that passes to products.

A contour variable is the ordered product of the $U$ along a path; the intrinsic logarithm is the inverse of $\exp$ on $\{|X|<\pi\}$, real-analytic on $\mathrm{SU}(2)\setminus\{-\mathbf 1\}$; $U[c]$ is the contour variable of the straight path from $c_-$ to $c_+$, and $x'=x+(c_+-c_-)$ for $x\in B(c_-)$. Equations~\YMMref{(37)--(39)}{20} give $\mathcal M(U)(c)$ by three cases, with disjoint domains that exhaust all configurations (Prop.~\YMMref{4.5}{20}). \emph{First case:} on the open set $\mathcal S_c$ of the configurations whose plaquettes with all corners in the double block of $c$ lie within $\omega_M=\frac1{200L^2}$ of $\mathbf 1$ (the small fields of the double block, a condition on its bonds alone), $\mathcal M(U)(c)=\exp(L^{-3}\sum_{x\in B(c_-)}\log W_x)U[c]$ with $W_x=U(c_-,x)U([x,x'])U(x',c_+)U[c]^{-1}$, the $U(y,x)$ being the group means of the contour variables along the staircase paths of a block from its centre $y$ to $x$, and $\log$ the series; the first case applies exactly on $\mathcal S_c$.

\emph{Second case:} off $\mathcal S_c$, where none of the closed contour variables 
\[
Y_{x,\Gamma,\Gamma'}=U(\Gamma)U([x,x'])U(\Gamma')^{-1}U[c]^{-1},
\]
$x\in B(c_-)$, $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$ staircase paths from $c_-$ to $x$ and from $c_+$ to $x'$, equals $-\mathbf 1$, 
\[
\mathcal M(U)(c)=\exp\bigl(L^{-3}\sum_x{\rm mean}_{\Gamma,\Gamma'}\log Y_{x,\Gamma,\Gamma'}\bigr)U[c]
\]
 with the intrinsic logarithm. \emph{Third case:} at all other configurations $\mathcal M(U)(c)=U[c]$. A contour variable $Y_{x,\Gamma,\Gamma'}$ with $x$ on the line through $c_-$ parallel to $c$ runs forth and back on that line and is identically $\mathbf 1$; every other one passes once through the bond of $X_c$ on $[x,x']$ and once through the bond of $X_c$ on $[c_-,c_+]$, two different bonds, all its other bonds lying inside the blocks; so the set where it equals $-\mathbf 1$ is the graph of one bond of $X_c$ over the other bonds, a closed real-analytic submanifold of codimension $3$.

The finite union $\mathcal N_c$ of these graphs is closed and null, and its section at every value $\iota$ of the bonds inside the blocks is null; its complement $\hat{\mathcal O}$ is open, connected, as the complement of finitely many closed submanifolds of codimension $3$ of a connected manifold, and holds $\mathbf 1$. The domain of the second case lies in $\hat{\mathcal O}$, that of the third in $\mathcal N_c$. In the formula of the second case every logarithm is taken of one of these closed contour variables, and no group mean occurs: products of bond variables, the intrinsic logarithm on $\mathrm{SU}(2)\setminus\{-\mathbf 1\}$ and the exponential make it a real-analytic map $F_c$ on $\hat{\mathcal O}$, jointly in the bonds inside the blocks and in $X_c$.

Its differential in the variables of $X_c$ at $\mathbf 1$: the factors $U(\Gamma)$, $U(\Gamma')$ do not read $X_c$, the differential of the logarithm at $\mathbf 1$ is the identity, so $dY_{x,\Gamma,\Gamma'}=dU([x,x'])-dU[c]$ there, and the differential of $F_c$ is $L^{-3}\sum_xdU([x,x'])=L^{-2}\sum_{b\in X_c}du_b$, each bond of $X_c$ lying on $L$ of the $L^3$ straight paths $[x,x']$: the mean over the $L^2$ bonds, the value that Lem.~\YMMref{4.6}{22} gives for the formula of the first case. The Gram determinant of this differential is a real-analytic function on the connected set $\hat{\mathcal O}$ with the value $L^{-6}$ at $\mathbf 1$; so its zero set $\mathcal Z_c$ is null, and off it $F_c$ is a submersion in the variables of $X_c$.

We now prove that the first branch is a submersion at every point of
$\mathcal S_c$. This avoids any assumption about its connected components.
Let $\nu$ be the direction of $c$. Index the $L^2$ lines parallel to $c$
in its double block by their transverse coordinates $z$. Each line has
one crossing bond $b_z\in X_c$; write $u_z=U(b_z)$ and let $z_0$ index
the line through $c_-$. For $x\in B(c_-)$ on the line $z$, factor the
straight transport as
\[
 U([x,x'])=P_xu_zQ_x,\qquad U[c]=g=P_0u_{z_0}Q_0.
\]
The factors $P_x,Q_x$ use only bonds inside the blocks. The contour means
also use only those bonds. Thus, with
\[
 a_x=U(c_-,x)P_x,\qquad
 b_x=Q_xU(c_+,x')^{-1},
\]
the first-branch variables are $W_x=a_xu_zb_xg^{-1}$, and $a_x,b_x$
stay fixed when the crossing variables vary.

Let $t_z$ be the point of the line $z$ whose $\nu$-coordinate is that of
$c_-$, so $t_{z_0}=c_-$ and $a_{c_-}=P_0$. Given
$\xi\in\mathfrak g$, vary all crossing bonds together by
\[
 u_z(\epsilon)=e^{i\epsilon X_z}u_z,
 \qquad X_z=\operatorname{Ad}(a_{t_z})^{-1}\xi.
\]
The norm of this tangent vector in the Euclidean product of the crossing
variables is $L|\xi|$, and $g(\epsilon)=e^{i\epsilon\xi}g$. Moreover,
\[
 W_x(\epsilon)
 =e^{i\epsilon(\xi+\rho_x)}W_xe^{-i\epsilon\xi},
 \qquad
 \xi+\rho_x=\operatorname{Ad}(a_xa_{t_z}^{-1})\xi.
\]
The error $\rho_x$ is small because the contour mean is close to every
contour in its family. Indeed,
\[
 a_xa_{t_z}^{-1}
 =U(c_-,x)U([x,t_z])U(c_-,t_z)^{-1}=h_1h_2.
\]
To obtain the last factorization, choose the contour from $c_-$ to $x$
which traverses the $\nu$ direction last. It is a contour
$\Gamma_\perp$ from $c_-$ to $t_z$ followed by $[t_z,x]$. Then
\[
 h_1=U(c_-,x)U(\Gamma)^{-1},\qquad
 h_2=U(\Gamma_\perp)U(c_-,t_z)^{-1}.
\]
Lem.~\YMMref{4.4}{19} gives $|h_i-\mathbf1|\le1/40$ and
$|W_x-\mathbf1|<1/14$. Unitarity and
$|\operatorname{Ad}(h)\xi-\xi|\le2|h-\mathbf1||\xi|$ therefore give
\[
 |h_1h_2-\mathbf1|\le\frac1{20},\qquad
 |\rho_x|\le\frac1{10}|\xi|.
\]
Write $W_x=e^{iw_x}$ with $w_x\in\mathfrak g$ and
$|w_x|<0.0715$. The differential of the logarithm gives
\[
 \left.\frac d{d\epsilon}\log W_x(\epsilon)\right|_{\epsilon=0}
 =i\eta_x,\qquad
 |\eta_x|\le\left(1.001\cdot\frac1{10}+2|w_x|\right)|\xi|
 <\frac14|\xi|.
\]
Here the first term bounds the logarithmic differential of the left
perturbation $\rho_x$, and the second is the commutator from conjugating
$w_x$ by $e^{i\epsilon\xi}$.

Put $\mathsf E=L^{-3}\sum_xw_x$ and
$\bar\eta=L^{-3}\sum_x\eta_x$. The formula for the average now yields
\[
 \left.-i\frac d{d\epsilon}\mathcal M(U(\epsilon))(c)
                 \mathcal M(U)(c)^{-1}\right|_{\epsilon=0}
 =\mathsf T_U\xi
 :=\mathsf f(\operatorname{ad}(i\mathsf E))\bar\eta
                 +\operatorname{Ad}(e^{i\mathsf E})\xi,
 \qquad \mathsf f(s)=\frac{e^s-1}{s}.
\]
The operator $\mathsf f(\operatorname{ad}(i\mathsf E))$ is the average,
for $0\le t\le1$, of the isometries
$\operatorname{Ad}(e^{it\mathsf E})$. Consequently
$|\mathsf T_U\xi|\ge3|\xi|/4$. It is an invertible map of
$\mathfrak g$, and
\[
 \zeta\longmapsto
 \bigl(\operatorname{Ad}(a_{t_z})^{-1}\mathsf T_U^{-1}\zeta\bigr)_z
\]
is a right inverse of the crossing-variable differential, of norm at
most $4L/3$.

A submersion pulls Haar-null sets back to null sets, since in local
coordinates it is a projection and Haar measure has a smooth positive
density. The first branch is a submersion everywhere on $\mathcal S_c$.
For the second branch, the exceptional set $\mathcal Z_c$ found above is
null; the third branch is contained in $\mathcal N_c$. Fubini's theorem
therefore gives, for almost every fixed internal configuration $\iota$,
the null-set property for $\Psi_c^\iota$. There are finitely many coarse
bonds, so these properties hold simultaneously outside one exceptional
set of $\iota$ of measure zero. The product map has the same property,
again by Fubini.

So $\mathcal M^{-1}(N)$ is null. Then $\mu^K_d(N)=Z_K^{-1}\int\mathbf 1_N(\mathcal M^{K-d}U)\,e^{-\beta\sum_pa_p}\,\mathrm{d}U=0$ for a null $N$, and $\mu_d(N)=\lim_K\mu^K_d(N)=0$, the laws converging uniformly on all Borel sets (Cor.~\textup{\ref{IV-62-66}}).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[One vertex]\label{C-363-27}
Let $V_{s_1},V_{s_2},V_{s_3}$ be irreducible representations of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$, $J_i=(J^a_i)_{a\le3}$ the spins acting in the $i$-th factor of $V_{s_1}\otimes V_{s_2}\otimes V_{s_3}$, $[J^a_i,J^b_i]=i\epsilon_{abc}J^c_i$, and $t_{ik}=\sum_aJ^a_iJ^a_k$. For every spin $J$ the algebra generated by $1$, $t_{12}$ and $t_{23}$ acts irreducibly on the multiplicity space $\mathsf M^J={\rm Hom}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)}(V_J,V_{s_1}\otimes V_{s_2}\otimes V_{s_3})$: it is the algebra of all operators of $\mathsf M^J$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The enveloping algebra $\mathfrak U$ of three copies of the Lie algebra of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ maps onto the algebra of all operators of the irreducible module $V_{s_1}\otimes V_{s_2}\otimes V_{s_3}$ (Burnside), equivariantly for the diagonal adjoint action, which is locally finite; averaging over the group shows that the invariant part $\mathfrak U^{\rm inv}$ maps onto the commutant of the diagonal action, the sum of the algebras of all operators of the spaces $\mathsf M^J$. By symmetrisation the graded algebra of $\mathfrak U^{\rm inv}$ is the algebra of the polynomial invariants of three vectors of $\mathbb C^3$ under $\mathrm{SO}(3)$, which is generated by the scalar products and the determinant (first fundamental theorem); by induction along the filtration of $\mathfrak U$ by the order, $\mathfrak U^{\rm inv}$ is generated by the $J_i^2$, the $t_{ik}$ and $T_3=\sum\epsilon_{abc}J^a_1J^b_2J^c_3$, and $[t_{12},t_{23}]=\sum J^a_1J^c_3[J^a_2,J^c_2]=-iT_3$. On the isotypic part $V_J\otimes\mathsf M^J$ the $J_i^2=s_i(s_i+1)$ are numbers and, the square of the total spin being $J(J+1)$, $t_{13}=\frac12\bigl(J(J+1)-\sum_is_i(s_i+1)\bigr)-t_{12}-t_{23}$. So $1$, $t_{12}$, $t_{23}$ generate the image of $\mathfrak U^{\rm inv}$ in the operators of $\mathsf M^J$, which is all of them.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Proof of Thm.~\ref{C-363-3}}

\emph{(a)} If $\eta\perp N^n\mathcal D_0$, then $\langle\eta,U(x)N^n\chi\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and $\chi\in\mathcal D_0$, as $U(x)$ keeps $\mathcal D_0$ and commutes with $N$; so the spectral measure of the pair $(\eta,N^n\chi)$ vanishes and $\langle\eta,\chi\rangle=\int(1+E)^{-n}\,\mathrm{d}m_{\eta,N^n\chi}=0$. If $\psi\perp N^n\mathcal D_0(O)$, the function $(a_k)_{k\le q}\mapsto\langle\psi,N^nU(a_1)\phi(f_1)\cdots U(a_q)\phi(f_q)\Omega\rangle$, $f_k\in\mathcal F(O_1)$, with arbitrary $q\ge1$ with $O_1+\{|a|<\delta\}\subset O$, vanishes for small $a_k$ and is the boundary value of a function holomorphic in $a_k+iV_+$ (spectrum condition); by the reflection principle it vanishes for all $a_k$, and a partition of unity gives $\psi\perp N^n\mathcal D_0$.

By the bound (b5) and the core $\mathcal D_0$ of $N^n$, $n\ge\wp$, the closures from $\mathcal D_0$ and from $\mathcal D_\infty$ agree, $\langle\phi(\bar f)\chi,\eta\rangle=\langle\chi,\bar\phi(f)\eta\rangle$ for $\chi\in\mathcal D_\infty$, $\eta\in D(\bar\phi(f))$, and the relation that defines $\mathcal C(O)$ passes from $\mathcal D_0$ to $\mathcal D_\infty$. A smoothing in time turns it into $Q\bar\phi(f)\subset\bar\phi(f)Q$. Let $Q\in\mathcal C(O)$, $f\in\mathcal F(O)$, $\delta>0$ with ${\rm supp}f+(-\delta,\delta)e_0\subset O$, $g\in C^\infty_c((-\delta,\delta))$ and $Q(g)=\int g(t)e^{itH}Qe^{-itH}\,\mathrm{d}t$. As $e^{-itH}\phi(f)=\phi(f(\cdot+te_0))e^{-itH}$ on $\mathcal D_\infty$ and $f(\cdot+te_0)\in\mathcal F(O)$ for $|t|<\delta$, $Q(g)$ has the same relation for this $f$ on $\mathcal D_\infty$; and $\langle N^n\chi,Q(g)\psi\rangle=\sum_{k\le n}\binom nki^k\langle\chi,Q(g^{(k)})N^{n-k}\psi\rangle$ for $\chi,\psi\in\mathcal D_\infty$ gives $Q(g)\mathcal D_\infty\subset\mathcal D_\infty$.

With $\phi(f)^\dagger=\phi(\bar f)$: $\phi(f)Q(g)=Q(g)\phi(f)$ on $\mathcal D_\infty$; as $\bar\phi(f)$ is closed, $Q(g)\bar\phi(f)\subset\bar\phi(f)Q(g)$; for an approximate unit $g_k$, $Q(g_k)\to Q$ strongly, and closedness once more gives $Q\bar\phi(f)\subset\bar\phi(f)Q$. Conversely a bounded $Q$ with $Q\bar\phi(f)\subset\bar\phi(f)Q$ for all $f\in\mathcal F(O)$ lies in $\mathcal C(O)$, by the relation between $\phi(\bar f)$ and $\bar\phi(f)$ above. So $\mathcal C(O)$ is closed under products; it holds $1$, is closed under adjoints and weakly closed: a von Neumann algebra; covariance is $U(\mathfrak g)\phi(f)U(\mathfrak g)^{-1}=\phi(f^{\mathfrak g})$ on $\mathcal D_0$. If $Q\in\mathcal C(O)$ and $Q\Omega=0$, then $\langle\psi,QX\Omega\rangle=\langle X^\dagger\psi,Q\Omega\rangle=0$ for products $X$ of fields of $O$, so $Q=0$.

The projection onto the closure of $\mathcal A(O)\Omega$ lies in $\mathcal A(O)'=\mathcal C(O)$, commutes with every $\bar\phi(f)$, $f\in\mathcal F(O)$, and fixes $\Omega$, so that closure holds $\mathcal D_0(O)$. The unitaries of $\mathcal A(O)'=\mathcal C(O)$ commute with $\bar\phi(f)$; and a net $\mathfrak N$ with this affiliation has $\mathfrak N(O)'\subset\mathcal C(O)$, so $\mathfrak N(O)\supset\mathcal A(O)$. A partition of unity writes $f\in\mathcal F(\bigcup O_i)$ as a finite sum of $f_i\in\mathcal F(O_i)$: $\mathcal C(\bigcup O_i)=\bigcap\mathcal C(O_i)$, and the commutants give $\mathcal A(\bigcup O_i)=\bigvee\mathcal A(O_i)$. For $O_2\subset O_1^\times$, $\mathcal L(O_1)\subset\mathcal C(O_1^\times)\subset\mathcal C(O_2)$ commutes with $\mathcal A(O_2)\supset\mathcal L(O_2)$. (W) says $\mathcal A(O_1)\subset\mathcal C(O_2)$ for all $O_2\subset O_1^\times$, that is $\mathcal A(O_1)\subset\mathcal C(O_1^\times)$ by additivity, that is $\mathcal L=\mathcal A$; and an open set is the union of the upright double cones in it, so additivity reduces (W) to such cones.

\emph{(b)} (b1) $P_m\phi(f)P_n=P_me^{sH}(e^{-sH}\phi(f)e^{-sH})e^{sH}P_n$ with $\|P_me^{sH}\|\le e^{s(m+1)}$; at $s=(m+n+2)^{-1}$, \eqref{C-363-2} gives $b_{mn}(f)\le e\,C_\wp\|f\|_{L^1}(m+n+2)^\wp$. (b2) With $X=P_m\phi(f)P_n$ and $[H,\phi(f)]=i\phi(\partial_tf)$,
$$(m-n)X=iP_m\phi(\partial_tf)P_n-(H-m-\tfrac12)X+X(H-n-\tfrac12),\qquad\|(H-m-\tfrac12)P_m\|\le\tfrac12,$$
so $(|m-n|-1)b_{mn}(f)\le b_{mn}(\partial_tf)$; iterate. (b3) If $\wp\le1$, then $k_1=0$ and the claim follows directly from (b1). Suppose $\wp>1$, so $k_1\ge1$. For $|m-n|>(m+n+2)^\epsilon\ge2^\epsilon$, $|m-n|\ge2$ and $|m-n|-1\ge\frac13|m-n|$, so (b2) at $k_1$ and (b1) at $\partial_t^{k_1}f$ give $b_{mn}(f)\le3^{k_1}|m-n|^{-k_1}eC_\wp\|\partial_t^{k_1}f\|_{L^1}(m+n+2)^\wp$, and $|m-n|^{k_1}>(m+n+2)^{\epsilon k_1}\ge(m+n+2)^{\wp-1}$. (b4) $\phi(h*f)=\int h(a)U(a)\phi(f)U(a)^{-1}\,\mathrm{d}a$, and $U(a)$ commutes with $P_m$. (b5) At $s=(1+\max\{m,n\})^{-1}$ the argument of (b1) gives $b_{mn}(f)\le e^2C_\wp\|f\|_{L^1}(1+\max\{m,n\})^\wp$, and with $\|(H-m)P_m\|\le1$ the argument of (b2) gives $(|m-n|-2)^kb_{mn}(f)\le b_{mn}(\partial_t^kf)$ for $|m-n|\ge3$. With $(1+\max\{m,n\})^2\le(1+m)(1+n)(1+|m-n|)$: $b_{mn}(f)\le e^2C_\wp(1+m)^{\wp/2}(1+n)^{\wp/2}\gamma(m-n)$, $\gamma(d)=(1+|d|)^{\wp/2}\|f\|_{L^1}$ for $|d|\le2$ and $\gamma(d)=(1+|d|)^{\wp/2}(|d|-2)^{-k_\flat}\|\partial_t^{k_\flat}f\|_{L^1}$ for $|d|\ge3$; $\sum_d\gamma(d)$ is the bracket of the form bound, and Schur's test with $\sum_a(1+a)^{2q}\|P_a\psi\|^2\le\|N^q\psi\|^2$ gives it. For the operator bound, $(2+a)^j\le2^j(1+b)^j(1+|a-b|)^j$ and $(1+\max\{a,b\})^\wp\le(1+b)^\wp(1+|a-b|)^\wp$, and the second form of Schur's test. At $\wp=4$: $\mathsf s_0(4)=195$, $2\mathsf s(4,6)<537.82$, $\mathsf s_0(2)=27$, $2\mathsf s(2,4)<37.20$. $\mathcal D_\infty$ is a core of $N^\wp$.

\emph{(c)} Put $J\phi(f_1)\cdots\phi(f_n)\Omega=\phi(\bar f_1\circ\mathsf j)\cdots\phi(\bar f_n\circ\mathsf j)\Omega$; it is antiunitary because $\mathcal W(F_1\circ\mathsf j\otimes\cdots\otimes F_N\circ\mathsf j)=\mathcal W(F_N\otimes\cdots\otimes F_1)$, which at Euclidean points is the invariance of $\sigma$ under the rotation $R_\pi$ by $\pi$ in the $(x_1,x_3)$-plane, the image of $\mathsf j=B(i\pi)$, which reverses the order of the Euclidean times, continued by {\cite[Lem.~G.5]{YMM2}}; uniqueness holds because $\mathcal D_0$ is dense. Call $X=\phi(f_1)\cdots\phi(f_n)$, $f_k\in C^\infty_c(\mathbb R^{1+2})$, an ordered product in $W$ if ${\rm supp}f_1\times\cdots\times{\rm supp}f_n$ lies in $W^{(n)}=\{(x_k)_k:\ x_1\in W,\ x_{k+1}-x_k\in W\ (1\le k<n)\}$ (an order in real time along the wedge, not the order of the Euclidean heights of the setting), and put $X^{\mathsf j}=\phi(f_1\circ\mathsf j)\cdots\phi(f_n\circ\mathsf j)$, in the same order, and $X^\dagger=\phi(\bar f_n)\cdots\phi(\bar f_1)$.

As $W$ is an open convex cone, $x_k\in W$ and $x_l-x_k\in W$ for $k<l$ on the supports: all $f_k$ lie in $\mathcal F(W)$, and their supports are pairwise spacelike separated. With $\mathsf m(y)=y^1-|y^0|$, so that $W=\{\mathsf m>0\}$ and $\mathsf m(B(s)y)\ge e^{-|s|}\mathsf m(y)$, one has $d(\iota B(s+i\tau)y)=\sin\tau\,\mathsf m(B(s)y)\ge\sin\tau\,e^{-|s|}\mathsf m(y)$ for $y\in W$, $0\le\tau\le\pi$; read at $y=x_1$ and at $y=x_{k+1}-x_k$, this puts $(\iota B(\zeta)x_k)_k$ into $\mathsf{Tb}^{(n)}$ for $0<{\rm Im}\,\zeta<\pi$, and $(\iota B(\zeta)x_k+k\eta e_3)_k$ for $0\le{\rm Im}\,\zeta\le\pi$, $\eta>0$. So the function $\zeta\mapsto\langle\chi,U(B(\zeta))X\Omega\rangle$ continues through the point vectors, by (Br) and $\eta\downarrow0$ at the edges, to a function continuous on the closed strip $0\le{\rm Im}\,\zeta\le\pi$ and holomorphic inside, with the boundary value $\langle\chi,U(B(s))X^{\mathsf j}\Omega\rangle$ at ${\rm Im}\,\zeta=\pi$, $B(s+i\pi)=B(s)\mathsf j$; the comparison with the spectral integrals of $K$ on its bounded spectral sets gives $X\Omega\in D(\Delta^{1/2})$ and $\Delta^{1/2}X\Omega=X^{\mathsf j}\Omega$.

By the definition of $J$ ($\mathsf j^2=1$), $JX^{\mathsf j}\Omega=\phi(\bar f_1)\cdots\phi(\bar f_n)\Omega$, and this is $X^\dagger\Omega$, the order being reversed by locality on $\mathcal D_0$, as the supports are pairwise spacelike separated. A boost-invariant dense subspace $\mathcal D$ of $D(\Delta^{1/2})$ is a core: if $\langle\xi,\chi\rangle+\langle\Delta^{1/2}\xi,\Delta^{1/2}\chi\rangle=0$ for $\chi\in\mathcal D$, then the measure $(1+e^{-2\pi k})dm^K_{\xi,\chi}$ has Fourier transform $0$, and $\langle\xi,\chi\rangle=0$ follows. The span of $\Omega$ and of the $X\Omega$, $X$ ordered in $W$, is such a subspace: it is boost invariant, as $B(s)^{\times n}W^{(n)}=W^{(n)}$, and it is dense by the argument of (a): products of fields in the balls of radius $\frac14$ about the points $(0,2k,0)$ stay ordered in $W$ under small translations of each factor, the reflection principle carries the orthogonality to all translations, and a partition of unity to all products of fields.

Locality removes the ordering: for $Y=\phi(h_1)\cdots\phi(h_r)$, $h_k\in\mathcal F(W)$ in any order, and $\xi=X\Omega$, $X$ ordered in $W$, the fields of $(X^{\mathsf j})^\dagger=\phi(\bar f_n\circ\mathsf j)\cdots\phi(\bar f_1\circ\mathsf j)$ lie in $\mathcal F(W')$, so they commute on $\mathcal D_0$ with those of $Y$, and $(X^{\mathsf j})^\dagger\Omega=J\xi$; hence $\langle\Delta^{1/2}\xi,Y\Omega\rangle=\langle\Omega,(X^{\mathsf j})^\dagger Y\Omega\rangle=\langle Y^\dagger\Omega,(X^{\mathsf j})^\dagger\Omega\rangle=\langle Y^\dagger\Omega,J\xi\rangle=\langle\xi,JY^\dagger\Omega\rangle$, also at $\xi=\Omega$; on the core this gives $Y\Omega\in D(\Delta^{1/2})$ and $J\Delta^{1/2}Y\Omega=Y^\dagger\Omega$ for all $h_k\in\mathcal F(W)$.

For $Q\in\mathcal C(W)$ the weak commutation, used $n$ times, gives $\langle Q^*\Omega,X\Omega\rangle=\langle X^\dagger\Omega,Q\Omega\rangle=\langle J\Delta^{1/2}X\Omega,Q\Omega\rangle$ on the core, so $\Delta^{1/2}JQ\Omega=Q^*\Omega$. Opposite wedges: let $Q\in\mathcal C(W)$, $Q'\in\mathcal C(W')$ and $Q'_g=\int g(a)U(a)Q'U(a)^{-1}\,\mathrm{d}a$, $g\in C^\infty_c(W)$; as $W'\subset W'+a$ for $a\in W$, $Q'_g\in\mathcal C(W')$; it keeps $\mathcal D_\infty$ (smoothness in the time translation) and commutes there with the fields of $W'$. With $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$, $J$ carries the graph of $\Delta^{1/2}$ onto that of $\Delta^{-1/2}$, so $\mathcal D_0(W')$ is a core of $S^*=J\Delta^{-1/2}$, and every $R$ on $\mathcal D_\infty$ with an adjoint there that commutes with the fields of $W'$ has $SR\Omega=R^\dagger\Omega$; and $S^*Q\Omega=Q^*\Omega$.

For products $X,Y$ of fields of $W$ and $R=Y^\dagger Q'_gX$:
$$\langle Y\Omega,QQ'_gX\Omega\rangle=\langle S^*Q\Omega,R\Omega\rangle=\langle SR\Omega,Q\Omega\rangle=\langle Y\Omega,Q'_gQX\Omega\rangle ;$$
so $QQ'_g=Q'_gQ$, and $g\to\delta$ gives $QQ'=Q'Q$. For a wedge $\tilde W\supset O$, $\tilde W'\subset O^\times$, so $\mathcal C(O^\times)\subset\mathcal C(\tilde W')\subset\mathcal C(\tilde W)'=\mathcal A(\tilde W)$, whence $\mathcal C(O^\times)\subset\mathcal A^d(O)$; two spacelike separated double cones are parted by a wedge, which gives the locality; if $\mathcal C(O^\times)=\mathcal A^d(O)$ for all double cones, then $\mathcal A(O)\subset\mathcal C(O^\times)$ and (W) holds by (a), and the converse is (e).

\emph{(d)} The function $f_*$ is that of Lem.~\ref{C-363-19}(a). (W) implies density: $\mathcal A(W')\subset\mathcal C(W)$ and $\mathcal A(W')\Omega$ is dense. Density implies wedge duality: $\Omega$ is then cyclic and separating for $\mathcal N=\mathcal C(W)$; by (c), $Q\Omega\mapsto Q^*\Omega$ is the restriction of $\Delta^{1/2}J=J\Delta^{-1/2}$ ($JKJ=-K$), and $J\mathcal N\Omega$ is a boost-invariant dense subspace of $D(\Delta^{1/2})$, hence a core; so modular theory gives the conjugation $J$, the modular operator $\Delta^{-1}$, and $\mathcal N'=J\mathcal NJ=\mathcal C(W')$. Wedge duality implies (W): spacelike separated upright double cones lie in some $\mathfrak gW'$ and $\mathfrak gW$, and $\mathcal C(K_1)'\subset\mathcal C(\mathfrak gW')'=\mathcal C(\mathfrak gW)\subset\mathcal C(K_2)$. $J\mathcal A(W)J=\mathcal C(W')'$, so $J\mathcal A(W)J\subset\mathcal C(W)$ is (W) for the pair $(W',W)$, equivalent to (W) by the same chain with $W$ and $W'$ exchanged. (W) implies (CP): $\bar\phi(f)$, $f\in\mathcal F(K)$ real, is affiliated with $\mathcal A(K)\subset\mathcal C(K^\times)$; the extension of Lem.~\ref{C-363-12}(b) has its bounded Borel functions in $\mathcal A(K)\otimes M_2$, which commute weakly with the fields of $K^\times$; Lem.~\ref{C-363-12}(a) at $\mathfrak A$ generated by $1$, $f$ and $\mathcal F(K^\times)$, $X_0=f$. (CP) implies (QCP$_f$), as $W\subset K^\times$ for $\bar K\subset W'$. (QCP$_f$) gives $\phi(f)\Omega\in\mathcal H_0$.

Let $\mathsf L(Y_0+\lambda Y_1+\lambda^2Y_2)=\langle\Omega,Y_0\Omega\rangle+\langle\Omega,Y_1\eta\rangle+\langle\eta,Y_2\eta\rangle$ on the quadratic polynomials in $\lambda$ with coefficients in $\mathfrak P(W)$; $f$ commutes with $\mathfrak P(W)$ in $\mathfrak P$, as $\bar K$ and $W$ are spacelike separated. On a square $(Z_0+\lambda Z_1)^*(Z_0+\lambda Z_1)$, $\mathsf L$ is $\|Z_0\Omega+Z_1\eta\|^2\ge0$ for all data; (QCP$_f$) is the positivity of $\mathsf L$ on the larger cone of the quadratic polynomials whose values at all real $\lambda$ lie in $\mathfrak P(W)^+$, and the extension below is positive on this cone. Let $\mathscr C$ be the space of the functions $G=\sum_kg_k(\lambda)Y_k$, $Y_k\in\mathfrak P(W)$, $g_k$ complex Borel with $|g_k|\le C(1+\lambda^2)$, and $\mathscr C^+$ the cone of those whose values at all real $\lambda$ lie in $\mathfrak P(W)^+$.

Every hermitian element of $\mathscr C$ is a sum of terms $gS$, $g$ real, $S=S^*$, and $\frac12q(S^2+1)-gS=\frac14(q-g)(S+1)^2+\frac14(q+g)(S-1)^2\in\mathscr C^+$ for $q=C(1+\lambda^2)$, $|g|\le q$, with $\frac12q(S^2+1)$ a quadratic polynomial: the step of the proof of Lem.~\ref{C-363-12}(a) at $r=1$. The extension theorem of M.~Riesz extends $\mathsf L$ to a linear $\hat\omega$ on $\mathscr C$ with $\hat\omega\ge0$ on $\mathscr C^+$. For $G,G'$ with $|g_k|\le C(1+|\lambda|)$, $G^*G\in\mathscr C^+$, so $\langle[G],[G']\rangle=\hat\omega(G^*G')$ gives a Hilbert space; $V\pi(Y)\Omega=[Y]$ on the dense $\mathcal D_0(W)$ is an isometry $V$ of $\mathcal H$ into it; $\hat\pi(g)[G]=[gG]$, $g$ bounded Borel, is bounded by $\sup|g|$, as $(\sup|g|^2-|g|^2)G^*G\in\mathscr C^+$; and $Q_g=V^*\hat\pi(g)V$ commutes weakly with the fields of $W$ on $\mathcal D_0(W)$, so on $\mathcal D_0$ by (a) and (b5): $Q_g\in\mathcal C(W)$, $\|Q_g\|\le\sup|g|$.

With $g_n(\lambda)=\lambda\mathbf 1_{|\lambda|\le n}$, $Q_{g_n}\Omega\to\phi(f)\Omega$, because $\|[\mathbf 1_{|\lambda|>n}Y]\|^2\le n^{-2}\mathcal W(f^2Y^*Y)$ and $V^*[\lambda]=\phi(f)\Omega$. The first order holds for all data: if $Y_0+\lambda Y_1\in\mathfrak P(W)^+$ for all real $\lambda$, then $\langle\psi,\pi(Y_1)\psi\rangle=0$ for $\psi\in\mathcal D_0$, so $\pi(Y_1)=0$ there by polarisation, and $\mathcal W(Y_0+fY_1)=\langle\Omega,Y_0\Omega\rangle\ge0$. One vector decides: $\mathcal H_0$ is invariant under $\mathcal C(W)$, under the boosts, and under the translations $U(-a)$, $a\in\bar W$ (as $\mathcal C(W)\subset\mathcal C(W+a)$), hence, by the spectrum condition and the reflection principle along the light rays $(\pm1,1,0)$ and along $e_2$, under all translations; so its projection $P_0$ commutes with $\mathcal P$, and $\mathsf D(f)=\|(1-P_0)\phi(f)\Omega\|$ is a seminorm invariant under translations and boosts, with $\mathsf D(h*f)\le\|h\|_{L^1}\mathsf D(f)$.

For $\chi\perp\mathcal H_0$ the tempered distribution $\mathsf T(h)=\langle\chi,\phi(h)\Omega\rangle$ vanishes on all $f*k$, $f\in\mathfrak F$, $k\in\mathcal S$; if the $\hat f$, $f\in\mathfrak F$, have no common real zero, a partition of unity shows that $\mathsf T$ vanishes on all $h$ with $\hat h\in C^\infty_c$, so $\phi(h)\Omega\in\mathcal H_0$ for all $h\in\mathcal S$. Then for $\chi\in\mathcal D_\infty\cap\mathcal H_0^\perp$ and $h\in\mathcal F(W)$, $\langle Q\Omega,\phi(\bar h)\chi\rangle=\langle\bar\phi(h)Q\Omega,\chi\rangle=\langle Q\phi(h)\Omega,\chi\rangle=0$ for $Q\in\mathcal C(W)$; for $\psi\in\mathcal H_0\cap\mathcal D_\infty$ the vector $\chi=(1-P_0)\phi(h)\psi$ has $\|\chi\|^2=\langle\phi(\bar h)\chi,\psi\rangle=0$; by induction $\mathcal D_0(W)\subset\mathcal H_0$, and $\mathcal H_0$ is dense.

The infimum over the boosts is the distance itself, by the boost invariance of $\mathcal H_0$; for one $f_0\ge0$ the transforms of its Lorentz images have no common real zero by Lem.~\ref{C-363-19}(d), and translations do not change zero sets. So all the conditions are equivalent, and the modular data under (W) are those of the density step, applied to $\mathcal A(W)=\mathcal C(W')$. (CP) gives (W) also without the wedge relation: for spacelike separated upright double cones $K_1,K_2$, $Q\in\mathcal C(K_1)'$ and real $g\in\mathcal F(K_2)$, the extension of Lem.~\ref{C-363-12}(a) for $(K_2,g)$ gives bounded $Q_h=V^*h(\hat T)V\in\mathcal C(K_2^\times)\subset\mathcal C(K_1)$, which commute with $Q$, and $Q_{g_n}\psi\to\phi(g)\psi$ for $\psi$ in the domain of the GNS representation, which holds $\mathcal D_0(K_2^\times)$; so $Q$ commutes weakly with $\phi(g)$ there, and the polynomial bound carries this to $\mathcal D_0$.

The inequalities: under (W) the closures of $\phi(g_1),\phi(g_2)$ are affiliated with commuting algebras, and Lem.~\ref{C-363-12}(c) gives strongly commuting self-adjoint extensions $\hat A_1,\hat A_2$; with $\psi=\phi(f)\Omega$ and their joint spectral measure,
\[
\begin{gathered}
|\mathcal W(fg_1g_2)|=\Bigl|\int\lambda_1\lambda_2\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{\psi,\Omega}\Bigr|\\
\le\Bigl(\int|\lambda_1\lambda_2|d\mu_\psi\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\int|\lambda_1\lambda_2|d\mu_\Omega\Bigr)^{1/2}\\
\le\bigl(\|\hat A_1\psi\|\|\hat A_2\psi\|\bigr)^{1/2}\|\hat A_1\hat A_2\Omega\|^{1/2},
\end{gathered}
\]
and locality on $\mathcal D_0$ identifies the squares of the three norms with $\mathcal W(f^2g_1^2)$, $\mathcal W(f^2g_2^2)$, $\mathcal W(g_1^2g_2^2)$; likewise $\mathcal W(p(f_1,f_2))=\int p\,\mathrm{d}\mu_\Omega\ge0$, and Motzkin's polynomial is covered by Lem.~\ref{C-363-12}(d).

\emph{(e)} Under (W), $\mathcal A(\tilde W)=\mathcal C(\tilde W')$ for every wedge by (d) and covariance. Two spacelike separated open convex sets are parted by a wedge (Hahn--Banach), so $O^\times=\bigcup\{\tilde W':\tilde W\supset O\}$, and additivity gives $\mathcal A^d(O)=\bigcap\mathcal C(\tilde W')=\mathcal C(O^\times)$. Locality: a wedge parts $O_1$ from $O_2$. Haag duality: $\mathcal A^d(O)'=\mathcal A(O^\times)=\bigvee\mathcal A(O_3)\subset\bigvee\mathcal A^d(O_3)=\mathcal A^d(O^\times)\subset\mathcal A^d(O)'$, the joins over the double cones $O_3\subset O^\times$; and as $O^\times=\bigcup\{\tilde W':\tilde W\supset O\}$, (a) gives $\mathcal A(O^\times)=\bigvee\{\mathcal A(\tilde W'):\tilde W\supset O\}$.

Outer regularity: a point with a neighbourhood spacelike to $O$ is spacelike to the compact set $\bar O$, hence to $\bar O_\epsilon$ for small $\epsilon$, the compact sets $\bar O_\epsilon$ decreasing to $\bar O$; so $O^\times=\bigcup_{\epsilon>0}O_\epsilon^\times$, and (a) gives $\mathcal A^d(O)=\mathcal C(O^\times)=\bigcap_\epsilon\mathcal C(O_\epsilon^\times)=\bigcap_\epsilon\mathcal A^d(O_\epsilon)$. An operator commuting with all $\mathcal A(O_1)$, $O_1\subset O^\times$, commutes with $\mathcal A(O^\times)$, so it lies in $\mathcal A^d(O)$. For $O\subset\tilde W$: $\mathcal A(O)\subset\mathcal A^d(O)\subset\mathcal A(\tilde W)$, so the wedge algebras of $\mathcal A^d$ are those of $\mathcal A$, and $(\mathcal A^d)^d=\mathcal A^d$. $\mathcal A(O)=\mathcal A^d(O)$ if and only if $\mathcal C(O^\times)\subset\mathcal A(O)=\mathcal C(O)'$.

Covariance, $J$, cyclicity and affiliation follow from (a) and (c). Without (W): if the intersections are local, then $\mathcal A(O_1)\subset\mathcal A^d(O_1)\subset\mathcal A^d(O_2)'\subset\mathcal A(O_2)'=\mathcal C(O_2)$ for spacelike separated double cones.

\emph{(f)} Let $A_j=\phi(\partial_t^jf)$ and $R_\epsilon=(1+\epsilon N)^{-1}$. From $[H,A_0]=iA_1$: $R^r_\epsilon A_0\chi=A_0R^r_\epsilon\chi-i\epsilon\sum_{j=1}^rR^j_\epsilon A_1R^{r-j+1}_\epsilon\chi$. For $A_0^*\eta=\pm i\eta$ and $\eta_\epsilon=R^{k_0}_\epsilon\eta$, the imaginary part of $\langle\eta_\epsilon,\bar A_0\eta_\epsilon\rangle$ and the form bound of $A_1$ give $\|\eta_\epsilon\|^2\le c\sum_j\epsilon^{1/2}\|N^{1/2}R_\epsilon^{k_0-j+1}\eta_\epsilon\|\,\epsilon^{1/2}\|N^{1/2}R^j_\epsilon\eta\|\to0$, while $\eta_\epsilon\to\eta$; so $\bar A_0$ is self-adjoint. $N^k\phi(f)=\sum_j\binom kji^j\phi(\partial_t^jf)N^{k-j}$ gives $\bar A_0N^{-k}=N^{-k}(\bar A_0+K_k)$ with $K_k$ bounded under the block bounds, whence the resolvents keep $D(H^k)$ off a strip and, through cores, commute with $\bar\phi(h)$ for $h$ spacelike to $f$; Neumann series reach all $z\notin\mathbb R$; so the resolvents lie in $\mathcal C(O)$. (f1) With the logarithm the self-adjointness and the commutation come from unitary groups along which the exponent of the energy falls.

Put $\mathsf w(x)=x(1+\log x)$, and for real $h\in C^\infty_c$ let $v=f_i*h$. Off the band (b3) bounds the blocks of $\partial_tf_i$ linearly, so $b_{mn}(\partial_tf_i)\le c\,\mathsf w(m+n+2)$ for all $m,n$; by (b4), $\partial_t^jv=(\partial_tf_i)*\partial_t^{j-1}h$ has the same bound with $c\|\partial_t^{j-1}h\|_{L^1}$, $j\ge1$, and (b2) adds the decay $(|m-n|-1)^{-3}$ for $|m-n|\ge2$; as $\mathsf w(m+n+2)\le3.4(1+|m-n|)\,\mathsf w(m+1)^{1/2}\mathsf w(n+1)^{1/2}$, Schur's test with the weights $\mathsf w(n+1)$ gives $|\langle\psi',\phi(\partial_t^jv)\psi\rangle|\le c_j\|\mathsf w(N)^{1/2}\psi'\|\|\mathsf w(N)^{1/2}\psi\|$ on $\mathcal D_\infty$, $j\ge1$. By $\log x=\int_0^\infty[(1+t)^{-1}-(x+t)^{-1}]dt$, $[N+t,\phi(\partial_t^jv)]=i\phi(\partial_t^{j+1}v)$ and $\int_0^\infty\mathsf w(x)(x+t)^{-2}dt=1+\log x$, this turns into $|\langle\log N\,\psi,\phi(\partial_t^jv)\psi\rangle-\langle\phi(\partial_t^jv)\psi,\log N\,\psi\rangle|\le c_{j+1}\langle\psi,(1+\log N)\psi\rangle$, $j\ge0$, the left member being $|\mathfrak l^{(j)}(\psi,\psi)|$ for the hermitian form $\mathfrak l^{(j)}(\psi',\psi)=\int_0^\infty\langle(N+t)^{-1}\psi',\phi(\partial_t^{j+1}v)(N+t)^{-1}\psi\rangle dt$.

The three-lines theorem, on vectors of bounded energy, carries the bound to $\mathfrak l^{(j)}(N^\tau\psi',N^{-\tau}\psi)$ with the constant $\sum_{l\le\lceil|\tau|\rceil}\binom{\lceil|\tau|\rceil}lc_{j+1+l}$; as $\frac d{d\tau}\langle N^\tau\chi',AN^{-\tau}\chi\rangle=i\,\mathfrak l^{(0)}(N^\tau\chi',N^{-\tau}\chi)$ for $A=\phi(v)$, and a second derivative brings in $\mathfrak l^{(1)}$, integration over $|\tau|\le\frac\rho2$ at $\chi'=\chi$ gives
$$|\langle N^\rho\chi,A\chi\rangle-\langle\chi,AN^\rho\chi\rangle|\le\rho\,c_1\langle\chi,N^\rho(1+\log N)\chi\rangle+\rho^2c'(\rho)\langle\chi,N^\rho\chi\rangle\qquad(\chi\in\mathcal D_\infty,\ \rho\ge0),$$
$c'(\rho)=\sum_{l\le\lceil\rho/2\rceil}\binom{\lceil\rho/2\rceil}lc_{l+2}$. The bounded $A_s=e^{-sH}Ae^{-sH}$ satisfy the same with the same numbers. For $\psi\in\mathcal D_\infty$ and $y(\lambda)=\|N^{\rho(\lambda)/2}e^{i\lambda A_s}\psi\|^2$ with the falling exponent $\rho(\lambda)=\rho_0e^{-c_1|\lambda|}$, the term $\rho'\langle N^\rho\log N\rangle$ of $y'$ cancels the term with the logarithm: $y'\le(\rho_0c_1+\rho_0^2c'(\rho_0))\,y$ for $\lambda\ge0$, and Gronwall's lemma bounds $\|N^{\rho(\lambda)/2}e^{i\lambda A_s}\psi\|$ uniformly in $s$. As $s\downarrow0$, $\|(A_s-A_{s'})\chi\|\le c|s-s'|\|N^{q+1}\chi\|$ ($q\ge\wp$ an integer) makes the groups $e^{i\lambda A_s}$ converge strongly to a unitary group $V$ with $V(\lambda)D(N^r)\subset D(N^{re^{-c_1|\lambda|}})$ for $r\ge0$, so $V(\lambda)\mathcal D_\infty=\mathcal D_\infty$, and $\lambda\mapsto V(\lambda)\psi$ is continuously differentiable in every norm $\|N^a\cdot\|$ with the derivative $iAV(\lambda)\psi$; its generator is the closure of $A$ on $\mathcal D_\infty$ (for $\eta$ with $(A|_{\mathcal D_\infty})^*\eta=\pm i\eta$, $\lambda\mapsto\langle V(\lambda)\psi,\eta\rangle$ is bounded with the derivative $\pm$ itself, hence $0$): $\phi(v)$ is essentially self-adjoint on $\mathcal D_\infty$ and on $\mathcal D_0$.

The group loses moments of the energy and keeps $\mathcal D_\infty$. For $h'\in\mathcal S$ whose support is spacelike separated from ${\rm supp}\,v$, $\phi(v)\phi(h')=\phi(h')\phi(v)$ on $\mathcal D_\infty$ (locality on $\mathcal D_0$, the core $\mathcal D_0$ of $N^n$, (b5)), and $\frac d{d\lambda}\langle\phi(\bar h')V(\lambda)\psi',V(\lambda)\psi\rangle=0$ gives $V(\lambda)\bar\phi(h')\subset\bar\phi(h')V(\lambda)$: by (a) the bounded Borel functions of $\bar\phi(v)$ lie in $\mathcal C(O)$ for every open $O$ spacelike separated from ${\rm supp}\,v$. For real $h\in\mathcal F(O)$ the $f_i*h$ lie in $\mathcal F(O)$ for large $i$ and tend to $h$ in $\mathcal S$; so $\mathcal C(O)$ is the commutant of the groups of the $\bar\phi(f_i*h)$ with ${\rm supp}(f_i*h)\subset O$ (by (a) every $Q\in\mathcal C(O)$ commutes with them; conversely weak commutation with the $\phi(f_i*h)$ passes to $\phi(h)$ by (b5)), and for spacelike separated $O_1,O_2$ the groups of $O_1$ lie in $\mathcal C(O_2)$: $\mathcal C(O_1)'\subset\mathcal C(O_2)$, which is (W) without a wedge, and (CP) by (d). (f2) The time reversal $[F]\mapsto[\bar F]$ gives the other sign for $f_0$ even in $t$; $\partial_t^j(h*f_0)=(\partial_t^{j-1}h)*\partial_tf_0$ gives the hypotheses of the first part at every $h*f_0$; by Lem.~\ref{C-363-19}(d) the images of $f_0$ under rotations, boosts and translations into $W'$ have no common real zero of their transforms, and the resolvents of the corresponding operators lie in $\mathcal C(W)$ and produce from $\Omega$ a total set; (d) applies. (f3) For products $X$ of fields spacelike to $f_0$, $\|\phi(f_0)^nX\Omega\|^2=\langle\phi(f_0)^{2n}\Omega,X^\dagger X\Omega\rangle\le\|\phi(f_0)^{2n}\Omega\|\|X^\dagger X\Omega\|$, so these total vectors are quasi-analytic, $\bar\phi(f_0)$ is self-adjoint with resolvents commuting with the outside fields, and the argument of (f2) applies. (f4) At $s=(m+n+2)^{-1}$ the argument of (b1) gives $b_{mn}(f)\le e\,C\|f\|_{L^1}(m+n+2)(1+\log(m+n+2))$ for every $f\in\mathcal S$ (for $\wp\le1$ (b1) gives it without the logarithm), so for every $\partial_t^jf$: the hypothesis of (f1) holds for every approximate unit $f_i$, and the argument of (f1) runs with $v=f$ itself; so every real $\phi(f)$ is essentially self-adjoint on $\mathcal D_0$, and $e^{i\lambda\bar\phi(f)}\bar\phi(h)\subset\bar\phi(h)e^{i\lambda\bar\phi(f)}$ for real $h$ whose support is spacelike separated from that of $f$; $\bar\phi(h)$ being self-adjoint, the group of $\bar\phi(f)$ commutes with its spectral projections: the closures commute strongly. (f5) Lem.~\ref{C-363-20}(b)--(d) gives (LB$_f$) for every real $f\in C^\infty_c$, so (f2) at every $f_0$.

The last assertion of (f): if (f2) holds at $f_*$, time reversal gives the two-sided bound $c_*(\partial_tf_*)<\infty$, and with Lem.~\ref{C-363-19}(b), (c) the functions $f_i=g^{\otimes3}_{1/i,3/2}=f_**\mu_i^{\otimes3}$ have $c_*(\partial_tf_i)\le\|\mu_i\|^3_{L^1}c_*(\partial_tf_*)$, hence $b_{mn}(\partial_tf_i)\le\|\mu_i\|_{L^1}^3c_*(\partial_tf_*)(m+n+2)$ by polarisation; these functions have the properties that (f1) asks of the $f_i$.

\emph{(g)} By Lem.~\ref{C-363-13}(ii), $\phi_u([F],M_{g^2}[F])=\int g^2\phi^\xi_u\,\mathrm{d}\lambda$ and $\langle[F],M_{g^2}N[F]\rangle=\int g^2\langle[F]_\xi,N_\xi[F]_\xi\rangle \,\mathrm{d}\lambda$; at $g=1$ the bound passes from all $\sigma_\xi$ to $\sigma$; conversely, the bound for $\sigma$ at the vectors $M_g[F]$ gives $\int g^2(c\,\mathsf n-\mathsf a)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda\ge0$ for all real $g$, with $\mathsf a(\xi)=\phi^\xi_u([F]_\xi,[F]_\xi)$ and $\mathsf n(\xi)=\langle[F]_\xi,N_\xi[F]_\xi\rangle$ continuous, and full support gives $\mathsf a\le c\,\mathsf n$ at every $\xi$; the classes $[F]_\xi$ form a core of $N_\xi$. The premise of (CP) speaks of $\mathfrak P$ alone, and $\mathcal W_\sigma=\int\mathcal W_\xi \,\mathrm{d}\lambda$ (Lem.~\ref{C-363-13}(iii)): (CP) passes from all $\sigma_\xi$ to $\sigma$, and so does every fixed inequality $\mathcal W(a)\ge0$.

Conversely, for $a=\sum f^nY_n$ as in (CP), which is hermitian, and $b$ formed as in Lem.~\ref{C-363-13}(iv), a polynomial in means of translates of elements $b_i$ of $\mathfrak P$ over pairwise different spatial translations of length $\ge R$, with $R$ so large that the translated $b_i$ are spacelike to $K$, which puts $b$ in the algebra of (CP), $\sum\lambda^nb^*Y_nb\in\mathfrak A^+$ and $f$ is central, so $\mathcal W_\sigma(b^*ab)\ge0$, and Lem.~\ref{C-363-13}(iv) gives (CP) for every $\sigma_\xi$; (d) turns (CP) into (W). The limits: Lem.~\ref{C-363-13}(v); inequalities $\mathcal W(a)\ge0$ pass to the limit.

\emph{(h)} (h1) Fix $\Lambda<\infty$; on $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ let $q$ be the bounded operator of the form 
\[
\int h'(\vec x)q_0(U(-\vec x)\cdot,U(-\vec x)\cdot)d^2x;
\]
then 
\[
\langle\psi',\mathsf I\psi\rangle=\int\mathsf l^{-1}\rho_1(\varsigma/\mathsf l)\langle e^{-(\frac{\mathsf l}2+\varsigma)H}\psi',q\,e^{-(\frac{\mathsf l}2-\varsigma)H}\psi\rangle \,\mathrm{d}\varsigma
\]
 and 
\[
\langle\psi',\phi(g_{\mathsf l}\otimes h')\psi\rangle=\int g_{\mathsf l}(t)\langle e^{-itH}\psi',q\,e^{-itH}\psi\rangle \,\mathrm{d}t.
\]
An operator integral $\int\alpha_\tau(H)q\beta_\tau(H)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(\tau)$ depends on $(\alpha,\beta,\mu)$ only through its symbol \[\int\alpha_\tau(E)\beta_\tau(E')\,\mathrm{d}\mu(\tau)\] (approximate the functions by step functions on a fine partition of $[0,\Lambda]$). With $A(x)=\hat D(x)+\epsilon$ and $\log A=\int_0^\infty[(1+t)^{-1}-(t+A)^{-1}]dt$, $L_\epsilon(x)=-\log(\hat D(x)+\epsilon)$ is $C^2$ in norm and $L_\epsilon'(0)=-\int_0^\infty R^\epsilon_t\hat D'(0)R^\epsilon_tdt$, $R^\epsilon_t=(t+\epsilon+e^{-\mathsf lH})^{-1}$. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$ on $\mathcal H_\Lambda$, $-L_\epsilon'(0)$ tends to the operator integral with the symbol
$$e^{-\frac{\mathsf l}2(E+E')}\int\mathsf l^{-1}\rho_1(\varsigma/\mathsf l)e^{-\varsigma(E-E')}\,\mathrm{d}\varsigma\int_0^\infty\frac{\,\mathrm{d}t}{(t+e^{-\mathsf lE})(t+e^{-\mathsf lE'})}=\mathsf G(\mathsf l(E-E')),$$
minus $\mathfrak m$; and $\phi(g_{\mathsf l}\otimes h')$ has the same symbol: this is the slope. Taylor's formula for $u_\epsilon(x)=\langle\psi,L_\epsilon(x)\psi\rangle$ at $x=\pm r$, with $L_\epsilon\ge-\log(Q+1)$ and $L_\epsilon(0)\le\mathsf lH$, gives 
\[
r|u'_\epsilon(0)|\le\mathsf l\langle H\rangle_\psi+\log(Q+1)\|\psi\|^2+\frac{r^2}2\max\{\sup_{|x|\le r}u_\epsilon'',0\};
\]
let $\epsilon\downarrow0$ and use (v); extend from $\bigcup_\Lambda\mathcal H_\Lambda$ to $\mathcal D_\infty$ by continuity in a norm $\|N^a\cdot\|$. For every real $k\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$, a dyadic partition $\chi_i$ of the energy transfer and the functions $\mu_i$ with $\hat\mu_i=\hat k\chi_i/\mathsf G(\mathsf l_i\,\cdot)$, $\|\mu_i\|_{L^1}\le C_N\mathsf l_i^N$, write $k=\sum_i\mu_i*g_{\mathsf l_i}$ in $L^1$, and Lem.~\ref{C-363-19}(c) sums the bounds. (h2) By Lorentz covariance on $\mathcal D_\infty$ the bound of (b1) holds in every frame for vectors with $n\cdot p\le\mu$: boost the two spectral sets to the rest frame of $n$, where the argument of (b1) gives $e^2C_\wp\|u\|_{L^1}\mu^\wp$.

The set $\{p\cdot p\le\mu^2\}$ is cut into cells: $\{p\cdot p\le\mu^2,\ E<2\mu\}$ and, for $a\ge1$, the cells $\{p\cdot p\le\mu^2,\ 2^a\mu\le E<2^{a+1}\mu\}$ on which the direction of $\vec p$ lies in one of $\lceil2\pi2^a\rceil$ equal sectors, of angle about $2^{-a}$. The frame of such a cell has the rapidity $a\log2$ in the direction of the middle of its sector, and $n\cdot p<3\mu$ on the cell. For two cells at the distance $D$ in momentum space let $n$ be the midpoint of the hyperbolic segment between their frames, whose length is $\mathsf d$: then $n\cdot p\le3\mu e^{\mathsf d/2}$ on both cells, and $e^{\mathsf d}\le4(1+2D/\mu)^2$, so $n\cdot p\le6\mu+12D$ there. A test function whose Fourier transform vanishes for $|k|\ge\frac34D$ has a vanishing block between the two cells, the spectral projections being smeared translations; so, cutting $\hat u=\hat\kappa(\cdot/D)\hat u+(1-\hat\kappa(\cdot/D))\hat u$ with a fixed smooth $\hat\kappa$ equal to $1$ on $\{|k|\le\frac12\}$ and to $0$ on $\{|k|\ge\frac34\}$, the block is that of a function of $L^1$ norm $\le c\,D^{-8}\|\mathcal L^4u\|_{L^1}$.

For $r\mu\le D<(r+1)\mu$, $r\ge1$, the block is therefore $\le e^2C_\wp\,c\,(r\mu)^{-8}\|\mathcal L^4u\|_{L^1}(6\mu(2r+3))^\wp$, and for $D<\mu$ it is $\le e^2C_\wp\|u\|_{L^1}(18\mu)^\wp$. At most $100(r+1)$ cells lie at a distance $<(r+1)\mu$ from a given cell; Schur's test over the cells, with the weight $r+1$ of this count, gives the bound with the constant $C_{\rm L}$, the sum over $r$ converging for $\wp<6$, with no dependence on the bound of the energy. For these two consequences let $\wp>0$. On $P_m\mathcal H\cap\mathcal P_<\mathcal H$ the invariant mass is $\le(m+n+2)^{1/\wp}$, which gives the bound of the blocks. For the last statement, $\Pi P_m=\mathcal P_<\Pi P_m$ and $P_n\Pi=P_n\Pi\mathcal P_<$ with the $\mathcal P_<$ of the pair $(m,n)$, since $p\cdot p\le(1+p^0)^{2/\wp}\le(m+n+2)^{2/\wp}$ on both ranges; $\Pi$ commutes with $H$, so the argument of (b2) gives $(|m-n|-1)^j\|\Pi P_m\phi(u)P_n\Pi\|\le\|\Pi P_m\phi(\partial_t^ju)P_n\Pi\|$; the blocks of $\Pi e^{-sH}\phi(u)e^{-sH}\Pi$ are then at most $c\,e^{-s(m+n)}(m+n+2)\min\{1,(|m-n|-1)^{-2}\}$, and Schur's test with $\sup_{x\ge0}(x+2)e^{-sx}\le e/s$ gives the bound.

The bound by $1+H+M^2$: cut momentum space into unit cubes; for two cubes at the sup-distance $d$, $D=\sqrt3(d+1)$, and a point $p_0$ of energy $E_0$ and invariant mass $m_0$ in one of them, a timelike vector $a$ with $|a|=(\sqrt2\mathsf M_1)^{-1}$, $\mathsf M_1^2\le2D^2(1+E_0+m_0^2)$, has $a\cdot p\le1$ on both cubes, and the point bound in the frame of $a$ bounds the block of $\phi(f)$ between the two cubes by $e^2C_\wp\|f\|_{L^1}(2D)^\wp$ times the least value of $(1+p^0+p\cdot p)^{\wp/2}$ on either cube; derivatives in a coordinate along which the cubes are $d$ apart give the decay $(d-1)^{-k}$ as in (b2), and Schur's test with the weights $(1+p^0+p\cdot p)^{\wp/2}$ of the cubes gives the form bound.

\subsubsection{Proof of Thm.~\ref{C-363-4}}

\emph{Step 1.} By Thm.~\textup{\YMMref{AP}{780}} among the construction results on the limits of periodic Gibbs states, $\sigma$ is data (Rec) with $(16C^g_{\rm pt},4,\frac12)$ and $S^\sigma_1=0$, and its truncated functions $S^\sigma_n$, $n\ge2$, are the limits of the joint cumulants $S^T_{n;j}$ of the $\mathcal O_{K_j}(f)$ under $\mu_j=\mu_{\beta_j}$ on $\Lambda_j$, with $\ell_j/a_j=2L^{K_j+m_j}$ even, $a_j=L^{-K_j}$ the spacing of $\Lambda_j$; every component is data (Rec) with one triple.

\emph{Step 2 (frames).} Let $\mathcal H_j,\iota_{\Lambda_j},\mathcal M_j,\pi_j,K_{\Lambda_j},\mathsf P_j$ be the objects of Prop.~\ref{C-363-14} on $\Lambda_j$ at $\beta_j$, and, for tuples $G=(h_k)$ over $\mathbb E_+$, $(G)_j=\prod_k(\mathcal O_{K_j}(h_k)-\mu_j(\mathcal O_{K_j}(h_k)))$, the functions $h_k$ periodised on $\Lambda_j$, and $\iota_jG=\iota_{\Lambda_j}((G)_j)$, both extended linearly. In Steps 2--7 the sign $(\cdot)_j$ is this product on the torus $\Lambda_j$, centred by $\mu_j$; it is not the product $(X)^{\nu_j}_{K_j}$ on $L^{-K_j}\mathbb Z^3$ of the setting, and for a tuple $G$ over a quadrant it is, for large $j$, a real function of the bonds of the closed quadrant of $\Lambda_j$, with $\mathsf r(G)_j=(\mathsf rG)_j$ for $\mathsf r\in\{\theta,\theta_1,R\}$ ($\mathsf r\mathcal O(f)=\mathcal O(\mathsf rf)$, $\mu_j$ being invariant).

For large $j$ the supports lie in $(-\frac{\ell_j}4,\frac{\ell_j}4)^3$ and farther than $2a_j$ from the time-zero plane. For $X=\theta G'\cdot G=(f_k)$, (L1) and the invariance of the weight give $\langle\iota_jG',\iota_jG\rangle=\mu_j\prod_k(\mathcal O(f_k)-\mu_j\mathcal O(f_k))=\sum_\varpi\prod_{\mathsf b\in\varpi}S^T_{|\mathsf b|;j}(X_{\mathsf b})$, the sum over the partitions without singletons (a moment of centred variables, and a cumulant of order $\ge2$ does not see the centring); by Step 1 it tends to $\sum_\varpi\prod S^\sigma_{|\mathsf b|}(X_{\mathsf b})=\sigma(X)=\langle[G'],[G]\rangle$. So $(\mathcal H_j,\iota_j)$ is a frame for $(\mathcal H(\sigma),[\cdot])$, and Lem.~\ref{C-363-8} applies.

\emph{Step 3 (limits of half-plane operators lie in $\mathcal C(W')$).} Let $Q_j\in\mathcal M_j$, $Q_j\rightharpoonup Q$ along a subsequence; take the $\tilde q_j$ of (L3), $\|\tilde q_j\|\le\sup\|Q_j\|$, and a further subsequence with $\tilde q_j\rightharpoonup\tilde q$. For tuples $G_1,G_2$ over $\mathsf{II}$ and large $j$, the $(G_i)_j$ are real functions of the bonds of $\bar{\mathsf Q}_2$, and $R^{-1}(\theta(G_1)_j\cdot(G_2)_j)=(R^{-1}(\theta G_1\cdot G_2))_j$; the limit of (L3) is the hypothesis of Lem.~\ref{C-363-11}, so $Q\in\mathcal C(W')$.

\emph{Step 4 (the lattice modular flows converge to the boosts).} Every subsequence of the support projections $e_{R,j}\in\mathcal M_j$ has a further one with $e_{R,j}\rightharpoonup\mathsf E$; by Step 3, $\mathsf E\in\mathcal C(W')$, and by Lem.~\ref{C-363-8}(iii), $\mathsf E\Omega$ is the weak limit of $e_{R,j}\Omega_{\Lambda_j}=\Omega_{\Lambda_j}=\iota_j\varnothing$: $\mathsf E\Omega=\Omega$. $\Omega$ separates $\mathcal C(W')$, so $\mathsf E=1$ and $\|(1-e_{R,j})\iota_jG\|^2=\langle\iota_jG,(1-e_{R,j})\iota_jG\rangle\to0$ along the full sequence; by (L1), $\|(1-e_{L,j})\iota_jG\|=\|(1-e_{R,j})\iota_j(\theta_1\bar G)\|\to0$. So Lem.~\ref{C-363-8}(iv) applies to $\pi_j$, and by (L4) (for $G\in\mathcal V_0$ and large $j$, $(G)_j$ is a function of $\bar{\mathsf Q}_1$ with $R(G)_j=(RG)_j$) and Lem.~\ref{C-363-9}(b), Lem.~\ref{C-363-8}(v) applies to $\mathsf P_j$, $\Delta^{1/4}$, $\mathsf r=R$:
$$\Phi(\mathsf P_j)\psi_j\Rightarrow\Phi(\Delta^{1/4})\psi\quad(\Phi\in C_0(\mathbb R)),\qquad e^{-2\pi itK_{\Lambda_j}}\psi_j\Rightarrow U(B(-2\pi t))\psi,$$
the second from the even functions $\Phi(x)=|x|^{4it}\chi_{\mathsf M}(x)$, $\chi_{\mathsf M}$ a cut-off near $0$ and $\infty$, since $|\mathsf P_j|=e^{-\frac\pi2K_{\Lambda_j}}$ and $\Delta^{1/4}$ is injective.

\emph{Step 5 (the field on the vacuum is reached).} For real $u\in C^\infty_c(\mathsf I)$ let $\Phi(x)=\mathsf F(-\frac2\pi\log|x|)$, $\Phi(0)=0$: an even function of $C_0(\mathbb R)$ with $\Phi(\mathsf P_j)=\mathsf F(K_{\Lambda_j})$ and $\Phi(\Delta^{1/4})=\mathsf F(K)$. Step 4 and \eqref{C-363-10} give $\xi_j=\mathsf F(K_{\Lambda_j})\pi_j\iota_j(u)\Rightarrow\phi(f_u)\Omega$. (L5) with $F=(u)_j$ gives $T^{(\epsilon)}_j\in\mathcal M_j$; along a subsequence $T^{(\epsilon)}_j\rightharpoonup T^{(\epsilon)}_u$, which lies in $\mathcal C(W')$ by Step 3, and by Lem.~\ref{C-363-8}(i), (iii) and Step 2
\begin{equation}\label{C-363-15}
\|T^{(\epsilon)}_u\Omega-\phi(f_u)\Omega\|\le\tfrac{\sqrt\epsilon}2\,\pi e^{5\pi^2/8}\|[\theta_1u\cdot u]\|,
\end{equation}
one Euclidean four-point function at separated points. With $\epsilon\to0$, $\phi(f_u)\Omega$ lies in the closure of $\mathcal C(W')\Omega$.

\emph{Step 6 (density, locality).} By Lem.~\ref{C-363-9}(c) the transforms of the $f_u$ have no common real zero; Thm.~\ref{C-363-3}(d), with $W$ and $W'$ exchanged, gives the density of $\mathcal C(W')\Omega$, (W), (CP), the duality for wedges and the modular data; Thm.~\ref{C-363-3}(a), (e) give (a)--(e) for $\tau=\sigma$; $\mathcal A(W)=\mathbb C1$ would make $\mathcal H=\overline{\mathcal A(W)\Omega}=\mathbb C\Omega$.

\emph{Step 7 (the wedge algebra is made of lattice limits).} Let $\mathfrak M$ be the von Neumann algebra generated by the operators of (f) and $\mathcal N=\mathcal C(W')=\mathcal A(W)$. For $\mathfrak gW\subset W$ one has $\mathfrak gW'\supset W'$, so $U(\mathfrak g)\mathcal C(W')U(\mathfrak g)^{-1}=\mathcal C(\mathfrak gW')\subset\mathcal C(W')$, and $\mathfrak M\subset\mathcal N$ by Step 3. The closure of $\mathfrak M\Omega$ is invariant under $\mathfrak M$ and under the $U(a)$, $a\in W$, hence under all translations, and it holds every $\phi(f_u)\Omega$ (Step 5); the one-vector argument of Thm.~\ref{C-363-3}(d), with $\mathfrak M$ in the place of $\mathcal C(W')$, makes $\mathfrak M\Omega$ dense. $\mathfrak M\Omega$ and $\mathcal N\Omega$ are boost-invariant dense subspaces of $D(\Delta^{1/2})$ on which $Q\Omega\mapsto Q^*\Omega$ is the restriction of $J\Delta^{1/2}$ (Thm.~\ref{C-363-3}(c) for $W'$), hence cores of it; so the two algebras have the one modular conjugation $J$, and $\mathfrak M'=J\mathfrak MJ\subset J\mathcal NJ=\mathcal N'$: $\mathcal N\subset\mathfrak M$.

\emph{Step 8 (components).} All $\sigma_\xi$ are data (Rec) with one triple. For $a=\sum f^nY_n$ as in (CP), which is hermitian, and $b$ formed as in Lem.~\ref{C-363-13}(iv), a polynomial in means of translates of elements $b_i$ of $\mathfrak P$ over pairwise different spatial translations of length $\ge R$, with $R$ so large that the translated $b_i$ are spacelike to $K$ and so in the algebra of (CP), $\sum\lambda^nb^*Y_nb\in\mathfrak A^+$ for all real $\lambda$ and $f$ is central, so $\mathcal W_\sigma(b^*ab)\ge0$ by Step 6; Lem.~\ref{C-363-13}(iv) gives (CP) for every $\sigma_\xi$, and Thm.~\ref{C-363-3}(d), (a), (e) give (a)--(e) for $\tau=\sigma_\xi$. The same follows from the vectors $M_g\Omega$ of Lem.~\ref{C-363-13}(i): $M_g\in\mathcal C(O)$ for every $O$, and the extension of the proof of (W)$\Rightarrow$(CP) to the vector $M_g\Omega$ gives $\int g^2\mathcal W_\xi(a)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda\ge0$ for all real $g\in C(\mathsf X)$.

\emph{Step 9 (fibres).} The operators $M_g$ of Lem.~\ref{C-363-13}(i) commute with the semigroup, the translations and the fields, so they lie in $\mathcal C_\sigma(O)$ for every $O$, hence in $\mathcal C_\sigma(W')\cap\mathcal C_\sigma(W)=\mathcal A_\sigma(W)\cap\mathcal A_\sigma(W)'$ (Step 6). The rest is reduction theory: on a separable Hilbert space that is a direct integral over $(\mathsf X,\lambda)$, $\mathsf X$ compact metrisable and $\lambda$ a Borel measure, the decomposable operators are the commutant $\mathcal Z'$ of the diagonal algebra $\mathcal Z$; a von Neumann algebra $\mathcal N$ with $\mathcal Z\subset\mathcal N\subset\mathcal Z'$ is $\int^\oplus\mathcal N_\xi\,\mathrm{d}\lambda$ for a measurable field of von Neumann algebras, whose fibres are those of a countable generating family and are fixed up to a $\lambda$-null set; and $(\int^\oplus\mathcal N_\xi\,\mathrm{d}\lambda)'=\int^\oplus\mathcal N_\xi'\,\mathrm{d}\lambda$. (1) The classes depend continuously on the entries, with constants of one triple for $\sigma$ and for all $\xi$; so $\mathcal H(\sigma)$ is separable, and there are countably many combinations $F_n$ whose classes $[F_n]_\xi$ are total in every $\mathcal H(\sigma_\xi)$; and $\xi\mapsto\sigma_\xi(\theta\bar F'\cdot F)$ is continuous: the fields $\xi\mapsto[F_n]_\xi$ are a fundamental sequence.

The Hilbert space $\mathfrak K$ of the proof of Lem.~\ref{C-363-13}(i) is the direct integral $\int^\oplus\mathcal H(\sigma_\xi)\lambda(\,\mathrm{d}\xi)$: $g\otimes F\mapsto(g(\xi)[F]_\xi)_\xi$ is isometric by the form of $\mathfrak K$, and onto, as a field orthogonal to all $g[F_n]$, $g\in C(\mathsf X)$, has $\langle[F_n]_\xi,x_\xi\rangle=0$ for almost every $\xi$ and all $n$. So $[F]\mapsto([F]_\xi)_\xi$ is unitary, $\mathcal H(\sigma)=\int^\oplus\mathcal H(\sigma_\xi)\lambda(\,\mathrm{d}\xi)$, and $M_g$ is the multiplication by $g$; the diagonal algebra $\mathcal Z$ is the weak closure of the $M_g$. (2) The semigroup, the translations and the insertions decompose, being given by one formula for $\sigma$ and for all $\sigma_\xi$; so do the bounded $e^{-sH}\phi(f)e^{-sH}$, by \eqref{C-363-2}; as the $e^{-sH_\xi}$ are injective and the polynomial bound holds with one triple, a subsequence converging fibrewise gives $(\phi(f)\psi)_\xi=\phi_\xi(f)\psi_\xi$ for almost every $\xi$, $\psi\in\mathcal D_\infty$, and by induction the fibres of $\phi(f_1)\cdots\phi(f_n)\Omega$ are $\phi_\xi(f_1)\cdots\phi_\xi(f_n)\Omega_\xi$ almost everywhere. (3) $M_g\in\mathcal A_\sigma(W)'$ and weak closure give $\mathcal Z\subset\mathcal A_\sigma(W)'$, so $\mathcal A_\sigma(W)\subset\mathcal Z'$ consists of decomposable operators; $M_g\in\mathcal A_\sigma(W)$ gives $\mathcal Z\subset\mathcal A_\sigma(W)$: $\mathcal Z$ lies in the centre of $\mathcal A_\sigma(W)$, and $\mathcal A_\sigma(W)=\int^\oplus\mathfrak A_\xi\,\mathrm{d}\lambda$ for a measurable field of von Neumann algebras $\mathfrak A_\xi$. (4) A decomposable bounded $Q$ lies in $\mathcal C_\sigma(W')$ if and only if $Q_\xi\in\mathcal C_{\sigma_\xi}(W')$ for almost every $\xi$, and the same with $W$ for $W'$: ``if'' by integration of the relation of the fibres, by (2); ``only if'' because $\mathcal C_\sigma(W')$ is an algebra that holds the $M_g$, so that $\int g\,[\langle\phi_\xi(\bar f)\psi_\xi,Q_\xi\psi'_\xi\rangle-\langle\psi_\xi,Q_\xi\phi_\xi(f)\psi'_\xi\rangle]\,\mathrm{d}\lambda=0$ for all $g\in C(\mathsf X)$; the bracket vanishes almost everywhere, with one null set for countably many test functions $f\in\mathcal F(W')$ and products of fields, and the polynomial bound with one triple carries it to all. (5) A countable family that generates $\mathcal A_\sigma(W)=\mathcal C_\sigma(W')$ has, by (4), its fibres in the von Neumann algebra $\mathcal C_{\sigma_\xi}(W')$ for almost every $\xi$, and these fibres generate $\mathfrak A_\xi$: $\mathfrak A_\xi\subset\mathcal C_{\sigma_\xi}(W')$ almost everywhere. (6) $\mathcal A_\sigma(W)'=\mathcal C_\sigma(W)=\int^\oplus\mathfrak A_\xi'\,\mathrm{d}\lambda$, and (4) for $W$, read on a countable generating family, gives $\mathfrak A_\xi'\subset\mathcal C_{\sigma_\xi}(W)$ almost everywhere; with wedge duality for each $\sigma_\xi$ (Step 8), $\mathfrak A_\xi\supset\mathcal C_{\sigma_\xi}(W)'=\mathcal C_{\sigma_\xi}(W')$.

So $\mathfrak A_\xi=\mathcal C_{\sigma_\xi}(W')=\mathcal A_{\sigma_\xi}(W)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $\xi$, every $\xi$ with $\lambda(\{\xi\})>0$ among them, as such a point is no null set, and $\mathcal A_\sigma(W)=\int^\oplus\mathcal A_{\sigma_\xi}(W)\,\lambda(\,\mathrm{d}\xi)$: for $\lambda$-almost every $\xi$ the wedge algebra of the component $\sigma_\xi$ is the fibre of the algebra of (f), the fibres of a direct integral being fixed up to null sets.

\emph{Step 10 (the supply).} Here $(F)_j=(F)^{\rho_j}_{K_j}$ is the product at $K_j$ centred by $\rho_j$, as in (h), also for a component, where the states $\rho_{j,\xi}$ integrate and the $\rho_j$ give the centring. Reflection positivity of $\rho_j$ at the site mirror $x_3=0$: a bounded Borel function $B$ of bonds in the mirror is fixed by $\theta$, and with $\mathsf c=(\sup|B|^2-|B|^2)^{1/2}$, $\sup|B|^2\rho_j(\overline{\theta G}G)-\rho_j(\overline{\theta(BG)}BG)=\rho_j(\overline{\theta(\mathsf cG)}\mathsf cG)\ge0$; the Schwarz inequality gives the first bound. $\mathcal H(\sigma')$ is separable; a diagonal subsequence over a countable set of combinations with dense classes, and the first bound, give the limit form and $Q$, $\|Q\|\le\mathsf b$. For $c=0$ and combinations $F,F'$ over $\mathsf Q_L$ put $A_j=B_j\overline{\theta(F')_j}(F)_j$; then $\ell^Q_{F',F}(h)=\lim_j\rho_j(A_j(h)_j)$, and the Schwarz inequality for the reflection positivity at the site mirror $x_1=0$ gives
$$|\rho_j(A_j(h)_j)|^2\le\rho_j(A_j\,\theta_1\bar A_j)\,\rho_j(\overline{\theta_1(h)_j}(h)_j),$$
whose second factor tends to $\sigma'(\theta_1\bar h\cdot h)$; in the first, with $Y=F\cdot\theta_1\bar F$, $Y'=F'\cdot\theta_1\bar F'$ and the function $B_j\theta_1\bar B_j$ of the bonds of the mirror $x_3=0$, $A_j\theta_1\bar A_j=\overline{\theta(Y')_j}\,B_j\theta_1\bar B_j\,(Y)_j$, and the first mirror, used a second time, bounds it by $\mathsf b^2\|[Y']\|\|[Y]\|$ in the limit. So the hypothesis of Lem.~\ref{C-363-17} holds and $Q\in\mathcal C_{\sigma'}(W)$. For $c\ne0$, $ce_1$ is a lattice vector for large $j$; the translate $\tau_{-ce_1}B_j$ is of the case $c=0$, and by the invariance of $\rho_j$ its limit is $U(ce_1)^{-1}QU(ce_1)$. The proof uses of the states that integrate only reflection positivity at the site mirrors $x_3=0$, $x_1=0$ and invariance under the lattice translations, which the lattice approximants of a component have; so the same holds for every component.

Thms.~\YMMref{D}{8}, \YMMref{AJ}{673} and~\YMMref{AD}{607} enter only through Thm.~\textup{\YMMref{AP}{780}}.

\subsubsection{Proof of Thm.~\ref{C-363-5}}

Every bound below passes to the components through the last sentence of Lem.~\ref{C-363-16}(d), which carries the norm bound of every insertion from $\sigma'$ to each component; every component is data (Rec) with one triple.

\emph{(a)} Step 1: the blocks at one time. Let $h\in C^1_c(\mathbb R^2)$ be real and carried by a square of side $2$, $q=T_{mn}(h)$, $A=(H-m)P_m$, $B=(H-n)P_n$, so that $0\le A,B\le1$. As $P_m\mathsf B_h(s,s')P_n=e^{-sH}q\,e^{-s'H}$,
$$e^{\frac{\mathsf l}2(m+n)}P_m\mathsf I_{\mathsf l}(h)P_n=\int\rho_{\mathsf l}(\varsigma)e^{-\varsigma(m-n)}\,e^{-(\frac{\mathsf l}2+\varsigma)A}\,q\,e^{-(\frac{\mathsf l}2-\varsigma)B}\,\mathrm{d}\varsigma ,$$
and $\|e^{-uA}qe^{-u'B}-q\|\le(u+u')\|q\|$ with $u+u'=\mathsf l$; since $\int\rho_{\mathsf l}(\varsigma)e^{-\varsigma(m-n)}\,\mathrm{d}\varsigma=\int\rho_{\mathsf l}(\varsigma)\cosh(\varsigma(m-n))\,\mathrm{d}\varsigma\ge1$, $\|q\|\le(1-\mathsf l)^{-1}e^{\frac{\mathsf l}2(m+n)}\|\mathsf I_{\mathsf l}(h)\|$. Take the least $i\ge1$ with $L^{-i}\le2/(m+n+2)$: then $e^{\frac{\mathsf l}2(m+n)}\le e$ and $\mathsf l^{-1}\le L(m+n+2)$, and Lem.~\ref{C-363-16}(c) gives
$$\|T_{mn}(h)\|\le\tfrac{3e}2L^3\mathsf C_3(m+n+2)^3|h|_{C^1}.$$
Step 2: the field. By \eqref{C-363-2}, $\langle\chi',P_m\phi(f)P_n\chi\rangle=\int\langle e^{-itH}\chi',T_{mn}(f_t)e^{-itH}\chi\rangle\,\mathrm{d}t$ with $f_t=f(t,\cdot)$; a partition of unity on $\mathbb R^2$ subordinate to the squares $\kappa+[-1,1]^2$, $\kappa\in\mathbb Z^2$, splits the real and imaginary parts of $f_t$ into pieces of norm $|\cdot|_{C^1}\le3.3\sup_{\kappa+[-1,1]^2}(|f_t|+|\nabla f_t|)$, and $2\cdot3.3\cdot\frac{3e}2<27$ gives $b_{mn}(f)\le\mathsf c_0(m+n+2)^3$; Thm.~\ref{C-363-3}(b2), which holds for all data, gives the decay. Step 3: the operator and form bounds. $\|P_m\phi(f)\psi\|\le\sum_nb_{mn}(f)\|P_n\psi\|$, and $m+n+2\le2(1+n)(1+|m-n|)$; so $\|\phi(f)\psi\|\le\|\kappa\|_{\ell^1}\|N^3\psi\|$ by Young's inequality, $\kappa(d)=8(1+|d|)^3\min\{\mathsf c_0,\mathsf c_5(|d|-1)^{-5}\}$, and $\sum_{|d|\le2}(1+|d|)^3=71$, $\sum_{|d|\ge3}(1+|d|)^3(|d|-1)^{-5}<6.3$; with a weight $(1+m)^a\le(1+n)^a(1+|d|)^{|a|}$ and a larger $k$ the same gives the bound with $N^{a+3}$.

For the form, $(m+n+2)^2\le4(1+m)(1+n)(1+|d|)$ and Schur's test with $\kappa'(d)=8(1+|d|)^{3/2}\min\{\mathsf c_0,\mathsf c_3(|d|-1)^{-3}\}$, whose two sums are less than $17.1$ and $5.7$, respectively. The blocks of $e^{-sH}\phi(f)e^{-sH}$ are $\le e^{-s(m+n)}b_{mn}(f)$, and $\sup_{x\ge0}(x+2)^3e^{-sx}\le(3/s)^3e^{2s}$. Step 4: growth. For $|m-n|=d\ge2$, the bound of Step 2 at $\partial_t^kf$ with $\|\partial_t^kf\|_\star\le A^{k+1}(k!)^{\mathsf s}\le A^{k+1}k^{\mathsf sk}$, at $k=\lfloor((d-1)/e^{\mathsf s}A)^{1/\mathsf s}\rfloor$, gives
$$b_{mn}(f)\le\mathsf G\,(m+n+2)^3e^{-\gamma'|m-n|^{1/\mathsf s}}\qquad\text{for all }m,n,\qquad\gamma'=\mathsf se^{-1}A^{-1/\mathsf s},\ \mathsf G=27L^3\mathsf C_3Ae^{\mathsf s+\gamma'} .$$
As $\Omega=P_0\Omega$, $\|\phi(f)^n\Omega\|\le\sum\prod_{k\le n}b_{m_km_{k-1}}(f)$ over paths $0=m_0,m_1,\dots,m_n$; with $\mathsf D=\sum_k|m_k-m_{k-1}|\ge\max_km_k$, at most $2^n$ paths for each sequence of steps, and $\sum_k|d_k|^{1/\mathsf s}\ge\mathsf D^{1/\mathsf s}$,
$$\|\phi(f)^n\Omega\|\le(2\mathsf G)^n\sup_{\mathsf D\ge0}(2\mathsf D+2)^{3n}e^{-\frac{\gamma'}2\mathsf D^{1/\mathsf s}}\Bigl(\sum_{d\ge0}e^{-\frac{\gamma'}2d^{1/\mathsf s}}\Bigr)^n\le C^n(n!)^{3\mathsf s}.$$
Such $f$ exist: $w\otimes b$ with $b\in C^\infty_c(\mathbb R^2)$, $b\ge0$, and $w$ the infinite convolution of the uniform probability densities on $[0,i^{-\mathsf s}]$, $i\ge1$, for which $\|w^{(k)}\|_{L^1}\le\prod_{i\le k}2i^{\mathsf s}=2^k(k!)^{\mathsf s}$, because the $k$-th derivative falls on the first $k$ factors, each becoming a difference of two point masses divided by the width.

\emph{(b)} The same four steps with the second bound of Lem.~\ref{C-363-16}(c), $\|T_{mn}(h)\|\le\frac{3e}2L^2\mathsf C_2(m+n+2)^2|h|_{C^1}$, the exponent $2$ in the place of $3$, the weight $(1+n)^2$ in Step 3 for the operator bound and $[(1+m)(1+n)]^{1}$ for the form bound, $\sup_x(x+2)^2e^{-sx}\le(2/s)^2e^{2s}$, and $(n!)^{2\mathsf s}$ at the end.

\emph{(c)} \emph{The point.} Put
$\bar B=B_\sharp L/(L-1)$, where $B_\sharp\ge0$ is one of the fixed
constants $\sigma^-$. Thus $\bar B$ is independent of the source
radius, $\gamma$ and $g$, and $\bar B<\gamma^{-2}\le g^{-2}$.
For an integer $z\ge2$ set
\[
 v_z^{-2}=L^{z-1}(g^{-2}+B_\sharp-L^{-1}\bar B)
                       +L^{-1}\bar B-B_\sharp,
 \qquad G=g^{-2}+2\bar B.
\]
Then $L^{z-1}g^{-2}\le v_z^{-2}\le L^zG$. Define
\[
 \Lambda_z=1+\log(L^zG),\qquad
 \varrho_z=\frac12\min\{
   \sigma^{\rm S}(v_z^{-2}-\bar B),\,
   \sigma^{\rm S}_{\rm L}v_z^{-1}
                         (\log v_z^{-2})^{-\mathfrak p_0}\}.
\]
Here $\sigma^{\rm S}$ and $\sigma^{\rm S}_{\rm L}$ depend only on
$\sigma^-$. We check explicitly that this radius is allowed.
The radius-independent conditions remain valid when the coupling
ceiling is decreased from $\gamma$ to $v_z$.
The two source-radius conditions in
Prop.~\YMMref{82.2}{668}, with source radius $2\varrho_z$, are
\[
 2\varrho_z\le\sigma^{\rm S}(x-\bar B),\qquad
 2\varrho_z x^{-1/2}(\log x)^{\mathfrak p_0}
                              \le\sigma^{\rm S}_{\rm L}
                 \quad(x\ge v_z^{-2}).
\]
The first left margin is smallest at $x=v_z^{-2}$. The calibration
also gives $\log\gamma^{-2}>2\mathfrak p_0$. Therefore
$x^{-1/2}(\log x)^{\mathfrak p_0}$ is decreasing for
$x\ge v_z^{-2}\ge\gamma^{-2}$, and the second condition is likewise
strongest at that endpoint. Both conditions hold by the definition
of $\varrho_z$. This proves the required admissibility and also
identifies $\varrho_z$ as the largest radius permitted by these two
source conditions at the fixed ceiling $v_z$.

Let $(K,\beta)$ be admitted at $g$, $K>z$. Its label $\mathsf b=L^{-K}\beta$ lies in the window \YMMref{(1531)}{615} of Prop.~\YMMref{74.1}{615}, $g^{-2}+B_\sharp\frac{L-2}{L-1}<\mathsf b\le L(g^{-2}+\bar B)$; so the running coupling $g'$, $g'^{-2}=L^{-1}(L^z\mathsf b+\bar B)-B_\sharp$, at which the label $L^z\mathsf b$ of $(K-z,\beta)$ passes first, has $v_z^{-2}<g'^{-2}\le L^zG$ and $1+\log g'^{-2}\le\Lambda_z$. At the radius $\varrho_z$ and the choice $(\sigma^-,v_z)$ the dilated pair $(K-z,\beta)$ is a first-passage datum at $g'\le v_z$, and it carries systems of localised source energies with the constants $(2\varrho_z;C_{\rm S},\kappa;C_{\rm S},C_{g'};C_{\rm gap})$ ({\cite[Lem.~N.1]{YMM2}}), where $C_{\rm S},\kappa,C_{\rm gap}$ are the numbers of the pairs admitted at $g$, formed from $\sigma^-$ alone, and $C_{g'}\le C_{\rm S}(1+\log g'^{-2})\le C_{\rm S}\Lambda_z$ {\cite[eq.~288]{YMM2}}.

As $v_z^{-2}-\bar B\ge\frac{12}{13}L^{z-1}g^{-2}$, $v_z\le gL^{-(z-1)/2}$, $\log v_z^{-2}<\Lambda_z$ and $g\le\frac12$,
$$\frac1{\varrho_z}\le2c_\sigma\,g\,L^{-(z-1)/2}\Lambda_z^{\mathfrak p_0},\qquad\Lambda_z=1+z\log L+\log G,\qquad G=g^{-2}+2\bar B,$$
$c_\sigma=\max\{\frac{13}{24\sigma^{\rm S}},\frac1{\sigma^{\rm S}_{\rm L}}\}$, formed from $\sigma^-$ alone: the radius of analyticity in the source grows like $1/g'$, the square root of the label $g'^{-2}$, up to logarithms. This is where Thms.~\YMMref{AJ}{673} and~\YMMref{AD}{607} are used at every radius and every admitted choice. Fix $0<\eta\le1$, a real $h\in C^1_c$ carried by a ball $B(y,\frac\eta{40L})$ with $|y_3|\le\frac\eta8$, and $F,F'$ over $\{x_3>\frac\eta4\}$. The cell: $\mathsf l=L^{-i}$ with $\frac\eta{5L}<\mathsf l\le\frac\eta5$ and a centre $y^*\in L^{-i-2}\mathbb Z^3$ within $\frac{\mathsf l}{2L^2}$ of $y$; then the ball lies in the middle of the cell, and the cell in $\{|x_3|<\frac\eta4\}$.

The dilation by $L^z$ among the construction results ({\cite[Lem.~K.1]{YMM2}}) carries periodic Gibbs states, mirrors and boards to the like and $\mathcal O_K(h)$ to $\mathcal O_{K-z}(L^zh(L^{-z}\cdot))$; it carries the cell to one of side $L^z\mathsf l\le L^z\eta/5$, and $h$ to a source of norm $\max\{L^z\sup|h|,40M\,{\rm Lip}\,h\}$, which is $\le\|h\|_\sharp$ as long as $L^z\eta\le5$, since $h$ vanishes on the boundary of its ball, so that $\sup|h|\le\frac\eta{40L}{\rm Lip}\,h$. The insertion bound on one lattice for a pair that carries systems, Lem.~\YMMref{104.4}{760} among the construction results, read on the dilated lattice at the radius $\varrho_z$, has the constant $2\mathsf Q_{\rm mid}(L^z\mathsf l)/\varrho_z$ at the side of the one cell, with $\log\mathsf Q_{\rm mid}(\mathsf l')=(C_{\rm S}+C_{g'}+C_{\rm gap})\mathsf l'^3+\Phi_1(\frac{\mathsf l'}4,\frac{\mathsf l'}4;\mathsf l')$ (equation~\YMMref{(2017)}{760}) and $\Phi_1(\frac{\mathsf l'}4,\frac{\mathsf l'}4;\mathsf l')\le\bar\Phi$ for $0<\mathsf l'\le1$, where
\[
 \bar\Phi=C_{\rm S}S(\kappa)
 \left[\frac{27}{26}
       +27\{32(C''_\Sigma+\log_L10)+4C'_\Sigma\}\right]
\]
is the contribution of $\Phi_1$ in equation~\YMMref{(2018)}{760}; so $\mathsf Q_{\rm mid}(L^z\mathsf l)\le Q_\star=e^{2C_{\rm S}+C_{\rm gap}+\bar\Phi}$, free of $z$, as long as $(L^z\eta/5)^3\Lambda_z\le1$.

This is the proof of Prop.~\YMMref{105.1}{762} up to its last step, with the side of the one cell in the place of the supremum over the sides. With $z$ fixed and the cutoff removed, $|\sigma'(\theta\bar F\cdot(h)\cdot F')|\le\frac{2Q_\star}{\varrho_z}\|h\|_\sharp\|[\tau_{-\frac\eta4e_3}F]\|\|[\tau_{-\frac\eta4e_3}F']\|$ for every $z\ge2$ with $(L^z\eta/5)^3\Lambda_z\le1$. As $z\mapsto(L^z\eta/5)^3\Lambda_z$ increases, such a $z$ exists if and only if $\eta\le\eta_1=5L^{-2}\Lambda_2^{-1/3}$, a number $<L^{-1}$.
