\emph{(h)} For continuous $h$ the first statement is Lem.~\ref{C-363-41} (Thm.~\ref{C-372-6} of \S\ref{C-372-1}, read at one polygon), applied to the polygon $C$, a closed path of some $\Lambda_{K_0,\ell}$ taken in every $\Lambda_{K,\ell}$, $K\ge K_0$, with the functions $F_K$ of the bonds at the distance $\ge\mathsf d$ from $C$, uniformly in them; a bounded $h$ that is continuous off a null set lies between continuous functions $h_-\le h\le h_+$ with $\overline{h_+}-\overline{h_-}$ as small as we please, and $F_K$ is a combination of four functions with values in $[0,1]$. The law of $\frac12{\rm tr}\,g$ under Haar measure is $\frac2\pi\sqrt{1-w^2}\,\mathrm{d}w$; so $\bar h=0$ for $h={\rm sign}$ and for the characters $\chi_j$, $j\ge\frac12$, written as functions of $w=\frac12{\rm tr}$, and $\bar h=\frac14$ for $h(w)=w^2$.

With $C$ in a site mirror and $F_K=\overline{\theta G'_K}G_K$, $|G_K|,|G'_K|\le1$ at a fixed distance, this is the fading between the vectors of the space of reflection positivity. The Bessel bound is Lem.~\ref{C-363-25}(a), and $\mathsf r(x)=1-\frac3{2x}+O(x^{-2})$, $n'\approx|\gamma|L^K$, $4\beta=4L^K\mathsf b$ give the limit $\exp(-3|\gamma|/8\mathsf b)$. The fading of the flips is Lem.~\ref{C-363-25}(b), (c), with $\omega_K(1-Q_0)\le\omega_K(M_{a_{p_0}})=\langle a_{p_0}\rangle_K$, the multiplication operators of one layer having the Wilson measure as their law in the state of the transfer operator.

\emph{(i)} \emph{Notation.} $x_{[D]}=L^D\mathsf b$ (\S\ref{sec:block-field-laws}) is the coupling at the depth $D$; $\varepsilon(\mathsf t)=A_0\mathsf t^{-1/2}(\log\mathsf t)^{\mathfrak p_0}$ and $\delta(\mathsf t)=(A_1/A_0)\varepsilon(\mathsf t)$ \YMMref{(634)}{339}, with the constants $A_0,A_1>0$, $\mathfrak p_0\in\mathbb N$ of the list of Thm.~\YMMref{D}{8}; $\varpi(V)=\max_p|\partial V(p)-\mathbf 1|$, $|\cdot|$ the operator norm; and the small fields of the depth $D$ are those of the inner ball $\mathsf{In}_{[D]}=\{V:\varpi(V)<2\varepsilon(x_{[D]})\}$ of Thm.~\YMMref{D}{8} (the common-depth definitions in Section~\YMMref{116}{807}, the definitions preceding Lem.~\YMMref{113.10}{796}), an open gauge-invariant set (Lem.~\YMMref{113.10}{796}). $\mathsf R_{[D]}=2M^{-3}(\ell L^D)^3\exp[-c'A_0^2(\log x_{[D]})^{2\mathfrak p_0}]\exp[(\mathsf C^\Sigma_{\rm maj}+2+C_{\rm low}(\mathsf b))\ell^3]$ is the number \YMMref{(2187)}{806} at the level of the depth $D$; it reads $D$ and not $K$, and it tends to $0$ as $D\to\infty$, since $c'A_0^2>0$ and $2\mathfrak p_0\ge2$. An element $g$ of $G$ with the eigenvalues $e^{\pm i\phi}$, $\phi\in[0,\pi]$, has $|g-\mathbf 1|=2\sin\frac\phi2\le\phi$, so $|e^{iw\sigma_3}-\mathbf 1|\le|w|$; and replacing the four factors of $\partial(kV)(p)$ by those of $\partial k(p)$ one by one, $|\partial(kV)(p)-\partial k(p)|\le\sum_{b\in\partial p}|V_b-\mathbf 1|$ for $G$-valued fields $k$, $V$ and the bondwise product $kV$.

\emph{The floor.} Let $D$ be so large that $x_{[D]}\ge\mathsf t_\natural$ and $\mathsf R_{[D]}<1$, let $K\ge D+1$, and let $t=K-D$ be the level of the depth $D$. The setting of the small-field chain of Thm.~\YMMref{D}{8} asks of its top level only that it lie between $1$ and $K-1$ and carry a coupling $\ge\mathsf t_\natural$ (\S\ref{sec:cutoff-calibration}); so it holds with the top level $t$, at a fixed depth. At the source $0$, Prop.~\textup{\YMMref{115.2}{806}} gives a bounded Borel weight $\mathfrak w^{\rm sf}_t\ge0$ defined before Prop.~\YMMref{115.2}{806} such that the image of $\mathfrak w^{\rm sf}_t\rho_0\,\mathrm{d}U$ under $\mathcal M^t$ is the measure $\mathbf 1_{\mathsf{In}_{[D]}}\nu_t$ of the chain \YMMref{(2188)}{806}, $\int F\mathfrak w^{\rm sf}_t\rho_0\,\mathrm{d}U\le\int F\rho_0\,\mathrm{d}U$ for gauge-invariant bounded Borel $F\ge0$ \YMMref{(2189)}{806}, and $0\le Z-\int\mathfrak w^{\rm sf}_t\rho_0\,\mathrm{d}U\le\mathsf R_{[D]}Z$ \YMMref{(2190)}{806}, $Z=\int\rho_0\,\mathrm{d}U$.

So the measure of the chain lies below $Z$ times the law on gauge-invariant functions (histories with a large field at a finer level, which may end in $\mathsf{In}_{[D]}$, are left out of it), and what it leaves out has a mass $\le\mathsf R_{[D]}Z$. On $\mathsf{In}_{[D]}$, which lies in the field cut (Lem.~\YMMref{113.10}{796}), the measure of the chain has the density $p=e^{\mathsf c}e^{\Phi_t}$ for $\mathsf h_D$, $\mathsf c$ a complex number (Prop.~\YMMref{114.2}{801}), and there $|\Phi_t|\le\mathsf O_D:=(\ell L^D)^3[\frac32c_\rho^2A_0^2(\log x_{[D]})^{2\mathfrak p_0}+C_{\rm old}\frac L{L-1}E_0]$: the bound \YMMref{(2161)}{796} of the action on a field cut, at the radius $c_\rho\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$ and the weight $x_{[D]}$, gives the first term, because $\mathsf t\,\varepsilon(\mathsf t)^2=A_0^2(\log\mathsf t)^{2\mathfrak p_0}$, and the bound $\mathsf m^S_t$ \YMMref{(2179)}{803} of the added action (equation~\YMMref{(2180)}{803}) gives the second; $\mathsf O_D$ reads $D$ and not $K$.

A complex density of a positive measure is $\ge0$ almost everywhere; so $p=e^{{\rm Re}\,\mathsf c}e^{{\rm Re}\,\Phi_t}$ lies in $e^{{\rm Re}\,\mathsf c}[e^{-\mathsf O_D},e^{\mathsf O_D}]$, and its mass, which lies in $[(1-\mathsf R_{[D]})Z,Z]$, puts $e^{{\rm Re}\,\mathsf c}/Z$ between $(1-\mathsf R_{[D]})e^{-\mathsf O_D}/\mathsf h_D(\mathsf{In}_{[D]})$ and $e^{\mathsf O_D}/\mathsf h_D(\mathsf{In}_{[D]})$: the constant $\mathsf c$, the sum of the vacuum energies of the steps, drops out. For a gauge-invariant Borel $F$ with $0\le F\le1$ on the fields of the depth $D$, $F\circ\mathcal M^t$ is gauge invariant, the block map being covariant, and this gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
\kappa_D\int_{\mathsf{In}_{[D]}}F\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf h_D\ \le\ \int F\,\mathrm{d}\mu^K_D\ \le\ \bar\kappa_D\int_{\mathsf{In}_{[D]}}F\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf h_D+\mathsf R_{[D]},\qquad\\
\kappa_D=\frac{(1-\mathsf R_{[D]})e^{-2\mathsf O_D}}{\mathsf h_D(\mathsf{In}_{[D]})},\quad\\
\bar\kappa_D=\frac{e^{2\mathsf O_D}}{\mathsf h_D(\mathsf{In}_{[D]})},
\end{gathered}
\]
the right inequality by \YMMref{(2189)}{806} at $1-F$ together with \YMMref{(2190)}{806}; at $F=\mathbf 1_{\mathsf{In}_{[D]}}$, $\mu^K_D(\mathsf{In}_{[D]})\ge1-\mathsf R_{[D]}$. For a Borel set $E$, $\mu^K_D(E)=\int\bar{\mathbf 1}_E\,\mathrm{d}\mu^K_D$ with the mean $\bar{\mathbf 1}_E$ of $\mathbf 1_E$ over the gauge group, the law being gauge invariant, while $\mathsf{In}_{[D]}$ and $\mathsf h_D$ are gauge invariant; so the floor $\mu^K_D(E)\ge\kappa_D\mathsf h_D(E\cap\mathsf{In}_{[D]})$ and the upper bound $\mu^K_D(E)\le\bar\kappa_D\mathsf h_D(E\cap\mathsf{In}_{[D]})+\mathsf R_{[D]}$ hold for all Borel $E$, free of $K$, and for the limit law, the laws converging on every Borel set (Cor.~\textup{\ref{IV-62-66}}).

\emph{The thick vortex.} On the bonds $c$ of the depth $D$ let $n(c)=\#(c\cap\mathsf S)$, let $j_0$ be an integer cycle carried by the dual bonds of the rim with $j_0\equiv dn$ modulo $2$ (the rim, with an even number of its dual bonds at every dual site, is a union of closed dual paths, which are oriented), and $\mathsf r=\lfloor L^{D-d}/4\rfloor$. The translates $\tau_vj_0$ by the $(2\mathsf r+1)^3$ lattice vectors $v$ of a box of radius $\mathsf rL^{-D}$ differ from $j_0$ by coboundaries $d\beta_v$, $\beta_v$ carried within the distance $<L^{-d}$ from the rim: with the prism $(\mathsf{pr}_\lambda j)(x;\mu)=j(x;\lambda\mu)$, which takes functions on plaquettes to functions on bonds and functions on cubes to functions on plaquettes, $d\,\mathsf{pr}_\lambda j+\mathsf{pr}_\lambda dj=\tau_\lambda j-j$ and $dj_0=0$, summed along a path to $v$.

With $\varphi$ the mean of the $\pi\beta_v$, $\omega$ the mean of the $\pi\tau_vj_0$, $\theta=\pi n+\varphi$ and $V^1_c=e^{i\theta(c)\sigma_3}$: $d\theta=\omega+2\pi\mathsf k$ with $\mathsf k$ integer, so $\partial V^1(p)=e^{i\omega_p\sigma_3}$, and $|\omega_p|\le\pi n_{\mathsf S}(2\mathsf r+1)^{-2}\le16\pi n_{\mathsf S}L^{-2(D-d)}$, as a segment of the rim normal to $p$ meets at most $2\mathsf r+1$ of the translates of $p$; the rim misses $\mathcal R$, so it keeps the distance $\ge L^{-d}$ from it (the closed cubes of side $L^{-d}$ about sites that touch a dual bond of $\Lambda_{d,\ell}$ in the rim cover its neighbourhood of that radius, and none of them belongs to $\mathcal R$), and on the bonds of $\mathcal R$, $\varphi=0$ and $V^1=\bar\xi$.

Counted in $\Lambda_{d,\ell}$, $n_{\mathsf S}$ is at most the number $3(\ell L^d)^3$ of all its dual bonds; so for $D$ so large that $48\pi(\ell L^d)^3L^{-2(D-d)}\le\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$, which holds for large $D$ as $\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$ decays only like $L^{-D/2}$ up to logarithms, the thick vortex of every flip has $\varpi(V^1)\le\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$: it is a small field, and one $D$ serves all surfaces. \emph{The common part.} Let $\eta=\frac14\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$ and ${\rm vol}(\eta)$ the Haar measure of $\{g\in G:|g-\mathbf 1|<\eta\}$. If every bond of a field $W$ is within $\eta$ of $\mathbf 1$, then $\varpi(W)<4\eta<2\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$ and $\varpi(V^1W)<\varpi(V^1)+4\eta\le2\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$, by the bound of a product of four: $W$ and $V^1W$ (bondwise product) are small fields, and $(V^1W)|_{\mathcal R}=\bar\xi\,W|_{\mathcal R}$.

By the floor, the law $\mu_{\mathcal R}$ of the block fields of $\mathcal R$ at the depth $D$ dominates the measure $\kappa_D\mathsf g(w)\,\mathrm{d}w$, $\mathsf g(w)$ the Haar measure of the continuations of $w$ to small fields; on the configurations $w$ of $\mathcal R$ within $\eta$ of $\mathbf 1$, $\mathsf g(w)$ and $\mathsf g(\bar\xi w)$ are $\ge c_\eta={\rm vol}(\eta)^{3(\ell L^D)^3-n_{\mathcal R}}$, $n_{\mathcal R}$ the number of the bonds of $\mathcal R$ at the depth $D$ (continue $w$ by bonds within $\eta$ of $\mathbf 1$, and $\bar\xi w$ by the same bonds times those of $V^1$); so $\theta_0=\kappa_Dc_\eta\mathbf 1_{\{|w_c-\mathbf 1|<\eta\ \forall c\}}\,\mathrm{d}w$ lies below $\mu_{\mathcal R}$ and below $\bar\xi_*\mu_{\mathcal R}$, for every flip of a surface whose rim misses $\mathcal R$ and at every cutoff $K\ge D+1$, and in the limit; it reads no surface and no cutoff, and its mass $\varkappa_D=\kappa_D{\rm vol}(\eta)^{3(\ell L^D)^3}$ reads $D$ alone.

The block map from the depth $D$ to the depth $d$, which reads on the bonds of $\mathcal R$ the bonds of $\mathcal R$ alone and turns $\bar\xi$ at the depth $D$ into $\bar\xi$ at the depth $d$ by the first clause of (g), carries this down. Then $\mu_{\mathcal R}\wedge\bar\xi_*\mu_{\mathcal R}$ has mass $\ge\varkappa_D$, which is the bound in total variation; for odd $F$ with values in $[-1,1]$, $\int F\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{\mathcal R}=\frac12\int F\,d(\mu_{\mathcal R}-\bar\xi_*\mu_{\mathcal R})$ lies in $[\varkappa_D-1,1-\varkappa_D]$; and for flip-invariant $\Phi$, since $\mu\ge\frac12(\theta_0+\bar\xi_*\theta_0)$ and $W_C\circ\bar\xi=-W_C$,
$$\int|W_C-\Phi|\,\mathrm{d}\mu\ge\frac12\int\bigl(|W_C-\Phi|+|W_C+\Phi|\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}\theta_0\ge\int|W_C|\,\mathrm{d}\theta_0=\mathsf m_C>0,$$
$|W_C|$ being near $1$ on the configurations near $1$; the same for ${\rm sign}\,W_C$. \emph{Densities.} If $\mathsf h_d(E)=0$, the preimage of $E$ under the block map from the depth $D$ is Haar-null by Lem.~\ref{C-363-26}, and the upper bound found with the floor gives $\mu_d(E)\le\mathsf R_{[D]}$ for every large $D$, so $\mu_d(E)=0$. \emph{The ceiling.} On the open set $X_0$ of full Haar measure of Lem.~\ref{C-363-24}(b), which has full $\mu$-measure, the four bricks with their overlaps determine a configuration up to a gauge transformation and one flip; Lem.~\ref{C-363-24}(b) with $\mathsf H=\mathbb Z_2$, $C_\kappa=C$ for the non-trivial character, gives $F=\Phi_0+\Phi_1u$ with $\Phi_i$ measurable for the bricks; for bricks three sites thick the cubes generate the bricks by the same lemma; the block field of a coarser depth in $\mathcal R$ is a function of that of the depth $d$ in $\mathcal R$.

Lem.~\ref{C-363-24}(c) gives the adjoint loop. \emph{The commutant.} $\mathfrak L$ is maximal abelian on $\mathfrak h$, the space of the gauge-invariant classes of $L^2(\mu)$, the density $\rho$ being chosen gauge invariant; $\mathfrak E$ is its part fixed by the flip $\alpha$; on $Y=\{\rho>0\}\cap\alpha\{\rho>0\}$ the flip is implemented by $v$, a partial isometry with $v^2=e$ and $vM_Fv=M_{F\circ\alpha}e$, and on the rest of $\{\rho>0\}$ the flip moves no mass inside; so $\mathfrak E'=\mathfrak L+\mathfrak Lv$, isomorphic to $L^\infty(Y_1)\oplus L^\infty(Y\cap\{u=1\})\otimes M_2(\mathbb C)$, $Y_1=\{\rho>0\}\setminus Y$; $vu=-uv$, and $v\ne0$ because $\mu(Y)\ge\varkappa_D$: the measure $\mu\wedge\alpha_*\mu$, of the density $\min\{\rho,\rho\circ\alpha\}$, vanishes off $Y$ and lies above $\theta_0$.

For this last point $\alpha$ is realised as the flip of a surface whose rim misses $\mathcal R$, at the depth $d+1$. In the units of $\Lambda_{d,\ell}$ let $y_0=(b_1+1,b_2+1)$, a site of the hole ($b_i'-b_i\ge2$), and $y_1=(a_1'+1,b_2+1)$, a site beyond $Q$ ($a_1'-a_1\le N-2$); let $\mathsf S_1$ be the flat sheet of $\Lambda_{d+1,\ell}$ in the plane $x_2=b_2+1+\frac1{2L}$ from the straight closed dual line of $\Lambda_{d+1,\ell}$ in the direction $3$ over $y_0+\frac1{2L}(1,1)$ to the one over $y_1+\frac1{2L}(1,1)$, across the arm of the ring at $x_1=b_1'$. Each line lies over the open square of side $1$ about $y_0$ or $y_1$, which meets no closed cube of $\mathcal R$: the rim misses $\mathcal R$; and $C$ crosses $\mathsf S_1$ once. $\mathcal R$ is a union of closed cubes of side $L^{-(d+1)}$ about sites of $\Lambda_{d+1,\ell}$, $L$ being odd; so the first half of (i) and (g) hold for $\mathsf S_1$ at the depth $d+1$.

The block map from the depth $d+1$ to the depth $d$ reads on the bonds of $\mathcal R$ the bonds of $\mathcal R$ alone, and by the first clause of (g), no plaquette in $\mathcal R$ being pierced by the rim, it turns the flip of $\mathsf S_1$ into the sign field $(-1)^{\#(c\cap\mathsf S_1)}$ on the bonds $c$ of $\mathcal R$ at the depth $d$; this sign field is closed on the plaquettes of the bricks and odd on $C$, so it differs from $\alpha$ by a coboundary, which acts trivially on the gauge-invariant functions. Hence $\theta_0$, carried down from the depth $d+1$, lies below $\mu$ and below $\alpha_*\mu$, and its mass is $\varkappa_D$. This holds for every ring admitted, $D$ and $\varkappa_D$ being those of the first half of (i) at the depth $d+1$.

If besides $b_i'-b_i\ge3$ $(i=1,2)$ and $a_i'-a_i\le N-3$ for one $i$, say $i=1$, a sheet of $\Lambda_{d,\ell}$ itself serves as well, with $D$ and $\varkappa_D$ at the depth $d$: in the units of $\Lambda_{d,\ell}$, the flat strip $\{x_2=b_2+\frac32,\ b_1+\frac32\le x_1\le a_1'+\frac32\}$ between the straight closed dual lines in the direction $3$ over $(b_1+\frac32,b_2+\frac32)$ and over $(a_1'+\frac32,b_2+\frac32)$. A closed cube of side $1$ about a site meets such a line only if the site lies in one of the four columns of sites nearest to the line, and these columns hold no site of $\mathcal R$: about the first line they lie over $b_1+1,b_1+2$ and $b_2+1,b_2+2$, in the hole, as $b_i+2<b_i'$; about the second they lie over $a_1'+1,a_1'+2$ in the direction $1$, beyond $Q$, as $a_1'+2<a_1+N$.

So the four cubes about each line, at every height, are free, and the rim of the strip misses $\mathcal R$; $C$ crosses the strip once, on its side $x_1=b_1'$, as $b_1<b_1+\frac32<b_1'<a_1'+\frac32$ and $b_2<b_2+\frac32<b_2'$; the flip of the strip is closed on the plaquettes of the bricks and odd on $C$, so it differs from $\alpha$ by a coboundary, and the first half of (i) at the depth $d$ puts the measure $\theta_0$ of that depth below $\mu$ and below $\alpha_*\mu$. \emph{The vortex line.} At the cutoff $K$ the flip of the block fields of $\mathcal R$ is the insertion of the closed vortex line $\partial\mathsf S_1$: (g) at the depth $d+1$, for the functions of the block fields of $\mathcal R$ at the depth $d+1$ that factor through the block map, together with the covariance just used, gives $\mu^K\circ\alpha=x_K\mu^K$ with $x_K=\mathbb E_K[X_K\,|\,V]$, $X_K$ the ratio of the twisted to the untwisted weight, at every $K$; so $x_K\cdot x_K\circ\alpha=1$, $v_KF=x_K^{1/2}F\circ\alpha$ is a self-adjoint unitary, and, with $\rho_K$ the density of $\mu^K$ for Haar measure (Lem.~\ref{C-363-26}), $|\langle F,v_KF'\rangle-\langle F,vF'\rangle|\le\sup|F|\sup|F'|\int|\sqrt{\rho_K\,\rho_K\circ\alpha}-\sqrt{\rho\,\rho\circ\alpha}|\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf h$, which the Schwarz inequality bounds by $2\sqrt2\sup|F|\sup|F'|$ times the square root of the total variation between $\mu^K$ and $\mu$, at most $\sum_{K'\ge K}\mathfrak o_{K'}$.

\emph{Wide rings.} Let moreover the hole be at least three bonds wide in both directions, and the ring be of positive height and lie in an open ball of radius $<\ell/4$. Then a sheet of $\Lambda_{d,\ell}$ itself realises $\alpha$: in the units of $\Lambda_{d,\ell}$, the flat sheet $\mathsf S$ in the plane $x_2=b_2+\frac32$ from the straight closed dual line in the direction $3$ over the centre $(b_1+\frac32,b_2+\frac32)$ of four cubes of the hole (here the width three is used) to the one over the centre of four cubes beyond the ring on the same row (for which the ball leaves room) has its rim off $\mathcal R$ and crosses $C$ once. Let $\xi^{(D)}$ be its flip at the depth $D$, $\pi_D$ the limit law of the block fields of $\mathcal R$ at the depth $D$, so that $\pi_d=\mu$, and $\Phi_D$ the block map from these fields to those at the depth $d$; by the first clause of (g), $\Phi_D\circ\xi^{(D)}=\bar\xi\circ\Phi_D$ with the flip $\bar\xi$ of $\mathsf S$ at the depth $d$, which differs from $\alpha$ by a coboundary; as $\mu$ is invariant under gauge transformations, we take $\alpha=\bar\xi$ here.

We show that $\mu(\alpha A)=0$ gives $\mu(A)=0$ for a Borel set $A$ of the block fields of $\mathcal R$ at the depth $d$.

(1) \emph{From the measure to the fields.} Let $\mathcal G_D$ be the set of the $V\in\mathsf{In}_{[D]}$ whose flipped restriction $\xi^{(D)}V|_{\mathcal R}$ continues to a field of $\mathsf{In}_{[D]}$. If $\mu(\alpha A)=0$, then $\mu(A)\le1-\mu_D(\mathcal G_D)+\mathsf R_{[D]}$. Indeed, with $\tilde A=\Phi_D^{-1}A$, $\pi_D(\xi^{(D)}\tilde A)=\mu(\alpha A)=0$; by the floor, $\int_{\xi^{(D)}\tilde A}q_D\,\mathrm{d}w=0$, $q_D(w)$ the Haar measure of the continuations of $w$ into $\mathsf{In}_{[D]}$, and $q_D>0$ exactly on the projection $\mathsf{Pr}_D$ of the open set $\mathsf{In}_{[D]}$ to the bonds of $\mathcal R$; so $\tilde A\cap\xi^{(D)}\mathsf{Pr}_D$ is Haar-null. The fields of $\mathcal G_D$ whose restriction to $\mathcal R$ lies in $\tilde A$ have it in $\tilde A\cap\xi^{(D)}\mathsf{Pr}_D$; they form a Haar-null set, of $\mu_D$-measure $\le\mathsf R_{[D]}$ by the upper bound; the others with the restriction in $\tilde A$ lie off $\mathcal G_D$.

(2) \emph{Insertion of a straight line into a small field.} In units of $L^{-D}$ let $\mathsf l_P$ be the straight closed dual line in the direction $3$ over a dual point $P$ of the $(1,2)$-plane, $\varrho_1\ge1$ an integer with $2\varrho_1+4<\ell L^D$, $\mathcal T$ the sites whose horizontal part lies within the sup-distance $\varrho_1+\frac32$ of $P$ (the tube), $s$ a sign field with $(ds)_p=-1$ exactly at the plaquettes with corners in $\mathcal T$ that $\mathsf l_P$ pierces, and $V$ a field with $|\partial V(p)-\mathbf 1|\le\delta_0$ at the plaquettes with corners in $\mathcal T$. Then there is a field $V'$ with $V'_c=s_cV_c$ on every bond that has not both ends in $\mathcal T$, $|\partial V'(p)-\mathbf 1|\le6\varrho_1^{-2}+3\delta_0$ at the plaquettes with all corners in $\mathcal T$, and $\partial V'(p)=(ds)_p\partial V(p)$ at all the others.

Idea: take an axial gauge $\gamma$ of $\mathcal T$, $\mathbf 1$ on the spanning tree made of all the bonds in the direction $3$ at a corner $o$ of the unit plaquette centred at $P$ but one, one line in the direction $1$ through $o$ in each layer, and all the bonds in the direction $2$, the holonomy $\Upsilon$ around the torus along the bonds in the direction $3$ at $o$ being made diagonal by a constant gauge transformation; then, $x$ measured from $o$, a bond in the direction $1$ at $x$ is within $|x_2|\delta_0$ of $\mathbf 1$, and a bond in the direction $3$ at $x$ is $\mathsf Y_x\Upsilon_x$ with $\Upsilon_x\in\{\mathbf 1,\Upsilon\}$ and $\mathsf Y_x$ within $|x|_1\delta_0$ of $\mathbf 1$. For positively oriented bonds put $V'_c=s_c\gamma(c_-)^{-1}e^{-i\varsigma_c\sigma_3}\gamma(c_-)V_c$ on the bonds with both ends in $\mathcal T$, with the profile $\varsigma_c=(1-f_c)\vartheta_c$ on the horizontal bonds, $\vartheta_c$ half the signed angle that $c$ subtends at $P$, $f_c=\min\{1,(r_c^2-\frac14)/\varrho_1^2\}$, $r_c$ the sup-distance of the midpoint of $c$ from $P$, and $\varsigma_c=0$ on the vertical bonds; define the values on reversed bonds by inversion.

Then $d\varsigma=\pi$ at the pierced plaquettes, which takes away the sign of $ds$ there, and $|d\varsigma|\le6\varrho_1^{-2}$ at the other horizontal ones, as $d\vartheta=0$ there: three terms $\pm(f_{c'}-f_c)\vartheta_c$ remain, each $\le\frac{2r}{\varrho_1^2}\cdot\frac1r$, $r\ge1$ the sup-distance of the centre of the plaquette from $P$; this is the source of the $6$. The rotations $e^{-i\varsigma_c\sigma_3}$ commute with one another and with $\Upsilon$. With $o=(0,0)$ and $P=(\frac12,\frac12)$ in a horizontal layer, the half-angle bound is $|\vartheta_c|\,|c_--o|_1\le1$ for the positively oriented horizontal bonds. It is paired with the gauge error measured from the same $o$. For a horizontal plaquette the direction-$2$ bonds are $\mathbf1$, leaving one commutator with a direction-$1$ bond. For a vertical plaquette first factor out the original plaquette product; the remaining error is one commutator with $\mathsf Y_x$ in $\mathsf Y_x\Upsilon_x$, since the inserted rotations commute with $\Upsilon_x$. Its cost is at most $2\delta_0$ in either case. Adding the original plaquette error $\delta_0$ gives $3\delta_0$. At the boundary $f_c=1$, so the insertion matches the prescribed exterior field; no boundary value of the gauge at $o$ is required.

(3) \emph{The witness.} Let $\varrho_1=\frac12(L^{D-d}-5)$. At the depth $D$ the hole holds a square of $(2\varrho_1+4)^2$ sites about a dual point $P_1$ of the $(1,2)$-plane, and beyond the ring, on its row, there is a dual point $P_2$ whose square of that size misses $Q$ (the ball leaves room); the tubes $\mathcal T_1,\mathcal T_2$ over them are disjoint and hold no site of $\mathcal R$. Let $s=-1$ on the bonds in the direction $2$ that cross the flat strip between the vertical lines over $P_1$ and $P_2$, and $s=1$ elsewhere: $(ds)_p=-1$ exactly at the plaquettes that the two lines pierce. On the bonds of $\mathcal R$ at the depth $D$, $s$ and $\xi^{(D)}$ are closed on the plaquettes of the bricks and odd on the loop around the hole, so $s=\xi^{(D)}dz$ there, with signs $z$ on the sites of $\mathcal R$ (Lem.~\ref{C-363-24}(b) for the four bricks, whose group $Z/B$ is $\mathbb Z_2$ and is read on that loop).

Let $\theta'<\frac23$ and $D$ be so large that $6\varrho_1^{-2}+3\theta'\varepsilon(x_{[D]})<2\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$, as $\varrho_1^{-2}$ is of the order of $L^{-2(D-d)}$ and $\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$ of the order of $L^{-D/2}$ up to logarithms. If $\varpi(V)<\theta'\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$, $V$ is a small field, and the insertion in both tubes with $\delta_0=\theta'\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$ gives $V'$ with $V'=sV$ off the tubes, so on the bonds of $\mathcal R$, and $\varpi(V')<2\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$; the gauge transform of $V'$ by $z$, continued by $1$, is a small field equal to $\xi^{(D)}V$ on the bonds of $\mathcal R$. So $\{\varpi<\theta'\varepsilon(x_{[D]})\}\subset\mathcal G_D$.

(4) \emph{The tail at a fraction of the threshold.} For integers $n\ge0$ and $D'=D-n$ with $x_{[D']}\ge\mathsf t_\natural$, let $\Theta_n=4B_3L^{-3n/2}+2\frac{C_HA_1}{A_0}\sum_{j<n}L^{-3j/2}$, where $B_3\ge1$ and $C_H\ge1$ are the constants of the list of Thm.~\YMMref{D}{8} that enter the bound of the background over a small field and the contraction of the backgrounds from one level to the next (Thm.~\YMMref{E}{10} and the curvature comparison in the proof of Lem.~\YMMref{113.10}{796}). Then $\mu^K_D\{\varpi\ge\Theta_n\varepsilon(x_{[D]})\}\le\mathsf R_{[D']}$ for $K\ge D+1$, and in the limit. Run the chain with its top level at the depth $D'$. On the histories with $\mathfrak w^{\rm sf}\ne0$ the field at the depth $D'$ lies in the inner ball, and the field of every finer level lies in the field cut and is the field over the next coarser one moved by a fluctuation from the ball of the step; so the regularity numbers $\mathsf m$ of the backgrounds obey $\mathsf m<2B_3\varepsilon(x_{[D']})$ at the top (Thm.~\YMMref{E}{10}) and $\mathsf m_k\le L^{-2}\mathsf m_{k+1}+C_H\delta(x_k)$ from the level $k+1$ to the finer level $k$ (the proof of Lem.~\YMMref{113.10}{796}).

Summed down the $n$ levels, with $\varepsilon(x_{[D-j]})\le L^{j/2}\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$ and the same for $\delta$, this gives $\mathsf m<\frac12\Theta_n\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$ at the depth $D$, and a field whose background has the regularity number below $\mathsf m$ has its plaquettes below $2\mathsf m$ (as in the inclusions \YMMref{(2159)}{796}): $\varpi<\Theta_n\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$. The other histories have the mass $\le\mathsf R_{[D']}Z$ by \YMMref{(2189)}{806} at $1-F$ and \YMMref{(2190)}{806}, $F$ the indicator of $\{\varpi(\mathcal M^{K-D}U)\ge\Theta_n\varepsilon(x_{[D]})\}$; the limit follows.

(5) \emph{The end.} Let $n_0$ be the least integer with $L^{3n_0/2}\ge80B_3$; it is fixed by $L$ and $B_3$, and chosen so that $\Theta_{n_0}<\frac35$: the first term of $\Theta_{n_0}$ is $\le\frac1{20}$, and the condition $A_0\ge4B_3C_HA_1$, one of the conditions on $A_0$ written in the proof of Lem.~\ref{lem:rarity-lowered-choice}, with $B_3\ge1$ and $L\ge13$, makes the second $\le\frac12(1-13^{-3/2})^{-1}<0.52$. For $D$ so large that $x_{[D-n_0]}\ge\mathsf t_\natural$, $\mathsf R_{[D]}<1$ and $6\varrho_1^{-2}<\frac15\varepsilon(x_{[D]})$, (1) and (3) at $\theta'=\frac35$ give $\mu(A)\le\mu_D\{\varpi\ge\frac35\varepsilon(x_{[D]})\}+\mathsf R_{[D]}$, and (4) at $n=n_0$ bounds the first term by $\mathsf R_{[D-n_0]}$. So $\mathsf R_{[D-n_0]}$ bounds the mass of the histories that the chain with its top level at the depth $D-n_0$ leaves out, this chain controlling the plaquettes at the depth $D$, and $\mathsf R_{[D]}$ comes from the upper bound in (1). Both tend to $0$ as $D\to\infty$, and $\mu(A)$ reads no $D$: $\mu(A)=0$. With $\alpha A$ in the place of $A$ the converse holds; so the law and its flip have the same null sets, $e=1$, $v$ is a self-adjoint unitary, and with the ceiling, whose hypothesis on the corners the positive height meets, $\mathfrak L=\mathfrak E\oplus\mathfrak Eu$ is a grading by $\mathbb Z_2$.

\emph{A band that winds.} The flip $\bar\xi_1$ of a band $\mathbb Z/N\times I_2\times I_3$ is the restriction of a flip of the torus, a symmetry of the law: $v$ is unitary, odd and even functions are orthogonal, $\mathfrak Eu_1\ne0$ as $u_1^2=1$, and the cubes of the band generate $\mathfrak E$ by Lem.~\ref{C-363-24}(b) with the cubes as boxes; the only closed sign fields on the cubes of the band modulo coboundaries are $1$ and the winding one.

\subsubsection{Scope of the conclusions}

Thm.~\ref{C-363-4}(a)--(g) concern the centred functionals of volume-first limits and their components, for which the proof uses a periodic lattice; for other limits of periodic Gibbs states only (h) is asserted. The proofs of Thms.~\ref{C-363-3} and~\ref{C-363-4} use no energy bound beyond the polynomial one of the reconstruction, no gap, no uniqueness of the vacuum of $\sigma$ and no rate of clustering. Thm.~\ref{C-363-5}(d) bounds from below the norms of the field at one instant and of one Euclidean slab. Thm.~\ref{C-363-7}(g)--(i) are statements on the commutative algebras of the Euclidean block fields at a fixed depth on one torus.


\section{A continuum Langevin process}\label{supp:C-367-1}

Fix the physical torus and the label $b$, and keep the invariant
thread law obtained from the compatible block-field marginals.
Put $A_K=\sum_pa_p$, and write $\mu^K$ for the Wilson probability
measure of {\cite[\S{}2]{YMM2}} on this fixed torus. On the cutoff lattice the stationary Wilson Langevin
process has generator and Dirichlet form
\[
 \mathcal L_K=a_K^{-1}\sum_{b,\alpha}(\partial_b^\alpha)^2
       -a_K^{-1}\beta\,\partial A_K\cdot\partial,
 \qquad
 \mathcal E_K(F)=a_K^{-1}\int|\partial F|^2\,\mathrm{d}\mu^K.
\]
The derivatives are along the three orthonormal colour directions
at each link.

\begin{sketch}[A nonfrozen reversible Markov limit]\label{supp:C-367-2}
Subsequences of the stationary lattice processes converge on
gauge-invariant cylinder observables to a nonconstant stationary
reversible Markov process on block-field threads. Its closed
Dirichlet form is the strong-and-weak limit of the lattice
forms, and its semigroup mixes to the invariant thread law.
The result is on a fixed torus and does not identify the limits
from different subsequences.
\end{sketch}

\paragraph{Sketch of the argument.}
Separate the fine field from a fixed block field using the
small-field chain. On each fluctuation box the conditional
Hamiltonian is strictly convex after the controlled nonlinear
remainder is included. The conditional law therefore has
Poincar\'e and logarithmic Sobolev bounds. Differentiate the
conditional expectation defining one averaging step. The
response of the background transports the coarse gradient,
while the fluctuation covariance controls the additional term.
The resulting multiplicative losses have the form
$1+C\delta(L^db)$, and their product is finite because
$\sum_d\delta(L^db)<\infty$.

At a selected coarse depth $n$, retain a connected region of
regular fields. Its finite-dimensional inequality supplies
the remaining top-scale bound. The small-field chain omits
mass $r_n\to0$, which appears as a defect rather than a
uniform spectral-gap constant:
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(F)\le C_n\mathcal E(F)
                         +r_n\operatorname{osc}(F)^2.
\]
Conditional versions control the fine field uniformly in the
cutoff; the constant $C_n$ at the top can depend on the torus.

These bounds give compactness for uniformly bounded observables
of bounded energy. Along a process subsequence, they provide the
lower bound for weakly convergent functions and recovery
sequences converging strongly. Resolvents and semigroups then
converge strongly, identifying a closed Markovian limiting
form and the reversible Markov process it generates. Let $Y_n$ be the selected coarse block field and take its plaquette
observable $F=a_p(Y_n)$. Apply the coarse-gradient estimate to a recovery
sequence for $F$. Lower semicontinuity of its Dirichlet integral on the
regular coarse-field set gives $\mathcal E(F)>0$. The limiting semigroup
therefore moves this observable, so the process is not frozen.

For mixing, fix $n$ in the weak variance inequality and let time
increase. Its exponential term disappears, leaving the defect
$r_n\operatorname{osc}(F)^2$. Now increase $n$ to remove that
defect. The analogous entropy estimate gives relaxation of
bounded probability densities in total variation on the
invariant algebra.

This order of limits matters. The argument supplies constants
uniform in the fine cutoff, not constants uniform in the torus
volume. Stronger gauge estimates across several block levels
would make the top-scale constants more explicit; the qualitative
conclusion above does not require them.




\subsection{Continuum limits of the lattice Langevin dynamics}\label{C-367-1}

At a fixed physical label and on a fixed torus, the Wilson Langevin
processes have subsequential limits on threads of block fields. We prove
that each limit is a nonconstant stationary reversible Markov process on
the gauge-invariant $\sigma$-algebra. The lattice Dirichlet forms converge
in the strong and weak sense. Conditional Poincar\'e and logarithmic
Sobolev inequalities control the fine field; a connected coarse-scale
region then gives weak inequalities with defects tending to zero. These
estimates imply mixing and entropy relaxation. Their constants may
depend on the fixed torus, and the result does not identify the processes
obtained along different subsequences.

We also study observables regularised by the Wilson gradient flow. The
finite-cutoff flow identities and upper bounds use no probabilistic
assumption. The moment estimates use the admissibility conclusion
\textup{(Adm)} of Prop.~\ref{C-367-12}, concerning conditional layer means and colour covariances.
Identifying the continuum flow limits requires the approximation step described below.
The nonlinear defect bounds are proved in Lem.~\ref{C-367-14}.
Lem.~\ref{lem:short-time-lower-propagation} proves lower propagation
on a regular time interval; Prop.~\ref{C-367-23}(c) applies it
on the interval of the short-time flow theorem and extends the lower
bound to every final time by current transport and the integrated
curvature. These estimates do not complete the continuum-flow identification, whose remaining work is described under \textup{(Flow approximation)}.

The generator requires separate treatment. Some bounded flowed
observables have generator images whose norms grow exponentially in the
inverse square of the spacing. We therefore first insert condenser
cutoffs, pass to the continuum limit, and then remove the cutoffs.
The resulting generator identity is distributional.

\subsubsection{The lattice process and its limiting objects}

$G=\mathrm{SU}(2)$; $\mathfrak g$ is the space of hermitian traceless $2\times2$ matrices, $\langle X,Y\rangle=\frac12\mathrm{tr}\,XY$, $|X|=\langle X,X\rangle^{1/2}$, so that $X^2=|X|^2\mathbf 1$ and $e^{iX}\in G$; $\mathsf d$ is the geodesic distance of $G$, the unit sphere $S^3$, with $\mathsf d(e^{iA},\mathbf 1)=|A|$ for $|A|\le\pi$ and $|g-h|=2\sin\frac12\mathsf d(g,h)$. The numbers $L$, $a_d=L^{-d}$, $\ell=2L^m$, the torus $T_\ell=\mathbb R^3/\ell\mathbb Z^3$ of side $\ell$, the lattices $\Lambda_{d,\ell}=a_d\mathbb Z^3/\ell\mathbb Z^3\subset T_\ell$ (Section~\YMMref{3}{13}) and the averaging map $\mathcal M$ (equations~\YMMref{(37)--(39)}{20}) have the conventions just stated. The label $\mathsf b$ and setting (E) are those of \S\ref{sec:cutoff-calibration}: the constants of the construction are an admissible choice $\varsigma=(\sigma^-,\gamma)$ of the canonical list of constants and conditions (\S\ref{sec:cutoff-calibration}), subject to the conditions (Th1) and (Th2) of \S\ref{sec:cutoff-calibration}, with $\gamma$ the fixed reference-coupling ceiling; the label satisfies $\mathsf b\ge\gamma^{-2}$ and $M\,R(\mathsf b)\le L^m$, with the cube size $M=L^{m'}$ and the function $R$ of \S\ref{sec:cutoff-calibration}, $R(x)$ the least power $L^j$, $j\ge0$, that is not smaller than a fixed power of $\log x$; and $\beta=L^K\mathsf b$, so that $\mathsf b=a_K\beta$.

$\Omega_d$ is the set of configurations on $\Lambda_{d,\ell}$, $dV$ (on $\Omega_K$: $dU$) its Haar probability measure, $V^u(b)=u(b_-)V(b)u(b_+)^{-1}$ the gauge action; invariant means gauge invariant. $\partial V(p)$ is the plaquette variable, $a_p=1-\frac12\mathrm{tr}\,\partial V(p)$, $\varpi_p=|\partial V(p)-\mathbf 1|=(2a_p)^{1/2}$, $\varpi(V)=\max_p\varpi_p$, $A_K=\sum_pa_p$, $A^a=a_K^{-1}A_K$, and $\mathcal O(f)=a_K^{-1}\sum_pf(x(p))\,a_p$ for real $f$ on $T_\ell$, $x(p)$ the barycentre of $p$. On $\Omega_K$ we write $N=\ell/a_K$ for the number of sites along an axis. Tangent vectors are real $\mathfrak g$-valued $1$-forms $X$, with the curves $s\mapsto e^{isX}V$; $\langle X,\partial F(V)\rangle=\frac d{ds}F(e^{isX}V)|_{s=0}$, $\|X\|^2=\sum_b|X(b)|^2$; $\partial_bF$ is the value of the $1$-form $\partial F$ at the bond $b$, and $\partial^\alpha_bF=\langle\sigma_\alpha,\partial_bF\rangle=\frac d{ds}F(e^{is\sigma_\alpha\delta_b}V)|_{s=0}$, with the Pauli matrices $\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3$, a basis of $\mathfrak g$ that is orthonormal for $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, and $\delta_b$ the function of the bonds that is $1$ at $b$ and $0$ at the others; $\Gamma_d(F)=a_d^{-1}|\partial F|^2$ on $\Omega_d$, and $\Gamma_d(F,F')$ is its polarisation.

The vectors $\mathrm{d}_V\lambda$, $(\mathrm{d}_V\lambda)(b)=\lambda(b_-)-\mathrm{Ad}(V(b))\lambda(b_+)$ for $\mathfrak g$-valued site functions $\lambda$, are the gauge directions at $V$; a tangent vector orthogonal to them is horizontal, and the gradient of an invariant function is horizontal. $\mathrm{osc}=\sup-\inf$.

\emph{Dynamics.} $\mu^K=Z_K^{-1}e^{-\beta A_K}dU$; $\Delta_K=a_K^{-1}\sum_{b,\alpha}(\partial_b^\alpha)^2$; $\mathcal L_K=\Delta_K-a_K^{-1}\beta\sum_b\langle\partial_bA_K,\partial_b\,\cdot\,\rangle$; $\mathcal E_K(F)=\int\Gamma_K(F)\,\mathrm{d}\mu^K$ on the closure $D(\mathcal E_K)$ of $C^\infty(\Omega_K)$, with $\mathcal E_K(F)=\infty$ off $D(\mathcal E_K)$; $P^K_t=e^{t\mathcal L_K}$, and $(U_t)_{t\in\mathbb R}$ is the stationary process. $J(U)=a_K^{-3}\partial A_K(U)$ is the current (\YMMref{9.2}{38}), $(J,J)_a=a_K^{-3}|\partial A_K|^2$; $\Phi_s$ is the gradient flow $\frac d{ds}U(b)=-ia_KJ(U)(b)U(b)$, $U_s=\Phi_sU$, $v=-a_K^{-2}\sum_b\langle\partial_bA_K,\partial_b\,\cdot\,\rangle$ its vector field, and $\Lambda_\sigma(U)=\int_0^\sigma a_K^{-2}\varpi(U_s)\,\mathrm{d}s$.

\emph{Threads and limits.} $\mathcal Y=\prod_{d\ge0}\Omega_d$ is compact and metrisable; a thread is a point $Y=(Y_d)$ of $\mathcal Y$ with $Y_d=\mathcal MY_{d+1}$ for all $d$; $\pi_{K,d}=\mathcal M^{K-d}$. The laws $\mu^K_d$ of $\pi_{K,d}U$ under $\mu^K$ converge in total variation to measures $\mu_d$, with $\mu_{d+1}\circ\mathcal M^{-1}=\mu_d$ (Cor.~\textup{\ref{IV-62-66}}), and $\mu=\mu_{\ell,\mathsf b}$ is the measure on threads with the marginals $\mu_d$. A cylinder function is $\Psi(Y_d)$, $\Psi$ bounded Borel on $\Omega_d$, and $\Psi_K=\Psi\circ\pi_{K,d}$; $L^2_{\rm inv}$ is the closure in $L^2(\mu)$ of the invariant cylinder functions, which generate the invariant $\sigma$-algebra, and $\Pi$ is the orthogonal projection onto $L^2_{\rm inv}$.

Along $K_j\to\infty$, $H_j\in L^2(\mu^{K_j})$ converge \emph{strongly} to $F\in L^2(\mu)$ if there are cylinder functions $\Psi_m\to F$ in $L^2(\mu)$ with $\lim_m\limsup_j\|H_j-\Psi_{m,K_j}\|_{L^2(\mu^{K_j})}=0$, and \emph{weakly} if $\sup_j\|H_j\|<\infty$ and $\int H_j\Psi_{K_j}\,\mathrm{d}\mu^{K_j}\to\int F\Psi\,\mathrm{d}\mu$ for every cylinder function $\Psi$. A \emph{limit} is a sequence $K_j\to\infty$ along which all means $\mathbb E\prod_i\Psi_i(\pi_{K_j,d}U_{t_i})$ of bounded Borel $\Psi_i$ converge, with its limit process $(Y_t)$ on threads; $(F,Q_tF')=\mathbb EF(Y_0)F'(Y_t)$, $\mathcal E_\star(F)=\sup_{t>0}t^{-1}(F,(1-Q_t)F)$, $A_\star$ is the operator of $\mathcal E_\star$, and the limit is frozen if $\mathcal E_\star$ vanishes on $L^2_{\rm inv}$, that is, if $Q_t=1$ on $L^2_{\rm inv}$ for all $t$ ($\mathcal E_\star$ is finite only on $L^2_{\rm inv}$, Lem.~\ref{C-367-6}(b)).

The forms converge \emph{in the strong and weak sense} if (M1) $\mathcal E_\star(F)\le\liminf_j\mathcal E_{K_j}(H_j)$ whenever $H_j\to F$ weakly, and (M2) every $F$ has $H_j\to F$ strongly with $\mathcal E_{K_j}(H_j)\to\mathcal E_\star(F)$.

\emph{The chain.} We recall the following objects of the small-field chain on one torus (Sections~\YMMref{113}{786}, \YMMref{114}{799}, \YMMref{115}{805}), which rests on the results on one step of Prop.~\ref{prop:source-entry}. $\delta(\mathsf t)=A_1\mathsf t^{-1/2}(\log\mathsf t)^{\mathfrak p_0}$, $\varepsilon=\frac{A_0}{A_1}\delta$, $\mathfrak b(\mathsf t)=\mathsf t^{1/2}\delta(\mathsf t)$, the threshold functions of equation~\YMMref{(634)}{339}, with the constants $A_0,A_1>0$ and $\mathfrak p_0\in\mathbb N$ of the construction; $\varepsilon_n=\varepsilon(L^n\mathsf b)$; $\sum_d\delta(L^d\mathsf b)<\infty$. For an integer $n\ge1$ with $L^n\mathsf b\ge\mathsf t_\natural$, $\mathsf t_\natural\ge\gamma^{-2}$ the fixed calibration of \S\ref{sec:cutoff-calibration}, a number formed from the constants alone, and for $K>n$, put $t=K-n$, so that $1\le t\le K-1$, as required of a top level in \S\ref{sec:cutoff-calibration}: level $k$ is depth $d=K-k$, $V_k=\mathcal M^kU$, $x_k=L^d\mathsf b$, so that $x_k^{-1}=a_d/\mathsf b$.

The cuts $\mathsf{In}_k\subset\mathsf{Cut}_k\subset\Omega_d$ of the definitions preceding Lem.~\YMMref{113.10}{796} are open and invariant (Lem.~\YMMref{113.10}{796}); $\mathsf{Cut}_k\subset\{\varpi<\theta_d\}$ with $\theta_d$ below; $\mathsf I_n=\mathsf{In}_t=\{\varpi<2\varepsilon_n\}\subset\Omega_n$, and $\mathsf D_n$ is the connected component of $\mathbf 1$ in $\mathsf I_n$. $\mathsf R_n$ is the number \YMMref{(2187)}{806} at the level $t=K-n$, which depends on $n$, $\ell$ and $\mathsf b$ but not on $K$; it bounds the mass of the large fields (Prop.~\textup{\YMMref{115.2}{806}}, lost-mass bound), and by \YMMref{(2187)}{806} $\mathsf R_n\le C(\ell,\mathsf b)\,L^{3n}\exp[-c'A_0^2(\log L^n\mathsf b)^{2\mathfrak p_0}]$ with the rate $c'>0$ of \S\ref{sec:cutoff-calibration} and $2\mathfrak p_0\ge2$, so that it tends to $0$ faster than every exponential in $n$.

The chain measure is $\sigma^K=Z_K^{-1}\mathfrak w^{\rm sf}_te^{-\beta A_K}dU$, with the constant $Z_K$ of $\mu^K$ and the weight of the small-field chain of level $t$, the function defined before Prop.~\YMMref{115.2}{806},
\[
\mathfrak w^{\rm sf}_t(U)=\mathbf 1_{\mathsf{In}_t}(V_t)\prod_{k=0}^{t-1}\bigl[\mathbf 1_{\mathsf{Cut}_k}\,\mathfrak G_k[x_k]\,\chi^{\rm sf}_{x_k}\bigr](V_k),
\]
where $\mathfrak G_k[x_k]$ is the gauge-fixing factor of the axial gauge on the blocks of the level $k+1$ and $\chi^{\rm sf}_{x_k}$ the fluctuation test of the step $k+1$ ({\cite[\S{}B.2]{YMM2}}); the weight is a bounded Borel function with values in $[0,\infty)$ (Prop.~\textup{\YMMref{115.2}{806}}, proof and the definitions preceding Prop.~\YMMref{115.2}{806}). So $\sigma^K$ is a positive measure of mass in $[1-\mathsf R_n,1]$ (Lem.~\ref{C-367-7}(i)), normalised by the constant of $\mu^K$ and not by its own mass; and as its weight carries gauge-fixing factors, $\sigma^K$ is not gauge invariant, and its comparisons with $\mu^K$ are made on invariant functions. $\sigma^K_d$ is its image at depth $d$, $\sigma^K_n$ the top law.

For $0\le k<t$ and $W\in\mathsf{Cut}_{k+1}$, a background $U_+$ over $W$ is any element of the minimal orbit over $W$ with $\mathcal M^kU_+$ in the axial gauge, and $V_W(B)$ is the chart of the fibre $\{\mathcal MV=W\}$ ({\cite[\S{}B.2]{YMM2}}), defined on the convex box $\{|B(b)|<\mathfrak b(x_k)\}$ of the bonds that are not pivot bonds, with $V_W(B)(b)=e^{ix_k^{-1/2}B(b)}(\mathcal M^kU_+)(b)$ there; it carries the box into $\mathsf{Cut}_k$ (Lem.~\YMMref{113.10}{796}). The fixed radii $0<\alpha_0<\alpha_1$ are two constants of the construction (Def.~\YMMref{49.1}{374} and Lem.~\YMMref{82.1}{665}, Lem.~\YMMref{82.1}{665}), free of $n$, at which the analyticity cores of the chain are taken (Def.~\YMMref{49.1}{374}); $\mathsf{Cut}_{k+1}$ lies in the class $\mathcal W_{k+1}(x_k;\alpha_0,\alpha_1)$ of the sum rule (Lem.~\YMMref{113.10}{796}).

One fluctuation integral $p_W$ is set at every $W\in\mathsf{Cut}_{k+1}$ by the chart integral $\mathsf I$ of {\cite[eq.~191]{YMM2}} at $\mathsf t=x_k$ ({\cite[Def.~B.2]{YMM2}} and equation~{\cite[eq.~191]{YMM2}}): it is the measure on the box with
\[
\int h(V_W(B))\,p_W(\,\mathrm{d}B)=\frac{\mathsf I[hF_k](W)}{\mathsf I[F_k](W)}\qquad\text{for every bounded Borel }h\text{ on }\Omega_d ,
\]
$F_k$ the integrand of the chain at the level $k$ and at the source $0$ (Prop.~\YMMref{114.2}{801}); that is, $p_W$ has on the box the density proportional to $\exp[-x_kG_W(B)+\mathsf J_W(B)]\,F_k(V_W(B))$, with the gauge-fixing form $G_W$ and the exponent $\mathsf J_W$ of the Jacobians of the chart ({\cite[\S{}B.2]{YMM2}}). The denominator vanishes at no $W\in\mathsf{Cut}_{k+1}$: on the class of the sum rule $\mathsf I[F_k]=e^{\mathsf c_{k+1}(0)}F_{k+1}\ne0$, $\mathsf c_{k+1}(0)$ the constant \YMMref{(2173)}{801} of the step (Prop.~\YMMref{114.2}{801}). $p_W$ depends on $K$, $k$ and $W$, and not on the top level; that it is a probability measure with a positive continuous density on the box, and that its images under $V_W$ form a regular conditional law of $V_k$ given $V_{k+1}=W$ under $\sigma^K$, is Lem.~\ref{C-367-7}(ii).

The tower of $H$ is $h_0=H$, $h_{k+1}(W)=\int h_k(V_W(B))\,p_W(\,\mathrm{d}B)$ at every $W\in\mathsf{Cut}_{k+1}$. For a finite measure $\nu$, $\mathrm{Ent}_\nu(f)=\inf_{c>0}\int\Xi(f,c)\,\mathrm{d}\nu$, $\Xi(x,c)=x\log\frac xc-x+c\ge0$.

\emph{Constants.} $\mathsf o_n=[2C_{\rm nl}\frac L{L-1}E_0+\frac32c_\rho^2A_0^2(\log L^n\mathsf b)^{2\mathfrak p_0}](\ell L^n)^3$, with the number $C_{\rm nl}=C'_{\rm A}+2C_{\mathrm E,0}(C_{\rm lg}+L^{4l_0})$, with $C'_{\rm A}$, $l_0$, $C_{\rm lg}$ and $C_{\mathrm E,0}$ defined exactly as in equation~\YMMref{(2163)}{798} and its following sentence, using $K_{\rm A}=K^\sharp_{\rm tw}$ and $a_{\rm A}=a^\sharp$. The proof following that equation gives the bound on the non-local action, that is, the action of a bare array at the background of a field in a cut (equation~\YMMref{(2180)}{803}). We also use the size $E_0>0$ of \S\ref{sec:step-input-conventions} and the constant $c_\rho$ of the field cuts \S\ref{sec:cutoff-calibration} (and $C_H$ defined in {\cite[\S{}P.1]{YMM2}}); $\theta_d=2c_\rho\varepsilon(L^d\mathsf b)$; $\gamma_{\rm r}\in(0,1]$ and $c_{\rm r}\ge1$ are the numbers of Thm.~\YMMref{U}{378}, entered through \S\ref{sec:step-input-conventions}, which depend on $L$ alone: the floor and the ceiling of a real reference form of the Gaussian integral of one step, from which the form of the step itself differs, in the $\ell^2$ operator norm, by at most the defect $\frac12\mathsf u_{\rm G}(LM)^{-3}\le\frac12\gamma_{\rm r}$ (the completeness (St4) of the Gaussian structure of the step, Def.~\YMMref{47.2}{359} and Thm.~\YMMref{W}{423}, with $\mathsf u_{\rm G}=4C_{\rm Str}$ of Thm.~\YMMref{U}{378} and the proof of Prop.~\YMMref{113.4}{791}); so the form of the step lies between $\frac12\gamma_{\rm r}$ and $c_{\rm r}+\frac12\gamma_{\rm r}$; $\Lambda_+=c_{\rm r}+\gamma_{\rm r}$; $C_Q$, $c_Q$, $a_Q$ are the constants defined in Lem.~\ref{lem:plain-average-remainder}, which depend only on $L$; for a $1$-form $X$ on $\Lambda_{K-j,\ell}$, $m^j_y(X)=\sum_{c'}e^{-\delta_0d(y,c'_-)}|X(c')|$, $\delta_0>0$ the rate of decay in the bounds of the response, are the averages that enter these bounds, and $\mathsf B$, $\mathsf S$ are the constants with $|\mathcal H_V(\zeta)(b)|\le\mathsf B\,m^j_y(\zeta)$ for $b_-$ in the block of $y$ and $\sum_ym^j_y(X)^2\le\mathsf S^2\|X\|^2$ (\S\ref{sec:background-step-complements}, Lem.~\ref{lem:response-current-zero}); $\mathsf M=\max\{1,\mathsf B\mathsf S\}$.

$C_{\rm P}=4C_{\rm ch}/\gamma_{\rm r}$ (Lem.~\ref{C-367-7}); $\epsilon^\flat_d=[1+(C_\flat+C_{\rm cov})\delta(L^d\mathsf b)]^2-1$ and $\Pi^\flat_n=\prod_{d>n}(1+\epsilon^\flat_d)$, finite and tending to $1$ (Prop.~\ref{C-367-9}); $C^\sigma=3\mathsf M^2\Pi^\flat_{n_{\rm a}}$. Thresholds: $n_2$ is the least integer $\ge1$ with $L^{n_2}\mathsf b\ge\mathsf t_\natural$ such that $C_{\rm Hs}\delta(L^d\mathsf b)\le\frac14\gamma_{\rm r}$ and $\theta_d\le\omega_L$ for $d\ge n_2$, with $C_{\rm Hs}$ the constant of Lem.~\ref{C-367-7}(iv) and a number $\omega_L\le(3200L^3)^{-1}$ that depends only on $L$; $n_3\ge n_2$ is the least integer such that for $d\ge n_3$ the number $\theta_d$ lies below the radius of \S\ref{sec:background-step-complements} and $2\theta_d\le\varepsilon_{\mathcal W}\alpha_0$, with the fixed radii $\alpha_0<\alpha_1$ of the chain and the number $\varepsilon_{\mathcal W}$ of Prop.~\YMMref{52.3}{433}, so that $\theta_d$ is at most the threshold $\varepsilon_{\mathcal W}\cdot\frac12\alpha_0$ of Prop.~\YMMref{52.3}{433} at the radii $(\frac12\alpha_0,\frac12\alpha_1)$; $n_{\rm a}$ is the least integer $\ge\max\{1,n_3\}$ such that for all $d\ge n_{\rm a}$: $L^d\mathsf b\ge\mathsf t_\natural$; $\theta_d\le\min\{a_Q,\varpi_{\rm db}\}$ (that $\theta_d$ lies below the radius of \S\ref{sec:background-step-complements} holds already for $d\ge n_3$); $4\delta(L^d\mathsf b)\le r_2$; $4C_{\rm db}\delta(L^d\mathsf b)\le r_1$; and $C_z\delta(L^d\mathsf b)\le\min\{\frac12r_{\rm h},\frac12,(36+6C_{\rm pz}^2)^{-1/2}\}$.

Here $\varpi_{\rm db}=r_{\mathsf y}^2/(8\pi L^3)$ and $C_{\rm db}=8L^3$ are the numbers of {\cite[Def.~B.2]{YMM2}}, $r_{\rm h}=\min\{r_{\mathrm B},\varrho^0_{\mathrm R}\}$ is the radius of holomorphy of the response in \S\ref{sec:background-step-complements}, $r_1=\min\{\frac{c_Q}{4L},\frac{c_Q}{32C_QL^4}\}$, $r_2=\frac{r_1}{8C_QL^3}$, $C_z=4C_QL^3$ and $C_{\rm pz}=24C_QL^3+128C_QL^4/c_Q$, so that these numbers depend only on $L$ and the constants of \S\ref{sec:background-step-complements}; $n''$ is the least integer $\ge n_{\rm a}$ with $\mathsf R_e\le\frac12$ for all $e\ge n''$; $n_1$ is the least $n\ge2$ with $L^{n-1}\mathsf b\ge\mathsf t_\natural$ and $4\theta_d\le(48000L^4)^{-1}$ for $d\ge n$.
\paragraph{A quantitative extension of the gauge construction.} The explicit top-scale bounds below require a compatible gauge construction across several block levels. The missing estimate, referred to as \emph{(Multiscale gauge)}, would provide finite constants $R_{\rm S},C_{\rm S}\ge1$, independent of the odd integer $L\ge13$, the side $\ell$, the integers $n,J$ and the field, with the following property. If $V\in\Omega_n$, $J\ge1$, $n-J\ge1$, $L^J\ge R_{\rm S}$, $\varpi(\mathcal M^jV)<(200L^2)^{-1}$ for $0\le j<J$, and $\frac\pi2L^J\varpi(\mathcal M^JV)\le1$, there is a periodic site gauge $u$ such that \[\mathsf d(V^u(b),\mathbf1)\le44\pi L^2\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}\varpi(\mathcal M^jV)+C_{\rm S}L^{-J}\quad\hbox{at every bond }b.\] This quantitative estimate remains to be proved. The branches (B1)(e), (B2)(d) and the explicit-top variants of (A4)(f) and (A5) below remain sketches at this estimate; the assertions using $j_1$, $w_n$ and $C^{\rm t}_n$ retain their stated hypotheses.
With $C_{\rm BG}=2\lambda_{{\rm BG},3}$ of \eqref{eq:uniform-box-gauge-constants}, $C''=1+20\pi^2C_{\rm BG}^2$, $\kappa_0=(8\pi C_{\rm BG})^{-2}$, $\vartheta_\infty=C_HA_1/((1-L^{-3/2})A_0)$, which is $<1$ under (E), and $j_1$ the least $j\ge1$ with $L^{-3j/2}c_\rho\le\min\{\frac12(1-\vartheta_\infty),1/C''\}$: $n_{\rm c}$ is the least integer such that for $n\ge n_{\rm c}$: $n-j_1\ge1$, $L^{n-j_1}\mathsf b\ge\mathsf t_\natural$, $2\varepsilon_n\le C''\kappa_0$, $\ell L^n\ge\max\{\lambda_{{\rm BG},3},(C''/2\varepsilon_n)^{1/2}\}$; $\mathsf r_n=\mathsf R_n+\mathsf R_{n-j_1}$. For the proposed variants requiring the multiscale gauge estimate, let $\alpha_n=\frac18(2\arcsin\varepsilon_n)^{1/2}$ for $n\ge2$ (the indices $0$ and $1$ belong to the fixed radii), and let $J_n$ be the least integer $J\ge1$ with $L^J\ge\max\{R_{\rm S},8C_{\rm S}/\alpha_n\}$. Then $J_n\le n/4+c$, with $c$ independent of $n$ and $K$.

For these proposed multiscale variants, $n_{\rm e}$ denotes the least integer $\ge2$ such that for $n\ge n_{\rm e}$: $\varepsilon_n\le\frac1{51}$, $\log L^n\mathsf b>2\mathfrak p_0$, $n-J_n\ge1$, $L^{n-J_n}\mathsf b\ge\mathsf t_\natural$, $\theta_d<(200L^2)^{-1}$ for $d\ge n-J_n$, $44\pi L^2\sum_{j<J_n}\theta_{n-j}\le\frac18\alpha_n$, and $\frac\pi2L^{J_n}\theta_{n-J_n}\le1$. No constant of this section depends on $K$; $n_1,n_2,n_3,n_{\rm a},n_{\rm e},C^\sigma,\Pi^\flat_n$ depend only on $\mathsf b$ and the constants of the construction, and $\mathsf R_n$, $\mathsf o_n$, $n''$, $n_{\rm c}$ and the constants defined from them ($\mathsf r_n$, $C^{\rm t}_n$, $C^\flat_n$, $\mathsf C_n$, $\mathsf C'_n$) depend besides on $\ell$.

\emph{Flowed observables.} Fix $0<\kappa<\frac16$. For $s>0$ and $V\in\Omega_K$, $\mathsf m_s(V)$ is the least 
\[
\max\{s^{1/4+\kappa/2}\|A\|_\infty,s^{3/4+\kappa/2}\|\nabla A\|_\infty\}
\]
 over the real $1$-forms $A$ with $e^{ia_KA}$ gauge equivalent to $V$ ($\nabla$ forward difference quotients); 
\[
\mathsf O_K(C,\bar s)=\{U:\mathsf m_s(U_s)\le C\text{ for }0<s\le\bar s\}.
\]
The \emph{flowed observables} are the functions $H^\sigma_K=\varphi(\mathcal O(f_1),\dots,\mathcal O(f_r))\circ\Phi_\sigma$, $\sigma>0$, $f_i\in C^\infty(T_\ell)$ real, $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^r)$ bounded with all its derivatives. For $0<\alpha<1$ let $\mathcal O^\alpha$ be the space of orbits of $\mathfrak g^3$-valued $C^{0,\alpha}$ connections $\mathfrak A$ on $T_\ell$ under $C^{1,\alpha}$ gauge transformations; a \emph{flow line} is a continuous map $(0,\infty)\to\mathcal O^\alpha$ that near every time is the orbit of a mild solution of $\partial_s\mathfrak A=-\mathrm{d}_{\mathfrak A}^*F_{\mathfrak A}+\mathrm{d}_{\mathfrak A}(\partial_\nu\mathfrak A_\nu)$, the Yang--Mills gradient flow up to an infinitesimal gauge transformation; $\mathcal O^0(f)(\mathfrak A)=\frac12\int f\sum_{\mu<\nu}|F_{\mu\nu}(\mathfrak A)|^2$.

With $P_s=e^{s\Delta_a}$ the heat semigroup of $\Lambda_{K,\ell}$, $a=a_K$, $|f|_{\eta;a}=\sup_{0<s\le1}s^{-\eta/2}\|P_sf\|_\infty$ and $X\wedge Y=\frac1{2i}[X,Y]$, the rough regularity quantity of a $1$-form $\mathbf B$ is
\[
\|\mathbf B\|_{\kappa;a}=|\mathbf B|_{-\frac12-\kappa;a}+\sup_{0<s\le1}s^{\frac34+\kappa}\max\bigl|(\tau_h\nabla_\lambda P_s\mathbf B_\nu)\wedge(\tau_{h'}P_s\mathbf B_{\nu'})\bigr|_{-\frac12;a},
\]
the maximum over directions $\lambda,\nu,\nu'$ and translations $\tau_h,\tau_{h'}$ in a fixed finite set containing every translation in the quadratic term of the gauge-fixed flow equation below; it bounds $s^{\frac14+\frac\kappa2}\|P_s\mathbf B\|_\infty$ and $\frac12s^{\frac34+\frac\kappa2}\|\nabla P_s\mathbf B\|_\infty$. The rough distance of $\mathbf B$, $\mathbf B'$ adds to $|\mathbf B-\mathbf B'|_{-\frac12-\kappa;a}$ the same supremum for the products $\nabla P_s(\mathbf B-\mathbf B')\wedge P_s\mathbf B$ and $\nabla P_s\mathbf B'\wedge P_s(\mathbf B-\mathbf B')$.

\subsubsection{Why the process limit is Markov}

At a fixed physical torus, the compatible block fields give a
common space on which to compare cutoff processes. An observable
of one block level can be evaluated at every finer cutoff by
pulling it back along the averaging map. Convergence of these
observables defines the one-time thread law. Convergence of their
multi-time expectations gives stationary reversible limiting
processes along subsequences. There is a further issue: projecting
a Markov process onto a smaller space can retain memory. The
semigroup identity must therefore be proved after taking the
limit.

The source makes that issue explicit. A subsequential transition
family has the form $Q_t=J^*R_tJ$, where $J$ embeds the limiting
$L^2$ space isometrically into another Hilbert space and $R_t$ is a
self-adjoint contraction semigroup there. The possible loss is
measured exactly by
\[
 (F,Q_{2t}F)-\|Q_tF\|^2
       =\|(1-JJ^*)R_tJF\|^2.
\]
Consequently, weak convergence of transition operators leaves open
whether their limit is a semigroup. Strong convergence will make
the two sides of the intermediate scalar-product identity agree
and remove this defect. The multiscale estimates are used to
obtain that strong convergence.

Fix a coarse depth $n$ and a finer cutoff $K$. Successively average
an invariant observable $H$ under the conditional fluctuation
probabilities. Denote the resulting conditional means by $h_k$.
These functions form a martingale when the small-field chain is
read from the coarse level to the fine level. Its variance
decomposition is a sum of conditional variances. The convexity of
each fluctuation integral bounds its variance by the Dirichlet
energy at that step. The response estimate transports that energy
to the next step with a multiplicative error whose product stays
bounded. Summing the physical scale factors gives the principal
approximation bound
\[
 \|H-(\mathbf1_{\mathsf I_n}h_{K-n})\circ\pi_{K,n}\|_{L^2(\mu^K)}^2
 \le \frac{C^\sigma C_{\rm P}}{L^2-1}
           \frac{a_n^2}{b}\mathcal E_K(H)
          +4\mathsf R_n\|H\|_\infty^2.
\]
Here $\mathsf I_n$ is the admitted open set at depth $n$,
$\pi_{K,n}$ is the block projection, and $\mathsf R_n$ is the mass
discarded by the chain. All these objects are defined precisely
below. The two errors have different origins. The factor $a_n^2$
comes from summing the conditional variances above depth $n$;
$\mathsf R_n$ accounts for the part of the Wilson measure on which
the chain was discarded. Both go to zero as $n$ increases, with
the physical torus held fixed.

This estimate reduces compactness to one finite-dimensional block
space. For bounded observables with bounded energies, the
conditional means have bounded Dirichlet integrals on compact
subsets of $\mathsf I_n$. Rellich compactness is applied on an
exhaustion of that open set; no smoothness of its boundary is
required. Comparison of the block law with Haar measure then
transfers convergence of the conditional means to the block
probability measure. Finally, the displayed approximation permits
$n$ to increase and gives strong compactness in the thread law.
The order is important: finite-dimensional compactness is used
at a fixed $n$, and the uniform approximation is used afterwards.

Apply this compactness statement to
$H_K=P_t^K\Psi_K$, where $\Psi$ is an invariant cylinder function.
The lattice spectral theorem supplies
\[
 \mathcal E_K(P_t^K\Psi_K)
       \le\frac{\|\Psi_K\|_2^2}{2et},\qquad t>0.
\]
Every subsequence therefore has a strongly convergent
subsequence. Its limit must equal the already determined weak
limit $Q_t\Psi$. Thus the entire chosen process subsequence
converges strongly at this observable and time. Density extends
this conclusion to the invariant $L^2$ space. It gives the
semigroup property and the Markov property on the invariant
sigma-algebra. It does not identify the limits arising from two
different process subsequences.

The form domain is recovered by cylinder functions multiplied by
smooth regularity cutoffs at all finer block levels. The
large-field tail makes these cutoffs converge to one, and their
Dirichlet costs tend to zero. This produces a common core rather
than merely a collection of cylinder functions with no energy
control. The lower semicontinuity and recovery-sequence arguments
then give convergence of forms in the weak and strong senses and
convergence of the resolvents.

Nonconstancy is checked on the limiting form $\mathcal E_\star$.
The conditional-mean
comparison passes a positive coarse Dirichlet integral to every
recovery sequence for a nonconstant plaquette observable. The
coarse measure has a positive density on its regular open set,
and the squared gradient of that observable is positive there
away from zero curvature. Hence the limiting energy is positive.
The spectral measure of the observable cannot be concentrated at
zero, so its transition correlation changes with time. A positive
lattice energy alone would not give this conclusion without the
comparison with recovery sequences.

For mixing, the connected part of the coarse regular region gives
a Poincar\'e inequality, while its complement contributes a defect.
After transport through the chain, its useful form is
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_\mu(F)
    \le C_n\mathcal E_\star(F)
          +r_n\operatorname{osc}(F)^2,
 \qquad r_n\longrightarrow0.
\]
At fixed $n$, apply this inequality along the semigroup and let
time increase; then let $n$ increase to remove the defect. The
constants $C_n$ may depend on the physical torus. This proves the
stated mixing without supplying a spectral gap uniform in volume.

\subsubsection{Markov limits, functional inequalities and flowed observables}

\begin{theorem}[Nontrivial Markov limits and mixing]\label{C-367-2}
Assume (E).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(A1)]

\emph{Motion.} For every limit, every integer $n\ge n''$ and every invariant $\Phi\in C^1(\Omega_n)$, with $|\mathsf I_n|$ the Haar measure of $\mathsf I_n$,
\begin{equation}\label{C-367-3}
\mathcal E_\star(\Phi(Y_n))\ge\frac{e^{-\mathsf o_n}}{2C^\sigma|\mathsf I_n|}\int_{\mathsf I_n}\Gamma_n(\Phi)\,\mathrm{d}V .
\end{equation}
Hence $(\Psi,Q_t\Psi)<\|\Psi\|^2$ for $\Psi=a_p(Y_n)$ and every $t>0$: no limit is frozen.
\item[(A2)]

\emph{Compactness.} Along every sequence $K_j\to\infty$, invariant $H_j\in D(\mathcal E_{K_j})$ with $\sup_j(\sup|H_j|+\mathcal E_{K_j}(H_j))<\infty$ have a strongly convergent subsequence; its limit $G$ has $|G|\le\sup_j\sup|H_j|$.
\item[(A3)]

\emph{The Markov property and form convergence.} For every limit, $\mathcal E_\star$ is a closed, densely defined Markovian form on $L^2_{\rm inv}$, and $Q_t=e^{-tA_\star}$ is a strongly continuous symmetric Markov semigroup on $L^2_{\rm inv}$; $P^{K_j}_tH_j\to Q_tF$ strongly for $t>0$ whenever $H_j\to F$ strongly, in particular $P^{K_j}_t\Psi_{K_j}\to Q_t\Psi$ for every invariant cylinder function $\Psi$; (M1) and (M2) hold, and $(\alpha-\mathcal L_{K_j})^{-1}W_j\to(\alpha+A_\star)^{-1}W$ strongly for $\alpha>0$ and invariant $W_j\to W$ strongly; $(Y_t)$ is a stationary reversible Markov process on the invariant $\sigma$-algebra with the transition operators $Q_t$ and the invariant measure $\mu_{\ell,\mathsf b}$; and $\{G\in L^2_{\rm inv}:|G|\le1,\ \mathcal E_\star(G)\le1\}$ is compact.

If invariant $H_j\in C^\infty(\Omega_{K_j})$ converge strongly to $F$ and $\sup_j\|\mathcal L_{K_j}H_j\|_{L^2(\mu^{K_j})}<\infty$, then $F\in D(A_\star)$, $\mathcal L_{K_j}H_j\to-A_\star F$ weakly and $\mathcal E_{K_j}(H_j)\to\mathcal E_\star(F)$; under the assumptions of (C7), this hypothesis fails at the flowed observables of (C7)(b), (c), (e). If invariant $u_j\to u$ strongly with $\mathcal E_{K_j}(u_j)\to\mathcal E_\star(u)$, and invariant $v_j\to v$ weakly with $\sup_j\mathcal E_{K_j}(v_j)<\infty$, then $\mathcal E_{K_j}(u_j,v_j)\to\mathcal E_\star(u,v)$.
\item[(A4)]

\emph{Variance bounds and mixing.} Let $n\ge\max\{n'',n_{\rm c}\}$ and $\mathsf C_n=C^\sigma[\frac{C_{\rm P}}{L^2-1}\frac{a_n^2}{\mathsf b}+\frac12C^{\rm t}_n]$, with $C^{\rm t}_n$ of (B1). For all $K>n$: (a) $\mathrm{Var}_{\mu^K}(H)\le\mathsf C_n\mathcal E_K(H)+\mathsf r_n\mathrm{osc}(H)^2$ for bounded invariant $H\in D(\mathcal E_K)$; (b) $\|P^K_tH-\mu^K(H)\|^2_{L^2(\mu^K)}\le(\mathsf r_n+\frac14e^{-2t/\mathsf C_n})\mathrm{osc}(H)^2$ for bounded Borel invariant $H$ and $t\ge0$. For every limit: (c) $\mathrm{Var}_\mu(F)\le\mathsf C_n\mathcal E_\star(F)+\mathsf r_n\mathrm{osc}(F)^2$ for bounded $F\in L^2_{\rm inv}$, so $\mathcal E_\star(F)=0$ only for constant $F$, and $(F,(1-Q_t)F)>0$ for every non-constant bounded $F\in L^2_{\rm inv}$ and $t>0$; (d) $0\le\mathbb EF(Y_0)F(Y_t)-(\int F\,\mathrm{d}\mu)^2\le\inf_n(\mathsf r_n+\frac14e^{-t/\mathsf C_n})\mathrm{osc}(F)^2$ for bounded $F\in L^2_{\rm inv}$, the infimum over the admitted $n$, which tends to $0$ as $t\to\infty$; and a probability measure $\rho\,\mu$, $\rho\in L^2_{\rm inv}$, with $Q_t\rho=\rho$ for one $t>0$ is $\mu$.

(e) If $F_K\to F$ strongly along the full sequence of cutoffs, $\sup_K\sup|F_K|\le M_F$, $F$ is not constant, and $H_K$ are invariant Lipschitz functions with $\|H_K-F_K\|_{L^2(\mu^K)}\to0$, then $\liminf_K\mathcal E_K(H_K)\ge\sup_n(\mathrm{Var}_\mu F-4\mathsf r_nM_F^2)/\mathsf C_n>0$; and for invariant Lipschitz $H_K$ with $\sup_K\mathrm{osc}(H_K)\le O$, $\liminf_K\mathcal E_K(H_K)\ge\sup_n[\liminf_K\mathrm{Var}_{\mu^K}(H_K)-\mathsf r_nO^2]/\mathsf C_n$. (f) The multiscale gauge extension remains a sketch. Completing that estimate would give all of (a)--(e) as well for $n\ge\max\{n'',n_{\rm e}\}$ with $\mathsf R_n<1$, with $C^\flat_n$ of (B1)(e) in the place of $C^{\rm t}_n$ and $\mathsf R_n+\mathsf R_{n-J_n}$ in the place of $\mathsf r_n$.
\item[(A5)]

\emph{Entropy relaxation.} Let $n\ge\max\{n_{\rm a},n_{\rm c}\}$, $\mathsf C'_n$ and $\varsigma^K$ as in (B2). For all $K>n$: (a) if $G\in C^1(\Omega_K)$ is real and invariant, $M_G=\sup|G|$ and $m_2=\int G^2\,\mathrm{d}\mu^K>\mathsf r_nM_G^2$, then
\[
\mathrm{Ent}_{\mu^K}(G^2)\le\mathsf C'_n\mathcal E_K(G)+\mathsf r_nM_G^2\Bigl[1+\log\frac{M_G^2}{m_2-\mathsf r_nM_G^2}\Bigr];
\]
(b) if $\psi\in C^1(\Omega_K)$ is real and invariant with $\Gamma_K(\psi)\le l^2$ and $\bar\psi=\int\psi\,\mathrm{d}\varsigma^K/\varsigma^K(\Omega_K)$, then $\mu^K(\psi-\bar\psi\ge u)\le e^{-u^2/(\mathsf C'_nl^2)}+\mathsf r_n$ for $u>0$; (c) if $f_0\ge0$ is bounded Borel invariant, $m_1=\int f_0\,\mathrm{d}\mu^K>0$, $\bar M=\sup f_0$ and $\mathsf r_n\bar M\le\frac12m_1$, then for $\tau\ge0$
\[
\mathrm{Ent}_{\mu^K}(P^K_\tau f_0)\le e^{-4\tau/\mathsf C'_n}\mathrm{Ent}_{\mu^K}(f_0)+\mathsf r_n\bar M\Bigl[1+\log\frac{2\bar M}{m_1}\Bigr].
\]
For every limit, (a) holds for bounded $F\in D(\mathcal E_\star)$ with $\mu,\mathcal E_\star$ in the places of $\mu^K,\mathcal E_K$; and if $F\in L^2_{\rm inv}$, $0\le F\le\bar M$, $m_1=\int F\,\mathrm{d}\mu>0$ and $\mathsf r_n\bar M<\frac12m_1$, then $\mathrm{Ent}_\mu(Q_\tau F)\le e^{-4\tau/\mathsf C'_n}\mathrm{Ent}_\mu(F)+\mathsf r_n\bar M[1+\log\frac{2\bar M}{m_1}]$; so $\mathrm{Ent}_\mu(Q_\tau F)\to0$ as $\tau\to\infty$, and $m_1^{-1}(Q_\tau F)\,\mu\to\mu$ in total variation on the invariant $\sigma$-algebra. The corresponding extension remains a sketch at the multiscale gauge estimate; its intended conclusion is the same for $n\ge\max\{n_{\rm a},n_{\rm e}\}$ with $\mathsf R_n<1$, with the explicit top of (B1)(e).
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Functional inequalities uniform in the cutoff]\label{C-367-4}
Assume (E).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(B1)]

\emph{The coarse-scale law.} For $n\ge n_{\rm c}$ there are an invariant Borel weight $w_n:\Omega_n\to[0,1]$ and a constant $C^{\rm t}_n<\infty$ such that for all $K>n$ and every bounded invariant locally Lipschitz $\phi$ on $\mathsf I_n$: (a) $w_n\le\mathbf 1_{\mathsf D_n}$ and $\sigma^K_n(w_n<1)\le\mathsf R_{n-j_1}$; (b) $\mathrm{Ent}_{w_n\sigma^K_n}(\phi^2)\le C^{\rm t}_n\int\Gamma_n(\phi)\,w_n\,\mathrm{d}\sigma^K_n$; (c) $\int(\phi-c)^2\,\mathrm{d}\sigma^K_n\le\frac12C^{\rm t}_n\int\Gamma_n(\phi)\,\mathrm{d}\sigma^K_n+\mathsf R_{n-j_1}\mathrm{osc}(\phi)^2$, $c$ the mean of $\phi$ under $w_n\sigma^K_n$; (d) $\mathrm{Ent}_{\sigma^K_n}(\phi^2)\le C^{\rm t}_n\int\Gamma_n(\phi)\,\mathrm{d}\sigma^K_n+\mathsf R_{n-j_1}\sup_{\mathsf I_n}\Xi(\phi^2,c')$, $c'$ the mean of $\phi^2$ under $w_n\sigma^K_n$.

Here $w_n=\min\{1,\rho/\rho_0\}$, $\rho(V)=\int\mathbf 1_{S'}(V^g)\,\mathrm{d}g$ for a connected open $S'\subset\mathsf D_n$ that is a finite union of chart balls, $\rho_0=\min_{\mathcal K_1}\rho>0$ on a compact invariant set $\mathcal K_1\subset\mathsf D_n$, and $C^{\rm t}_n=a_n\,c(S')\,e^{\mathsf o_n}/\rho_0$, $c(S')$ the log-Sobolev constant of Haar measure on $S'$. (e) (An explicit top.) The following variant remains a sketch at the multiscale gauge estimate. Let $n\ge n_{\rm e}$, $\mathsf R_n<1$, $N=\ell L^n$, $w^{\rm e}_n(V)=\int\mathbf 1\{\mathsf d(V^u(b),\mathbf 1)<\alpha_n\text{ for all }b\}\,\mathrm{d}u$ ($du$ Haar measure of the gauge group), $c_n=[(\frac12\alpha_n-\sin\frac12\alpha_n)/2\pi]^{N^3}$ and $\chi_n=\min\{1,w^{\rm e}_n/c_n\}$.

Completing that estimate would give (a)--(d) with $\chi_n\mathbf 1_{\mathsf I_n}$ in the place of $w_n$, $\mathsf R_{n-J_n}$ in the place of $\mathsf R_{n-j_1}$, and the constant
\[
\begin{multlined}
C^\flat_n=\frac{a_ne^{2\mathsf o_n}C_{\mathscr D}}{(1-\mathsf R_n)c_n},\quad C_{\mathscr D}=2\sqrt e\Bigl(\frac{\alpha_n}{\sin\alpha_n}\Bigr)^{6N^3}\Bigl(\frac{2\rho_{\max}}{r'}\Bigr)^{9N^3}\Bigl(\rho_{\max}+\frac{8\pi\rho_{\max}^2}{r'}\Bigr)^2,\quad\rho_{\max} \\
=\alpha_n\sqrt{3N^3},\ \relax r'=64\alpha_n^2,
\end{multlined}
\]
in the place of $C^{\rm t}_n$; the set $\{\chi_n>0\}\cap\mathsf I_n$ is open, invariant, path connected and contained in $\mathsf D_n$; and for bounded invariant $\Phi\in C^1(\Omega_n)$, $\mathrm{Var}_{\mu^K_n}(\Phi)\le\frac12C^\flat_n\int_{\mathsf I_n}\Gamma_n(\Phi)\,\mathrm{d}\mu^K_n+(\mathsf R_n+\mathsf R_{n-J_n})\mathrm{osc}(\Phi)^2$, and the same with $\mu_n$ in the place of $\mu^K_n$.
\item[(B2)]

\emph{The chain with a connected coarse-scale region.} Let $n\ge\max\{n_{\rm a},n_{\rm c}\}$, $K>n$, $\varsigma^K=w_n(V_t)\,\sigma^K$ and
\[
\mathsf C'_n=\Bigl[\frac{2C_{\rm P}}{L^2-1}\frac{a_n^2}{\mathsf b}+C^{\rm t}_n\Bigr]\,3\mathsf M^2\,\Pi^\flat_n .
\]
(a) $\int f\,\mathrm{d}\varsigma^K\le\int f\,\mathrm{d}\sigma^K\le\int f\,\mathrm{d}\mu^K\le\int f\,\mathrm{d}\varsigma^K+\mathsf r_n\sup f$ for bounded Borel invariant $f\ge0$; (b) $\mathrm{Ent}_{\varsigma^K}(G^2)\le\mathsf C'_n\int\Gamma_K(G)\,\mathrm{d}\varsigma^K$ for real invariant $G\in C^1(\Omega_K)$; (c) for $\nu\in\{\sigma^K,\mu^K\}$: $\mathrm{Ent}_\nu(G^2)\le\mathsf C'_n\int\Gamma_K(G)\,\mathrm{d}\nu+\mathsf r_n\sup_U\Xi(G(U)^2,c')$, $c'$ the mean of $G^2$ under $\varsigma^K$. (d) This variant remains a sketch at the multiscale gauge estimate. Its intended conclusion is: for Lebesgue-almost every label $\mathsf b$, all $m$ and all $n\ge\max\{n_{\rm a},n_{\rm e}\}$ with $\mathsf R_n<1$, (a)--(c) hold with $\mathbf 1_{\mathsf D_n}(V_t)\,\sigma^K$ in the place of $\varsigma^K$, a finite constant $C^\sharp_n$ in the place of $C^{\rm t}_n$, and $\mathsf R_n+\mathsf R_{n-J_n}$ in the place of $\mathsf r_n$; for every $\mathsf b$ and $\eta>0$ they hold with the component of $\mathbf 1$ in $\{\varpi<\tilde r\}$, for some $\tilde r\in(\varepsilon_n,2\varepsilon_n)$ that does not depend on $K$, in the place of $\mathsf D_n$, and $\mathsf R_n+\mathsf R_{n-J_n}+\eta$ in the place of $\mathsf r_n$; with the explicit top of (B1)(e) they hold with $\chi_n(V_t)\sigma^K$, $C^\flat_n$ and $\mathsf R_n+\mathsf R_{n-J_n}$.

(e) (No weight.) For $n\ge n_{\rm a}$, $K>n$, real invariant $G\in C^1(\Omega_K)$, $f_t$ the top of the tower of $G^2$ and $\epsilon>0$:
\[
\begin{multlined}
\mathrm{Ent}_{\sigma^K}(G^2)\le\frac{6C_{\rm P}\mathsf M^2\Pi^\flat_n}{L^2-1}\frac{a_n^2}{\mathsf b}\int\Gamma_K(G)\,\mathrm{d}\sigma^K+\mathrm{Ent}_{\sigma^K_n}(f_t),\qquad\int\Gamma_n\bigl((f_t+\epsilon)^{1/2}\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}\sigma^K_n \\
\le3\mathsf M^2\Pi^\flat_n\int\Gamma_K(G)\,\mathrm{d}\sigma^K .
\end{multlined}
\]
\item[(B3)]

\emph{The fine field conditioned on a block field.} Let $n\ge n_{\rm a}$, $K>n$, $1\le t'\le K-n$, $e=K-t'$, $W\in\mathsf{Cut}_{t'}$, and let $\mathsf P_W$ be the law of $V_0$ when $V_{t'}=W$ and $V_k=V_{V_{k+1}}(B_k)$, $B_k$ of law $p_{V_{k+1}}$. Then $\mathsf P_W$ is a regular conditional law of $U$ given $\mathcal M^{t'}U=W$ under $\sigma^K$ and under $\varsigma^K$, and for real invariant $G\in C^1(\Omega_K)$ with tower $(g_k)$ and every $W\in\mathsf{Cut}_{t'}$
\[
\begin{multlined}
\mathrm{Ent}_{\mathsf P_W}(G^2)\le C^{\rm fib}_e\!\int\Gamma_K(G)\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf P_W,\qquad\Gamma_e(g_{t'})(W)\le3\mathsf M^2\Pi^\flat_e\!\int\Gamma_K(G)\,\mathrm{d}\mathsf P_W,\qquad C^{\rm fib}_e \\
=\frac{6\mathsf M^2C_{\rm P}\Pi^\flat_e}{L^2-1}\frac{a_e^2}{\mathsf b},
\end{multlined}
\]
a constant that depends neither on $K$ nor on $\ell$. If $\psi\in C^1(\Omega_K)$ is real and invariant and $\Gamma_K(\psi)\le l^2$ $\mathsf P_W$-almost everywhere, then $\mathsf P_W(\psi-\psi_{t'}(W)\ge u)\le e^{-u^2/(C^{\rm fib}_el^2)}$, $\psi_{t'}$ the member of the tower of $\psi$; and if $\Gamma_K(\psi)\le l^2$ on all of $\Omega_K$, then, with $\psi_{t'}:=0$ off $\mathsf{Cut}_{t'}$, $\mu^K(|\psi-\psi_{t'}(\mathcal M^{t'}U)|\ge u)\le2e^{-u^2/(C^{\rm fib}_el^2)}+\mathsf R_n$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\paragraph{Admissible top depths.}
The assertions about flowed observables use the following condition, in
the notation of Prop.~\ref{C-367-12}.

A top depth $d_0$ is \emph{admissible with constant $C_{\rm adm}$} if
$d_0\ge n_{\rm a}$, $d_0\ge d_{\rm num}(\ell,\mathsf b)$,
$c_\rho\varepsilon(L^{d_0}\mathsf b)\le C_{\rm BG}^{-2}$ and
$4c_{\mathsf h}\delta(L^{d_0}\mathsf b)\le1/4$,
and, for every $K>d_0$ and $d_0<d\le K$, (M) and (Col) hold
with that same constant.
Here $d_{\rm num}$ is the explicit numerical depth in the proof below.
The mean and covariance-error estimates hold at every
$W\in\mathsf{Cut}_{K-d+1}$; the Gaussian layer-kernel estimates hold
almost surely in the chain gauge, at every pair of bare bonds.
\textup{(Adm)} Under (E), there are $d_{\rm adm}$ and $C_{\rm adm}$,
depending on $\ell$, $\mathsf b$ and the construction constants but not
on $K$ or the chosen top depth, such that every $d_0\ge d_{\rm adm}$
is admissible with $C_{\rm adm}$. This is proved in
Prop.~\ref{C-367-12} below.

The proof of Prop.~\ref{C-367-12} establishes \textup{(M)} and
\textup{(Col)} uniformly in the cutoff and top depth whenever
$d_0\ge d_{\rm adm}$. Thus the flowed estimates use \textup{(Adm)}
as a consequence of \textup{(E)}.

A top depth $d_0$ is admissible when it meets the numerical and uniform-estimate conditions stated before Thm.~\ref{C-367-5}; under (Adm) the chains of all the large top depths give the moments under $\mu^K$. The statements made for all $K$, $m$ and $\beta>0$, namely Lem.~\ref{C-367-6}(a), (C1), the short-time theory of the gauge-fixed flow in Prop.~\ref{C-367-12}(a) (the flow on $[0,s_0(R)]$ with its four bounds, the Lipschitz bound in the rough distance and the bound of the flowed action), Lems.~\ref{C-367-13}, \ref{C-367-21} and \ref{C-367-15}, Lem.~\ref{C-367-14}, Prop.~\ref{C-367-22}(a), (b) and Prop.~\ref{C-367-23}(a), (b) and the upper bound in (c), use no continuum-limit result. The lower bound in Prop.~\ref{C-367-23}(c) follows from the adjoint frequency estimate and exact current transport, with the integrated curvature and current ratio displayed there. The continuum identification requires the separate \textup{(Flow approximation)} step.

\subsubsection{The lattice dynamics and a common core}

\begin{lemma}[Lattice dynamics, subsequential limits and a common core]\label{C-367-6}
(a) For all $K$, $m$, $\beta>0$: $\int G\,\mathcal L_KF\,\mathrm{d}\mu^K=-\int\Gamma_K(G,F)\,\mathrm{d}\mu^K$ for $F,G\in C^\infty(\Omega_K)$; $\beta\,\partial_bA_K=\mathsf b\,a_K^2J(U)(b)$, so $\mathcal L_K=\Delta_K+\mathsf b\,v$ is the generator of $dA=-\mathsf b\,J(U)\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt2\,\mathrm{d}\mathcal W$, $dU(b)=ia_K\circ dA(b)\,U(b)$, with $\mathcal W$ the Brownian motion of the $1$-forms for the scalar product $a_K^3\sum_b\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$: no constant is tuned. $P^K_t$ is a symmetric Markov semigroup on $L^2(\mu^K)$ that commutes with gauge transformations; $(U_{-t})$ has the law of $(U_t)$; $\mathbb E|F(U_t)-F(U_0)|^2=2(F,(1-P^K_t)F)\le2t\,\mathcal E_K(F)$; for $F\in D(\mathcal L_K)$, $\mathbb E|F(U_t)-F(U_0)|^2=2t\,\mathcal E_K(F)-\mathbb E|\int_0^t\mathcal L_KF(U_s)\,\mathrm{d}s|^2\ge2t\,\mathcal E_K(F)-t^2\|\mathcal L_KF\|^2$; and $\mathcal E_K(P^K_tF)\le\|F\|^2/2et$; $v(G\circ\Phi_\sigma)=\partial_\sigma(G\circ\Phi_\sigma)$.

With $\Pi_y$ the Haar average over the gauge transformations at a site $y$ and $\Pi_S=\prod_{y\in S}\Pi_y$: $\mathcal E_K(F)\ge(2a_K)^{-1}\|F-\Pi_yF\|^2$ and $\|P^K_t(F-\Pi_SF)\|\le e^{-t/2a_K}\|F-\Pi_SF\|$.

(b) Assume (E). Every sequence of cutoffs has a subsequence that is a limit. For every limit: $(Y_t)$ is stationary, reversible and positive under time reflection ($\mathbb E[\overline{\theta\mathsf F}\,\mathsf F]\ge0$ for finite sums $\mathsf F$ of products of cylinder functions at times $\ge0$, $\theta$ the reflection of the times), with one-time law $\mu$; its multi-time means are real-analytic functions of the strictly positive consecutive time differences; its finite-dimensional laws are invariant under gauge transformations chosen independently at different times; $Q_t$ is a symmetric positivity preserving contraction of $L^2(\mu)$, $Q_t1=1$, $Q_t=\Pi Q_t\Pi$, and $\|Q_tF\|^2\le(F,Q_{2t}F)$.

If $H_j\to F$ strongly, the spectral measures of $H_j$ for $-\mathcal L_{K_j}$, taken as measures on $[0,\infty]$, converge weakly to a measure $\nu_F$ of mass $\|F\|^2$ with $(F,Q_tF)=\int e^{-t\lambda}d\nu_F$ for $t>0$; $\mathcal E_\star(F)=\int\lambda\,\mathrm{d}\nu_F$; $\mathcal E_\star$ is closed, Markovian and finite only on $L^2_{\rm inv}$; (M2) holds, and $\mathcal E_\star(F)\le\liminf_j\mathcal E_{K_j}(H_j)$ whenever $H_j\to F$ strongly. The following are equivalent: $\|Q_t\Psi\|^2=(\Psi,Q_{2t}\Psi)$ for invariant cylinder functions $\Psi$ and $t>0$; $Q_{t+s}=Q_tQ_s$; $P^{K_j}_t\Psi_{K_j}\to Q_t\Psi$ strongly for these $\Psi$; $(Y_t)$ is a Markov process on the invariant $\sigma$-algebra with the transition operators $Q_t$.

They imply (M1), and $P^{K_j}_tH_j\to Q_tF$ strongly whenever $H_j\to F$ strongly. In general $Q_t=J^*R_tJ$, where $J$ is an isometry of $L^2(\mu)$ into a Hilbert space $\mathcal K$ and $(R_t)$ is a semigroup of positive self-adjoint contractions of $\mathcal K$, and $(F,Q_{2t}F)-\|Q_tF\|^2=\|(1-JJ^*)R_tJF\|^2$; the four properties hold if and only if $R_tJL^2_{\rm inv}\subset JL^2_{\rm inv}$ for all $t$.

(c) Assume (E). For every integer $n\ge1$ with $L^n\mathsf b\ge\mathsf t_\natural$ and every $K>n$, $\mu^K(\varpi(\pi_{K,d}U)<\theta_d$ for all $n\le d\le K)\ge1-\mathsf R_n$, and $\mu(\varpi(Y_d)<\theta_d$ for all $d\ge n)\ge1-\mathsf R_n$. Fix $\varphi_{\rm cut}\in C^\infty([0,\infty);[0,1])$ with $\varphi_{\rm cut}=1$ on $[0,1]$, $\varphi_{\rm cut}=0$ on $[4,\infty)$ and $|\varphi_{\rm cut}'|\le1$, and put
\[
\chi_d=\prod_p\varphi_{\rm cut}\bigl(\varpi_p^2/(2\theta_d)^2\bigr)\quad\text{on }\Omega_d,\qquad\mathsf k_d=24L^{d/2}\theta_d^{-1}(\ell L^d)^3,
\]
the product over the plaquettes of $\Lambda_{d,\ell}$: $\chi_d$ is smooth and invariant, takes its values in $[0,1]$, is $1$ on $\{\varpi\le2\theta_d\}$ and $0$ on $\{\varpi\ge4\theta_d\}$, and $\Gamma_d(\chi_d)^{1/2}\le\mathsf k_d\mathbf 1\{\varpi\ge\theta_d\}$; the number $\mathsf k_d$ depends on $\ell$ and not on $K$, and it is at most a constant times $\ell^3L^{4d}$. The span $\mathcal C$ of the functions $F=\Phi(Y_n)\prod_{d\ge n}\chi_d(Y_d)$, $n\ge n_1$, $\Phi\in C^\infty(\Omega_n)$ invariant, is dense in $L^2_{\rm inv}$; the lattice forms $F_K=\Phi\circ\pi_{K,n}\prod_{n\le d\le K}\chi_d\circ\pi_{K,d}$ are smooth and invariant, $|F_K|\le\sup|\Phi|$, $F_K\to F$ strongly along the full sequence, and $\sup_K\int\Gamma_K(F_K)^pd\mu^K<\infty$ for every $p<\infty$; the cutoffs $\chi^K_n=\prod_{n\le d\le K}\chi_d\circ\pi_{K,d}$ have $\mu^K(\chi^K_n<1)\le\mathsf R_n$ and $\|\Gamma_K(\chi^K_n)^{1/2}\|_{L^{2p}(\mu^K)}\to0$ as $n\to\infty$, uniformly in $K$.

Consequently, for every limit, $\mathcal E_\star$ is densely defined, $\nu_F(\{\infty\})=\|F-\Pi F\|^2$ for $F\in L^2(\mu)$, $(F,Q_tF)\to\|\Pi F\|^2$ and $Q_t\to1$ strongly on $L^2_{\rm inv}$ as $t\to0$, and $\frac12\mathbb E|F(Y_t)-F(Y_0)|^2\le t\sup_K\mathcal E_K(F_K)$ for $F\in\mathcal C$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(a) Haar measure is invariant under left translations in each factor, so 
\[
\int\partial^\alpha_b(FGe^{-\beta A_K})\,\mathrm{d}U=0,
\]
which is the integration by parts; (\YMMref{9.2}{38}) and $\beta=\mathsf b/a_K$ give the drift. Writing a tangent vector as $X=a_KB$ with a $1$-form $B$ per unit length, $a_K\|X\|^2=(B,B)_{a_K}$, and $\Gamma_K(F)$ is the square of the gradient for $(\cdot,\cdot)_{a_K}$: this is the stochastic equation. The closure of $(\mathcal E_K,C^\infty)$ is a Dirichlet form, gauge transformations act unitarily and preserve it, so they commute with $P^K_t$; the two bounds are $1-e^{-t\lambda}\le t\lambda$ and $\lambda e^{-2t\lambda}\le1/2et$ under the spectral measures of the spectral theorem, and the identity is 
\[
